units.la: POstquam mihi, integro jam quadriennio & quod excurrit, quicquid est hoc professorii sive muneris delegatum, sive oneris impositum esse sensi: dici vix potest (Auditores) quam horrucrim totus; quam variæ adversantesque sibi cogitationes mox animum alternatim incesserint meum. Observabuntur imprimis ante oculos quamplurima, quæ virum longe virilius præstabiliorem, audentioremque; quam ego me aut esse puto, aut haberi velim, a suscipiendo tam arduo munere prorsus absterrerent, Prov. cum omni tempore difficilisstum illis, nisi papejora insecuta essent, pessimis temporibus, post tot enatas novas, veteres renatas hæreses, multo difficilior: Vires, cum vel maxime vigerent, admodum exiguæ; & tunc accrescentibus annis fractæ plurimum imminutæque: Memoria fragilis & infida: Impediti oris, in hac etiam balbescente fenestute, infantia: Vel ipsius Latini sermonis, post quinque tum superque lustrorum absentiam, insolentia. Perorandi, prælegendi, disputandi, determinandi, cæteraque quæ hujusce sunt muneris præstandi (quæ fortassis ab his exigi fas est, qui assidui sunt in hac palæstra) facultas siqua olim inerat, quum in his studiis aliquantulum versaremur, (& quantilla tum illa!) exoleta jam prorsus, & plane nulla. Denique, ut minutiora illa præteream, longinquæ migrationis cum famulatu & supellectile qua libraria qua domestica, tædium, reliquaque ab re familiari incommoda: vel is unus, quem & fateri pudet, pudor plusquam subrusticus, & (quam facile patior amicos amoris quodam errore Modestiam interpretari) invirilis quædam verecundia. Insuperabilis illa quidem; ut quam natura infevit, firmavit educatio, fovit hactenus, atque etiamnum fovet tenuitatis proprię conscientia: sed qua tamen vix aliud comperi quidquam a prima pueritia ad hunc usque diem, aut rationibus meis aut existimationi magis adversarium. Retundit hæc assidue generociores quosque animi impetus: eximium quid ausuri conatus frangit: memoriam pessime labefactat, sermonis vim aut præripit, aut sistit: ut, quod mihi visus sum quandoque mente concepisse haud prorsus incommode aut abs re, hoc aut non ausim proloqui statua taciturnior; aut si tente, sic timide, sic gelide, sic id faciam hæsitans, ut aliquanto nonnunquam præ-staret staret non tentasse, Dicam verbo, & quod res est suna hæc timiditas, & (si dabitis vocabulo veniam) hæc infiducia mei, ut de munere hoc detrectando serio cogitarim, atque etiam aliud eam in rem tentarim plus efficit, quam cætera illa, quantumuis gravia, quæ hactenus commemini, universa.
units.tr: Ever since, for four years now and a little more, I have felt that this professorship, or whatever this office is, has been assigned to me as a duty or laid on me as a burden, I have been utterly dismayed, gentlemen, and I can hardly say how many and how conflicting thoughts have by turns troubled my mind. Above all, very many things present themselves to my eyes, which would frighten off from undertaking so arduous a charge a man far more manly, more eminent and bolder than I am or wish to be thought. The times are especially hard, when the task would have been difficult at any time, and it has become far harder since so many new heresies have sprung up and old ones have been revived. My powers, though at their height they were very slight, have now been worn down and diminished as my years have increased. My memory is frail and unreliable. My speech is impeded, and in this stammering old age I am like a child. Even my command of the Latin language itself has grown rusty after an absence of more than twenty-five years. Whatever ability I once had for speaking at length, reading lectures, disputing, determining questions, and the other things this office requires (which perhaps may fairly be demanded of those who are constantly in this arena), if I had any at all when I was engaged in these studies for some time (and how small it was then!), has now faded away entirely and is quite gone. Finally, to pass over smaller matters: the weariness of a long removal with servants and furniture, both of books and of household goods, and the other inconveniences that come from my private affairs. Above all, there is one thing which I am ashamed to confess: a shame more than rustic, and (as I readily allow my friends to mistake modesty for it through some error of affection) a certain unmanly bashfulness. It is indeed insurmountable; as nature planted it, and upbringing strengthened and has hitherto fostered it, so it still fosters the consciousness of my own slightness. Yet I have found almost nothing else, from my earliest boyhood to this day, that is more hostile either to my reasoning or to my reputation. It constantly blunts even the most spirited impulses of mind; it breaks off attempts at anything outstanding; it badly weakens my memory, and either snatches away or halts the force of my speech. So that what I have sometimes seemed to conceive in my mind, not at all unsuitably or irrelevantly, I either dare not put into words, being more silent than a statue; or, if I venture to, I do it so timidly, so coldly, so hesitantly, that it would sometimes have been better not to have tried at all. To put it plainly: this timidity is my own doing, and (if you will pardon the word) this distrust of myself. It has done more to make me seriously consider refusing this office, and even to attempt to refuse it, than all those other matters, however weighty, which I have so far mentioned, taken together.

units.la: Occurrebant dum istæc cogito, ex adverso pauca quædam, nec aspernanda, quæ labantem animum nonnihil erigerent, cunctantemque subinde velut subjectis stimulis in hanc arenam propellerent. Optimi Regis judicium: crebri amicorum hortatus: vester multorum (ut illi submonebant, et ego haud inexpertus humanitatem vestram facile credebam) in me proni affectus. Repulerunt ista fateor, (ut par erat) animum meum; quin & commoverunt: sed hactenus, ut tamen si meo unius arbitratu res statuenda foret, nec longa nec difficilis ficilis futura effet deliberatio. Quidenim? Patererne ego me ætate jam declivi, defectis viribus, memoria lubrica balbum & pertimidum senem, ex suavissimo quo perfruebar otio & umbra, in apricum & in pulverem, iniquissimo tempore, post 25 annorum missionem, quasi post-liminio, & invitum rapiet quæ me poterant satis expurgasse cicutæ, si lubens consensissem? Quis non omnem mihi Anticyram destinatam crederit, ni abnuissem & quoad verecunde licuit, restitissem.
units.tr: While I was thinking these things, a few considerations also came to mind on the other side, not to be despised, which somewhat lifted my faltering spirit and from time to time urged me, as if with goads, to push forward into this arena when I hesitated. These were the judgement of the best of kings, the frequent exhortations of friends, and the favourable disposition towards me of many of you, which, as they reminded me, and as I, not without experience of your kindness, readily believed. I confess these things did move my mind, as was right, and indeed stirred it; yet only to this extent, that if the matter had been for me alone to decide, the deliberation would have been neither long nor difficult. For what? Should I allow myself, now in declining years, with my strength spent, my memory slippery, a stammering and very timid old man, to be dragged out of the most pleasant leisure and shade I enjoyed, into the sunlight and the dust, at a most unfavourable time, after twenty-five years of dismissal, as if by a right of return, and against my will, by a hemlock which might well have cleansed me enough, had I willingly consented? Everyone would believe that I had been destined for a voyage to Anticyra, unless I had refused, and resisted as far as modesty allowed.

units.la: Ergo ne perduci poteras, inquietis, ut conditioni tam iniquæ acquiescere tandem, sanus utrisque auribus atque oculis? Poteram, ut videtis, & perductus sum; ita sunt ut res humanæ, sic & consilia incerta: Sanusne an secus ubi facti rationem edidero, vosmet judicate. Certe non ego hac in re vel ingenio meo obsecutus sum, vel etiam judicio: cui ut optatius fuit, ita visum est salutarius, in tenebris latitare securum, quam cum labore & periculo prodire in scenam. Imo vero egi cum amicis, qui apud serenissimam Regiam majestatem videbantur aliquid posse; idque non una vice, coram & per literas semel atque iterum obtestatus per omnem amicitiam, Regis animum pertentarent fieri ne posset sine ipsius offensione, ut de hac Cathedra aliter statueretur, nec ego tam importunum onus tam imparibus humeris sustinere cogerer. Pertentant: renunciant fieri non posse; perstare in sententia Regem, quod ante jussisset & id ratum esse velle: non utique obniterer porro frustra, sed onus quod excutere non possem, qua possem animi alacritate subirem & perferrem. Hæc admonitus, officii conscientia, cujus voluntati obtemperare debui, ejus authoritati cessi: Maxime cum altius assurgerem, (nam quæ hactenus dicta sunt ad humanas tantum rationes pertinent,) & ut decuit hominem & Christianum & Theologum, summam Dei Opt. Max. providentiam, singula quæ in terris aguntur vel minutissima quæque, prout ipsi collibitum est, & suaviter & fortiter moderantis, diligentius cogitarem : Scilicet est cor Regis in manu domini, sicut derivationes aquarum;& pro bene-placito suo convertit ipsum. Hæc ego quo sæpius & attentius cum animo reputavi meo, eo mihi propius conjunctam cum Regia voluntate divinam etiam vocationem visus sum contueri. Siquidem nihil aliud est, quantum ego quidem adhuc intelligere potui, ordinaria Dei ad aliquod munus vocatio, quam ab his penes quos est plena & legitima de ejufmodi rebus statuendi potestas, personæ ipsorum judicio non inidoneæ, nulla intercedente prava ambitione, dolo, malisve artibus, designatio. Pervicit itaque omnia impedimenta, omnia obječtamenta deluit, duplex illa parendi necessitas, voluntati Regiæ, divinæ vocationi. Quo mihi paratiorem apud omnes bonos, apud omnes æquos rerum æstimatores excusationem fore confido, si (quod indubie futurum prospicio) in obeundo hoc tam illustri tam arduo munere, nec votis meis, nec vestræ expectationi satisfacerem. Dabo tamen operam officio utcunq; ut satisfaciam meo: & sane, ut aliquid saltem de me fidenter dicam, spero me aliqua ex parte satisfaɖturum: illud si concedatis,quod omnino concedi debet & est verissimum,non satisfecisse officio qui se ingessit,ni fecerit,quod debuit:satisfecisse qui admotus est,si fecerit quod potuit.
units.tr: "Then could you not be persuaded," you may say, "to finally submit to so unfair a condition, sound in both ears and eyes?" I could, as you see, and I have been persuaded. Human affairs are uncertain, and so are plans. Whether I am sound or not, when I have given an account of what was done, you yourselves may judge. Certainly I did not in this matter yield to my own nature, or even to my judgement, though it would have been more welcome to me, and it seemed more wholesome, to lie hidden in the dark in safety than to come forward onto the stage with toil and danger. Indeed I dealt with friends who seemed able to accomplish something with the most serene Majesty of the King, and I called upon them, more than once, both in person and by letter, to try, by all the friendship they had, whether the King's mind could be moved, without offence to himself, so that this chair might be decided otherwise, and I need not be compelled to bear so troublesome a burden on shoulders so unequal to it. They tried, and reported that it could not be done: the King persisted in his opinion, and wished what he had earlier ordered to stand. I would not then struggle on in vain, but would take up with what cheerfulness of mind I could the burden I could not throw off, and bear it. Warned by these things, and by a sense of duty, to whose will I ought to submit, I yielded to his authority. Especially as I rose higher (for what has been said so far pertains only to human reasons), and as became a man, a Christian and a theologian, I considered more carefully the supreme providence of God Most Good and Most Great, who governs, both sweetly and strongly, each of the things done on earth, even the very smallest, as it pleases him. Surely "the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord, like the watercourses; he turns it wherever he pleases" [Prov. 21.1]. The more often and attentively I weighed these things in my mind, the more it seemed to me that the divine calling is joined most closely with the will of the King. For, as far as I have so far been able to understand, an ordinary calling of God to some office is nothing other than the designation of a person, not unfit in the judgement of those in whom lies the full and lawful power of deciding such matters, and with no wicked ambition, deceit or evil arts intervening. So that double necessity of obeying, to the King's will and to the divine calling, overcame all hindrances and wiped away all obstacles. I trust I shall have a readier excuse before all good men and all fair judges of affairs, if (as I clearly foresee it will be) in discharging this so illustrious and so arduous office I satisfy neither my own wishes nor your expectation. Yet I shall take pains, in whatever way I can, to satisfy my duty: and indeed, that I may say at least something confidently about myself, I hope to satisfy it in some measure. Let this be granted, which must be granted altogether and is most true: that he who thrust himself into an office has not satisfied his duty unless he has done what he ought; and that he who was called to it has satisfied it if he has done what he could.

units.la: Exposui pluribus,auditores,provinciam hanc quo concilio jam olim susceperim : cur in ea administranda toto quadriennio nil gestum sit,si forte requiratis,paucioribus expediam. Quo tempore reverendus in Christo Pater Vigorniæ Episcopus, cathedra pastorali conconsensa, doctoralem hanc quam permultis jam annis plurimum ornaverat mihi successori designato reliquit (fuit id æstiva vacatione circiter Kal. Sextiles:)discessi tum hinc ea mente, ut proximo termino Michaelis certo etiam die constituto, Kal. sc. Novembribus revertetur res domesticas interea componerem, eaque curarem quæ reditum maturarent. Quid multa? Curo, compono, &c totus in hac sum. Gliscere jam tum simultates publicæ, magis magisq, indies universa in pejus ruere, ardere passim omnia discordiis civilibus: versari in ore, in auribus, in oculis omnium nil nisi bellici apparatus, armorum strepi- tus, tumultus militum. Ego tamen pergo, sed segnius aliquanto quam occaperam, vasa colligere, sarcinas complicare, capsas &c cistulas rebus necessariis implere ex quibus una, magno meo cum infortunio, paulo longius domo mea eo fine premissa ut huc com-modius asportaretur, post aliquot menses cum supellectile quam habui pretiosissima incidit in glutinosas manus borum illorum virorum, quibus pro jure vis est, & arma pro legibus: unde eam mihi reglutinandi nulla jamdu reliqua est aut facultas, aut spes. Sed quod amissum est, missum facio; & pergo.
units.tr: I have explained at more length, gentlemen, on what grounds I took up this charge long ago. If perhaps you ask why nothing has been accomplished in its administration during the whole of these four years, I shall explain in fewer words. At the time when the reverend Father in Christ, the Bishop of Worcester, having resigned his pastoral see, left this doctoral chair, which he had adorned for very many years, to me as his designated successor (this was in the summer vacation, about the Kalends of August), I departed from here with the intention of returning by a fixed day, namely at Michaelmas term, that is on the Kalends of November. Meanwhile I would arrange my domestic affairs and take care of those things which would hasten my return. What more? I took care, I arranged, and so on, and I was wholly intent on this. But already public quarrels were growing, and day by day everything was tending more and more for the worse, and everywhere things were burning with civil discord. Nothing but warlike preparations, the clash of arms and the tumult of soldiers was on everyone's lips, in their ears and before their eyes. Still I went on, but rather more slowly than I had begun, collecting my vessels, packing my baggage, and filling chests and boxes with necessary things. Of these, one, sent on a little ahead of my house for the purpose of being more conveniently carried here, fell, to my great misfortune, after some months, together with the most valuable of my furniture, into the sticky hands of those men who have force for their law and arms for their rights; and so I have now neither the means nor the hope of having it glued together again. But what is lost I let go, and I go on.

units.la: Instat tandem destinatus itineri dies; & erant quae ad profectionem videbantur necessaria, pleraque expedita: praestolabar tantum tabellarium hinc cum literis ex quibus nonnulla, quae mihi usui forent, & rescire interrerat, intelligerem. Miror hominem condicto die non adesse: expecto adhuc diem alterum, tertium, quartum; comparet nullus: quinta demum luce venit, sed pedes, inops, squalidus, & maestus. Nempe acciderat forte per illa tempora, (ipsissima hac fere anni tempestate,) praelium illud atrox, & utriusque parti satis funestum Monticlivensce, sive ad Edge-hill hill: unde disjecti sparsique per oppida longe lateque milites vicina quæque loca occuparant, & vias undique publicas nefariis deprædationibus infestabant. Narrat misellus homuncio, ut in hos incideret, ut se minis contumeli-sque pessime exceptum, equo, vestitu, nummis, & tabellis expoliaverint: docet omnia rapinis, latrociniis, concufsionibus, terroribus plena: quoad ardor ille belli refrxierit, intuta omnia viatoribus. Quibus auditis, necessitati iterum parendum ratus, abjeci professionis consilium, certus manet domi continere, donec resideret nonnihil belli æstus, & immutata rerum facies spem ostenderet commodioris profectionis: quod ego sane, ut eram illarum rerum inexpertus, intra paucos saltem menses futurum non dubitavi. Sed heu! quam inanis fuit spes illa! Exarsit ex illo tempore multo quam ante æstuosius belli furor, pervagatusque est latius; & aafflictiores indies res evasere publicæ: Venit interea Oxonium cum exercitu serenissimus Rex Carolus : urbem vallo & fossa cingit, præsidio firmat: sigunt hic stativa pretoriani milites. Abjecta igitur protinus omni spe & pacis publicæ, & reditus huc mei : quod reliquum erat, experire statui, veterum illud λαθε βιώσας an aliquid contineret sanæ ac solidæ Philosophiæ. Periculum feci, latui, eaque fui in proposita sententia, (postquam ita constitueram) sive constantia mentis sive pertinacia: ut cum alias quam parcissime, idque non nisi magna cogente necessitate, tum integro propemodum biennio, non omnino aut ocreas induerim aut equum conscenderim, aut parochiolæ meæ angustissimos fines (qui ubi maxime patent vix sunt millenum passuum) vel latum pedem unquam excesserim. Quod quam animo meo fuerit jucundum, quam rebus meis salutare ; nec ego fatis oratione complecti, nec vos existimationi consequi poteritis. Qua in re ingratissimus essem quot quot sunt usquam mortalium, si non providentiae divinae vim, sapientiam, bonitatem et agnoscerem lubens et laetus praedicarem: cujus singulari beneficio factum est, ut quod paucissimis in tanta rerum perturbatione contigisse reor, mihi domi meae inter meos considere licuerit; libris, literis, otio frui: et quod ad animi mei fructum maximum duco, illibatam una cum libertate conscientiam et dignitatem conservare. Sc. ab domo abductus sum mea, iniqua ut tum videbatur conditione, sed (Deo providente) non infelici tamen ut alium quendam verbi praeconem belli lege captivum in libertatem redimerem; virum sane gravem et disertum, quicum interceperat mihi a multis ante annis ex vicinia et longo usu non levis animorum conjunctio junctio et amicitiæ quædam necessitudo. Ne longam faciam; uterque tandem data utrinque fide publica ita domum remissi sumus, ut communis incolumitatis mutui invicem obsides essemus. Hæc fides sancte servata, utrique nostrum in hoc tanto rerum æstu tranquillitatem securam præstitit. Sicque mihi, auspice Dei bonitate, brevis procella longam peperit halcyoniam.
units.tr: At last the day fixed for the journey arrived, and most of what seemed necessary for departure was ready. I was only waiting for a messenger from here with letters, from which I could learn some things that would be useful to me and that I was eager to know. I wondered that the man did not come on the appointed day. I waited a second day, a third, a fourth, and no one appeared. On the fifth day he finally came, but on foot, penniless, filthy, and sad. It had happened by chance in those times, at almost this very season of the year, that the savage battle of Edgehill had been fought, deadly enough to both sides. As a result, soldiers scattered far and wide through the towns had occupied the nearby places and were harassing the public roads everywhere with wicked plundering. The poor little fellow related how he had fallen into their hands, and how, after being very badly treated with threats and insults, they had stripped him of his horse, clothes, money, and papers. He reported that everything was full of robberies, brigandage, extortion, and terror, and that travel would be safe only once the fury of war had cooled. Having heard this, and thinking that I must once more yield to necessity, I gave up my plan of lecturing. I resolved to stay at home until the heat of the war had subsided somewhat and a changed state of affairs offered hope of a more convenient journey. As I was inexperienced in such matters, I did not doubt that this would happen within a few months at least. But alas, how empty that hope proved! From that time the fury of war flared up far more fiercely than before and spread more widely, and public affairs grew more troubled by the day. Meanwhile the most serene King Charles came to Oxford with his army. He surrounded the city with a rampart and ditch and strengthened it with a garrison, and the king's guards pitched their camp here. Therefore, with all hope of public peace and of my return here abandoned at once, I resolved to try what remained of the old saying λάθε βιώσας [live unnoticed], to see whether it contained anything of sound and solid philosophy. I made the attempt. I kept out of sight, and I held fast to the course I had chosen, whether from steadiness of mind or from obstinacy. So, going out as sparingly as possible, and only under strong necessity, for almost two whole years I did not put on boots or mount a horse, nor did I ever step a single foot beyond the very narrow bounds of my little parish, which at their widest scarcely measure a thousand paces. How pleasant this was to my mind, how beneficial to my affairs, I can neither express adequately in words nor can you appreciate it in your estimation. In this matter I would be the most ungrateful of all mortals if I did not gladly acknowledge and cheerfully proclaim the power, wisdom, and goodness of divine providence. By its singular kindness it came about that, which I believe fell to very few amid such great upheaval, I was allowed to remain at home among my own people, to enjoy books, letters, and leisure; and, what I count as the greatest fruit for my mind, to keep my conscience and dignity unimpaired along with my liberty. For I was taken from my home under a condition that then seemed hard, but, God providing, not unhappy, so that I might redeem to liberty another preacher of the Word, a man taken captive under the law of war, a man indeed grave and eloquent. With him, for many years past, through our neighbourhood and long acquaintance, there had grown no slight union of spirits and a certain bond of friendship. To make a long story short, we were at last both sent home, each giving public assurance, on condition that we would be mutual hostages for each other's common safety. This pledge was faithfully kept, and it secured for each of us tranquillity and safety in this great turmoil. And so for me, under the auspices of God's goodness, a brief storm brought forth a long halcyon calm.

units.la: Verum, ubi postea deditam hanc urbem, immutatamque in tantum rerum conditionem, ut saltem itinerantibus securiores essent viarum transitus, oblatam mihi opportunitatem sensi Academiam revisendi: de ornanda hac quæ mihi obtigisset Sparta denuo cogitare cœpi: Nempe contractam longo situ seu rubiginem, seu scabritiem ocyus abradendam, excutiendum omnem torporem: reptandum e latebris in apricum; ingenium deses & inurbanum qua potest exitandum, et ad Academicos mores, Studia, instituta|q; paulatim efformandum: hoc est, ut ego interpretor, vim naturæ faciendam, et vel invita Minerva Minervam colendam. Statui itaque, sed communicato prius per literas cum amicis concilio, ad medium Octob. adesse, si & illis id oportunum videretur. Rescribunt non sibi id oportunum videri, sed necessarium, adeoq; ab omnibus expectar. Iproinde advolarem, de prælegendo aut disputando ne sollicitus esfem; nec enim in tanta Academiæ solitudine, in mediis castris & inter arma (ubi silere solent leges) iustarum rerum rationem ullam haberi, nedum expectationem. Pergratum id fuit homini et semper cunctatori, & subire omnis ignavo, maxime & imparato. Quamprimum itaque per alias occupationes, & continuos imbres licuit, huc advolo : ita securus ab omni publici officii metu, ut ne vel solitariam schedam adversariarum annotatiuncularum mecum attulerim rim. Alium enim mihi proposueram istiusce itineris finem duplicem : alterum, ut de Academicarum rerum praefenti statu certius aliquid praefens cognoscerem : alterum, ut de futura praelegendi ratione cum viris amicis & prudentibus consilium caperem. Sciebam enim vi statuti atque etiam officii praelectiones habendas esse : sed in praelegendo quam potissimum viam insisterem, ut id sequerer quod Theologiae studiosis & gratissimum esse posset & utilissimum, id vero nisi ab his edoctus qui quid maxime effct ad gustum & sensum eorum qui nunc sunt hominum, exploratum haberent, scire non poteram. Asi ubi advenissem, vix salutatum resalutatumque est invicem, cum mihi nova occinitur cantilena : praelectiones ordinarias pro more solito a professoribus expectari : Egone ut aliquid sic insperatum praestem, hac temporis angustia, hospes, & harum rerum insolens, & quem tot alia premunt incommoda ? Fieri non potest, iniquam : Illi contra, At fieri oportet. Tunc ego mecum, Jam ergo teneris: nec est aut elabendi spes, aut deliberandi locus. Sed bono es animo; Non est impossibile, nisi nos dialectici fallant, quodcunque est necessarium :--Ἀνάγκης ἐνῇ ... Audendum ergo aliquid; & nunc tertium, quod a te bis antea factum est, necessitati parendum. Protinus ergo & calamum et chartas, & scrinia posco : & dum meditor (pro more publice profitentium) aliquid ipso in limine præfari, quod apud humanitatem vestram habiturum esset justæ excusationis instar, dum eam in rem scriptur io nescio quid subsecivis horis & subsultoria opera; exit tandem de re nihili, hoc est de me, & de rebus, factis, consiliis meis jejuna hæc & ( ut vereor) nimium importuna narratiuncula.
units.tr: But when afterwards this city surrendered, and the state of affairs changed so far that at least travellers had safer passage along the roads, I perceived an opportunity offered to me of revisiting the university, and I began again to think about adorning this Sparta that had fallen to me. For the rust or roughness contracted by long idleness had to be rubbed off quickly, all torpor shaken off, and I had to crawl out of my hiding places into the sunshine. My sluggish and unpolished talent had to be stirred up as far as possible and gradually shaped to academic manners, studies, and customs. That is, as I understand it, violence must be done to nature, and Minerva must be cultivated even against Minerva's will. I resolved, therefore, though first consulting my friends by letter, to be present about the middle of October, if this also seemed opportune to them. They replied that it seemed not merely opportune but necessary, and that everyone expected it. So I should hasten there, and need not be anxious about lecturing or disputing. For in such a deserted university, in the midst of camps and among arms, where the laws are wont to fall silent, no account of just matters could be taken, much less any expectation. That was most welcome to a man who was always a procrastinator, who shrinks from every task, especially one for which he is unprepared. So as soon as other business and continual rains allowed, I hastened here, so free from any fear of public duty that I did not even bring with me a single sheet of my little notes of objections. For I had set myself a twofold aim for this journey: first, to learn with more certainty something about the present state of academic affairs; second, to take counsel about the future manner of lecturing with wise and friendly men. For I knew that lectures were to be given by virtue of statute and also of duty. But in what way especially I should proceed in lecturing, so as to follow what might be most pleasing and most useful to students of theology, I could not know unless I were informed by those who had ascertained what would best suit the taste and feeling of the men of the present day. But as soon as I arrived, scarcely had we greeted and returned greetings when a new tune was sung to me: that the professors were expected to give their ordinary lectures as usual. "Am I, a stranger and unaccustomed to these matters, and burdened by so many other troubles, to perform something so unexpected in this narrowness of time, and such a guest? It cannot be done; it is unfair!" They, on the contrary: "But it must be done." Then I said to myself: "So you are held fast; there is neither hope of escape nor room for deliberation. But be of good courage. It is not impossible, unless the dialecticians deceive us, whatever is necessary: [Ἀνάγκης ἐνῇ ...] ('there is necessity in it'). So I must dare something. Now, a third time, which you have done twice before, necessity must be obeyed." So at once I call for pen, paper, and writing boxes; and while I consider (as is the custom of those who profess publicly) to preface something on the very threshold, which would serve before your kindness as a just excuse, while I write I know not what in spare hours and by way of diversion, this barren and (as I fear) too troublesome little narrative about nothing, that is, about myself and my affairs, deeds, and plans, at last comes forth.

units.la: Quam,quo mihi videmini pronioribus animis & auribus excepisse,eo confiͤentius ad illa accedo quæ supersunt dicenda: & spero vos facile exoratum iri,ut qua me attentione & patientia baſien us prosecuti estis de præteritis rebus deserentem,eadem prosequamini porro,dum quid ego vobis in posterum spondeam,quidque a vobis viciſsim petam,qua potero brevitate exposuero. Prius illud quod attinet,imprimis aperte profiteor non esse me ex illorum numero,quibus cordi est litem ex lite serere, rixas ciere doctiores quam componere, quique controversias novas movere malunt quam summovere veteres,& contentionis funem trahere quam abrumpere: ingeniosi suo,fortassis & aliorum judicio;sed certe malo publico. Est hæc gens hominum numerosa satis & multigena: sed in triplici fere discrimine. Sunt qui suo nescio quo malo genio,vel etiam odii invidiaeve æstri perciti, alienorum operum Aristarchi siunt & censores severissimi. Excutiunt hi non sententias modo & locutiones hominum, sed & vocum et syllabarum minutissimos quisque apices. Si erratum est in re aliqua quamvis levissima, si quid forte aut vehementius, aut temperatius dictum quam pro ipsorum palato vociferantur continuo, insectantur, damnant, & tantum non diro anathemate feriunt. Si quid obscurius prolatum aut ambigue, trahunt semper in deteriorem partem, et ne desit calumniae lo-cus, sensum ei de suo affingunt. Quod ita sanum, solidum, pulchrum est, ut non audeant vituperare, (quod vituperio proximum est) maligne laudant. Est alterum genus eorum, qui aut ex inanis gloriolae cupiditate, nova & inaudita opiniomum monstra in Ecclesiam invehunt, quorum est hoc infœlix seculum longe feracissimum; aut φιλοπονισ quadam laborantes pulchrum esse du-cunt {C}unt inutilibus distinctiunculis & subtilitatibus, aut puerilibus inaniis, gratiam apud adolescentes captare, aut risu diducere risum Auditoris: Disputaturientes Theologi, nec veteri Stoicorum vulgo multum abfimiles; qui feveriorem profeffi philofophiam, in exilibus tamen Grammaticorum λεπτολογίας vel Dialecticorum argutiolis omne aevum transfegere. Tertium genus latiffime patet, eftque eorum hominum qui aut ftudio partium fic illos admirantur, quibus fe magiftris addixerunt ut fibi nefas effe putant ab eorum placitis vel latam unguem difcedere; aut odio partium ita fe demum fatis effe religiofos exiftimant, fi ab eorum fententia, quos fibi adversarios conftituerunt, quam longiffime receffierint. Hinc alios effectus videas ἀμετρέα & ἀνθολογίας ex Antipapismo Semianabaptistas, alios ex Antipuritanismo Semipapistas, alios--Sed piget ista ulterius profequi.
units.tr: Since you seem to have received what I have said so far with the more eager minds and ears, I approach what remains to be said with the greater confidence. I hope you will easily be persuaded to follow on, with the same attention and patience with which you have followed me in discussing past matters, while I set out as briefly as I can what I promise you for the future and what I ask in return. As to the former, I first declare openly that I am not one of those who delight in sowing strife upon strife, who stir up quarrels more than they settle them, who prefer to raise new controversies rather than remove old ones, and who would rather pull the rope of contention than break it. They may be ingenious in their own judgement, and perhaps in that of others, but certainly to the public harm. This class of men is quite numerous and of many kinds, but falls into roughly three divisions. There are those who, goaded by some evil genius of their own, or by the sting of hatred or envy, become Aristarchuses of other people's works and very severe critics. These men examine not only the opinions and expressions of others but each tiniest point of words and syllables. If something has been mistaken in any matter, however slight, or if anything has been said more vehemently or more moderately than their own palate demands, they at once clamour, pursue, condemn, and all but strike with dire anathema. If anything has been stated somewhat obscurely or ambiguously, they always drag it to the worse side, and lest there be no room for calumny, they attach a meaning of their own to it. What is so sound, solid, and beautiful that they do not dare to blame it (which is next to blame), they praise grudgingly. There is a second kind of men who, either from a desire for empty glory, bring new and unheard-of monstrosities of opinion into the Church, a kind of which this unhappy age is by far the most fruitful; or, labouring under a certain love of toil, think it a fine thing to win the favour of young men with useless little distinctions and subtleties, or with childish trivialities, or to draw laughter from their hearers with jokes. These are theologians who dispute with itching ears, not much unlike the common run of the old Stoics, who, though professing a stricter philosophy, nonetheless spent their whole lives on the trifling hair-splitting of grammarians or the little quibbles of dialecticians. The third kind extends very widely, and consists of those who, either from zeal for a party, so admire the leaders to whom they have bound themselves as masters that they think it wrong to depart a finger's breadth from their opinions; or, from hatred of a party, think themselves religious enough only if they have withdrawn as far as possible from the opinion of those whom they have set up as adversaries. Hence from one cause you may see semi-Anabaptists arising out of excessive anti-Popery, from another semi-Papists out of anti-Puritanism, and from others... But it grieves me to pursue these things further.

units.la: λεπτολογίας, ἀμετρέα, ἀνθολογίας: Greek words as printed in the text. prosequi tam innumera, tam ingrata: & ad alia festino. Harum ne in nulla classe nomen censeri merear meum, Deum cordis mei conscium testem advoco, cui servire in spiritu filii sui ante omnia cupio, ea me mente ad hoc munus accedere, non ut propria existimationi aut affectibus, non ut alterius cujusquam voluntati aut gratiæ, sed ut unis his tribus litarem, Veritati, Pietati, paci. Et quidem spero præcorque eundem illum Deum, cujus gratia hanc miserecordiam hactenus consecutus sum vilissimus licet peccator, ut tamen essem fidelis: largiturum mihi in posterum, pro sua bonitate, ne ab eadem hac mente ullis aut mundi illecebris, aut machinis tentationum, aut temporum inclinationibus unquam dimovear. Cujus ope fretus, ut cætera non ausim polliceri quæ non sunt mearum virium, spondeo vobis tamen in fungendo hoc munere, quoad
units.tr: Quibbling, immoderation and gleaning [λεπτολογίας, ἀμετρέα, ἀνθολογίας]: I shall not pursue such innumerable and unwelcome matters, and I hasten on to others. Lest I be counted in any of these classes, I call God, the witness of my heart, to witness. Above all I desire to serve him in the spirit of his Son, and I approach this office with this purpose: not for my own reputation or feelings, not for the will or favour of any other person, but to offer these three things alone as a sacrifice: Truth, Piety, Peace. And indeed I hope and pray that the same God, by whose grace I have obtained this mercy so far, vilest sinner though I am, that I might be faithful, will grant me in future, in his goodness, that I may never be moved from this same purpose by any allurements of the world, any machinations of temptation, or any shifts of the times. Relying on his help, I will not presume to promise other things that are beyond my powers, but I pledge to you, in discharging this office, as far as God permits, sincerity and faith, and, once I have ceased to be a guest, diligence.

units.la: Text is set in italic type throughout the main body. quoad Deus permiferet, fincerit atem, fidem, & postquam hospes esse desiero, diligentiam.
units.tr: Text is set in italic type throughout the main body. So far as God permits: sincerity, faith and, once I have ceased to be a stranger, diligence.

units.la: Sunt & nonnulla, viri, patres & fratres, ut ad ultimum illud orationis meae caput tandem accedam, quae a vobis ego vicissim expecto, vel saltem expeto; compluria illa quidem, si aut mihi vacaret exequi, aut vobis audire singula. Sed praeterquam quod id nimis longum esset, est quoqe ut mihi videtur non multum necessarium; tam qui humanitatem dixerit, hunc ego omnia illa una voce complexum esse arbitror. Cogitate object, quanta sit molis, non cum uno jam Typhone Romano (qui fuit quondam praecipua & pene singularis in hac arena concertatio) secum tot efferis gigantibus, Socinianis, Pelagianis, Antinomis, Anabaptistis, Erastianis, aliisque succrescentibus quotidie velut Hydrae capitibus novis haereseon monstris, quorum vix audita vulgo nomina, nedum satis
units.tr: There are also some things, gentlemen, fathers and brothers, which I now come to at last, the final head of my address, and which I in turn expect from you, or at least desire. Many of them I would name, if I had time to pursue them or you to hear each one. But apart from the fact that this would be far too long, it is also, I think, not very necessary, for whoever has said "kindness" [humanitas] has, I believe, embraced all of them in that one word. Consider, too, what a burden it is to contend not with the single Roman Typhon alone (who was once the chief and almost the only contest in this arena), but with so many savage giants: Socinians, Pelagians, Antinomians, Anabaptists, Erastians, and others sprouting daily like new heads of the Hydra, monstrous heresies whose names are scarcely known to the common people, let alone

units.la: [illegible, ~2 letters] tis explorata dogmata, manus conferere cogitate cujus sit artis, anguillas illas lubricas et cœno gaudentes, sed quid ego anguillas dico? apage deminutiva; quin angues potius [Greek: μεταμορφωμένους] (Sectarios, inquam, & sophistas) e cavis et limo quibus se abdiderunt eruere, in lucem protrahere, ita constrictos tenere, neque aut toxico noceant, aut elabantur lubrico. Cogitate quanta sit folertia, latentem sub ovilla veste lupum deprehendere; Detrahere & pellem nitidus qua quisque per ora Cederet introrsum. turpis: hypocritarum & Enthusiastarum, qui obtentu Reformationis orbi illudunt, qui sub larva Spiritus carni militant, qui libertatem prophetandi sibi arrogant ut aliis licentius imponant, quid sibi velint & quo tendant occulta consilia sapienter perspicere, eorumque conatibus tempestive & prudenter obvenire, [Greek: τίς πρὸς τοῦτο]; Quotu quisque est ea naturarum sagacitate, ea perspicacia oculorum, ea lacertorum & laterum firmitate, ut ad ista omnia debite peragenda unus sufficiat? Ista si cogitabitis, facile ut opinor & illud una existimabitis, mihi cui omnia jam dicta ex officio incumbunt facienda, omnino sub tam impari onere succumbendum esse, ni vos me fatiscentem usque & languentem cum omni humanitate vestra subinde sublevetis. Condonabitis itaque uti spero ingenio, pudori, memoriae, aetati, defuctudini, quicquid quacunque in re nolens peccavero: si quid forte inter disputandum aut alias exciderit non mature cogitatum, incongrue dictum, aut incommode enunciatum: si dictio aut phrasis non occurrerit rei de qua agitur exprimendae satis idoneae: si memoriae diffusius (quod me praedico, & alias quoties opus est facturum, et inter praelegendum constanter,) quae apud vos dicturus sum e chartis recitavero: si denique quod est ab antecessori-bus Ius meis quacunque in re egregie præstitum, id ego vel non præstitero, vel admodum tenuiter.
units.tr: [illegible] thoroughly explored doctrines. Consider what skill it takes to grapple with those slippery eels that delight in mud. But why do I say eels? Away with diminutives! Rather, consider how one must drag the snakes [μεταμορφωμένους] (I mean the sectaries and sophists) out of the hollows and slime where they have hidden themselves, bring them into the light, and hold them so fast that they can neither harm with their poison nor slip away on their slippery coils. Consider how keen-sighted one must be to detect a wolf lurking under a sheep's fleece: "to strip off the skin under which each man, gleaming on the surface, is foul within." I mean the hypocrites and enthusiasts who mock the world under the pretext of reformation, who serve the flesh beneath the mask of the Spirit, who claim for themselves the freedom to prophesy so that they may impose more licentiously on others. To perceive wisely what they mean and where their hidden designs tend, and to meet their attempts in good time and with prudence: "Who is sufficient for these things?" [τίς πρὸς τοῦτο]. How rare is the person with such quickness of mind, such sharpness of eye, and such strength of arm and side that one man alone is enough to carry all of this out as it should be done? If you consider these things, I think you will also easily judge that I, on whom all the duties just mentioned rest, must altogether succumb under so unequal a burden, unless you, with all your kindness, keep raising me up again and again as I flag and grow faint. You will therefore, I hope, pardon my natural talent, my modesty, my memory, my age and my lack of practice, and whatever I may unwillingly err in, in any matter: if something slips out in disputation or otherwise that has not been thought through in time, is said unfittingly or is expressed inappropriately; if a word or phrase does not come to hand that is suitable enough to express the matter in hand; if, for the sake of memory (which I confess I shall do, and at other times whenever need requires, and constantly while reading aloud), I recite at greater length from my papers what I am about to say among you; and finally, if what has been excellently accomplished in any matter by my predecessors, I either do not accomplish, or accomplish only very meagrely.

units.la: Hujus autem vestræ in me humanitatis certius mihi pignus dare non potestis, quam si præsentis instituti mei consilium resciero vobis non improbari. Dixi modo, & veredixi nihil mihi adhuc certi constitutum esse, in hoc prælegendi officio, quam viam insisterem.
units.tr: You cannot give me a surer pledge of this your kindness towards me than if I learn that the purpose of my present undertaking is not disapproved by you. I have just said, and truly said, that nothing has yet been settled for me with certainty in this office of lecturing, as to which course I should pursue.

units.la: Utrumne primo quod a multis factum video, Epistolam aliquam Apostolicam analytice explicarem & scholiis illustrarem, corollaria inde ad fidem et pietatem utilia breviter deducerem, controversias emergentes digressione facta fusius pertractarem, loca revincendis hæreticis et sectariis opportuna urgerem et confirmarem, vicissim quæ sunt ab iis in rem suam prave detorta nativo sensui restituerem, utraq; ab ipsorum sophismatis & cavillationibus vindicarem ?
units.tr: Shall I first do what I see many have done: expound some Apostolic epistle analytically and illustrate it with notes, briefly draw from it corollaries useful for faith and piety, treat the controversies that arise at greater length by way of digression, press and confirm passages suited to refuting heretics and sectaries, and conversely restore to their native sense what they have wrongly twisted to their own advantage, defending both against their sophistries and cavils?

units.la: An potius secundo historiam Evangelicam domini nostri J. Chr. vel juxta filium narrationis unius alicujus quatuor Evangelistarum vel etiam magis ex omnibus harmonice contextam præponerem et explicarem; et nodos hiftoricos aliafq; difficultates, qua ἐκ φαινομένης ἀπλοΐας qua ex rei subjecta qualitate aut circumstantiis ortas dissolverem?
units.tr: Or secondly, should I set before you and explain the Gospel history of our Lord Jesus Christ, either following the narrative of one of the four Evangelists, or, better, woven together harmonically from all of them; and should I resolve the historical knots and other difficulties, whether arising from the apparent simplicity of the text or from the nature of the subject or its circumstances?

units.la: An tertio pari ratione historiam facram Ecclesiasticam ex Apostolorum Actibus & Epistolis fecundum temporum ordinem dispositam?
units.tr: Or thirdly, in the same way, should I arrange the sacred ecclesiastical history, from the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles, in the order of time?

units.la: Vel etiam quarto integram historiam Biblicam utriufq; Testamenti a mundo condito ad constitutam ufq; ab Apoftolis Ecclesiam Christianam perpetuo filio deducerem, et rerum gestarum exempla ad usum conscientiæ et vitæ institutionem, quoad res ferret, accommodarem?
units.tr: Or fourthly, should I lead the whole Biblical history of both Testaments, from the creation of the world down to the Christian Church established by the Apostles, in one continuous thread, and adapt examples of deeds, as far as the material allows, to the use of conscience and the guidance of life?

units.la: An quinto ex textu aliquo scripturæ breviter exposito, locum communem Theologicum, maxime de re aliqua fidei controversa proponerem methodice exexplicandum:ut de Scripturæ perfectione, de satisfactione Christi de authoritate Ecclesiæ, de Peccato Originali, de Justificatione fidei, de Merito operum, de Purgatorio, Transubstantiatione, & id genus aliis?
units.tr: Or fifthly, from some passage of Scripture briefly expounded, should I set out a theological commonplace methodically, especially on some controverted article of faith explicating: such as the perfection of Scripture, the satisfaction of Christ, the authority of the Church, original sin, justification by faith, the merit of works, Purgatory, transubstantiation, and others of that kind?

units.la: An sexto locum aliquem communem Theologiæ practicæ sive Moralis pari modo explicarem; & casus dubios conscientiæ eo pertinentes ex certis agendi regulis & principiis illustrarem et dissolverem: ut, de Votis, de Juramentis, de scandalo, de Rebus Adiaphoris, de libertate Christiana, de obedientia et Subjectione, de civilibus Contractibus, de Divortiis, de Restitutionibus, aliisque ad Dei cultum aut ad fraternæ dilectionis & justitiæ officia spectantibus?
units.tr: Or sixthly, should I in the same way explain some commonplace of practical or moral theology, and illustrate and resolve doubtful cases of conscience belonging to it from fixed rules and principles of action: concerning vows, oaths, scandal, things indifferent, Christian liberty, obedience and subjection, civil contracts, divorces, restitutions, and other matters pertaining to the worship of God or to the duties of brotherly love and justice?

units.la: An denique utramque Theologiæ partem (Scholasticam dico, & moralem) sic pariter excolerem, ut neutra se merito conqueri posset neglectam penitus aut exclusam; sed alternis terminis ac vicissim nunc in controversiis fidei dirimendis, nunc in conscientiæ casibus enucleandis, exercerer ?
units.tr: Or finally, should I cultivate both parts of theology (I mean the scholastic and the moral) equally, so that neither could justly complain of being neglected or shut out, but exercise myself by turns, now in settling controversies of faith, now in unravelling cases of conscience?

units.la: En vobis indicavi quotquot estis Theologiæ studiosi, quæ cum aliqua vestra utilitate fieri posse videbantur, singula: vestrum erit statuere ex his quid fieri velitis. Qua vestra inclinant studia, hac me comparabo: et quod plerisq; vestrum gratissimum esse sensero, id universis utile judicabo. Sed enim hoc unum interim non possum dissimulare, ad practicam hanc Casuum Theologiam sponte sua & quasi natali genio multo propensiorem esse animum meum, quam ad illam rixosam Controversiarum. Cum itaq; mihi nunc aliquid esset necessariò & subito faciendum, nec qua spiraret favoris vestri aura in hac tanta temporis angustia satis explorare possem: obsecutus ingenio meo, ad Moralem Theologiam inflexi cursum. Cumque cogitarem quam sit grave Perjurii peccatum Deo pariter & hominibus exosum si-mmul-
units.tr: Behold, I have set out for you, who are all students of theology, each of the things that seemed capable of being done with some profit to you. It will be yours to decide from these what you wish done. I shall adapt myself to whatever your inclinations are; and what I perceive to be most pleasing to most of you, I shall judge useful to all. But this one thing I cannot conceal for now: my mind is, of its own accord and by its natural bent, far more inclined to this practical theology of cases than to that quarrelsome theology of controversies. Since therefore something had to be done by me at once and of necessity, and I could not sufficiently test, in so short a space of time, which breeze of your favour was blowing, I yielded to my own disposition and turned my course to moral theology. And when I considered how grave a sin perjury is, hateful to God and men alike, simul-

units.la: mulqs animadverterem quot hominum myriades his perturbatissimis temporibus tam nefario crimine se implicuerint dum aut vobis metu adacti, aut inducti dolo, juramentis se obstrinxerunt variis et interdum, sic inter se adversis, ut alterutrum sine certa perjurii periculo nec suscipi potuerit, nec praestari: existimavi non potuisse me utilius operam collocare, quam si aliquid, quod ad Juramenti & Perjurii rationem pertineret, discutiendum susciperem. Atque ex tota hac materia delegi potissimum eam partem hoc termino explicandam, quae est de Obligatione Juramenti, de Juramenti, inquam, promissorii obligatione. Ordiar autem hanc tractationem, Deo volente & auspice, comite patientia vestra die Veneris proximo, hora consueta. Unicum illud interea a me exorandi estis, viri, patres & fratres perdilecti in Christo, pro summa vestra humanitate & pietate, Deum Opt. Max. omnis boni
units.tr: and when I noticed how many myriads of men in these most troubled times have entangled themselves in so wicked a crime, bound by oaths, some sworn under fear or induced by deceit, and some so various and at times so mutually opposed that one of them could be neither undertaken nor performed without a certain danger of perjury: I judged that I could not spend my labour more usefully than by taking up for discussion something that pertains to the nature of oath and perjury. And from this whole matter I chose especially that part to be explained under this heading, which concerns the obligation of an oath: the obligation, I mean, of a promissory oath. I shall begin this treatment, God willing and with his guidance, on next Friday at the usual hour, with your patience as my companion. Meanwhile there is one thing I must ask of you, gentlemen, fathers and brothers most dearly beloved in Christ, by your great kindness and piety: join me in praying to God, Best and Greatest, the fount and giver of every good.

units.la: Note: the text is italic throughout, with the page's printed lines reading as above. boni fontem et largitorem mecum comprecemini: ut in omnibus meis studiis et conatibus sic me spiritu suo regat, verbo dirigat, benedictione prosequatur: ut ea sola sentiam, faciam, doceam, cum omni sobrietate et prudentia, quae ipsius gloriae, Ecclesiae Christi aedificationi, matris Academiae honori et ornatui, studiosorum in vera fidei et conscientiae puritate profectui, meae denique ipsius et paci internae et aeternae saluti aliqua ex parte inserviant: per et propter merita Domini nostri Jesu Christi, cui cum Patre et spiritu sancto Tri-uni Deo, sit omnis honos, laus et gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.
units.tr: boni fontem et largitorem mecum comprecemini: that, in all my studies and endeavours, he may guide me by his Spirit, direct me by his Word, and bless me, so that I may think, do and teach only those things which, with all sobriety and prudence, serve in some measure the glory of God himself, the building up of the Church of Christ, the honour and adornment of our mother the Academy, the advancement of students in the true faith and purity of conscience, and finally my own peace of mind and eternal salvation: through and for the sake of the merits of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the one triune God, be all honour, praise and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
