units.la: DE qua expeditius, & vestro majori cum fructu dicturum me arbitror, si in ipso statim vestibulo futurae tractationis generalem quasi typum & σχεδιαγραφίαν vobis ante oculos posuero. Sic enim & vobis melius constabit instituti mei ratio; & ego certas orationi meae metas figam: ut aut intra debitos fines usque se contineat; aut siquando forte extra oleas paululum procurrerit, non tamen ita laxe evagetur, quin ut possit mature & cito in ordinem cogi, & ad lineas revocari. Tribus itaque capitibus rem totam absolvam. Primum, ut qua de re agitur clarius intelligatur, ostendam quid sit Juramentum in genere, quid in specie Promissorium juramentum, quid item Obligatio. Deinde, quoniam de rebus incertis ex certis statuendum est, proponam Axiomata quaedam, sive κανόνες, hoc est regulas generales e fonte juris naturalis haustas, & communi gentium consensu comprobatas; velut hypotheses & futurae dissimilitudinis ἀξιώματα: e quibus (ut conclusiones ex principiis, in quibus virtualiter continentur,)deducendæ; & ad quas, sicut ad Canonem & normam, exigendæ sunt particularium casuum decisiones. His duobus necessario premissis, quorum ex altero lumen accipiant quæ sunt posit dicenda, ex altero robur & firmamentum: tertio denum loco ad dubia illa dissolvenda deveniam,quæ aut nodum aliquem vindice dignum in se continere, aut piorum hominum mentibus & conscientiis scrupulum injicere posse videbuntur. Quæ quum sit totius negotii præcipua pars, eaque longe diffusissima; conabor universam illam casuum varietatem in certas classes redigere; idque secundum quatuor Causarum genera, quod ad Obligationis Vinculum attinet: rejectis in calcem operis, tum quæ ad vinculi illius λύσιν solutionem spectant, tum si quod aliud aut fuisse a me debito loco prætermissum deprehendero, aut alias ad vitæ conscientiæque institutionem posse utiliter attexi indicavero.
units.tr: On this subject I think I shall speak more readily, and with greater profit to you, if at the very threshold of the coming treatment I set before your eyes a general outline, as it were, and a σχεδιαγραφία [σχεδιαγραφίαν]. For in this way the plan of my undertaking will be clearer to you too, and I shall fix certain limits for my discourse, so that it either keeps itself within its proper bounds, or, should it perhaps run a little beyond the olive groves, it does not wander so loosely that it cannot be brought promptly and quickly back into order and recalled to its lines. I shall therefore complete the whole matter under three heads. First, so that what is under discussion may be understood more clearly, I will show what an Oath is in general, what a promissory oath is in particular, and likewise what Obligation is. Next, since uncertain matters must be decided from certain ones, I shall propose certain axioms, or canons [κανόνες], that is, general rules drawn from the source of natural law and approved by the common consent of nations; as it were hypotheses and axioms [ἀξιώματα] of the dissimilarity to come, from which (as conclusions from the principles in which they are virtually contained) the decisions of particular cases are to be deduced, and by which, as by a rule and standard, they are to be tested. With these two things necessarily laid down beforehand, of which the one gives light to what is to be said and the other strength and firmness, thirdly and lastly I shall come to resolve those doubts which either seem to contain some knot worthy of untying, or seem able to cast a scruple into the minds and consciences of pious people. Since this is the principal part of the whole business, and by far the most extensive, I shall try to reduce that whole variety of cases into certain classes, and this according to the four kinds of causes, so far as they concern the Bond of Obligation. I shall leave to the end of the work both what pertains to the release and solution [λύσιν] of that bond, and anything else that I may find I have omitted in its proper place, or that I point out can usefully be added for the training of life and conscience.

units.la: II. Exhibito hunc in modum σχήματος totius futuræ tractationis diagrammate, rem ipsam nunc tandem aggredior. Ubi primo explicandum occurrit, quid sit Juramentum. De voce nulli litem moveo, seu quis Jusjurandum malit vocari,sive alia quacunque appellatione. Neque vero opus est, ut hac in re vocis alicujus Latinæ, Græcæ, aut Hebrææ vim & originem, vel etiam ἱμωνυμίαν, συνωνυμίαν aut παρωνυμίαν, operosius exequar. Efficit enim jurandi passim cacoethes, & rei sanctissimæ his tam profanis moribus nimium familiaris abusus, ut Quid sit Nominis nemini, ne pueruliis quidem, possit esse ignoratum. Rei ipsius definitionem varie (ut fit) authores expressere, pro suo quisque ingenio. Brevissima est illa Ciceronis: Est, inquit, Jusjurandum affirmatio religiosa. Quo magis, ut illud obiter dicam, præcoces hujus ævi adolescentulos, nescio quo præjudicii errore, sed magno suo cum damno, Ciceronem ut nimiæ prolixitatis scriptorem defugere, & miror & indignor. Sed redeo. Pleniorem Juramenti definitionem siquis desideret, hæc esto: Juramentum est actus religiosus, in quo ad confirmandam rem dubiam Deus testis invocatur. Hanc definitionem membratim per partes explico.
units.tr: II. Having thus set out the diagram of the whole future treatment in its σχήματος [σχήματος] form, I now at last come to the thing itself. Here the first thing to be explained is what an Oath is. I raise no dispute about the word, whether one prefers to call it Jusjurandum or by any other name. Nor is there any need for me to go laboriously into the force and origin of some Latin, Greek or Hebrew word in this matter, or even into its homonymy [ὁμωνυμίαν], synonymy [συνωνυμίαν] or paronymy [παρωνυμίαν]. For the widespread itch of swearing, and the abuse of a most holy thing that is far too familiar in these profane customs, make it so that what the name means can be unknown to no one, not even to small children. Authors have expressed the definition of the thing itself in various ways, as is usual, each according to his own talent. The shortest is that of Cicero: It is, he says, an oath is a religious affirmation. The more so, to say this in passing, do I both marvel at and resent the precocious young men of this age, who, through I know not what error of prejudice, but to their great loss, shun Cicero as a writer of excessive prolixity. But I return. If anyone wants a fuller definition of an oath, let this be it: an oath is a religious act, in which God is invoked as witness to confirm a doubtful matter. I will explain this definition member by member, part by part.

units.la: III. Dixi primo, quod sit Actus religiosus. Actus hic ponitur loco generis. Quamvis enim Juramentum sit proprie in Prædicamento Relationis: quia tamen respectus ille relativus qui in Juramento est, fundatur in actione jurantis, idcirco non incommode per talem actum definitur: siquidem in definiendis Relativis plerunque adhibetur Generis loco aut Materia, aut fundamentum illi-
units.tr: III. I said first that it is an act of religion. This act is put in place of the genus. For although an oath properly belongs to the predicament of Relation, yet because the relative respect that is in an oath is grounded in the action of the one swearing, it is therefore not inappropriately defined through such an act; for in defining relatives it is usually the matter or the foundation that is used in place of the genus.

units.la: Cic. lib. 3. Offic. us Relationis. Quod autem sit actus Religiosus, constat primo ex authoritate Scripturæ, Deut. 6. 13. ubi Moses ita populum alloquitur, Dominum Deum tuum timebis, & ipsi servies, & per nomen ejus jurabis. Ex quo loco concludunt uno ore Scholastici Juramentum esse actum a cultus (ut illi vocant) Latriæ, i.e. cultus sacri soli Deo debiti. Constat secundo, ex consensu omnium populorum: apud quos, etsi unius naturæ lumine ducerentur, sanctissima semper est habita Juramenti religio; usque adeo ut ipsa Sanctitatis, Religionis, aliaque his cognata vocabula apud rerum Gentilium scriptores vix ulla alia in re frequentius usurpata occurrant, quam in hac materia Juramentorum: & quum plurima ipsis alia sacra haberentur, Juri-jurando tamen soli, non alia de causa quam quod inter tot sacra lacerrimum quodammodo esset, peculiari quodam jure Sacramenti nomen remansit. Unde id nomen effluxit postea in Ecclesiam, nempe ob similitudinem aliquam cum militari Romanorum sacramento, ad alia tamen quædam significanda. Quin & Gallis hodie ipsum etiam Juramentum, ex inclinato ad suæ linguæ formam Latino nomine, pro Sacramento un Serement appellatur. Constat tertio ex evidentissima ratione: quia Juramentum tendit in honorem Dei; per agnitionem tionem Veritatis, Scientiæ, Justitiæ, & Potentiæ divinæ. Etsi enim Juramentum falsum, vel level, vel mere aliud vel indebite susceptum, procul dubio ex parte jurantis irreverentiam quandam vel potius contemptum Dei, & nimis sapit Atheismum: inde tamen juramenti actus ex natura sua divini nominis reverentiam includit. Quum enim omne juramentum ad hoc tendat, ad id confirmandum quod a jurante dicitur, & fieri debeat omnis confirmatio per aliquod certius & majoris authoritatis, (ἄνθρωποι μὲν γὰρ κατὰ μείζονος ὀμνύουσιν) Heb. 6. Homines per majorem jurant :) qui jurat, ipso facto agnoscit Deum se superiorem, summæ authoritatis testem, intallibilis veritatis, καὶ ... omnisque perjurii ac falsitatis justissimum & potentissimum vindicem. Est ergo Juramentum Actus Religiosus.
units.tr: Cic. lib. 3. Offic. ...of the relation. That it is an act of religion is established first by the authority of Scripture, Deut. 6. 13, where Moses thus addresses the people: You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him, and swear by his name. From this passage the Schoolmen unanimously conclude that an oath is an act of the worship (as they call it) of latria, that is, of sacred worship owed to God alone. It is established secondly by the consensus of all peoples, among whom, although they were guided by the light of one nature, the sanctity of the oath has always been held most sacred; so much so that the words sanctity, religion, and other words akin to these, occur among the writers of the pagan nations hardly more often in any other matter than in this matter of oaths. And although many other things were held sacred by them, the oath alone, for no other reason than that among so many sacred things it was in a sense the most solemn, kept by a peculiar right the name of sacrament. Hence that name afterwards flowed into the Church, namely on account of some likeness to the military sacrament of the Romans, though to signify certain other things. Indeed, even today the French call the oath itself, by a Latin name bent to the form of their own language, un Serement in place of sacrament. It is established thirdly by a most evident reason: because an oath tends to the honour of God, through the acknowledgement of the truth, knowledge, justice and power of God. For although a false oath, or a light one, or one taken in some other way or without due cause, undoubtedly shows on the part of the one swearing a certain irreverence, or rather contempt, of God, and smacks too much of atheism, yet the act of an oath by its nature includes reverence for the divine name. For since every oath tends to this, to confirm what is said by the one swearing, and every confirmation ought to be made through something more certain and of greater authority (for men swear by the greater [ἄνθρωποι μὲν γὰρ κατὰ μείζονος ὀμνύουσιν], Heb. 6. 16), the one who swears by that very fact acknowledges God as superior to himself, the witness of supreme authority, of infallible truth, [and] and [καὶ] ...and the most just and most powerful avenger of every perjury and falsehood. An oath is therefore an act of religion.

units.la: IV. Dixi secundo, In quo Deus testis invocatur. Ubi sunt tria, Deum adhiberi & ut testem, idque per modum invocationis. c Deus impiis in omni Juramento advocatur. Quantumvis enim & Ethnicis, & Judæis, & Christianis solenne olim fuerit, aut per creaturas jurare, aut saltem inter jurandum tacito Dei nomine creaturas solum nominare, ut infinitis testimoniis e scriptura sacra & aliunde petitis, si id opus esset, probari possit; (quorum utrumque, an & quatenus fieri
units.tr: IV. I said secondly, in which God is invoked as witness. Here there are three things: that God is brought in, and as witness, and that this is done by way of invocation. God is called upon as witness in every oath, even by the impious. For although it was once customary both among the heathen, the Jews and the Christians to swear by creatures, or at least, while swearing, to name creatures alone with God's name tacitly understood (as this could be proved, if it were needed, by countless testimonies from Holy Scripture and elsewhere), (whether either of these may be done, and how far, is not the business of the present subject to discuss:) yet in every oath which is properly and formally an oath, the testimony of God is brought in either explicitly or at least implicitly.

units.la: {c} Deus impiis in omni juramento advocatur. tieri liceat, differere non est præsentis instituti:) in omni tamen Juramento, quod quidem est proprie & formaliter Juramentum, aut explicite, aut saltem implicite Dei testimonium adhibetur. Nam & qui per Idola jurat, quæ revera nihil sunt, & e non Deus, jurat per ea quæ putat esse Deos: & qui per aliquam creaturam jurat, id facit aliquo modo in ordine & relatione ad Deum; quia creaturam testem advocat tanquam aliquid Dei, in quo sc. refulget Dei veritas, bonitas & potentia, & quo se tum agnoscit per Dei misericordiam frui, tum nolle per Dei justitiam privari. Verbi gratia: si quis juret per vitam, per animam, per caput, per salutem suam, &c. per inde est ac si diceret, Per illum Deum cui vitam, animam, caput debeo; a quo salutem expecto, &c. Et per hanc particulam distinguitur Juramentum a nuda assertione vel promissione; quæ ambæ fiunt hominibus sine aliqua nominis divini aut expressa aut tacita interventione. Adhibetur autem Deus ut testis: & per hoc distinguitur Juramentum a Voto. In Voto enim transfigitur cum Deo ipso, ut cum Parte; cui vota immediate nuncupantur: aut in Juramento transfigitur cum Homine; Deus autem adducitur, non ut Pars, sed ut Testis. Dixi autem in definitione Deum Testem & præcise, non autem Judicem aut Vindicem, quod tamen est a nonnullis additum: vere quidem, sed fortassis non necessario; & abesse debet a definitione omne superfluum. Fateor utrumque facere eum qui jurat; viz. Deum & testem adducere veritatis ejus quod dicitur, & vindicem falsitatis: sed illud primario & per se, hoc secundario & ex consequenti. Nam ut Deus attestetur veritati, pertinet per se ad naturam testimonii: sed ut puniat falsitatem, non tam ad naturam spectat testimonii, quam ad effectum. Sed nec satis est ad Juramenti rationem, ut Deus testis adducatur, nisi & invocetur. Potest enim Deus ut testis adhiberi, idque ad rei dubiae confirmationem etiam sine Juramento. Ut si ad confirmandam hanc thesin, non esse imagines adorandas, adducerem aliquot Scripturae loca: proculdubio hoc esset adducere Dei testimonium ad confirmationem rei dubiae; & tamen proculdubio hoc non esset Juramentum. Est enim longe aliud citare Deum testem, respectu testimonii jam olim exhibiti, quod citra invocationem fieri potest: aliud invocare Deum testem, respectu testimonii jam nunc exhibendi, in quo Juramenti quasi formalis ratio consistit.
units.tr: {c} God is called upon as witness in every oath, even by the impious. For the one who swears by idols, which in truth are nothing and not God at all, swears by those things which he thinks to be gods; and the one who swears by some creature does so in some way in order and relation to God, because he calls the creature as witness as something of God's, in which, namely, the truth, goodness and power of God shine forth, and by which he at once acknowledges that he enjoys God's mercy and is unwilling to be deprived of God's justice. For example: if someone swears by his life, by his soul, by his head, by his salvation, and so on, it is just as if he were to say, By that God to whom I owe my life, soul and head, and from whom I expect my salvation, and so on. And by this particle an oath is distinguished from a bare assertion or promise, which are both made to men without any express or tacit interposition of the divine name. But God is brought in as witness, and by this an oath is distinguished from a vow. For in a vow one deals with God himself, as with a party, to whom vows are made directly; but in an oath one deals with a man, and God is brought in not as a party but as a witness. I said in the definition that God is Witness, and precisely that, not Judge or Avenger, although this has been added by some: truly, indeed, but perhaps not necessarily; and everything superfluous ought to be absent from a definition. I grant that the one who swears does both things, namely brings in God both as witness of the truth of what is said and as avenger of its falsity; but the former primarily and in itself, the latter secondarily and by consequence. For that God should attest to the truth belongs in itself to the nature of testimony; but that he should punish falsehood belongs not so much to the nature of testimony as to its effect. Yet it is not enough for the notion of an oath that God be brought in as witness, unless he is also invoked. For God can be brought in as witness, and that for the confirmation of a doubtful matter, even without an oath. As if, to confirm this thesis, that images are not to be worshipped, I were to adduce several passages of Scripture: without doubt this would be to bring in the testimony of God for the confirmation of a doubtful matter; and yet without doubt this would not be an oath. For it is one thing to cite God as witness with respect to a testimony already given long ago, which can be done without invocation; it is another to invoke God as witness with respect to a testimony yet to be given, in which the quasi-formal nature of an oath consists.

units.la: V. Dixi tertio, & est ultimum definitionis membrum, invocari Deum testem ad hoc ut confirmetur res dubia. Quibus in verbis continetur Juramenti tum Finis, tum Materia sive Objectum. Juramenti Materia circa quam, sive Objectum est Res dubia: hoc est, cujus certitudo ita pendet ex fide dicentis, ut non possit ulla alia ratione commode investigari. μαρτυρία δὲ [?] ὡς [?] ἀμφιβάλλεσθαι [?], inquit Philo. Unde primo Scibilia, qualia sunt res Universales, quæ certæ sunt semper sibique similes, nec possunt aliter se habere; secundo res particulares quæ nituntur sensuum testimonio, aut sunt ita indubie certa ex monumentis historiarum traditione universali, aut alio publico & ab omni falsi suspicione immuni testimonio, ut apud eos qui sunt sanæ mentis nullus possit esse dubitandi locus; non sunt idonea Juramenti materia. Quam enim ridiculum foret, & a sobria ratione alienum, si quis juramento confirmare velit Triangulum habere tres angulos æquales duobus rectis, aut Virtutem esse propter se expetendam, aut Aristotelem fuisse Philosophum, vel Ciceronem oratorem? Aut si adolescens disputans in scholis, cui propositio negata incumberet probanda, destitutus argumento, a jurarer eam esse veram?
units.tr: V. I said thirdly, and this is the last part of the definition, that God is called as witness to confirm a matter in doubt. These words contain both the end and the matter, or object, of the oath. The matter about which an oath is made, its object, is a doubtful thing: that is, a thing whose certainty depends so much on the word of the one speaking that it cannot conveniently be established by any other means. As Philo says, testimony [μαρτυρία δὲ [?] ὡς [?] ἀμφιβάλλεσθαι [?]]. Hence, first, things that can be known, such as universal truths, which are always certain and like themselves and cannot be otherwise, are not fit matter for an oath. Second, particular things that rest on the testimony of the senses, or are so beyond doubt from the records of history, or from common tradition or some other public testimony free from any suspicion of falsehood, that there is no room for doubt among sane people, are not fit matter for an oath either. How ridiculous, and how far from sound reason, it would be if someone wished to confirm by oath that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, or that virtue is to be sought for its own sake, or that Aristotle was a philosopher, or Cicero an orator! Or if a young man disputing in the schools, who was obliged to prove a proposition that had been denied, and who had run out of arguments, swore that it was true!

units.la: Res ergo particulares, ut sunt facta singularium hominum cum suis circumstantiis, quæ propter varios casus & contingentias quibus sunt obnoxiæ, ita sunt mutabiles & dubiæ, ut de his nulla posset haberi certitudo b per demonstrationem, aut alia nisi quæ pendet ex fide humana : sunt eæ, quibus confirmandis proprie inservit Juramentum. Quod innuit Apostolus Heb. 6. per illud Quasi diceret, Ibi juri-jurando locus est, ubi contradicendi finis nullus est; uno, puta Accusatore, affirmante; altero, puta Reo, negante : nisi interposito juramento altera parte contradictionis confirmata, cessaret pars altera, & sic tota lis terminaretur.
units.tr: Therefore particular things, such as the deeds of individual men with their circumstances, which are so changeable and uncertain because of the various chances and contingencies to which they are subject, that no certainty about them can be had b by demonstration, or by any means other than human trust, are the things an oath is properly for. The Apostle hints at this in Heb. 6, where he says that an oath is the end of dispute: as if he were saying that an oath has its place where there is no end to contradiction, when one party, say the accuser, affirms and the other, say the defendant, denies. Unless an oath is interposed to confirm one side of the contradiction, the other side would cease and the whole dispute would be settled.

units.la: VI. Et hæc Confirmatio (βεβαίωσιν vocat Apostolus loco jam dicto,) est ipsissimus Juramenti Finis. Nam cum res particulares incertæ essent & dubiæ ob earum contingentiam, nec possent probari nisi per testes, esset autem humanum omne testimonium valde infirmum & fallibile, ex duplici maxime defectu ; Scientiæ (multa enim nos latent,) & Conscientiæ (cum sit omnis homo mendax;) & tamen expediret hominibus, ut de rebus inter ipsos controversis & mutuo agitatis haberetur aliqua certitudo ; qua sine nulla esset inter homines fides aut justitia. quæ sunt firmissima vincula humanæ societatis : necesse fuit recurrere ad testimonium Dei, qui nec fallere potest nec falli. Sicque receptum est apud omnes gentes, ex instituto Dei vi juris naturalis, velut huic malo congruum e remedium Juramentum. Omnium judicio μεγίστη πίστις, inquit Diodorus Siculus; & Dionysius Halicarnassus πλεῖστα πίστις: & utrobique elegantius major utroque Apostolus πάσης ἀντιλογίας πέρας Heb. 6. Huc ubi ventum est, Ne plus ultra: sistat fe opportet omnis humana disceptatio & contradiatio. Non quod omne quod juramento confirmatur fit simpliciter certum, (tum enim nulla essent perjuria, quorum heu nimium plena sunt omnia:) Sed quod in hac mortalium conditione, (ubi per utile visum est divinæ sapientiæ humanum genus in multa rerum caligine & incertitudine versari, quo magis supernis rebus quæ certiores sunt animum adjicerent,) nulla potest esse major fides humana, quam quæ juramento, per invocationem divini nominis, quasi de cælo attestata & confirmata est .
units.tr: VI. This confirmation (the Apostle in the passage just cited calls it βεβαίωσιν [bebaiōsin]) is the very end of the oath. For since particular things are uncertain and doubtful because of their contingency, and can be proved only by witnesses, and since all human testimony is very weak and fallible, owing chiefly to two defects, that of knowledge (for many things escape us) and that of conscience (since every man is a liar), and yet it was useful to men that some certainty should be had about things disputed between them and dealt with mutually, without which there would be no faith or justice among men, which are the firmest bonds of human society, it was necessary to have recourse to the testimony of God, who can neither deceive nor be deceived. And so it has been received among all nations, by the institution of God and by the force of natural law, that an oath is the remedy suited to this evil. In the judgment of all, it is μεγίστη πίστις [megistē pistis], the greatest assurance, says Diodorus Siculus; and Dionysius of Halicarnassus says πλεῖστα πίστις [pleista pistis]; and the Apostle, more elegantly than either, says πάσης ἀντιλογίας πέρας [pasēs antilogias peras], the end of all contradiction (Heb. 6). Once we have come to this point, Ne plus ultra: all human debate and contradiction must stop here. Not that everything confirmed by oath is simply certain (for then there would be no perjuries, of which, alas, everything is only too full), but because in this condition of mortals, where it has seemed good to divine wisdom that the human race should live in much obscurity and uncertainty of things, so that they might give more heed to heavenly things, which are more certain, no greater human trust can exist than that which is attested and confirmed as if from heaven by an oath, through the invocation of the divine name.

units.la: VII. In hac juramenti definitione ita ut audivistis evoluta, continentur aliquo modo omnes Juramenti Causæ. Primum illud membrum, quo dicitur esse Actus Religiosus, cujus nimirum qui jurat, necessario includit Agentis, hoc est Jurantis, Voluntatem (cum sit omnis homo agens liberum, & actus humanus omnis Voluntarius) ut causam Efficientem primariam. Secundum Membrum exprimit Formale Juramenti, quod est divini nominis attestatio, five Dei ut testis Invocatio. Tertium membrum reliquam utramque causam complectitur: Materiam sc. & Finem. Est enim propria Juramenti Materia circa quam versatur Res dubia; cujus sc. ex nudo dicentis testimonio apud eum quicum agitur non est satis firma fides: & proprius Juramenti Finis, ut ex invocato Dei testimonio res dubia habeat eam certitudinem, qua circa res humanas contingentes nulla potest esse major. Hoc eo dixi, Auditores, quo excusatior apud vos esset hæc mea in explicanda Juramenti definitione prolixitas. Siquidem ubi ad casus dubios statuminandos Deo volente pervenero quod me sacturum pollicitus sum per respectum ad quatuor causarum genera: tum demum vos omnes non dubito facile perspecturos, quam studiosis utile fuerit, quam instituto meo conducibile, ista quæ sunt a me de Juramenti natura paulo explicatius dicta, præcognita habuisse.
units.tr: VII. In this definition of the oath, as you have heard it unfolded, all the causes of the oath are in some way contained. The first part, which says that it is a religious act, necessarily includes the will of the agent, that is, of the one swearing, as the primary efficient cause (since every man is a free agent and every human act is voluntary). The second part expresses the formal element of the oath, which is the attestation of the divine name, or the invocation of God as witness. The third part embraces the remaining two causes, namely the matter and the end. For the proper matter about which an oath is concerned is a doubtful thing, of which, I mean, the bare testimony of the speaker does not provide sufficiently firm trust for the one with whom the business is being done; and the proper end of the oath is that, by the invoked testimony of God, the doubtful thing should have that certainty than which, concerning contingent human affairs, none can be greater. I have said this, listeners, so that my lengthy explanation of the definition of the oath may seem more excusable to you. For when, God willing, I come to settle doubtful cases, which I promised to do by considering the four kinds of causes, then at last I do not doubt that you will all readily see how useful it has been for students, and how suitable to my plan, to have known in advance what I have said somewhat more fully about the nature of the oath.

units.la: VIII. Sed de Juramento in genere hactenus: explicandum proxime, sed paucioribus, quid in specie sit Juramentum Promissorium. Variæ extant apud Theologos & Jureconsultos, pro diverso respectu, Juramentorum seu divisiones, seu distinctiones. Dividitur alias in Judiciale, & extrajudiciale: alias in Publicum, & privatum: in simplex, &
units.tr: VIII. So far, then, concerning the oath in general. Next, in fewer words, I must explain what a promissory oath is in particular. Theologians and jurists have various divisions or distinctions of oaths, according to different points of view. Oaths are divided, on the one hand, into judicial and extrajudicial; on the other, into public and private; into simple and solemn.

units.la: Solenne : in Nudum, & Execratorium : in Absolutum,& conditionale ; & alias aliter. Sed nobilissima omnium, nec ulli eorum qui de Juramentis scripsere (quod sciam) praetermissa, ea est qua distinguitur in Assertorium & Promissorium. Quum enim in omni Juramento, ut ante dictum est, assumatur a jurante nomen Dei per modum invocationis in testimonium rei alicujus dubiae : advertendum est id posse contingere tribus modis. Potest enim res aliqua in dubium vocari, vel de praeterito, Itane fuerit, vel non fuerit : ut videstine heri Caium in foro, vel non vidisti? Vel de praesenti, Itane sit, vel non sit : ut, Habesne pecunias quas apud te depositi, vel non habes? Vel denique de futuro, Itane futurum sit, vel non: ut Dabisne mihi cras mutuo centum, vel non dabis? Quoties ergo adhibito Juramento Deus advocatur in testimonium rei praeteritae, vel praesentis, dici solet ejusmodi Juramentum Assertorium : quia jurans sine ulla in futurum sponsione, asserit tantum rem ita esse vel fuisse sicut ipse tunc jurat. Quod si Deus interposito juramento invocetur in testimonium rei futurae, dicitur id Juramentum promissorium : quia jurans polliceatur se aliquid in posterum facturum vel non facturum. Assertorii usus praecipuus est in judiciis, ad lites terminandas maxime in Quæstione facti: Promissorii exiguus usus est in judiciis; sed in Promissis, pactionibus & contractibus plurimus. Extant hujus generis juramenti multa in historia sacra, & alibi passim, exempla. Jurat pie Abraham servum, se Domini mandata in assumenda herili filio uxore fideliter observaturum. Jurant, sed incaute Josue & viri Principes populi Israelitici fœdus cum Gabaonitis. Juravit Rex Herodes, sed perquam temere, filiæ Herodiadis daturum se quicquid postularet.
units.tr: Into nude and execratory; into absolute and conditional; and in other ways too. But the most noble of all these divisions, and one that (as far as I know) none of those who have written about oaths has passed over, is the division into assertory and promissory. For since, as was said before, in every oath the one swearing takes the name of God by way of invocation as witness to some doubtful matter, it must be noted that this can happen in three ways. A thing may be called into doubt either about the past: Did it happen or not? As in, Did you see Gaius in the forum yesterday, or did you not? Or about the present: Is it so, or is it not? As in, Do you have the money that I deposited with you, or do you not? Or finally about the future: Will it be so, or not? As in, Will you lend me a hundred tomorrow, or will you not? Whenever, then, by an oath God is called as witness to a past or present thing, such an oath is usually called assertory, because the one swearing, without any promise for the future, only affirms that the thing is or was just as he then swears. But if God is called as witness by an interposed oath to a future thing, it is called a promissory oath, because the one swearing pledges that he will do or not do something in time to come. The principal use of the assertory oath is in judicial proceedings, chiefly to end suits on a question of fact. The use of the promissory oath in judicial proceedings is slight, but in promises, agreements and contracts it is very frequent. Many examples of this kind of oath are found in sacred history and elsewhere everywhere. Abraham piously swore to his servant that he would faithfully observe the Lord's commands in taking a wife for his master's son. Joshua and the princes of the people of Israel swore, but rashly, a covenant with the Gibeonites. King Herod swore, but very rashly, that he would give the daughter of Herodias whatever she asked.

units.la: IX. Advertendum est ulterius, sub Juramenti Promissorii appellatione comprehendi & Comminatorium: quale fuit illud Davidis de perdendo Nabale temerarium juramentum; & impium illud quorundam Judeorum Zelotarum, quo se devoverunt nihil gustaturos, donec occidissent Paulum. Hæc, & alia id genus, non sunt proprie Promissiones; quæ vox potius rem alteri gratam significare videtur: Sed per Synechochen quandam cum Catachresi conjunctam, (cum alias familiare apud bonos authores, tum præsertim in his dictionibus quæ futurum aliquod spectant, ut Sperare pro Timere, & similibus,) extendi potest Metalepsice Promissionis nomen & ad Comminationes. Ita Dei juramentum illud, quo juravit in ira sua, Israelitas qui ipsum variis provocationibus tentatentaverant in eremo non ingressuros in requiem suam, non minus promissorium dici poterit & solet, (etsi minus proprie, quam illud ejusdem quo juravit patribus eorum ei daturum eis terram Chananeorum in hæreditatem.
units.tr: IX. It must further be noted that under the name of promissory oath are included also comminatory oaths: such as David's rash oath to destroy Nabal, and that impious oath of certain Jewish Zealots, by which they bound themselves to taste nothing until they had killed Paul. These and others of that kind are not properly promises, a word which seems rather to signify something pleasing to another. But by a certain synecdoche joined with catachresis (a figure common among good authors, and especially in those expressions that look to something in the future, such as "to hope" for "to fear" and the like), the name of promise can be extended by metalepsis to threats as well. So God's oath, by which in his anger he swore that the Israelites, who had tested him by various provocations in the wilderness, would not enter his rest, can be and is commonly called promissory no less (though less properly) than that other oath by which he swore to their fathers that he would give them the land of Canaan as an inheritance.

units.la: X. Neque vero, quod ad Juramenti Promissorii rationem aut effectum attinet, quicquam omnino interest nude proferatur Juramentum, an cum adjecta execratione. Etsi enim sint e Scholasticorum grege, quibus videtur Juramentum illud, quod fit per simplicem contestationem, specie differre ab eo quod fit per adjunctam insuper execrationem; ea ratione adducti, quod in illo Deus advocetur solum ut Testis; in hoc etiam ut Judex: tamen si rem attentius consideremus, ex antedictis facile constat utrumvis fiat, perinde esse. Omne enim Juramentum, quocunque modo prolatum, sive nude sive execratorie, aut expresse, aut saltem implicite, Deum & ut Testem invocat, & ut Judicem: sed ut testem, primario & per se; ut Judicem, secundario & consequenter: & est ea forma Juramenti explicatissima, cum explicite & Deus adducitur testis, & execratio vel imprecatio adiungitur: ut si quis sic juraret, Deum testor qui me perdat ni fecero, me hoc vel illud facturum. Sed plerumque fit, ut omissa nunc hac, nunc illa parte, contractius juretur: ut
units.tr: X. Nor, as far as the nature or effect of a promissory oath is concerned, does it make any difference at all whether an oath is spoken bare or with an added curse. Some of the Schoolmen think that the oath made by simple attestation differs in kind from the oath made with an added curse, because in the first God is called upon only as witness, while in the second he is also called upon as judge. But if we consider the matter more carefully, it is easily seen from what was said above that it makes no difference which is done. Every oath, however it is uttered, whether bare or cursing, invokes God both as witness and as judge, expressly or at least implicitly: as witness primarily and in itself, as judge secondarily and consequently. The most explicit form of oath is the one in which God is expressly called as witness and a curse or imprecation is added, as if someone should swear thus: I call God to witness that I will do this or that; may he destroy me if I do not. But it often happens that, with one part or another omitted, the oath is made more briefly, as

units.la: ex illis exemplis sacræ Scripturæ, in quibus Deus pro more humano jurans inducitur, facis manifestum est. Ubi Deum jurantem reperire est, modo per simplicem attestationem sine ulla execratione; qualia sunt illa, l Vivo ego dicit dominus, m Per memetipsum juravi, n per sanctitatem meam, &c. modo sine aliqua expressa attestatione per solam execrationem, sed & illam (ob honorem & reverentiam tantæ majestatis, atque etiam pro more hominum verba o mali ominis per apofiopesin fere reticentium,) elliptice & diminute enunciatam, in particulis כ & אלוא involutam & subauditam; ut in illo Psalmi, si introibunt in requiem meam. Illud interim videtur esse certum, omne juramentum promissorium, quacunque forma concipiatur, explicatione vel contractione, modo sit Juramentum & non mera Asseveratio vel Obtestatio, utramque virtualiter continere; Attestationem sc. & Execrationem. Nam in Juramento & Execratio supponit attestationem ut quid sibi natura prius: & Attestatio subinfert Execrationem, ut suum necessarium consequens. Scitum est illud, Plutarchi, Et hæc de Juramenti promissorii natura sufficiant.
units.tr: the examples of Holy Scripture make clear, in which God is introduced swearing after the manner of men. Where we find God swearing, it is sometimes by simple attestation without any curse, as in As I live, saith the Lord, I have sworn by myself, by my holiness, and so on. Sometimes it is by the curse alone, without any express attestation, and even then (out of honour and reverence for so great a majesty, and also following the custom of men, who almost pass over words of ill omen by aposiopesis) it is uttered elliptically and incompletely, wrapped up and understood in the particles כ and אלוא, as in that verse of the Psalm, If they shall enter into my rest. Meanwhile it seems certain that every promissory oath, in whatever form it is conceived, whether full or abbreviated, provided it is an oath and not a mere asseveration or obtestation, virtually contains both: namely attestation and execration. For in an oath the execration presupposes the attestation as prior by nature, and the attestation brings in the execration as its necessary consequence. That saying of Plutarch is apt. And let these remarks on the nature of a promissory oath suffice.

units.la: XI. Reliquum est, ut de Obligationis etiam natura & vi aliquid ultimo demum loco attexam.
units.tr: XI. It remains for me to add, last of all, something on the nature and force of the obligation.

units.la: attexam. De Obligationibus multa & satis prolixe Jurisconsulti: Definiunt autem illi Obligationem, quod sit vinculum juris, quo quis astringitur ad solvendum id quod debet. Quæ definitio non minus commoda erit iis rebus explicandis quæ pertinent ad forum internum Conscientiæ, quam illis quæ versantur in foro externo Ecclesiæ aut Reipublicæ: si Juris vocabulum non contrahatur ad Jus humanum positivum, sed ita extendatur, ut universum etiam Jus divinum & naturale complectatur. Quum autem, ut ex ipsa illa definitione colligitur, vinculum omne obligatorium ex aliquo jure originem ducat: quemadmodum duplex est Jus, alterum divinum & naturale, civile & humanum alterum; ita duplex est vinculum sive obligatio inde consurgens. Vinculum Naturale, quod obligat naturaliter & in foro externo, ex vi legis divinæ: & Vinculum Civile, quod obligat civiliter & in foro interno, ex vi legis humanæ. Illud nonnulli Æquitatis obligationem vocant; hoc obligationem Justitiæ. Sive id illi commode loquantur, sive incommode, non disputo: nam ubi convenit de re, quid opus est de verbis contendere? Sed quod iidem illi tertium addunt Obligationis genus, quod sit ex utroque priore mixtum: id certe aut parum commode faciunt, aut saltem minus necessario. Nam si quis ad idem officium præstandum, (ut exempli gratia ad alendum parentes in senectute) & lege naturali, & lege civili teneretur : non hoc esset nova Obligationis species ex utraque mista, sed potius duæ obligationes ; conjunctæ quidem Subjecto simul & Objecto, (Subjecto, in quantum obligant eandem personam ; & Objecto, in quantum obligant ad idem officium) natura tamen & origine distincta. Ratio manifesta. Plures enim res non possunt producere ex mistione sui novam speciem, nisi cum aliqua sui immutatione reali. Unde Aristoteles mistionem definit miscibilium alterationem unionem. Oportet enim esse in omni mistione alterationem; & omnis alteratio est mutatio realis : ut patet in generatione misti ex quatuor elementis, non integris, sed refractis & alteratis. Alt ubi accedit priori obligationi obligatio nova, ut in præsenti negotio civilis naturali, nulla fit realis mutatio utrinque : sed prior illa obligatio manet in eodem omnino statu in quo fuit ante accessionem novæ posterioris. Sed nolo his subtilitatibus diutius immorari. Obligationem is hac juramenti materia Naturalem sive Moralem vel solum vel præcipue intelligimus : Jurisconsultis illam alteram Civilem relinquimus.
units.tr: Lawyers have much to say about obligations, and at some length. They define an obligation as a bond of right by which someone is bound to pay what he owes. This definition will be no less useful for explaining matters that belong to the internal forum of conscience than for those that lie in the external forum of Church or Commonwealth, provided that the word right is not restricted to positive human law but is extended to embrace the whole of divine and natural law as well. Since, as is gathered from that very definition, every binding bond derives from some right, and since right is twofold, the one divine and natural, the other civil and human, so the bond or obligation arising from it is also twofold. There is a natural bond, which binds naturally and in the external forum, by the force of divine law; and a civil bond, which binds civilly and in the internal forum, by the force of human law. Some call the former an obligation of equity and the latter an obligation of justice. Whether they speak fittingly or unfittingly I do not dispute: where there is agreement about the thing, why contend about words? But the same men add a third kind of obligation, mixed from both of the earlier kinds, and this they either do without good reason or at least without necessity. For if someone were bound to perform the same duty (for example, to support his parents in old age) both by natural law and by civil law, this would not be a new species of obligation mixed from both, but rather two obligations. They are joined in subject and in object (in subject, in so far as they bind the same person; in object, in so far as they bind to the same duty), yet they are distinct in nature and origin. The reason is plain. Several things cannot produce a new species by mixing with one another unless each undergoes some real change. Hence Aristotle defines mixture as the alteration and union of things capable of mixing. For there must be alteration in every mixture, and every alteration is a real change, as is clear in the generation of a compound from the four elements, which are not whole but broken down and altered. But when a new obligation is added to a prior one, as in the present case the civil to the natural, no real change takes place on either side. The prior obligation remains in exactly the same state in which it was before the later one was added. But I do not want to linger longer over these subtleties. In this matter of oaths, we understand obligation as natural or moral, either solely or chiefly; the other, civil, we leave to the lawyers.

units.la: XII. Præter illam Obligationis distinctionem ex Origine natam, per respectum ad Jus Jus unde oritur obligatio: est & alia ab Objecto sumpta, per respectum sc. ad Debitum solvendum, quo tendit & in quod fertur Obligatio. Duplex autem est Debitum. Debitum Officii, quod quis ex præcepto juris tenetur facere: & Debitum Supplicii, quod quis ex sanctione juris tenetur pati, si officium suum neglexerit. Priori sensu dicimus mutua caritatis officia esse debita, quia lex Dei illa præcipit, juxta illud Rom. 13. {f}Nihil cuiquam debete, nisi ut diligatis invicem. Posteriori sensu dicimus Peccata esse debita, ut in oratione Dominica, {t}Dimitte nobis debita nostra: & mortem æternam esse debitam, juxta illud Rom. 6. {u}Stipendium peccati mors. Observandum tamen debitum posterius contrahi ex infoluto priori: ita ut si quis debitum officii plenarie dissolveret, faciendo id quod lex imperat, non teneretur aliquo debito supplicii ad patiendum id quod lex minatur. Respondet duplici huic Debito duplex item Obligatio, ejusdem plane denominationis: Obligatio sc. ad officium faciendum, & Obligatio ad supplicium perferendum; vel quod communiter dicitur & eodem recidit, Obligatio ad Culpam, & Obligatio ad Pœnam. Ita tamen ut illa sit prior & potior, sicut natura sua, sic & intentione juris. Tyrannidis enim est, non juris, pœnam intendere aliter quam in ordine ad culpam: & verum est illud Apostoli dictum etiam in hoc sensu, etsi fortassis alio rectius intelligendum,Lex Justo non est posita. Intendit ergo Lex primario, directe, per se, & ἀπλῶς obligare ad officium & obedientiam: ad supplicium autem & poenam non obligat nisi secundario, indirecte, consequenter, & ex hypothesi; supposito sc. officii aut contemptu aut neglectu. Utramque hanc obligationem conjunxisse videtur Apostolus, Rom. 13. ubi agit de subjectione Supremae potestati debita: y Necesse est, inquit, subjici, non solum propter iram, sed & propter conscientiam. E quibus verbis tria colligo ad praesens institutum pertinentia. Primum, duplici vinculo posse nos obligari ad idem praestandum; vinculo officii, & vinculo supplicii: hoc enim volunt illa, διὰ τὴν ὑποταγὴν, & διὰ τὴν ὀργήν. Alterum, priorem & potiorem apud omnes pios esse debere officii conscientiam, quam supplicii metum. Tertium, ex debito officii praecise exurgere obligationem conscientiae. Unde etiam manifestum est, nos, cum de Juramenti obligatione loquimur, quatenus conscientiae res est, Obligationem illam intelligere primario & potissimum, qua tenemur officium praestare; non eam, qua tenemur poenam perjurio debitam sustinere.
units.tr: XII. Besides the distinction of obligations arising from their origin, according to the right from which the obligation arises, there is another distinction taken from the object, that is, with respect to the debt to be discharged, to which the obligation tends and toward which it is directed. Now debt is twofold: the debt of duty, which someone is bound by precept of law to perform, and the debt of punishment, which someone is bound by the sanction of law to suffer if he has neglected his duty. In the former sense we say that mutual duties of love are owed, because God's law commands them, according to Rom. 13. {f}Owe no one anything, except to love one another. In the latter sense we say that sins are debts, as in the Lord's Prayer, {t}Forgive us our debts, and that eternal death is a debt, according to Rom. 6. {u}The wages of sin is death. It must be observed, however, that the latter debt is contracted from the former, unpaid. So if someone fully discharged the debt of duty by doing what the law commands, he would not be held by any debt of punishment to suffer what the law threatens. To this twofold debt there corresponds a twofold obligation of the same name: the obligation to perform the duty, and the obligation to bear the punishment. Or, as it is commonly put, and it comes to the same thing, the obligation to the fault and the obligation to the penalty. Yet the former is prior and more important, both by its nature and in the intention of the law. For it is tyranny, not law, to aim at punishment otherwise than in relation to the fault. The Apostle's saying is true even in this sense, though perhaps it is to be understood more rightly in another: The law is not laid down for the righteous (1 Tim. 1). The law therefore intends primarily, directly, in itself, and simply [ἁπλῶς], to bind to duty and obedience. It binds to punishment and penalty only secondarily, indirectly, consequently and by hypothesis, namely on the supposition of contempt or neglect of duty. The Apostle seems to have joined both these obligations in Rom. 13, where he treats of the subjection owed to the supreme power: It is necessary, he says, to be subject, not only for wrath's sake but also for conscience' sake. From these words I gather three things pertinent to the present purpose. First, that we can be bound by a twofold bond to render the same thing: the bond of duty and the bond of punishment, for the words mean (1) because of subjection [διὰ τὴν ὑποταγήν] and (2) because of wrath [διὰ τὴν ὀργήν]. Second, that among all the godly the awareness of duty ought to be prior and weightier than the fear of punishment. Third, that the obligation of conscience arises precisely from the debt of duty. Whence it is also clear that when we speak of the obligation of an oath, insofar as it is a matter of conscience, we understand primarily and chiefly that obligation by which we are bound to render the duty, not that by which we are bound to bear the punishment owed for perjury.

units.la: XIII. Positis duabus his Obligationum distinctionibus, illud porro sciendum est, Juramentum omne ex sua natura esse obligatorium.Ita ut si quis juret, non intendens se obligare,imo etiamsi juraret intendens se non obligare, nihil ominus tamen suscipiendo juramentum ipso facto obligetur:ut posthac suo loco(si Deo volente eo pervenero) plenius ostendam. Recte Cicero, Nullum vinculum ad astringendam fidem majores nostri juLLrando arctius esse voluerunt. Sed quid dilucidius hanc in rem dici potuit, quam quod est a Mose dictum in ipso textu ? Cum vir voverit votum, vel juraverit juramentum, לאסר ... ligando ligamen super animam suam. Ubi geminatio illa ex Hebraeorum idiotismo plurimam habet emphasin, & auget significationem vocis. Ut multiplicans multiplicabo, & benedicens benedicam.id est, valde multiplicabo, valde benedicam, &c.sic ligando ligamen,id est valde ligando. Quasi diceret, Etsi promissio vel nuda obliget conscientiam,addita etiam asseveratione aut obtestatione, fortius adhuc obliget : omnium tamen fortissime obligat votum, quod ipsi Deo nuncupatur,& Juramentum quod homini,sed Deo tamen teste,praestatur. Obligat ergo omne Juramentum conscientiam;tam Assertorium, quam Promissorium. De Promissorio,quandoquidem tempus futurum respicit,nulli potest esse dubium : sed de Assertorio fortassis non sine ratione dubitari posset ex eo,quod omnis Obligatio est ad aliquod futurum ; dictum
units.tr: XIII. With these two distinctions of obligation laid down, we must further note that every oath is by its nature binding. So if someone swears without intending to bind himself, or even if he swears while intending not to be bound, nevertheless by taking the oath he is bound by the very fact of taking it. I will show this more fully in its proper place, God willing, if I come to it. Cicero rightly says: Our ancestors wished that no bond for binding faith be tighter than an oath. But what could be said more clearly on this point than what Moses says in the text itself: When a man vows a vow, or swears an oath, to bind [לאסר] ... binding a bond upon his soul. Here the doubling, which is a Hebrew idiom, carries great emphasis and intensifies the meaning of the word, as in multiplying I will multiply, and blessing I will bless, that is, I will multiply greatly, I will bless greatly, and so on. So too binding a bond means binding firmly. It is as if he said: even if a bare promise binds the conscience, a promise with the added assertion or appeal to witness binds more strongly still; yet most strongly of all binds a vow, which is made to God himself, and an oath, which is given to a man but nonetheless with God as witness. Every oath therefore binds the conscience, both assertory and promissory. That a promissory oath binds is beyond doubt, since it looks to the future. But it might perhaps reasonably be doubted of an assertory oath, since all obligation concerns something future. The reply is that the difference between the assertory and the promissory oath is said to lie in this, that the one concerns a present or past thing and the other a future thing.

units.la: Gen. 22. 16. autem sit prius Assertorii juramenti a Promissorio discrimen in hoc consistere, quod illud rem praesentem vel praeteritam respiceret, hoc futuram. Sed facilis est solutio. Nimirum juramenti qua tale Obligatio non cadit primario super Objectum, sive Materiam juramenti; sic enim Assertorium juramentum, cujus objectum est res praeterita aut praesens, non posset obligationem de futuro inducere: sed obligatio cadit immediate & directe super Subjectum, hoc est conscientiam jurantis, qui in utraque Juramenti specie tenetur ad aliquod officium de futuro praestandum.
units.tr: Gen. 22. 16. But the answer is easy. The obligation of an oath as such does not fall primarily upon the object, or matter, of the oath; for then an assertory oath, whose object is a past or present thing, could not bring about an obligation concerning the future. Rather the obligation falls immediately and directly upon the subject, that is, the conscience of the one swearing, who in either kind of oath is bound to perform some duty in the future.

units.la: XIV. Quod ut manifestius fiat, simulque liquido constet, (quod explicandum suscepi) quae sit juramenti promissorii obligatio: ostendam ut potero utrique Juramenti speciei quid sit commune, quantum ad obligationis effectum; & quid sit Promissorio juramento peculiare. Concedendum autem est imprimis, quod est ex se ita evidens, ut ejus contradictorium manifestam implicet contradictionem, Obligationem omnem ad officium respicere officium de futuro praestandum; hoc est, aliquanto saltem tempore, etsi fortassis minutissimo, post contractam obligationem. Neque est observatu difficile, rem attentius paulo consideranti, hoc in omni Juramento tam Assertorio quam Promisforio contingere. Obligat enim se quisquis jurat ipso facto [?]ὡς τὸ ἀληθές[?], hoc est ad manifestandam veritatem in eo quod dicturus est, sive illud sit de re praeterita aut praesenti in Assertorio; sive de re futura in Promissorio Juramento. Et est ista obligatio hactenus utrique speciei pariter communis: ita ut in utravis si jurantis verba animo non congruant, violati officii culpae reus sit, & inde per necessariam consequentiam etiam & poenae.Sed in juramento Promissorio, praeter hanc obligationem quae cadit super conscientiam juramentis, & est ipsi cum Assertorio communis, quatenus est Juramentum; est & alia ulterior obligatio, ipsi propria & peculiaris quatenus Promissorium est, quae cadit super Materiam Juramenti; Cujus virtute tenetur promissorie jurans, non solum intendere de praesenti id facere quod juravit, quod est [?]τὸ ἀληθές[?], ut sc. verba animo congruant: sed etiam conari de futuro (quantum in ipso est) id implere quod juravit, ut facta verbis congruant. Hoc est, non modo obligat se ad id solum promittendum quod revera intendit: sed etiam ultra obligat se ad id omne faciendum quod jurando promisit. Quod vel ipsa verba Mosis in hoc versu clare ostendunt: Vir, inquit, qui juraverit juramentum ligando ligamen super animam suam, secundum omne quod egressum est ex ore suo faciet. Atque ita quam debui plene, & quam potui dilucide, exposui vobis sensum meum de primo capite hujus tractationis ; Quid Juramentum, Quid promiffiorium, & Quid Obligatio. Pergam reliqua, quo ordine proposui, proxima prælectione (Deo volente) persequi.
units.tr: XIV. To make this clearer, and so that it may plainly be established what the obligation of a promissory oath is (which is what I have undertaken to explain), I will show as well as I can what is common to both kinds of oath as regards the effect of obligation, and what is peculiar to the promissory oath. First, it must be granted, since it is so evident in itself that its contradiction would involve a manifest contradiction, that every obligation looks to a duty to be performed in the future; that is, after some time at least, however brief, following the undertaking of the obligation. Nor is it hard to observe, for anyone who considers the matter a little more carefully, that this holds for every oath, assertory as well as promissory. For whoever swears binds himself by the very act to the truth [τὸ ἀληθές], that is, to make the truth manifest in what he is about to say, whether it concerns a past or present thing in an assertory oath, or a future thing in a promissory oath. Up to this point the obligation is equally common to both kinds: so that in either, if the swearer's words do not agree with his mind, he is guilty of the fault of violating his duty, and from this, by necessary consequence, also of punishment. But in a promissory oath, besides this obligation, which falls upon the conscience in swearing and is common to it with the assertory oath insofar as it is an oath, there is another, further obligation, proper and peculiar to it insofar as it is promissory, which falls upon the matter of the oath. By virtue of this, the one swearing a promise is bound not only to intend at the present time to do what he has sworn, which is the truth [τὸ ἀληθές], so that his words agree with his mind; but also to strive in the future (as far as lies in him) to fulfil what he has sworn, so that his deeds agree with his words. That is, he binds himself not only to promise only that which he truly intends, but further binds himself to do all that he has promised by swearing. Moses' own words in this verse show this clearly: The man, he says, who swears an oath, binding a bond upon his soul, shall do according to all that has gone out of his mouth. And so I have set forth to you, as fully as I ought and as clearly as I can, my view of the first head of this treatment: what an oath is, what a promissory oath is, and what obligation is. In the next lecture, God willing, I will proceed to the remaining matters in the order I have proposed.
