units.la: EXposito superiore lectione quid Juramentum in genere, quid in specie promissorium Juramentum, & quid Obligatio: pergendum nunc porro ad proponendum, quod proxime pollicitus sum, quasdam τετάρτας five Hypotheses instituto nostro accommodas, velut fundamenta, aut (si malitis) Canones & κανόνες totius futuræ disquisitionis: e quibus sc. petendæ sunt, & ad quas exigendæ, pleroramque dubiorum determinationes. Sed unum vos interim, antiquam id faciam, non jam exoratum eo, (quod facerem si aut suspecta mihi esset vestra humanitas, aut res ipsa non esset multo justissima:) sed præmonitos tantum velim; mihi constitutum esse, dum reperiam quod rei de qua agitur utcunque significandæ sufficiat, de verbis non ultra laborare, multo minus de sermonis puritate, nedum elegantia sollicitum esse. Curent ista scilicet, quibus vacat, & cordi est, negotium faccessere sibi non necessarium. Repetere soleo cum amicis non sine aliquo risuque jocoque, quantum sudarit, ut tandem incipiret magis, vir alias sane non ineruditus,
units.tr: Having set out in the previous lecture what an oath is in general, what a promissory oath is in particular, and what obligation is, I must now go on to propose, as I promised next, certain theses [τετάρτας] or hypotheses suited to our purpose, serving as foundations, or (if you prefer) as canons and rules [κανόνες] for the whole of the coming inquiry. From these the answers to most doubts are to be drawn, and by these they are to be settled. But I will say one thing first. I do not do this because I need your indulgence, which I would ask only if I suspected your kindness or if the matter were not most just. I want only to forewarn you. I have resolved, until I find a word that can in some way signify the matter in hand, not to labour further over words, and much less to be anxious about purity of speech, let alone elegance. Let those who have leisure and a taste for such things attend to them, and make for themselves a task that is not necessary. I am accustomed to recount to friends, not without some laughter and jesting, how much a certain man, otherwise certainly not unlearned, sweated before he at last got on

units.la: Paulus Cortesius: Qui dum, post Thomam & Scotum & complures alios meditatur in quatuor libros Sententiarum commentarios pertæßus, sc. voces in Scholis receptas ut minus Ciceronianas, pro Ecclesia (delicias hominis!) maluit ubique Senatum dicere, pro Legibus Ecclesiasticis Senatus-Consulta, pro Prædestinatione Præfignationem, pro Sacerdotum Ordinatione Initiationem, pro Angelis, Genios, pro Episcopis Flamines, & alia passim ad eundem modum plurima. Quo eodem morbo laborasse invenio & alios quosdam, ut Petrum Bembum Cardinalem, & Sebastianum Castalionem: sed eos & paucos admodum, & aliquanto temperatius. At nobis non liber, nobis non licet esse tam difertis. Oratori condonabitur, imo laudi erit, si fit verborum paulo diligentior: cujus inter virtutes est, non apte modo & dilucide, sed etiam pure & ornate dicere; quemque non dedecebit floridius quandoque & pictura-tius incedere. Ait Philosophum, aut Theologum, præsertim in Scholasticis meditationibus & nodis Controversiarum, tam decet compta & ornata oratio, quam bovem arator em bullatæ phaleræ. Materia in qua operam sumimus, doceri contenta, non postulat ornatum; sed nec patitur. Nimirum non est idem in Rostris & in Scholis versari: & aliud longe est liberiore campo frui, in quo cum copia quadam & ubertate exultare possit oratio; aliud spinas inter & vepreta impeditum teneri, unde fe quovifmodo expedire fine sanguine & vulnere opimus est triumphus. Sed quid ego ilta tam operose? Si vocibus & locutionibus in hoc tractandi genere receptis passim utar, quod est omnino faciendum: quin fit ea res veniam apud vos habitura nullus dubito; verendum magis ut fi habitura hæc tam prolixa defensio. Desino itaque orare; & ad Hypotheses festino.
units.tr: Paulus Cortesius, who, while meditating on Thomas, Scotus and many others in his commentaries on the four books of the Sentences, grew weary, wanting the terms received in the schools to be less Ciceronian. So for "Church" (the darling of the man!) he preferred everywhere to say Senatum; for ecclesiastical laws, Senatus-Consulta; for predestination, Praefignationem; for the ordination of priests, Initiationem; for angels, Genios; for bishops, Flamines; and many other things in the same manner throughout. I find that some others laboured under the same disease, such as Cardinal Pietro Bembo and Sebastian Castellio, but these were few and rather more moderate. But we are not free, and we are not allowed to be so eloquent. An orator will be pardoned, indeed praised, if he is somewhat more careful with words; for among his virtues is to speak not only aptly and clearly but also purely and elegantly, and it does not disgrace him sometimes to advance in a more florid and embroidered style. But he says that for a philosopher or theologian, especially in scholastic meditations and the knots of controversies, an elaborate and ornate style suits as ill as a ploughman's ox wearing a studded trapping. The matter we are engaged with is content to be taught, and it does not require ornament; indeed it does not allow it. Of course it is not the same to speak in the Rostra as in the Schools. It is one thing to enjoy a freer field, where speech may exult with a certain abundance and richness; it is another to be held entangled among thorns and brambles, where to extricate oneself in any way without blood and wounds is a rich triumph. But why do I labour over this so elaborately? If I use words and expressions commonly received in this kind of treatment, as must be done, I do not doubt that the matter will be pardoned by you. I fear rather that this so lengthy defence will be. So I will stop begging, and hasten on to the hypotheses.

units.la: II. Quarum esto Prima, Juramentum ante omnia decet simplicitas.
units.tr: II. The first of these shall be: An oath above all requires simplicity.

units.la: Hoc est, Ea est Juramenti natura & obligatio, ut quisquis fe ad aliquid faciendum tam sacro vinculo obstrinxerit, juramenti religione omnino teneatur, & ex animo ferio intendere, & quantum in ipso est sedulo conari, id omne facere bona fide quod fe facturum promisit, fine omni astu, fraude, dolove malo aut simulatione. Recte, ut pleraque omnia in hoc genere Cicero, Quod affirmate quasi Deo teste promiseris, id tenendum est. Secus qui fecerit, nec curaverit id re ipsa præstare ad quod fe jurejurando obligavit, cum hic Moses censet polluisse verbum suum: hoc est, rem sacram nec temere prophanandam sede & indigne confpurcasse, & perjurii reum esse, aut aperti aut palliati. Cum enim tradantur fere tria
units.tr: That is, this is the nature and obligation of an oath: whoever binds himself to do something by so sacred a bond is wholly held by the religion of the oath, must intend it in earnest, and must strive diligently, as far as lies in him, to do in good faith everything he promised to do, without any cunning, fraud, evil deceit or pretence. Cicero rightly says, as he does in most matters of this kind: What you have promised with affirmation, as if God were your witness, must be kept. Whoever acts otherwise, and takes no care to perform in fact what he bound himself to by his oath, is judged by Moses to have polluted his word. That is, he has profaned and defiled a holy thing, which is not to be lightly profaned, and he is guilty of perjury, whether open or disguised. For since there are commonly given about three

units.la: Perjuriorum genera, quorum primum est Assertorio Juramentorum generi pene peculiare, viz. cum quis jurat aliquid esse verum, quod aut falsum esse putat, aut saltem sit necne verum dubitat; reliqua duo ad promissorium hoc genus pertinent; Secundum nimirum, cum quis jurando promittit quod nec intendit implere; & Tertium, cum non studet implere quod promiserat & intenderat: non sane multum refert, quod quidem ad Perjurii rationem attinet, maxime in foro conscientiae, apertene; aliquod trium fiat & an simulate & Scilicet est illud prophani cordis indicium; hoc dolosi: quorum utrumque, nisi sit a fraus odio digna majore, pariter b abominatur sanctissimus ille Deus, qui amat simplices corde, & diligit c veritatem in intimis; d declinantes autem in perversitates suas, id est, hypocritas & dolosos facit ambulare cum operantibus iniquitatem, id est, pariter habet cum palam impiis & facinorosis.
units.tr: kinds of perjury, of which the first is almost peculiar to the assertory kind of oath, namely when someone swears that something is true which he thinks false, or at least doubts whether it is true; the other two pertain to this promissory kind: the second, namely when someone swears a promise he does not intend to fulfil, and the third, when he does not care to fulfil what he promised and intended. It does not much matter, as far as the nature of perjury goes, especially in the court of conscience, whether one of these three occurs openly or in disguise. The former is a sign of a profane heart, the latter of a deceitful one. Both of these, unless there is a fraud deserving of greater hatred, the most holy God abhors equally: he who loves those simple of heart and delights in truth in the inward parts. But those who turn aside to their perversities, that is, hypocrites and deceivers, he makes to walk with workers of iniquity, that is, he counts them together with openly impious and wicked men.

units.la: III. Pugnat cum hac Juramenti simplicitate duplex Simulationis genus: alterum a parte ante, quod ad actum jurandi aut antecedenter se habet aut concomitanter; a parte post alterum, quod consequenter: quorum illud etsi deterius sit, neutrum tamen perjurio vacat. Utrumque
units.tr: III. Two kinds of simulation conflict with this simplicity of swearing. One lies on the part before the oath (a parte ante), which either precedes the act of swearing or accompanies it. The other lies on the part after (a parte post), which follows the oath. The former is the worse, but neither is free from perjury. Both of these

units.la: {a} Eccles. 1. (Greek marginal reference). {b} Psal. 51. {c} Psal. 51. {d} Psal. 11. que complexus videtur David, locis diversis, sed propemodum parallelis;Psalmis viz. decimo quinto & vicesimo quarto. Quorum in altero, illi quaestioni e Quis ascendet in mox{c}tem Domini? inter alia respondetur, Qui non juravit in dolo, (למרמה) id est, qui non juravit cum animo fallendi: ubi excluditur omnis simulatio a parte ante, ipso, sc. tempore, & inter ipsum factum jurandi. In altero, consimili quaestioni, Quis habitabit in tabernaculo Domini, &c. inter alia respondetur non multum diffimiliter, Qui juravit in malum, (לא־ימר [?]) & non mutavit; id est, qui postquam se juramento obligavit, maluit vel cum magno suo damno praestare quod incommode juravit, quam alicujus temporalis commodi intuitu datam fidem violare: ubi excluditur omnis simulatio a parte post. Ista mihi aut non cogitare videntur, aut non scrio, eorum qui nunc sunt hominum pleraque pars: qui in omne illud quodcunque demum fuerit, quod est ab his quibus nocendi potestas est propositum, sine ulla ambage prolixe & conceptis verbis jurare non verentur: quin sibi potius soli sapere videntur, ridentque non sine aliquo fastu eorum simplicitatem & inanem metum, qui ne conscientiam laedant, nodum in scirpo quaerunt scilicet & perscriptas ab iis qui proscribere possunt formulas follicitant. Securi interim se ab omni perjurii crimine metuque liberant, sibique & conscientiæ suæ egregie consultum existimant, sive inter jurandum, Jesuitarum more tacitæ alicujus æquivocationis, aut mentalis reservationis, aut subtilis coactive & a verbis proprie alieni interpretamenti adminiculo se quoquo modo tueri utcunque possint; vel etiam postquam juraverint, rimam qua elabantur, artificiosam aliquam evasionem reperire queant, velut σοφὶ φάρμακον, quo juramento sic fraus fiat, ut salvis verbis sententia tamen sophismate aliquo eludatur, & vis ejus omnis penitus enervetur. Non agnoverunt hanc Theologiam veteres Christiani: non hanc morum Philosophiam saniores Ethnici. Multo aliter ex illis Augustinus, {g} Perjuri sunt, qui servatis verbis, expectationem eorum quibus juratum est deceperunt. Aliter & ex his Cicero, {h} Quod ita juratum est, ut mens deferentis conciperet fieri oportere, id servandum est.
units.tr: {a} Eccles. 1. (Greek marginal reference). {b} Psal. 51. {c} Psal. 51. {d} Psal. 11. David seems to have embraced both, in different places but in nearly parallel terms, namely in Psalms fifteen and twenty-four. In the one, to the question "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord?" it is answered, among other things, "He who has not sworn deceitfully" [למרמה], that is, he who has not sworn with intent to deceive. Here every simulation on the part before is excluded, namely at the very time of swearing and in the act itself. In the other, to a similar question, "Who shall dwell in the tabernacle of the Lord?", etc., it is answered, not very differently, among other things, "He who has sworn to his hurt and has not changed" [לא־ימר], that is, he who, having bound himself by an oath, has preferred to perform what he swore, even at great loss to himself, rather than break his given word for the sake of some temporal advantage. Here every simulation on the part after is excluded. These people, who now make up the greater part of mankind, seem either not to think about these things or not to care about them. They do not hesitate to swear openly, at length and in express words, to whatever is proposed by those who have the power to harm them. Indeed they seem to themselves alone to be wise, and they laugh, not without some disdain, at the simplicity and empty fear of those who, lest they wound their conscience, seek a knot in a rush, and who court formulas written out by those who can dictate them. Meanwhile they feel safe and free from every charge and fear of perjury, and they think they have looked well to themselves and their conscience, whether while swearing, after the manner of the Jesuits, by some tacit equivocation, or mental reservation, or by the aid of a subtle, restrictive interpretation foreign to the proper sense of the words, they can somehow protect themselves in whatever way they can; or even after they have sworn, they can find some clever escape through which they slip away, like a sophistic remedy, so that the oath is so defrauded that, while the words are kept, the meaning is nonetheless eluded by some sophism, and all its force is utterly weakened. The early Christians did not acknowledge this theology, nor did the saner Gentiles acknowledge this moral philosophy. Augustine speaks quite differently: "They are perjurers who, keeping the words, have deceived the expectation of those to whom the oath was made." Cicero too, differently: "What has been sworn in such a way that the mind of the one who swore understood it ought to be done, that must be kept."

units.la: IV. Sed ne aut declamare videar, aut authoritate sola pugnare: confirmabo aliquot rationibus, neutra simulatione tolli Perjurium. Ratio prima. Ex permultis illis Scripturæ locis, in quibus cordis simplicitas, cum in omni cultu Dei & officiis vitæ communis, tum vel maxime in contractibus, promissis, votis, & juramentis exigitur. Ut alia mittam, in texu propolito diuersis verbis requiritur ab homine iurante, ut omnino faciat secundum id quod egressum est ex ore suo. Ut omnino faciat, id est, ut & tunc temporis bona fide intendat facere, & postea bona fide quantum in ipso est conetur facere; secundum id quod egressum est ex ore suo, id est, secundum eum sensum quem verba ab ipso prolata juxta communem & receptum morem loquendi apta sunt ingenerare in mente audientium, & non secundum eum sensum, quem ipse fortassis inter jurandum intra semetipsum tacita mentis cogitatione reservatum dolose intendit. Quo facit illud quod ex Isidoro solet afferri, {i}Quacunque arte verborum quis juret, Deus tamen qui conscientiae testis est, ita hoc accipit sicut ille cui juratur intelligit. Neque etiam secundum eum sensum, quem juratus, postquam caepit eum facti poenitere, de novo tandem comminiscitur ἀποφάσεως χάριν, seu dicis causa ut loquuntur; non ut integre & sincere exolvat sicut debet Sacramenti fidem, sed ut sibi aliisque videatur quoquo modo officio functum esse, & perjurii crimen isthoc artificio caute & provide admodum declinasse.
units.tr: IV. But lest I seem either to declaim or to fight with authority alone, I will confirm by several reasons that perjury is not removed by any mental reservation. First reason. From the many passages of Scripture in which simplicity of heart is required in all worship of God and all the duties of common life, but above all in contracts, promises, vows and oaths. To pass over the others: in the text proposed, the one swearing is required in different words to do altogether what has gone out of his mouth. To do altogether means both to intend in good faith to perform it at the time, and afterwards to strive in good faith, as far as lies in him, to perform it. What has gone out of his mouth means the sense which the words he utters, according to common and accepted usage of speech, are fitted to produce in the minds of the hearers, and not the sense which he perhaps, while swearing, has kept to himself by silent thought and deceitfully intends. To this bears the saying commonly cited from Isidore: By whatever artifice of words one swears, God, who is witness of the conscience, takes it as the one to whom it is sworn understands it. Nor is it the sense which the one who swore, after he began to regret the deed, now at last contrives anew ἀποφάσεως χάριν [for the sake of denial], or, as they say, for the sake of appearance. He does not do this to discharge fully and sincerely the faith of the oath as he ought, but so that he may seem to himself and to others to have fulfilled his duty in some way, and by this artifice carefully and very cleverly to have avoided the crime of perjury.

units.la: V. Ratio secunda. Ab exemplo ipsius Dei: quem scribit Apostolus Heb. 6. ea ipsa de causa promissiones suas fidelibus sta-tas jurejurando confirmatas esse voluisse, ut k ἀμετάθετον abundantius, id est, quam heri po-test cumulatissime, & ita ut nullus possit esse ultra dubitandi locus, testatur: ipsis fa-ceret τὸ ἀμετάβλητον τῆς βουλῆς αὐτοῦ, quam immutabile esset consilium ipsius in eo praestando quod se juravisset praestiturum: atque hoc omne eo fine, ut haberent credituri in ipsum ἰσχυρὰν παράκλησιν, validam consolationem, spem firmam. Quam tamen non haberent, si in his quae jurando promisit posssibile esset ἀδύνατον ψεύσασθαι, id est (ut l docti vim ejus vocis exprimunt) si fallere posset Deus eos quibus juravit, frustrando ipsorum expectationem. Falleret autem, & frustaret credentium spem, & ex spe consolationem, si, aut cum juraret non intenderet facere quod promisit, aut mutato postmodum consilio idipsum debito tempore non praestaret, idque eo ipso sensu quo ab eis promissiones illas par erat juxta verborum tenorem intelligi. Juravit m Deus, & non poenitebit eum. Juravit Dominus n Davidi veritatem, nec disce-det ab ea.
units.tr: V. Second reason. From the example of God himself: whom the Apostle writes in Heb. 6 to have wished, for this very reason, his promises made to the faithful to be confirmed by an oath, so that, as he testifies, the ἀμετάθετον [unchangeableness] might be shown more abundantly, that is, as fully as can be, and so that there should be no place left for doubt. He would make τὸ ἀμετάβλητον τῆς βουλῆς αὐτοῦ [the immutability of his counsel] evident, how unchangeable his purpose was in performing what he had sworn he would perform. And all this to the end that they who believed might have ἰσχυρὰν παράκλησιν [a strong consolation], a valid comfort, and firm hope. They would not have this if it were possible for God to lie in those things which he promised with an oath, ἀδύνατον ψεύσασθαι [impossible to lie]; that is (as learned men express the force of that word), if God could deceive those to whom he swore by frustrating their expectation. He would deceive and frustrate the hope of believers, and with it their consolation, if either when he swore he did not intend to do what he promised, or his purpose changed afterwards and he did not perform it at the due time; and this in the very sense in which those promises ought to have been understood by them according to the tenor of the words. God swore, and will not repent. The Lord swore to David the truth, and will not depart from it.

units.la: IV. Ratio tertia, Ex natura Veritatis: quae prima est & potissima e tribus illis decantatissimis Juramenti conditionibus, quae extant apud Jeremiam prophetam, & ab omnibus inculcantur, & a Scholasticis Tres juramenti comites appellantur. Veritas &c. Judicium, & Justitia. Cui Veritati repugnat, non modo quod talsum est, sed & quod fallum est: nec mendacium solum apertum & nudum, sed opertum quoque & qualitercunque palliatum. Polluit certe verbum suum mendacio, quicunque falsum dixerit proximo suo, & falsum is dixisse putandus est proximo suo, per quem stetit ut sallus esset proximus suus ea spe, quam ex dictis ipsius rationabiliter conceperat. Quum ergo per istiusmodi utriusve generis simulationem non evitatur Mendacium, dummodo id nostra culpa fiat ut decipiatur proximus adhibendo fidem dictis nostris: certe nec Periurium evitatur, si nostra culpa decipiatur adhibendo fidem juramento nostro: Siquidem nihil aliud est Periurium, quam Mendacium juramento firmatum. Ita ut omnino idem fit accedente juramento Periurium, quod est in nuda pollicitatione Mendacium.
units.tr: IV. Third reason. From the nature of Truth, which is the first and chief of those three much-repeated conditions of an oath found in the prophet Jeremiah, which everyone inculcates and which the Schoolmen call the three companions of an oath: Truth, Judgment, and Righteousness. To this Truth is opposed not only what is false but also what is deceitful: not only an open and bare lie, but also a hidden one, and one disguised in whatever way. Certainly whoever speaks falsely to his neighbour pollutes his word with a lie; and he is to be thought to have spoken falsely to his neighbour through whom it came about that his neighbour was deceived in the hope which he had reasonably conceived from his words. Since, therefore, a lie is not avoided by simulation of this or that kind, provided it happens through our fault that the neighbour is deceived by giving credit to our words, surely neither is perjury avoided if, through our fault, someone is deceived by giving credit to our oath. For perjury is nothing other than a lie confirmed by an oath. So the same thing that is a lie in a bare promise becomes perjury when an oath is added.

units.la: VII. Ratio Quarta: A fine Juramenti proprio: qui, ut ex antecedictis cum explicaremus Juramenti definitionem manifestum fit, est rei dubiæ confirmatio; nempe ut habeatur, de rebus alias incertis & ex humana fide pendentibus, certitudo quantum expedit rebus humanis. Est enim Juramentum a Deo institutum vi
units.tr: VII. Fourth reason: from the proper end of an oath. As is clear from what was said before, when we explained the definition of an oath, this end is the confirmation of a doubtful matter: namely, that concerning matters otherwise uncertain and depending on human faith, there may be obtained as much certainty as is useful for human affairs. For an oath was instituted by God, by the force of natural light,

units.la: * Num. 7. luminis naturalis, in remedium defectuum humanorum circa veritatem: ut esset tuendæ veritatis ultimum inter mortales præsidium, quoties omnia alia probationum genera deficiunt. Everteretur autem omnino hic finis, nec posset ulla esse apud homines certa fides, si liberum esset juranti pro suo arbitrio, quod verbis enunciat ad fidem faciendam; id aut tacita aliqua ambiguitate inter jurandum, aut postquam juraverit exquisito aliquo novo & quasi posthumo commento ita subnervare, ut vim suam, omnem amittat, & effectu penitus careat. Horum alterum si liceret, non esset juramentum q ἀπλοῦς τὶς sed ἀρχή; & ansam novis contradictionibus & litibus præberet potius quam sedaret veteres. Hac aperta semel fenestra, quid cogitari posset tam falsum, pro quo tuendo non posset excogitari aliquod saltem effugium aut diverticulum, quo a mendacio liberaretur? Interim quanta perversitatis est, ut quod est a sapientissimo Deo in subsidium fidei institutum, id ab improbis hominibus verteretur in instrumentum fallendi. πρὸς ἀπάτην ἐκ τῆς οἰκονομίας. Profecto nisi quis sacro Dei instituto aliorsum uti maluerit, quam in eum in quem institutum est finem, (quod non facile commiserit vir pius) qui juramenti finis est, idem debet esse & jurantis: is autem est, ita audienti fidem facere, ut de rei prius dubiæ veritate certior fiat & securior. At qui simulat, falsam fidem audientibus ingenerare studet: atque ita non solum alterum falli permittit, (quod tamen est contra charitatem, cum potest & debet impedire) sed etiam fallere intendit, quod præterquam quod est contra omnem justitiam & honestatem, est etiam cum summa Dei injuria & nominis divini contemptu conjunctum. Et mihi sane vix aliud Periurii genus Tertii Decalogi præcepti aut scopo; aut ipsis etiam verbis (de non assumendo in vanum Dei nomine) magis ex diametro adversari videtur, quam quod ex ista simulatione exurgit. Vanitatis enim vox ut proprie & adæquate omne id quod quovismodo falsum est complectitur: si peculiari quodam modo & propriissime id significat, quod ita falsum est, ut tamen veri speciem aliquam præ se ferat. Adeo ut si quis Vanitatis (cum sit Ens rationis tantum nec habeat veram essentiam, per analogiam tamen quandam ad Ens reale) naturam & essentiam definiendo exprimere conaretur, non posset id commodius facere, quam si mentis imaginatione ideam quandam sibi fingat rei compositæ ex Nihilo velut Materia, & mendacio velut Forma. Nimirum Spes, quæ se alit interim Mendacio, & tandem dem frustra est, nec invenit quicquam, ea Vana spes est. Et in praesenti negotio, qui promittit aliquid quasi revera futurum, assumpto in veritatis confirmationem Dei nomine, quod tamen totum abit in nihil, aut non intento aut non praestito, quod promissum est, is directe & ad literam assumit Dei nomen in vanum, violat praeceptum Dei, & gravissimi criminis (perjurii) reus est. Atque ita sat confirmatam habetis primam Hypothesin, de Juramenti Simplicitate.
units.tr: * Num. 7. as a remedy for human defects concerning truth, so that it might be the last safeguard among mortals for defending the truth whenever all other kinds of proof fail. But this end would be wholly overturned, and no certain faith could exist among men, if it were left free to the one swearing, at his own pleasure, to weaken by some tacit ambiguity during the swearing, or after he has sworn, by some far-fetched new and as it were posthumous contrivance, what he has uttered in words to make faith, so that it loses all its power and is wholly without effect. If the former were allowed, an oath would not be a simple thing ἀπλοῦς τὶς but a principle ἀρχή, and it would furnish occasion for new contradictions and lawsuits rather than settle the old ones. Once this window is opened, what could be conceived so false that some evasion or by-way could not be devised for defending it, by which one might be freed from lying? Meanwhile, how great is the perversity that what the most wise God instituted as a support of faith should be turned by wicked men into an instrument of deceiving: πρὸς ἀπάτην ἐκ τῆς οἰκονομίας [for deceit by means of economy]. Surely, unless someone prefers to use the sacred institution of God for another purpose than that for which it was instituted (which a pious man will hardly commit), the end of the oath must also be the end of the one swearing. That end is to make faith for the hearer, so that he may become more certain and secure about the previously doubtful truth. But he who dissembles strives to produce false faith in the hearers; and thus he not only permits the other to be deceived (which is against charity, since he can and ought to prevent it), but also intends to deceive, which, besides being against all justice and honesty, is also joined with the greatest injury to God and contempt of the divine name. And to me indeed hardly any other kind of perjury seems more directly opposed either to the aim of the Third Commandment or even to its very words (about not taking the name of God in vain) than what arises from this simulation. For the word vanity properly and adequately embraces whatever is in any way false; but in a particular and most proper sense it signifies that which is so false that yet it bears some appearance of truth. So that if someone, trying to express the nature and essence of vanity (since it is a being of reason only and has no true essence, yet by a certain analogy to real being), wished to explain it by definition, he could not do so more fittingly than by forming in his mind an idea of a thing composed out of Nothing as its matter and a lie as its form. Certainly hope which feeds itself meanwhile on a lie, and at last comes to nothing and finds nothing, is vain hope. And in the present matter, whoever promises something as though it were truly going to be, taking the name of God to confirm the truth, which yet wholly passes into nothing, the thing promised being neither intended nor performed, he directly and literally takes the name of God in vain, violates the precept of God, and is guilty of the gravest crime (perjury). And so you have the first hypothesis, concerning the simplicity of an oath, sufficiently confirmed.

units.la: VIII. Secunda sequitur, huic cognata: quae ad Juramenti juitam interpretationem pertinet; estque breviter haec, Juramenti obligatio est strikti juris. Jus strictum hic intelligo, non ea significatione qua saepissime occurrit apud Jurisconsultos, pro illo rigore juris quod ἀκριβὲς vocant, & apponitur τῷ ἐπιεικεῖ sive Aequitati: quo sc. convertitur judicium in arbitrium, quodque est ita cum injuria lere conjunctum, ut pene in proverbium abiit illud, Summum jus summa injuria. Sed mitius aliquanto, pro interpretatione juris ita justa & suis cancellis circumscripta, ut non trahantur verba juris ultra quam par est in alicujus parris gratiam & favorem, sed ut cujuscunque facto vel interpretari cogantur.
units.tr: VIII. The second proposition follows from this and is closely related to it. It concerns the correct interpretation of an oath, and in brief it is this: the obligation of an oath is of strict law. By strict law I do not mean the sense in which the lawyers most often use the phrase, for that rigour of law which the Greeks call [ἀκριβές], and which is opposed to [τῷ ἐπιεικεῖ] or Equity. In that sense judgement is turned into arbitrary decision, and this is so bound up with injustice that the saying The highest law is the highest injustice has nearly become a proverb. I mean something somewhat milder: an interpretation of the law so just and so confined within its own limits that the words of the law are not stretched beyond what is fitting, for the sake of favour toward anyone, but are made to yield to the facts of each case.

units.la: Ut verbo dicam, Strictum jus hic ita accipitur, non ut excludat juris interpretationem æquitate temperatam, sed ut excludat juris interpretationem gratia corruptam. Quum autem sit Interpretari nihil aliud, quam rem cui subest aliquid aut obscuri aut ambigui, exponere : sciendum est dari posse ejusdem rei triplicem expositionem sive interpretationem : Rigidam, Favorabilem, Justam. Extremæ sunt Rigida & Favorabilis : & est utraque, ut pleræque res extremæ, in vitio. Et ut est plerunque Extremorum coincidentia quædam, sed adeo infelix dum utrinq; a Medio recessum est, ut semper conveniant in eo quod malum est, & ut plurimum in eo quod pessimum: ita rigida nimis & nimium favorabilis interpretatio Juris in eo conveniunt, quod utraq; per iniquam virn quodammodo faciat legi, torquendo eam nimium subtili expositione, in compendium unius partis, & gravamen alterius; Sed cum hoc discrimine, ut rigidiorem premat interpretationem qui agitur odio partium, favorabiliorem sectetur qui studio ducitur. Justa autem & inter utramque media interpretatio ea est, quæ citra respectum omnem ad personas, ex naturali æquitate & justitia, & ex verbis ipsis quatenus congrua sunt æquitati justitiæ, verum & genuinum sensum legis venatur. Et hæc, si possit aperte satis ex verbis constare, est in omni re simpliciter retinenda. Verum quoniam fieri potest, & sæpenumero fit, ut de Legum aliorumque quæ indigent interpretatione proprio & naturali sensu oriatur controversia: ubi justa interpretatio ob rei dubietatem haberi non potest, concedenda est ex necessitate huic mediocritati sua quædam (ut ita dicam) latitudo prudentialis. Quemadmodum Ethici negant virtutis Mediocritatem in puncto indivisibili positam esse, aut constare proportione Arithmetica, sed Geometrica. In jure ergo dubio suppleat vicem justæ interpretationis, pro rei natura de qua agitur, nunc strictior, nunc benignior Interpretatio: quarum Stricta, a favorabili remotior, vergit magis ad Rigidam; Benigna vero favorabili proprior a rigida magis declinat. Perinde atque in Moralibus, Virtus ea, quæ Avaritiam inter & Prodigalitatem media est, prout remotior est ab alterutra extremarum, aut liberalitatis nomine censetur, aut Frugalitatis. Sunt ergo res aliquæ ita natura comparatæ, ut benignam sibi interpretationem suo quodam jure concedi postulent; quæ sic non fit interclusa verborum angustiis, sed cum quodam (ut Ciceronis verbo utar) laxamento liberior : qualis habetur exempli gratia in jure nostrati Res Testamentaria. Sic ex lege charitatis aliena dicta & facta, præsertim Principum, parentum, aliorumque Rectorum; scripta item hominum priorum & eruditorum, (nili ubi justa admodum subest suspicionis causa in contrarium) lenienda sunt benigna interpretatione: juxta id quod dici solet, Dubia esse interpretanda in meliorem partem. At sunt aliæ res permultæ ut Privilegia, Contractuum ex debito Syngraphæ, & pleraque eorum quæ inducunt obligationem juris, inque his Juramentum: in quibus ubi de justo sensu ambigitur, longe ratius est & naturæ rei accommodatius, strictiore quam benigniore uti interpretatione.
units.tr: To put it in a word, strict law is taken here not to exclude an interpretation of the law tempered by equity, but to exclude an interpretation corrupted by favour. Since to interpret is nothing other than to explain a matter that has something obscure or ambiguous lying under it, we must note that the same matter can receive a threefold exposition or interpretation: the Rigid, the Favourable, and the Just. The Rigid and the Favourable are the extremes, and each of them, like most extremes, is a fault. And just as there is often a certain coincidence of extremes, yet so unhappily that, the further each departs from the mean, the more they meet in what is bad, and most of all in what is worst, so an interpretation of law that is too rigid and one that is too favourable agree in this: each in some measure does violence to the law by an unjust course, twisting it by an overly subtle exposition for the advantage of one party and the burden of the other. But with this difference: the one who acts from hatred of a party presses the more rigid interpretation, while the one who is led by zeal pursues the more favourable. The just interpretation, which lies between the two, is that which, without any regard to persons, seeks from natural equity and justice, and from the words themselves insofar as they agree with equity and justice, the true and genuine sense of the law. If this can be plainly enough established from the words, it is to be kept simply in every matter. But since it can happen, and very often does happen, that a controversy arises over the proper and natural sense of laws and other things that need interpretation, and where a just interpretation cannot be had because the matter is doubtful, some prudential latitude, as I may call it, must of necessity be allowed to this mean. Just as the moralists deny that the mean of virtue lies at an indivisible point, or that it consists in arithmetical proportion, but in geometrical. In a doubtful law, therefore, an interpretation that is now stricter, now more benign, takes the place of the just interpretation, according to the nature of the matter in question. The strict one, which is further from the favourable, tends more toward the rigid; the benign one, which is nearer the favourable, departs more from the rigid. Just as in ethics the virtue that lies between avarice and prodigality is called liberality or frugality according as it stands further from one or the other extreme. Some things, then, are by their nature such that they demand a benign interpretation by a certain right of their own; these are not confined by the narrowness of words, but are rendered more liberal with a certain (to use Cicero's word) looseness. Such is, for example, testamentary matters in our law. Likewise, the sayings and deeds of others, especially of princes, parents and other rulers, and also the writings of learned men of former times, must be softened by a benign interpretation, unless there is a very just cause for suspicion to the contrary, in line with the saying commonly repeated: doubtful matters are to be interpreted in the better sense. But there are very many other things, such as privileges, bonds of debt in contracts, and most of those things which produce an obligation in law, and among these the oath. In these, where the just sense is in doubt, it is far more common and better suited to the nature of the thing to use the stricter rather than the more benign interpretation.

units.la: IX. Cum ergo dico Juramentum esse stricti juris, id ita intelligendum est, Juramenti sententiam ubi ea ex verbis satis manifesta est, omnino tenendam esse: at ubi sententia dubia est, unicuique sedulo cavendum, ne nobis nostrisque affectibus nimium indulgeamus, aut nimis liberam laxamque interpretandi licentiam nobismetipsis concedamus, quo facilius nos vinculo juramenti quo obligati sumus eximamus; neve sensum aliquem juramento a nobis præstito aut ejus alicui parti affingamus, proprii commodi aut utilitatis causa quem non quivis vir alius pius & prudens (qui est liberioris judicii, utpote cuja nihil interest) ex ipsis verbis facile eliceret. Ratio duplex. Altera refpectu aliorum, ob metum fc. scandali: nequis alius infirmior nostro exemplo adductus quod a nobis factum videt id sibi quoque licere putet, etsi ignaro illarum subtilitatum, quibus tamen solis nofmetipfos a perjurii crimine tueri solemus. Altera respectu nostri ipsorum, ob metum fc. Perjurii: quod gravissimum crimen fine dubio in nos admittimus, fi nos forte fallat benignior illa interpretatio, quae nobis jurandi fecit audaciam. Nititur autem haec ratio generali illa & utiliffima regula, quae jubet in dubiis partem sequi tutiorem. Tutius autem est non jurare, ubi verba juramenti propositi fecundum communem & obvium sensum verborum videntur aliquid illiciti in fe continere, quam laxa interpretatione ita ea lenire in rem nostram, ut securius possimus in ea jurare: Quatenus istiusmodi juramentum fine perjurii periculo constat recusari posse; non constat fine aliquo aut periculo aut metu posse suscipi.
units.tr: IX. When I say therefore that an oath is of strict law, this must be understood as follows: where the sense of an oath is plain enough from its words, it is altogether to be kept; but where the sense is doubtful, each person must take careful heed not to indulge too much his own affections, nor to grant himself too free and loose a licence of interpreting, by which he might more easily release himself from the bond of the oath by which he is obliged; nor to attach to the oath he has sworn some sense, or to some part of it, for the sake of his own advantage or convenience, which no other good and prudent man (one who has a freer judgement, since he has no stake in the matter) would readily draw from the words themselves. The reason is twofold. The first is with respect to others, out of fear of scandal: lest some weaker person, moved by our example, seeing that we have done something, should think it is lawful for himself too, even though he is ignorant of those subtleties by which we alone are accustomed to protect ourselves from the crime of perjury. The second is with respect to ourselves, out of fear of perjury: for we undoubtedly commit a most grievous crime if that more benign interpretation, which has given us the boldness to swear, happens to deceive us. This reasoning rests on that general and most useful rule which bids us in doubtful matters follow the safer part. Now it is safer not to swear where the words of the proposed oath, according to their common and obvious sense, seem to contain something unlawful, than to soften them by a loose interpretation in our own favour, so that we may swear to them with more confidence. For while it is certain that such an oath can be refused without danger of perjury, it is not certain that it can be taken without some danger or fear.

units.la: X. Sed tamen est & ex altera parte cavendum, ne ftrifta haec de qua loquimur interpretatio abeat in rigidam. Quod enim de Privilegiis dicunt Jurisconsulti, id & in aliis universim obtinent, quae sunt ejusdem rationis, & speciatim in Juramentis: neque ea nimis strictè, neque nimis large esse interpretanda. Quum ergo dicimus Juramentum esse stricti juris, non est id ita intelligendum, quin ut in omni juramento utcunque simpliciter enunciato & sine exceptione, subintelligi tamen possint & debeant omnes illæ sive Exceptiones, sive Conditiones, quæ de jure communi subintelligi solent ad hoc ut Juramentum obliget. Quarum sunt præcipuæ, & ad quas fortasse reliquarum pleræque reduci possunt, illæ quæ sequuntur. Subintelligendum primo, Si Deus permiserit: secundum illud Jacobi, Si Dominus voluerit & vixerimus, faciemus hoc vel illud. Unde si Cajus Titio juret se ad kal. Januarias Londoni affuturum, & pecunias quas ei debet allaturum; si ad id tempus gravi morbo correptus decubuerit; aut in itinere a latronibus expoliatus nummos amiserit: in hoc casu non tenetur perjurii. Ratio est: quia cum omnia divinæ providentiæ & voluntati subsint, nec fit in cujusvis hominis potestate omnes suturos casus præstare: qui fecit quod in se fuit ut adimpleret quod promiserat, juramenti fidem exolvit. Nam cum rei impossibilis nulla sit obligatio, ut mox audietis: omne juramentum ex lege communi debet intelligi cum clausula Nisi Deo aliter visum fuerit. aut alia similia. Subintelligendum secundo, Quoad licet: quia nec rei illicitæ ulla obligatio est. Ut siquis juret indefinite observare omnia statuta & consuetudines alicujus communitatis; non obligatur ad observandum nisi ea tantum quæ sunt licita & honesta. Subintelligendum tertio, z Salva potestate superioris. Unde si filius familias juret se facturum aliquid in se licitum, pater autem rei ignarus aliud ei faciendum imperet quod impediat id fieri quod juratum est, filius non tenetur juramento: quia lege divina naturali tenetur parere imperio patris. Et qui juravit non exire domo, citatus a legitimo judice ad comparandum, non obstante juramento tenetur exire. Ratio est, quia actus unius non debet præjudicare juri alterius. Subintelligendum quarto, Rebus sic stantibus: id est, si res in eodem statu permanserint quo nunc sunt. Unde qui juravit reddere gladium, non tenetur reddere furioso. Et qui juravit ducere aliquam uxorem, non tenetur ducere si deprehendat eam esse ex alio viro gravidam. Has & itiusmodi conditiones, quarum est perspicua ratio, in omni Juramento subintelligi fas est, etsi non exprimantur: & rigidus nimis esset juramenti interpres, qui istarum aliquam exclusum iret. Sed si quis exceptiones admiserit magis dubias, & non a verbis juramenti solum sed & ab omni recta ratione alienas, nec jure communi & consensu populorum approbatas : næ is ausu temerario fines Juramenti a Deo præstitutos : loco moverit, & omni perjuriorum generi latam portam aperuerit. Maneat ergo secunda hæc nostra hypothesis, de stricta Juramenti interpretatione.
units.tr: X. Yet on the other side, care must also be taken that this strict interpretation of which we speak does not pass into the rigid. For what the lawyers say about privileges holds in general for other things of the same kind, and especially for oaths: they are not to be interpreted either too strictly or too loosely. When therefore we say that an oath is of strict law, it is not to be understood in such a way that, in every oath however simply stated and without exception, all those exceptions or conditions which by common law are customarily understood, may not and should not be understood to be implied, so that the oath binds. The chief of these, and perhaps the majority of the rest may be reduced to them, are the following. First, it must be understood: if God permits, according to that saying of James: If the Lord will, and we live, we shall do this or that. Hence if Caius swears to Titius that he will be present at London on the Kalends of January and bring the money he owes him, and if he is then stricken with a serious illness and confined to bed, or on the journey is robbed by thieves and loses his money, in this case he is not guilty of perjury. The reason is that since all things are subject to divine providence and will, and it is not in the power of any man to guarantee all the events that will occur, whoever has done what lay in him to fulfil what he promised has discharged the faith of the oath. For since there is no obligation to an impossible thing, as you will shortly hear, every oath under the common law ought to be understood with the clause unless God has otherwise willed, or others of like kind. Second, it must be understood: so far as it is lawful, because there is no obligation to an unlawful thing. Thus if anyone swears indefinitely to observe all the statutes and customs of some community, he is bound to observe only those that are lawful and honourable. Third, it must be understood: saving the authority of a superior. Hence if a son under his father's authority swears that he will do something lawful in itself, but the father, ignorant of the matter, commands him to do something else which prevents the thing sworn from being done, the son is not bound by the oath, because by the divine natural law he is bound to obey his father's command. And one who has sworn not to leave his house, if summoned by a lawful judge to appear, is bound to go out notwithstanding the oath. The reason is that the act of one person ought not to prejudice the right of another. Fourth, it must be understood: with things remaining as they are, that is, if the circumstances continue in the same state in which they now are. Hence one who has sworn to return a sword is not bound to return it to a madman; and one who has sworn to marry a certain woman is not bound to marry her if he discovers that she is pregnant by another man. These and similar conditions, whose reasoning is plain, may rightly be understood to be implied in every oath, even though they are not expressed; and he would be too rigid an interpreter of an oath who should wish to exclude any one of them. But if anyone admits exceptions that are more doubtful, and that are foreign not only to the words of the oath but to all sound reason, and not approved by common law and the consent of peoples, then by rash audacity he has moved the bounds that God has set for oaths, and has opened a wide gate to every kind of perjury. Let this, then, our second proposition stand: concerning the strict interpretation of an oath.

units.la: XI. Cujus, ut & superioris de Juramenti Simplicitate, propterea fusiorem instituti tractationem, (etsi plurima alia meditandi mihi in mentem venerint, scitu non indigna, quæ tamen brevitatis causa prætermittenda judicavi : ) tum quod rerum istarum clarior explicatio visa est mihi his dissolutissimis maxime temporibus admodum necessaria, in quibus viri passim ludunt juramentis, ut pueri astragalis ; tum quod utriusque hypothefeos permagnus erit usus, in his quæ Deo volente futuris prælectionibus a me dicenda sunt. Reliquas absolvam brevius.
units.tr: XI. Since I have treated this matter at greater length in the case of the earlier point, on the simplicity of an oath, (though many other points worth knowing have come to mind, which I have judged should be passed over for the sake of brevity), I have done so for two reasons: first, because a clearer explanation of these matters seems to me very necessary in these most dissolute times, when men everywhere trifle with oaths like boys with knucklebones; and second, because each of the two hypotheses will be of very great use in the lectures I am to deliver, God willing, hereafter. I will deal with the remaining points more briefly.

units.la: Hypothesis tertia. Juramentum non tollit obligationem priorem. Habet quidem Juramentum ex natura suam vim obligatoriam : sed constructivam tantum, non item destructivam. Hoc est, potest inducere novam obligationem ubi nulla fuit, vel etiam confirmare eam quæ præfuit : sed non potest tollere eam quam invenit, aut aliam ei repugnantem superinducere. Cujus ratio est ;
units.tr: Hypothesis the third. An oath does not cancel a prior obligation. An oath does indeed have by its nature a binding force, but only constructive, not destructive. That is, it can create a new obligation where none existed, or confirm one that was already present; but it cannot cancel an obligation it finds in place, nor superimpose another that is contrary to it. The reason for this is:

units.la: quia per omnem obligationem jus alteri accrescit; quisquis enim obligatur, alteri obligatur: & iniquissimum videtur, ut per merum actum unius laedatur jus alterius sine ipsius consensu. Neque vero interest quicquam hac in re, fuerit ne prior illa quam supponimus obligatio, Naturalis an Adquisita. Obligatio Naturalis & necessaria est, qua astringimur ad aliquod officium alteri praestandum, quod ei debemus ratione personae nostrae vi legis Naturae: ut dicitur quibusdam (ut superiore lectione monui) Obligatio Æquitatis; quia ex lege naturali, qua & aequissima est & omnis aequitatis norma, originem ducit. Talis est mutua obligatio, quae est inter virum & uxorem, inter patrem & filium, inter dominum & famulum, inter principem & subditos. Obligatio Acquisita & Voluntaria, quae & Civilis (per synecdochen specici dicitur) & Justitiae, quia justum est ut quod quis voluntate sua fecit eo teneatur; est qua astringimur ad aliquod officium alteri praestandum, quod ei debemus ex conducto, virtute alicujus voluntarii actus proprii. Talis est illa obligatio, quae ex promissis, votis, juramentis, foederibus, aliisque humanis contractibus & conventionibus oritur. Si cui ergo Juramentum suscipiendum deferatur continens aliquod quod obligationi priori, sive naturali sive adquisitae adversatur, ut
units.tr: because every obligation gives a right to another person; for whoever is bound is bound to someone else, and it seems most unjust that the right of another should be harmed by the mere act of one party without that other's consent. Nor does it matter in this respect whether the prior obligation we are supposing is natural or acquired. A natural obligation is necessary: it binds us to perform some duty towards another, which we owe him by reason of our person under the force of the law of nature. Some call it (as I noted in the previous lecture) an obligation of equity, because it arises from the natural law, which is both most equitable and the rule of all equity. Such is the mutual obligation between husband and wife, between father and son, between master and servant, between prince and subjects. An acquired and voluntary obligation, which is also called civil (by a specific term used for the general, through synecdoche) and of justice, because it is just that a person be held to what he has done by his own will, is that by which we are bound to perform some duty towards another, which we owe him by contract, by virtue of some voluntary act of our own. Such is that obligation which arises from promises, vows, oaths, covenants, and other human contracts and agreements. If therefore an oath is offered to someone to be taken which contains something opposed to a prior obligation, whether natural or acquired, as follows

units.la: Prælectio Secunda.
units.tr: Prælectio Secunda.

units.la: ut si adversetur officio quod parenti debetur aut principi;vel si repugnet ei quod ante licite juratum fuit, vel promissum, ejusmodi juramentum non potest a quoquam salva conscientia vel præstari,vel præstitum adimpleri.Qui utrumvis fecerit,pejeraverit.
units.tr: as when it is opposed to the duty owed to a parent or to a prince, or when it conflicts with something previously and lawfully sworn or promised. An oath of this kind cannot be either taken or, once taken, fulfilled by anyone without violating conscience. Whoever does either of these has committed perjury.

units.la: XII. Sequitur Hypothesis quarta, quæ est ita ex se evidens,ut sit Regula juris,nec probatione indigeat. b Rei impossibilis nulla est Obligatio.Extenditur autem ad omne genus impossibilitatis, quæ in materia Juramenti potest contingere. Contingit autem rem aliquam esse impossibilem;aut per se, aut ex accidente.Per se autem tripliciter. Primo c impossibilitate Naturæ: quomodo impossibile est hominem volare, piscem loqui. Secundo, impossibilitate Facti: quomodo impossibile est Caium hodie Londini commorantem cras convenire Titium Venetiis. Tertio, d impossibilitate Juris, quomodo illud dicitur impossibile alicui, ad quod non habet potestatem legitimam; de quo etiam illud intelligendum est, quod dici solet, Id tantum possumus, quod jure possumus. Sic impossibile est Prætorem istius Urbis conferre alicui gradum Doctoratus. Si quis aliquod in aliquo istorum trium generum impossibile se facturum juraret; vanum esset juramentum, & ab initio nullum; & per consequens non cum omnino obligaret, non modo ad faciendum quod juravit, sed ne ad conandum quidem. Sed Rei Impossibilis ex accidente tantum, aliquantum diversa est ratio. Ut si quis juratus solvere centum infra mensem, quod non est per se impossibile, casu aliquo inopino interim impeditur, ut non posit tantam pecuniae summam tempore praefinito conficere; etsi non obligetur in foro Conscientiae ad faciendum id quod promisit, &c. ad solvendum totum debitum debito tempore, quod jam redditum est ei impossibile; obligatur tamen ad faciendum quod in se est, viz. ad solvendum quantum potest, & quam cito potest. Ratio utriusque est, quia cum in hoc casu sola impossibilitas impediat obligationem; obligatio tollitur quoad id solum quod est factu impossibile; quoad reliquum vero manet. Et qui non potest omne quod debet, debet tamen omne quod potest.
units.tr: XII. There follows Hypothesis quarta, which is so self-evident that it is a Rule of law and needs no proof: There is no obligation to an impossible thing. It extends to every kind of impossibility that can arise in the matter of an oath. A thing may be impossible either in itself or by accident. In itself it is impossible in three ways. First, by impossibility of nature, as it is impossible for a man to fly or a fish to speak. Second, by impossibility of fact, as it is impossible for Caius, who is staying in London today, to meet Titius in Venice tomorrow. Third, by impossibility of law: a thing is said to be impossible for someone when he has no lawful power over it. This is also what is meant by the common saying, We can only do what we have the right to do. Thus it is impossible for the praetor of this city to confer the degree of Doctor on anyone. If someone swore that he would do something that is impossible in any of these three ways, the oath would be empty and void from the beginning, and consequently it would not bind him at all, not even to attempt the thing, let alone to do it. But the reasoning is somewhat different for a thing that is impossible only by accident. Suppose someone has sworn to pay one hundred within a month, which is not impossible in itself, but by some unforeseen chance he is prevented in the meantime from raising so large a sum within the set time. Then, although in the forum of conscience he is not obliged to do what he promised, that is, to pay the whole debt on time, since this has now become impossible for him, he is still obliged to do what lies in his power, namely to pay as much as he can and as soon as he can. The reason for both is this: where in such a case only the impossibility removes the obligation, the obligation is cancelled only with regard to what has become impossible, and remains with regard to the rest. And he who cannot pay all that he owes nevertheless owes all that he can pay.

units.la: XIII. Hypothesis Quinta. Rei illicitae nulla est Obligatio.
units.tr: XIII. Hypothesis Fifth. There is no obligation to an unlawful thing.

units.la: Est autem Illicitum, quicquid est contra aliquod Dei praeceptum in decalogo, aut contra bonos mores; quicquid repugnat pietati erga Deum, aut charitati erga proximum; quicquid bono publico adversatur, aut paci Ecclesiasticae, Politicae, Domesticae: ut semel dicam, quicquid in se continet aliquam rationem peccati. Huc illa pertinent vulgatissima, Juramenta non est
units.tr: By unlawful I mean whatever is against any precept of God in the Decalogue, or against good morals; whatever is contrary to piety toward God or charity toward one's neighbour; whatever opposes the public good or the peace of the Church, the state, or the household. To put it in a word, whatever contains in itself some reason for sin. To this belong the very common maxims, Oaths are not to be kept,

units.la: {g} Vide Canonas 22. q. 4. st vinculum iniquitatis. In malis promissis rescinde fidem, &c. Ratio est: quia omne illicitum est contra officium. Obligatio autem omnis est ad officium. Præterea, quicquid est illicitum, est aliquo modo a Deo prohibitum, (aut immediate, aut per consequentiam;) prohibitio autem Dei obligat ad non faciendum id quod prohibitum est, quam obligationem ex tertia hypothesi subsequens Juramentum tollere non potest. Imo qui juravit facere id quod sine peccato fieri nequit, tantum abest ut obligetur ad id faciendum, ut potius obligetur omnino ad non faciendum. At juratum non adimplere perjurium est, inquies. Imo vero si res sit illicita in quam juratum est, tunc pejerasti cum jurasti, non pejeras, cum contra facis. Et rem illicitam ideo adimplere quia juravisti, nihil aliud est, quam perjurio flagitium adjicere velut Pelion Offæ & siti ebrietatem; quam juramenti vice perjurii potius mensuram implere; quam in perjurio obdurate & sine pœnitentia perseverare.
units.tr: {g} See Canons, 22 q. 4: there is no bond of iniquity; and In wicked promises break faith, and so on. The reason is that everything unlawful is contrary to duty, while every obligation is to duty. Moreover, whatever is unlawful is in some way forbidden by God, either directly or by consequence; and the prohibition of God obliges us not to do what is forbidden. A subsequent oath cannot remove this obligation, which we have from the third hypothesis. Indeed, one who has sworn to do what cannot be done without sin is so far from being obliged to do it that he is rather obliged altogether not to do it. "But not to fulfil what one has sworn is perjury," you will object. On the contrary: if the thing sworn to is unlawful, then you committed perjury when you swore, and you do not commit perjury when you act against the oath. To carry out an unlawful thing merely because you have sworn to it is nothing other than to add a crime to perjury, like Pelion on Ossa, and drunkenness on thirst; it is to fill up the measure of perjury, as it were, rather than to persist obstinately and without repentance in the perjury.

units.la: XIV. Est tamen advertendum circa hanc hypothefin; multum distare quæstionem hanc An hoc vel illud Juramentum sit licitum? ab ista, An hoc vel illud juramentum obliget? Etsi enim certum est, quod constat præstari non debere: re jurari quidem debere, potest tamen fieri, & fit sæpissime, ut quod jurari non debuit debet tamen præstari. Exemplum clarissimum, fœdus a Iosue cum Gabaonitis pactum. Discriminis autem ratio hæc est. Ubi Juramentum ideo est illicitum, quia id in quod juratur est res illicita; ibi utrobique peccatur, & jurando & adimplendo: ut si quis juraret occidere innocentem, & idipsum taceret, & perjurii reus esset, & homicidii. Et revera tale juramentum nullatenus obligat: quæ ultimæ istius hypothesis ipsissima mens est. Verum ubi juramentum de re non illicita fit aliunde illicitum, ex aliquo externo defectu, & propter aliquam indebitam circumstantiam: obligare potest jurantem ad implendum quod promisit, nisi appareat aliud impedimentum. In quo casu locum habet quod vulgo dicitur, Fieri non debet, factum valet. Possumus ergo distinguere, Juramentum dici posse illicitum duobus modis; vel respectu rei juratæ, vel respectu actus jurandi. Juramentum illicitum respectu rei juratæ nullatenus obligat: juramentum illicitum respectu actus jurandi obligat, nisi aliunde impediatur. Sed de his hactenus. Icтæ sunt illæ ὑποθέσεις sive hypotheses quas præponendas duxi insecuturæ tractationi: quibus velut pedamentis & tibicinibus suffulciantur quæ posthac de juramenti vinculo, & ejus vinculi solutione dicturus sum. Quæ quamvis sit materia valde diffusa. fusa : ex his tamen duabus præmissis partibus confido tertiæ parti tantum & luminis & roboris accessurum, ut non desperem posse hoc Termino universam de re propositā dissertationem absolvi. Conabor certe (si Deus permiserit) omnem illam Cesium varietatem ita compingere & in arctum cogere, ut Quinq; Prælectionibus, (quatuor sc. de Vinculo juxta totidem Causarum genera, & quinta de ejus vinculi Solutione) totam quæ superest partem, si potero, complectar.
units.tr: XIV. Yet in this hypothesis it must be noted that the question Whether this or that oath is lawful? is very different from the question Whether this or that oath binds? For although it is certain that what is unlawful must not be done, it is still possible, and very often happens, that what ought not to have been sworn must nevertheless be performed. The clearest example is the covenant made by Joshua with the Gibeonites. The reason for the distinction is this. Where an oath is unlawful because the thing sworn to is itself unlawful, there sin is committed both in swearing and in performing, as when someone swears to kill an innocent man and then does it: he is guilty of perjury and of murder. Such an oath truly binds in no way at all, and this is the very meaning of the last part of this hypothesis. But where an oath concerning a thing that is not unlawful becomes unlawful from some external defect, or on account of some improper circumstance, it can bind the one swearing to fulfil what he promised, unless some other impediment appears. In that case the common saying applies: What ought not to be done, once done, holds good. We can therefore distinguish: an oath can be called unlawful in two ways, either with respect to the thing sworn or with respect to the act of swearing. An oath unlawful with respect to the thing sworn does not bind at all; an oath unlawful with respect to the act of swearing does bind, unless it is otherwise hindered. But so much for these matters. These are the hypotheses [ὑποθέσεις] which I thought should be set forth before the following treatment, so that what I am going to say hereafter about the bond of an oath and its release may rest upon them as on props and buttresses. Although this is a very wide-ranging subject, I trust that from these two preliminary parts the third part will gain enough light and strength that I do not despair of being able to complete the whole dissertation on this matter within this compass. I shall certainly try, God permitting, to gather that whole chaotic variety into order and confine it within a small space, so that in five lectures (four on the bond according to as many kinds of causes, and a fifth on the release of that bond) I may, if I am able, embrace the whole of the remaining part.
