units.tr: SECT. I.

units.la: IMmensum jam tandem pelagus ingredior: de dubiis Conscientiæ casibus, quod ad Juramenti vinculum attinet, idque quoad quatuor Casuarum genera, prout policitus sum disturus. Sed antequam e portu solvam, illud vos adhuc præmoneo, non me fore de Methodo communi quæ sunt dicenda nimis sollicitum. Est quidem Ordinis in omni genere studii & tractationis plurimus & necessarius usus: quo sine, poterit fortasse quis vasta & assidua lectione comparare sibi variæ eruditionis molem; sed eam confusam & indigestam, nec multum utilem. Aut illam ex altera parte ἀκριβολογίαν & nimiam Methodi accurationem, (quam video nonnullos nimis anxie sectari,) ut molestam quandam superstitionem, & non levem studiorum remoram, vitandam semper judicavi. Mihi sat erit, omnia dicenda ad certas classes ita revocare, ut aliqua saltem cognationis vel analogiæ ratio appareat cur id factum sit: parum sollicito, nequis excipiat Juramenti sensum & interpretationem ad Formalem, aut effectum aliquem ad Finalem Causam non satis concinne reduci. Cum autem, ubi omnes causæ concurrunt ad effectum producendum, Materia imprimis requiratur, ut primum Subjectum generationis; proxime Efficiens causa, quæ agendo formam producat; tertio Forma, quæ in materiam per actionem efficientis introducatur; Finis denique cujus gratia efficiens operatur: nos hunc quasi naturæ ordinem sequuti, a Materia ordinemur; hinc ad reliquas suo ordine progredimur.
units.tr: Now at last I enter an immense sea: concerning doubtful cases of conscience, so far as the bond of an oath is concerned, and that with respect to the four kinds of cases, as I promised to discuss. But before I cast off from harbour, let me give you this warning: I shall not be overly anxious about the common method in what is to be said. There is indeed a very great and necessary use of order in every kind of study and treatment; without it, someone may perhaps, by vast and constant reading, gather a heap of varied learning, but one that is confused and undigested, and not very useful. On the other hand, I have always judged that excessive precision [ἀκριβολογίαν] and an overly exact method (which I see some pursuing too anxiously) should be avoided as a troublesome superstition and no small hindrance to study. It will be enough for me to reduce everything to be said into certain classes, in such a way that at least some ground of kinship or analogy appears for why this was done. I shall care little lest anyone object that the sense and interpretation of an oath are not neatly reduced to the Formal cause, or that some effect is not fitted neatly to the Final Cause. But since, where all causes concur to produce an effect, Matter is required first, as the first subject of generation; next the Efficient cause, which by acting produces the form; third the Form, which is introduced into the matter by the action of the efficient; and lastly the End for whose sake the efficient works: we, following this order, as it were, of nature, will take our order from the Matter, and from there proceed to the rest in their turn.

units.la: II. Materiam Juramenti intelligo rem illam circa quam versatur, & in cujus confirmationem adhibetur Juramentum: sive ea res spectetur ut Juranda, sive ut Jurata. Ad rem Jurandam pertinet illa quæstio, Liceatne hoc vel illo modo jurare? ad rem Juratam ista, Posito quod juratum sit, juramentum illud sive licitum sive illicitum, An & quatenus obligat in conscientia? cum ex facto etiam illicito possit oriri obligatio. Et est hæc quæstio sola instituti nostri propria: Exponam tamen plerumque obiter & ut ut τὴ παρὰ saltem ubi eadem fidelia utrumque parietem dealbari posse arbitrabor, quid de illa etiam quæstione sentiam: maxime cum id & a quibusdam expectari, & plerisque vestrum gratum fore, ab amicis admonitus nuper intellexerim. Est ergo Juramenti Materia, ut tandem rem ipsam aggrediar, aut Definita aut Indefinita. Quæ certa & definita est, considerari potest, vel quoad suum Esse Naturale sive ratione Existentiæ; utrum scilicet res facta possibilis sit an impossibilis: vel quoad esse Morale sive ratione Qualitatis; utrum scilicet res sit facta Necessaria, Illicita, an Licita?
units.tr: II. By the matter of an oath I understand the thing about which it is concerned, and in confirmation of which the oath is employed, whether that thing is regarded as to be sworn or as sworn. To the thing to be sworn belongs the question, Is it lawful to swear in this or that way? To the thing sworn belongs this: granted that something has been sworn, is that oath, whether lawful or unlawful, binding in conscience, and if so how far? For an obligation may arise even from an unlawful deed. This question alone is proper to our present undertaking. Yet I shall for the most part set out the other question too, in passing, and at least where I think both walls can be whitewashed with the same brush, what I think about that question as well: especially since I have recently learned, admonished by friends, that some expect this and that it will be welcome to most of you. So the matter of an oath, to come at last to the thing itself, is either defined or indefinite. A matter that is certain and defined can be considered either as to its natural being, that is with respect to existence, namely whether the thing is possible or impossible to do; or as to its moral being, that is with respect to quality, namely whether the thing is necessary, unlawful, or lawful to do.

units.la: III. Primum ergo Dubium est, qualis sit obligatio juramenti de re impossibili: Hoc est: Siquis juraverit id se facturum quod adimplere non poterit, an & quatenus obligetur? Ubi tres potissimum occurrunt Casus. Primus, ubi res juranda fuit ab initio & in ipso tempore jurandi palam & simpliciter impossibilis, sive impossibilitate Naturæ: cum res ipsa in se & nude considerata, citra respectum ad circumstantias, implicat apertam contradictionem, aut repugnat naturæ alicujus speciei entium; ut si quis promitteret se allinum docturum literas. Sive impossibilitate facti: cum res est in potentia (ut loquuntur) remota ad fieri, hoc est cum nulla est repugnantia ex parte naturæ rei ipsius quin ut possit fieri, tamen propter defectum in aliqua circumstantia, ut (verbi gratia) ob nimiam loci distantiam, aut præ angustia temporis, aut a quavis alia causa, illa potentia ita impeditur ut non possit exire in actum: ut si Caius hodie Oxonii existens promitteret se cras cum Titio una cænatum in Parisiis. Sive denique impossibilitate Juris: cum quis aliquid se recipit facturum quod ei a jure prohibitum, & ad quod non habet legitimam potestatem; ut si Caius non hæres promitteret de Titii defuncti bonis daturum se Julio trientem.
units.tr: III. The first doubt, therefore, is what kind of obligation an oath about an impossible thing creates; that is, if someone has sworn that he will do what he cannot accomplish, is he bound, and how far? Three main cases arise here. The first is where the thing sworn was from the beginning, and at the very time of swearing, plainly and simply impossible, by impossibility of nature: when the thing itself, considered bare and in itself, apart from circumstances, involves a plain contradiction or conflicts with the nature of some kind of being; as if someone promised that he would teach an ass letters. Or by impossibility of fact: when the thing is in potency (as they say) remote from becoming, that is, when there is no repugnance on the part of the nature of the thing itself why it could not come about, yet through a defect in some circumstance, as for example because of the great distance of a place, or the shortness of time, or any other cause, that potency is so hindered that it cannot pass into act; as if Gaius, existing today at Oxford, promised that tomorrow he would dine with Titius in Paris. Or finally by impossibility of law: when someone undertakes to do something that is forbidden him by law, and for which he has no lawful power; as if Gaius, who is not an heir, promised that he would give Julius a third of the goods of the dead Titius.

units.la: Pro responsione ad Dubium in hoc primo Casu, dico breviter; Juramentum de re simpliciter impossibili, nec licitum esse, nec obligare. Non est licitum, quia & judicio destituitur, & veritate. Quis enim homo, aut sani judicii sperare, aut bonæ fidei intendere posset id facere, quod ipse sciret fieri non posse? Nec etiam obligat, non modo ad faciendum, sed ne ad conandum quidem. Rei enim impossibilis, in quantum impossibilis, nullam esse obligationem, ante dictum est: Et itultum est conari, quod nequeas efficere.
units.tr: For the answer to the doubt in this first case I say briefly: an oath about a thing simply impossible is neither lawful nor binding. It is not lawful, because it lacks both sound judgment and truth. For what man of sound judgment could hope, or what man of good faith could intend, to do what he himself knows cannot be done? Nor does it bind, not only to doing it, but not even to attempting it. For it has been said before that there is no obligation to a thing insofar as it is impossible; and it is foolish to attempt what you cannot accomplish.

units.la: IV. Casus secundus est, Cum res in se non impossibilis, sed tamen ipso tempore juramenti præstiti ita improbabilis visa, ut eam multo verisimilius esset non posse quam posse postea præstari, ex aliquo objecto impedimento evadit tandem impossibilis. Ubi enim ad efficiendum ali.
units.tr: IV. The second case is when a thing not impossible in itself, yet at the very time of the oath appeared so improbable that it was far more likely it could not be done than that it could be performed afterwards, becomes at last impossible through some obstacle that arises. For where, to bring about some end,

units.la: Casus 2. aliquod intentum ita necessario requiritur complurium rerum concursus, ut si ex multis unum defuerit, reliquas necesse sit frustra esse universas; veluti si subtraheretur horologiæ machinæ rotula aut clavicula quantumvis exigua, inutilis esset reliqua compages: fieri vix potest quin ut inanis futura sit omnis in eam rem opera collocata. Ut si Caius Titium hominem novum & obscurum sua opera futuris Comitiis consulem creandum reciperet, adversus competitores natalibus, gloria, virtute authoritate totius urbis præstantissimos. Respondeo, tale juramentum non esse licitum, nisi difertim additur istiusmodi clausula, Si potero, Quantum in me est, aut alia similis. Si dicas, non opus esse addi clausulam, quæ de lege communi subintelligi debet. Respondeo, subintelligi licere ejusmodi clausulas ex interpretatione juris, ubi præsumitur jurans non potuisse prævidere aliquid quod impediret adimpletionem promissi: verum ubi id præsumi non potest, sed contrarium magis, nempe cum ignorare non potuisse multa contingere posse quæ impedirent, non concedi de lege communi tam benignam interpretationem. Obligat tamen hoc genus juramenti: non ad effectum quem supponimus esse impossibilem; sed ad conatum, quamdiu superat spes ulla, quantumvis debilis, rem fieri posse. Imo, quo plures & majores objiciuntur difficultates, eo obnixius conandum, & fortioribus animis obnitendum. At postquam palam desperata est, & constat fieri non posse; cessat obligatio: ex jam dicto fundamento, quod nemo teneatur ad impossibile.
units.tr: Case 2. some end requires such a concurrence of several things that if one of many is missing, the rest must necessarily be wholly in vain; as if the smallest little wheel or pin of a clockwork machine were removed, the remaining structure would be useless: it can hardly happen but that all labour spent on that matter will be made void. As if Gaius were to undertake that, by his efforts, he would have Titius, a new and obscure man, created consul at the coming elections, against competitors most outstanding in birth, glory, virtue and the authority of the whole city. I answer that such an oath is not lawful unless a clause is expressly added, If I can, As far as is in me, or some other similar one. If you say that there is no need to add a clause, since it ought to be understood from common law: I answer that such clauses may be understood by interpretation of law, where it is presumed that the swearer could not foresee anything that would hinder the fulfilment of the promise; but where this cannot be presumed, but rather the contrary, namely that he could not have failed to know that many things could happen that would hinder it, so kind an interpretation is not granted by common law. Yet this kind of oath binds: not to the result, which we suppose to be impossible, but to the attempt, as long as any hope, however weak, remains that the thing can be done. Indeed, the more and greater the difficulties that are raised, the more earnestly one must strive, and resist with the stronger spirit. But once it is openly despaired of, and it is clear that it cannot be done, the obligation ceases, from the foundation already stated: that no one is bound to the impossible.

units.la: V. Casus tertius est, Cum jurans ex animi sententia, rem probabilem ratus, & bona fide intendens facere, nec dubitat (Deo volente) quin possit efficere, quod promisit; postea tamen emergente aliquo inspérato casu, qui nullis rationibus humanis aut prævideri potuit aut præcaveri, sentit tandem rem factam esse impossibilem. Ut si Callias Thebis habitans, juratus solvere Socrati Athenis quinque talenta die condicto, pecunias diligenter comparatas, furto, rapina, aut aliquo dolo malo amiserit, aut in vita captivus alio abducatur, ita ut æs alienum debito tempore dissolvere non poterit. Tale juramentum est licitum: etiamsi non addatur illa clausula; Si potero, &c. quæ tamen ex communi juris interpretatione intelligi censenda est. Qua ex parte, discriminis inter hunc Casum & cum qui præcessit, hæc mihi videtur idonea ratio. Cum juramenti finis sit, ut fiat ei cui juratur promissi fides: expedit, ut id omne inter jurandum diserte exprimatur, quod videtur conducere ad hoc, ut firmior sit apud alterum fides nostra; illud vero e contra reticeatur, quod fidem nostram reddere posset suspectiorem. In re itaque parum probabili juranti non facile crederetur, ut hominí praecipiti, temerario, & nimium praesidenti, si nulla adjecta exceptione, aut difficultatis significatione, rem plenam alicae simpliciter fe facturum sponderet. E contra, addita exceptio, ubi nullus appareret periculi metus, suspectum redderet jurantem, quasi nihil aliud tam importuna diligentia quaereretur, quam fidei violandae φανταστικ quaedam & σαφηνισμ. Obligat autem jurantem hoc juramenti genus ad faciendum quantum poterit, siquidem non poterit totum: &, si grave damnum alteri ex non praestito juramento acciderit, ad sariendum illud aliqua saltem ex parte aliquo alio beneficio pro oblata sibi opportunitate, praesertim si impedimentum illud aliqua sua negligentia, imprudentia, aliave lata culpa contigerit. Et haec de Dubio primo.
units.tr: V. The third case is when someone swears from his honest conviction, thinking the thing probable and intending in good faith to do it, and trusting (God willing) that he can bring about what he promised. Afterwards, however, some unforeseen event arises which no human foresight could anticipate or guard against, and he at last finds the thing has become impossible. For example, suppose Callias, living at Thebes, swore to pay Socrates five talents at Athens on the agreed day, and had carefully gathered the money, but lost it through theft, robbery or some other wrongful act, or was taken captive and carried off elsewhere, so that he cannot pay the debt when it is due. Such an oath is lawful, even if the clause If I am able, and so on, is not added, since by the common interpretation of law that clause is to be understood. On this point I think the following is a sound reason for distinguishing this case from the one that came before. The purpose of an oath is that the person to whom it is sworn may have the assurance of a promise. So it is advantageous that everything which seems to make our faith more firm in the other's eyes should be stated plainly when we swear, while whatever might make our faith more suspect should be passed over. Thus, in a matter that is hardly probable, a rash and reckless man who is overconfident would not easily be believed if he swore simply, with no exception added and no mention of difficulty, that he would certainly do the whole thing. On the other hand, where no danger is apparent, an added exception would make the swearer suspect, as if such troublesome caution were aimed at nothing but the evasion of faith through certain fanciful [φανταστικά] and superfluous clarifications [σαφηνισμοί]. This kind of oath obliges the swearer, however, to do as much as he is able, since he cannot do all of it. And if great harm befalls another from the oath not being kept, he is obliged to make amends, at least in part, by some other benefit, using whatever opportunity is offered to him, especially if that hindrance came about through some negligence, imprudence or other gross fault of his own. And so much for the first doubt.

units.la: VI. Secundum sequitur, de juramento rei Necessariae.
units.tr: VI. Next follows the second, concerning an oath about a necessary thing.

units.la: Rem necessariam intelligo, quae nobis ex officio incumbit vi praecepti divini etiam citra juramentum; ita ut si eam debitis loco & tempore etiam injurati non faceremus, omnino peccaremus: ut alere pa-
units.tr: By a necessary thing I mean one which lies upon us as a duty by virtue of a divine precept, even apart from any oath; so that if we did not do it at the proper place and time, even without having sworn, we would certainly sin: such as feeding our

units.la: * Videtur excusari esse a faciendo quod juravit, licet teneatur facere quod in se est. Aquin. 2.2.qu.89 art.7. parentes egenos,depositum reddere & similia. Quo pertinent illa Juramenta, quæ a subditis exigi solent de fidelitate Regi servanda, & de suprematu regio agnoscendo tuendoque, quæque conceptis verbis ab iis præstantur, qui ad Magistratum aut munus aliquod publicum admittuntur, ut quæ sui sunt muneris fideliter faciant. De obligatione hoc genus Juramentorum nulla potest esse controversia. Ad quæ enim præstanda vel injurati tenemur, jurari cer-te b multo tenemur magis : accedente sci quæ præscripto expræcepto, nova obligatione ex jure jurando. Non ergo isti Dubio ulterius immorabimur.
units.tr: * It seems one may be excused from doing what he has sworn, though he is bound to do what lies in his power. Aquinas, 2.2, qu. 89, art. 7. needy parents, returning a deposit and the like. To this belong those oaths which subjects are customarily required to take, to keep fidelity to the king and to acknowledge and defend the royal supremacy, and which are made in set words by those who are admitted to a magistracy or some public office, that they will faithfully perform what belongs to their office. There can be no controversy about the obligation of this kind of oath. For whatever we are bound to do even without an oath, we are certainly bound to do much more when we have sworn, since a new obligation arises from the oath added to the prescribed command. Therefore we will not linger any longer on this doubt.

units.la: VII. Dubitum Tertium, de Juramento rei Illicitæ : Rem illicitam dico, quæ sine peccato fieri non potest, in quantum obviat (ut loquuntur) alicui præcepto divino: quam sit peccatum omne & legi Dei adversetur. Est autem hoc genus Juramenti adeo illicitum, ut non solum is peccet qui sic jurat, sed & is quoque qui alium ad sic jurandum authoritate, consilio, aut alio quocunque modo impellit inducitve. Sed de impellente fortasis alias. Peccat interim qui sic jurat, sive intendat facere quod juravit, sive non intendat. Si intendat; peccat volendo rem illicitam, & sic non jurat in Justitia : Si non intendat,peccat menmentiendo, & sic non jurat in veritate. Sed sive intendat, sive non; certum est nullatenus obligari. Fit quidem saepissime (qui est apud homines divinae majestatis contemptus) ut aut irae impatientia, aut metu periculi, aut spe commodi, aut amicorum impulsu, aut verecundia quadam & obsequio, aut alia quavis causa inducti plurimi (dum affectibus suis nimium indulgent) ea se facturos Deo adhibito telte confirmant; quae ipsi aut jam tum certo sciunt esse illicita, aut saltem postea cum sunt a pravis affectibus liberiores facile intelligunt, non posse a se sine peccato praestari. Et tamen, quae est humani judicii perversitas, peritissimi istiusmodi technarum artificis Satanae offuciis & praestigiis effascinati; plurimos videas quos nulla officii conscientia ad recte agendum compuleris, juramenti tamen religione ad prava agendum ita constrictos teneri, ut quod malo consilio juratum est ad idipsum adimplendum pessimo errore se putent ex juramenti vinculo obligatos.
units.tr: VII. The third doubt concerns an oath about an unlawful thing. By an unlawful thing I mean what cannot be done without sin, insofar as it runs counter (as they say) to some divine precept; for all sin is opposed to the law of God. Now this kind of oath is so unlawful that not only does the one who swears in this way sin, but so too does the one who by authority, counsel or any other means urges or induces another to swear so. But I will perhaps speak of the one who urges it elsewhere. Meanwhile, the one who swears in this way sins, whether he intends to do what he swore or does not intend it. If he intends it, he sins by willing an unlawful thing, and so he does not swear in justice. If he does not intend it, he sins by lying, and so he does not swear in truth. But whether he intends it or not, it is certain that he is in no way bound. Indeed it happens very often (which is a contempt of the divine majesty among men) that many people, indulging their passions too freely, are led by impatience of anger, or fear of danger, or hope of gain, or the urging of friends, or a certain shame and deference, or some other cause, to confirm with God as witness that they will do things which they either already know for certain to be unlawful, or at least afterwards, once they are freed from wicked passions, readily understand cannot be performed by them without sin. And yet, such is the perversity of human judgment, that you may see very many people, whom no sense of duty would move to act rightly, bound by the bond of an oath to act wickedly, and beguiled by the deceptions and illusions of Satan, the most skilled artificer of such tricks, who believe themselves bound by the chain of their oath, through a dreadful error, to fulfil what was sworn with a bad purpose.

units.la: {d} Et juravit illicite, & perseveravit injuste. Verum tamen non voluntate, sed verecundia. Nam probro ducitur apud Franci-genas juramentum solvere, quamlibet male publice juratum sit. Eccl. cp. 21. Atqui dictum est jam ante in quinta noltra hypothesi, & apertis rationibus confirmatum; nec rei illicitæ quatenus illicita est ullam esse obligationem, nec rem malam ullam vim accipere a Juramento.
units.tr: {d} And he swore unlawfully and persisted unjustly. Yet not by will, but by shame. For among the Franks it is counted a disgrace to break an oath, however wickedly it was sworn in public. Eccl. ch. 21. But it has already been said before in our fifth hypothesis, and confirmed by clear reasons, that there is no obligation to an unlawful thing insofar as it is unlawful, and that an evil thing receives no force from an oath.

units.la: VIII. Quod ut rectius intelligatur, & accommodatius ad Casus particulares, cum non sint omnes res illicitæ ejusdem generis & gradus: distinctius mihi paulo hac in re agendum esse sentio. Quicquid ergo illicitum est, aut ex se illicitum est, aut ex accidente: Ex le rursus dupliciter; Primario & Secundario. Illud dicitur illicitum ex se primario, & ut ita dicam in summo gradu, quod est ita illicitum ex natura ipsius rei, ut sit universo humano generi a Deo prohibitum. Sic illicitum est, quicquid est contra sacram Dei legem duabus Decalogi tabulis comprehensam: quicquid aut pietati in cultu dei, aut charitati fraternæ in operibus justitiæ & misericordiæ adversatur.
units.tr: VIII. So that this may be understood more correctly, and more suitably for particular cases, since not all unlawful things are of the same kind and degree, I think I must treat this matter a little more distinctly. Whatever is unlawful is either unlawful in itself or by accident. The former again in two ways: primarily and secondarily. That is called unlawful in itself primarily, and, so to speak, in the highest degree, which is so unlawful by the very nature of the thing that it is forbidden by God to the whole human race. Thus whatever is against the holy law of God, comprised in the two tables of the Decalogue, is unlawful: whatever opposes either piety in the worship of God or brotherly love in the works of justice and mercy.

units.la: Et de re hoc primo modo illicita, fit primus Casus. Ut si quis juraret se sacrificaturum Idolis, aut B. Virginis imaginem adoraturum; quæ sunt peccata Admissionis: vel si juraret nunquam se divinis officiis interfuturum, aut sacras conciones auditurum, aut Cœnæ dominicæ participaturum, aut sanctificaturum Diem dominicum; quæ sunt peccata Omissionis adversus præcepta Primæ Tabulæ. Aut si quis juraret occidere patrem, natum infantem exponere, adulteram dictis loco & hora convenire, aut cum aliis conjuraret in societatem furti, latrocinii, fraudis, aut alterius cujuslibet criminis; quæ sunt peccata Admissionis: vel si juraret patrem senem & egenum non alere, pauperibus eleemosynam non erogare, depositum non reddere, &c, quæ sunt peccata Omissionis adversus præcepta Secundæ Tabulæ. In iis & istiusmodi rebus simpliciter & universim illicitis, ex omnium consensu etiam simpliciter & universim obtinet Hypothesis antedicta, nullam esse posse ex Voto, Promisso, Juramento vel aliunde Obligationem. d Pacta quæ turpem causam continent, non sunt observanda: inquiunt Jesu Christi. Imo etsi graviter peccatum fuerit vovendi, pacisci endo, jurando, aliave promittendo rem in genere illicitam: multo tamen gravius peccatur e adimplendo promissum. Quod qui facit, duplicis peccati se reum constituit: unius, ejus speciei cujus est factum in se consideratum, puta homicidii aut furti; alterius, violatæ religionis ex irreverentia &
units.tr: The first case arises from a thing unlawful in this first way. For example, if someone swore that he would sacrifice to idols or worship the image of the Blessed Virgin, these are sins of commission; or if he swore that he would never attend the divine services, or hear sacred sermons, or take part in the Lord's Supper, or sanctify the Lord's Day, these are sins of omission against the precepts of the First Table. Or if someone swore that he would kill his father, expose a newborn infant, meet an adulteress at an appointed place and hour, or conspire with others in a partnership of theft, robbery, fraud, or any other crime, these are sins of commission; or if he swore that he would not support his aged and needy father, not give alms to the poor, not return a deposit, and so on, these are sins of omission against the precepts of the Second Table. In such matters and things of this kind, which are simply and universally unlawful, by the agreement of all, the aforesaid hypothesis holds good, in the simple and universal sense, that no obligation can arise from a vow, a promise, an oath, or any other source. Pacts which contain a shameful cause are not to be kept, say the words of Jesus Christ. Indeed, even if it is a grave sin to vow, bargain, swear, or promise in any way a thing that is unlawful in general, it is a far graver sin to carry out the promise. Whoever does so makes himself guilty of a double sin: one of the kind to which the deed itself belongs when considered in itself, such as murder or theft; the other, of violated religion, through irreverence and

units.la: d Si unus. tf de pactis.
units.tr: d Si unus. ff. de pactis.

units.la: e Imptia est promissio quæcunque adimplenda. 22. qu.4. c. in malis. & abusu Nominis divini, quatenus res mala ejus authoritate quantum in ipso est confirmatur.
units.tr: e An impious promise is any promise to be fulfilled. Caus. 22, qu. 4, c. In malis. And by abuse of the divine name, insofar as an evil thing is confirmed by its authority, so far as lies in it.

units.la: IX. Secundus Casus est de re ex se illicita secundario: id est, non ex natura ipsius rei omnibus illicita, sed quibusdam tantum pro conditione suarum personarum, prout sunt membra alicujus communitatis, aut in certo aliquo vitae genere versantur. Illicitum enim est (idque ex se, non ex accidente tantum) his qui sunt membra alicujus communitatis, quicquid f legibus illius communitatis repugnat: quod tamen illicitum est ut a Deo prohibitum, non primario, immediate, & in specie; sed secundario, mediate, & in genere, vi illius generalis mandati divini quod praecipit obedientiam rectoribus in omnibus licitis & honestis. Illicitum item est eodem fere gradu, & ex eodem fundamento, his qui aliquo munere aut officio funguntur, aut in certo aliquo vitae statu aut conditione constituti sunt, (quam nostrates vocabulo minus proprio fortasis, sed tamen usu recepto, particularem Vocationem appellant) quicquid naturae aut rationi illius muneris sive Vocationis non est consentaneum. Poterit enim id licere Magistratui politico, quod non licet verbi Ministro. aut e contra: itemque mercatori, quod non agricolae; domino, quod non servo: conjugi, quod non cælibi ; & sic de cæteris. Quibus omnibus Deus in genere legem hanc fixit, ut quisque quod suæ vocationis est fideliter faciat, intraque fines ejus modeste se contineat. Siquis ergo mercator Anglus juraret lanas, aut alias merces extra regnum Angliæ lege deportari prohibitas Hamburgum mittere; aut si Magistratus aliquis furaret se non puniturum furtum aut adulterium; aut Episcopus vel Presbyter se nunquam concionaturum, aut Sacramenta administraturum; Aut servus rusticus se domino jubenti boves jungere vel fruges demetere non parituram : quorum primum illud legibus Regni, reliqua conditionibus propriæ vocationis adversantur. Effecit ista omnia Juramenti rei eo quo jam dixi gradu illicitæ; & ipsa etiam propterea Juramenta illicita & ordinarie non obligarent. Dico Ordinarie : Qiia fortassis possunt dari casus: in quibus Juramentum quod videtur alicui legi communitatis aut vocationis adversari, etsi non debuerit suscipi, suceptum tamen poterit obligare. Ut exempli causa, in lege poenali disjuncta. Sit lex civitatis; Nemo civis Prætoris munus, ad id electus, detrectato : qui faxit, centum aureorum multa esto. Caius civis, quod se imparem putet muneri, aut ut caveat sibi ab aliquo quod inde metuit incommodo, jurat se nunquam urbana Prætura functurum. Eligitur a civibus: jurejurando se tuetur: ab illis poscitur tamen ad gerendam præturam, posthabito jurejurando. In hac specie facti quæritur, In foro conscientiæ quid juris? Respondeo, debuit non jurasse; nulla præsertim cogente necessitate: potuit enim vel injuratus recusasse. Juratus tamen videtur obligari, nec posse sine perjurio poscentibus civibus morem gerere: tenetur itaque multam solvere, Prœturam recusare. Intelligi velim præcise quantum spectat ad id de quo nunc agitur, materiam sc. juramenti, atque etiam præcise in quantum adversatur legi civitatis. Nam respectu finis, aut alterius causæ, imo respectu ipsius etiam materiæ quatenus est impeditiva majoris boni publici, aut aliunde, poterit justa subesse ratio quæ obligationem tollat. Ordinarie tamen ut dixi, Juramentum præstitum contra leges totius Communitatis aut propriæ vocationis non obligat. Atque hæc de rebus ex se illicitis dicta sunto.
units.tr: IX. The Second Case concerns a thing unlawful in itself but secondarily: that is, not unlawful in every case from the nature of the thing itself, but only for certain persons, insofar as they are members of some community or live in a certain walk of life. For it is unlawful (and this in itself, not merely by accident) for those who are members of some community to do whatever conflicts with the laws of that community. Yet this is unlawful as forbidden by God not primarily, immediately and specifically, but secondarily, mediately and generally, by virtue of that general divine command which enjoins obedience to rulers in all things lawful and honest. Likewise it is unlawful, to nearly the same degree and on the same ground, for those who hold some office or duty, or are placed in some definite state or condition of life (which we English, with a less proper word but one in common use, call particular Vocation), to do whatever does not agree with the nature and reason of that office or Vocation. For what is lawful for the civil Magistrate may not be lawful for a minister of the Word, or conversely; likewise what is lawful for a merchant may not be lawful for a farmer; for a master, what is not lawful for a servant; for a married man, what is not lawful for an unmarried one; and so on for the rest. God has laid down this general law for all of these: that each should faithfully do what belongs to his vocation, and keep himself modestly within its bounds. If therefore an English merchant should swear to send wool, or other goods forbidden by law to be exported from the kingdom of England, to Hamburg; or if some Magistrate should swear that he will not punish theft or adultery; or a Bishop or Presbyter that he will never preach or administer the Sacraments; or a rustic servant that he will not yoke the oxen or reap the crops when his master orders him: the first of these conflicts with the laws of the Kingdom, the rest with the conditions of his proper vocation. All these oaths are unlawful to the degree I have just described, and for that very reason such oaths, being unlawful, would not bind as a rule. I say ordinarily, for perhaps cases can be given in which an oath that seems to conflict with some law of the community or of the vocation, though it ought not to have been taken, may nevertheless, once taken, bind. For example, in a disjunctive penal law. Let there be a city law: "No citizen shall refuse the office of praetor to which he is elected; whoever does so shall pay a fine of a hundred gold pieces." Caius, a citizen, thinking himself unequal to the office, or wishing to guard himself against some harm he fears from it, swears that he will never serve as urban praetor. He is elected by the citizens; he protects himself by his oath; yet they demand that he take up the praetorship, the oath notwithstanding. In this case of fact the question is: what is the law in the court of conscience? I answer: he ought not to have sworn, especially with no compelling necessity, for he could have refused even without swearing. Yet having sworn, he seems bound, and cannot comply with the citizens' demand without perjury. Therefore he is bound to pay the fine and decline the praetorship. I wish this to be understood precisely as far as concerns what is now under discussion, namely the matter of the oath, and precisely insofar as it conflicts with the law of the city. For with respect to the end, or some other cause, or even with respect to the matter itself insofar as it hinders a greater public good, or for some other reason, there may be a just ground that removes the obligation. Ordinarily, however, as I said, an oath taken against the laws of the whole community or of one's own vocation does not bind. And let these things be said about what is unlawful in itself.

units.la: X. Sequuntur quæ ex se non illicitæ, sunt tamen illicitæ ex accidente. Accidit autem rei licitæ, ut fiat illicita; aut ex errore personæ jurantis, aut ex effectu malo rei juratæ. Tertius ergo Casus est, cum quis juramento pollicetur se facturum aliquid in se fortasse licitum, quod tamen ipse putat esse illicitum, aut certe veretur ne non sit licitum. Ut si quis ante hæc tempora admittendus ad beneficium (ut vocant) Ecclesiasticum, promisisset in publicis sacris observare omnes ritus legibus Ecclesiasticis imperatos; veltem sc. lineam crucis signum ad sacrum fontem, ingeniculationem in percipiendis symbolis in sacra cœna, & id genus alios; quos ipse tamen ex aliquo levi præjudicio putaret esse superstitiosos & Papisticos. Quæritur in hoc casu quæ sit Obligatio? Pro responsione dico tria. Dico primo, non posse tale juramentum, durante tali errore, sine gravi peccato suscipi. Peccat enim graviter, qui contra conscientiam peccat, etli erroneam. Judicium enim intellectus cum sit unicuique proxima agendi regula: voluntas, si judicium illud non sequatur, deficiens a regula sua necesse est ut in obliquum feratur. Tritum est illud. Qui facit contra conscientiam, ædificat ad gehennam. Sane qui jurat in id quod putat esse illicitum, nihilo minus juraturus esset, si esset revera illicitum: atque ita res illa, ut alii licita, est tamen ipsi illicita; sententiam ferente Apostolo, Rom. 14. 14. Ubi distinguit quit inter κοινὸν ἑαυτῷ, & ἐκείνῳ κοινόν, & aperte docet, posse id quod non est κοινὸν ἑαυτῷ, impurum & illicitum in se, esse tamen ἐκείνῳ κοινόν impurum & illicitum homini, τῷ λογιζομένῳ τὶ κοινὸν εἶναι, nempe illi mini qui æstimat aliquid esse impurum aut illicitum. Dico secundo, tale juramentum non obligare. Ratio manifesta, ex tertia hypothesi: quia juramentum non potest tollere obligationem priorem, nec inducere obligationem aliam ei contrariam. Ast illi juramento quod suscipitur contra dictamen Conscientiæ, præfuit alia prior ex illo dictamine orta. Conscientiæ enim dictamen sive rectæ sive erroneæ semper obligat, saltem ad non faciendum contra eam. Istam autem obligationem Juramentum subsequens removere non potest: quin ipsum potius invalidum fit, & vim obligandi amittit. Dico tertio, Si jurans postea melius edoctus errorem suum agnoscat & corrigat; Juramentum quod prius non obligabat, exinde incipere de novo obligare. Juramento enim inest obligandi potentia quasi naturalis & inseparabilis; sicut lapidi naturaliter & inseparabiliter inest potentia movendi deorsum: quæ potentia semper nata est exerere vires suas, & prodire in actum, nisi ab aliquo impediente prohibeatur: Quemadmodum ergo lapis, ut moveatur postquam aliquandiu quievit, non indiget nova aliqua potentia sibi aliunde indita, sed remoto prohibente statim suapte vi deorsum fertur: sic Juramentum, remota illa errantis conscientiae obligatione quae ipsius vim prius impediebat, sine omni mora aut alterius rei ope, ex vi sua obligat.
units.tr: X. What follows is not unlawful in itself but is unlawful by accident. A lawful thing, however, becomes unlawful either through the error of the person swearing or through the evil effect of the thing sworn. The third case, then, is when someone swears to do something perhaps lawful in itself, which yet he himself thinks unlawful, or at least fears may not be lawful. For example, if someone, admitted before these times to an ecclesiastical benefice (as they call it), had promised to observe in public worship all the rites enjoined by ecclesiastical laws, such as making the sign of the cross at the font, kneeling when receiving the elements at the Lord's Supper, and others of that kind, which he himself thought, from some slight prejudice, to be superstitious and Papistical. In this case the question is: what is the obligation? In reply I say three things. I say first, that such an oath cannot be taken, while this error lasts, without grave sin. For he sins gravely who acts against his conscience, even an erroneous one. For the judgment of the intellect, since it is the nearest rule of acting for each person, if the will does not follow that judgment, must necessarily deviate from its rule and be carried off course. The saying is commonplace: He who acts against conscience builds up to hell. Indeed, one who swears to what he thinks unlawful would nonetheless swear if it were really unlawful; and so the thing, though lawful for others, is unlawful for him, the Apostle so pronouncing (Rom. 14. 14.), where he distinguishes between not common to himself [κοινὸν ἑαυτῷ] and common to that one [ἐκείνῳ κοινόν], and plainly teaches that what is not not common to himself [κοινὸν ἑαυτῷ], impure and unlawful in itself, may yet be common to that one [ἐκείνῳ κοινόν], impure and unlawful to a man, to the one who reckons something to be common [τῷ λογιζομένῳ τὶ κοινὸν εἶναι], namely to him who judges something to be impure or unlawful. I say secondly, that such an oath does not bind. The reason is plain from the third hypothesis: because an oath cannot remove a prior obligation, nor induce another obligation contrary to it. But that oath which is taken against the dictate of conscience is preceded by another, prior obligation arising from that dictate. For the dictate of conscience, whether right or erroneous, always binds, at least to not acting against it. Yet the oath that follows cannot remove this obligation; rather, the oath itself becomes invalid and loses its power to bind. I say thirdly, that if the one swearing, better instructed afterwards, recognises and corrects his error, the oath which did not bind before begins to bind anew from that point. For an oath has a power of binding that is, as it were, natural and inseparable, just as a stone has naturally and inseparably the power of moving downward. This power is always ready to exert its strength and pass into act, unless it is restrained by some hindrance. Just as a stone, to be set in motion after resting for a while, needs no new power implanted in it from elsewhere, but as soon as the hindrance is removed, it is carried downward by its own force, so an oath, once the obligation of the erring conscience which previously hindered its force is removed, binds by its own power, without any delay or the help of anything else.

units.la: XI. Alii sunt Casus de re illicita ex accidente, ratione mali effectus ipsius rei: quatenus sc. potest esse impeditiva boni, aut causativa vel saltem (sic enim loquendum est) occasionativa mali: Impediri autem bonum supponitur aut Antecedens, aut Futurum. Quartus ergo Casus est, ubi res jurata videtur illicita, eo quod impediat effectum alicujus boni antecedentis; puta Voti, aut Promissi prius facti: ut si is qui voto se prius obstrinxerat ad aliquod opus pietatis aut charitatis, postea juramentum susciperet, quod impediret adimpletionem prioris voti. Veluti si Voto obstrictus dimidiam lucri partem hebdomadatim pauperibus dare; juraret postea totum lucrum in usus belli conferre: vel si Caius pollicitus Titio fundum vendere certo pretio, Julio postea se venditurum juret
units.tr: XI. There are other cases of a thing unlawful by accident, with respect to the evil effect of the thing itself: insofar as it can be hindering of a good, or causing or at least (for so we must speak) occasioning an evil. Now a good is hindered either a good that precedes or a good that is future. The fourth case, then, is when a sworn thing seems unlawful because it hinders the effect of some earlier good, such as a vow or a previously made promise. For example, if one who had earlier bound himself by a vow to some work of piety or charity should afterwards swear to something that would prevent fulfilment of the earlier vow; as if one bound by a vow to give half his weekly gain to the poor should then swear to devote all his gain to the uses of war; or if Caius, having promised Titius to sell him a field for a certain price, should afterwards swear to Julius that he will sell it for a higher price.

units.la: {8} Casus 8. juret majori pretio. Hic casus nihil habet difficultatis. Clare enim respondetur, & fundatur responsio in tertia hypothesi; ejusmodi juramentum nec licitum esse, nec obligatorium. Quia obligatio illa prior, undecunque contracta, sive ex pacto, sive ex voto, sive ex nuda promissione, sive ex officio mero, valida manet, & ponit obicem omni actui contrario subsequenti.
units.tr: {8} Case 8: he swears to sell at a higher price. This case presents no difficulty. The answer is clear, and it rests on the third hypothesis: such an oath is neither lawful nor binding. The earlier obligation, however it was contracted, whether by agreement, by vow, by bare promise, or by mere duty, remains valid and places a barrier in the way of any later act contrary to it.

units.la: XII. Quintus Casus est, cum id quod juratur videtur esse impeditivum alicujus boni futuri. Ut siquis juraret se nunquam futurum fide justorem alieni debi- ti ; aut verbi ministrum, cum sit tamen ad illud munus valde idoneus ; aut artem utilem quem solus novit nemini communicaturum ; & similia. Ratio dubii est, quia minus bonum respectu majoris boni habet quodammodo rationem mali : ergo juramentum etsi alias honestum, si sit impeditivum majoris boni, videtur esse malum. Solutio dubii in hoc casu non potest aliqua afferri generalis & certa, quæ factis singularibus universis conveniat : quia versatur in comparatione magis & minus boni, quæ plurimum pendent ex circumstantiarum collatione ; quæ cum sint infinitæ varietatis, non possunt omnes certis & definitis regulis ita comprehendi; quin ut viri prudentis arbitrio res plurima ex parte fit permittenda, ut id demum faciat; quod expensis qua licet fide & diligentia utrinque rationibus sibi videbitur tandem pro hic & nunc magis expedire. Interim tamen, quum non sit simpliciter verum (nisi caute intelligatur) unumquemque semper obligari ad id faciendum quod est melius: pro solutione dubii in hoc casu dici potest, Juramentum non esse illicitum, aut obligandi vim amittere; praecise ob hoc quod videatur esse impeditivum majoris boni; nisi concurrant aliae etiam circumstantiae (ut quidem fere fit, )quae illud evincant aut non licere, aut non obligare. Exemplo res erit illustrior. Caius pharmacum eximiae virtutis, aut aliud artificium insigne a Titio inventore edoctus, sed ea conditione, ut cum nemine alio, ipso superstite & inconsulto, juret se communicaturum. Non-communicatio tanti arcani videtur esse contra bonum publicum: & tamen ratio dictat Caium obligari, & teneri bona fide observare quod promisit. Alias Titio fieret injuria, cujus interest arcanum non communicari: quod nec ipsi Caio ab initio, nisi tali interposito juramento communicatum fuisset.
units.tr: XII. The fifth case is when what is sworn seems to be an impediment to some future good. For example, someone might swear that he will never stand surety for another's debt; or that he will never become a minister of the Word, although he is very well fitted for that office; or that he will never share with anyone a useful art that he alone knows; and the like. The reason for doubt is that a lesser good, compared with a greater good, has in some sense the character of an evil. Therefore an oath, although otherwise honest, seems to be evil if it impedes a greater good. In this case no general and certain solution can be offered that suits all particular cases, because the matter turns on comparing greater and lesser goods, which depends very much on weighing the circumstances. These are of endless variety and cannot all be embraced under fixed and definite rules. So in most cases the matter must be left largely to the judgement of a prudent person, so that he may do whatever, after weighing the reasons on both sides with as much honesty and care as he can, seems to him in the present circumstances the more expedient. Meanwhile, since it is not simply true (unless it is understood with caution) that each person is always bound to do what is better, the solution to this doubt may be stated as follows: the oath is not unlawful, nor does it lose its binding force, merely because it seems to impede a greater good, unless other circumstances also concur (as usually happens) which show that it is either unlawful or not binding. The matter will be clearer by an example. Caius has been taught by Titius, the inventor, a drug of remarkable virtue, or some other notable invention, on the condition that he swear not to share it with anyone else while Titius lives and without his consent. Not sharing so great a secret seems to be against the public good. Yet reason dictates that Caius is bound, and must in good faith keep what he has promised. Otherwise an injury would be done to Titius, whose interest lies in the secret not being shared; and this would not even have been communicated to Caius at the beginning, had such an oath not been interposed.

units.la: XIII.Restat proxime ut de re agamusper accidens illicita ex eo quod videatur esse causativa, vel saltem occasionativa alicujus mali, idque vel ipsi juranti, vel alteri. Sextus ergo Casus est, ubi quod juratur incommodum est ipsi juranti: vel inferendo ei certum damnum temporale, vel exponendo cum periculo tentationis. Ut si Caius juraret se Titio decoctori mutuo daturum centum aureos, nunquam fortassis recepturus; quod ei cederet in damnum. Aut si Fabius petente id uxore jam morti vicina, ex qua liberos aliquot sustulisset; ne induceretur eis noverca, juraret ad secundas nuptias se non transituram; unde se fortassis periculo exponeret ustionis. Pro responsione dico primum, istiusmodi promissionem non esse temere aut sine magna deliberatione faciendam, nec nisi gravis causa subsit: non tamen simpliciter esse illicitam. Etsi enim omnis mali occasio sit diligenter vitanda: tamen cum nihil quod non est ex se & alia ratione illicitum, sit necessario & universaliter mali occasio; nec sit aliquid simpliciter & de sua specie illicitum ob hoc solum quod possit esse occasio mali: non videtur simpliciter damnanda omnis istiusmodi promissio; praesertim si juranti quo tem-
units.tr: XIII. It remains next to deal with things unlawful per accidens, that is, those which seem to be causative or at least occasioning of some evil, whether for the one swearing or for another. The sixth case therefore is where what is sworn is a disadvantage to the one swearing, either by bringing upon him a certain temporal loss, or by exposing him to the danger of temptation. For example, if Caius should swear that he will lend a hundred gold pieces to Titius, a spendthrift, whom he will perhaps never repay, which would turn to his loss. Or if Fabius, at the request of his wife, who is near death and by whom he has raised several children, swears, so that no stepmother will be brought in for them, that he will not marry again, he perhaps exposes himself to the danger of burning. In answer I say, first, that a promise of this kind is not to be made rashly or without great deliberation, nor unless a grave cause lies behind it; yet it is not simply unlawful. For although every occasion of evil is to be carefully avoided, yet since nothing which is not unlawful in itself and for some other reason is necessarily and universally an occasion of evil, and nothing is simply and by its kind unlawful merely because it may be an occasion of evil, it does not seem that every promise of this kind should be simply condemned, especially if, with due diligence applied, no probable danger of some great disadvantage appeared at the time when the one swearing swore.

units.la: Caf. 10. tempore juravit, debita adhibita diligentia, non appareret alicujus magni incommodi periculum probabile. Dico secundo, si cedat juramentum in damnum temporale ipsius jurantis solum, citra injuriam tertiae personae, jurantem obligari etsi cum gravi suo damno, nisi is cui juratum est velit remittere. Verba diserta sunt, Psalm. 15. Juravit in malum, & non mutabit. Ubi in Hebraeo prius verbum praeteriti temporis est (juravit in malum) posterius futuri (& non mutabit) quasi diceret, Viri pii officium est, postquam juravit proximo suo, quod sine magno suo malo praestari nequit, constare tamen sibi, & quod promisit ratum esse jubere, & (ut est in hoc textu) secundum omne quod egressum est ex ore suo facere. Dico tertio, Juramentum obligare; etiamsi videatur exponere periculo tentationis, nisi sit aliunde vitiosum. Quia sid sufficeret tollendae obligationi, vix remaneret quidquam quod posset obligare: quum ex astu Satanae & corruptione cordis humani nihil sit a mali periculo tam immune, quin ut inde necti possit in perniciem nostram (nisi nos Dei gratia praestaret incolumes) laqueus tentationis. Quin potius ex adjutorio divinæ gratiæ poterit ista obligatio, velut clypeus repellendæ tentationi idoneus, ex adversum objici: nempe tentationi non cedendum, sed animosius obnitendum; quia juramenti religione teneris, ne id facias ad quod tentaris.
units.tr: Caf. 10. I say secondly, that if the oath turns to the temporal loss of the one swearing alone, without injury to a third person, he is bound by it, even at his own grave loss, unless the one to whom he swore is willing to release him. The words are plain, Psalm 15: He has sworn to his hurt, and will not change. Here in the Hebrew the first verb is in the past tense (he has sworn to his hurt) and the second in the future (and will not change), as if to say: it is the duty of a godly man, once he has sworn to his neighbour something which cannot be performed without great loss to himself, nevertheless to remain true to himself, and, as the text has it, to do according to all that has gone out of his mouth. I say thirdly, that an oath binds even if it seems to expose one to the danger of temptation, unless it is otherwise wrongful. For if this were enough to annul the obligation, hardly anything would remain that could bind, since through the cunning of Satan and the corruption of the human heart nothing is so free from the danger of evil that a snare of temptation cannot be tied from it to our ruin (unless the grace of God keeps us safe). Rather, by the help of divine grace this obligation can be set against temptation like a shield suited to repelling it: namely, that one should not yield to temptation but resist it more bravely, because by the bond of an oath you are restrained from doing what you are tempted to do.

units.la: XIV. Casus Septimus est, ubi id quod juratur videtur ex eo illicitum, quod alteri possit inde creari periculum Scandali; præbendo sc. ei ex facto nostro occasionem ruinæ. Plurima exstant eaque gravissima in Epistolis Paulinis de vitando scandalo monita: præsertim Rom. 14. & 1 Cor. 8. & 10. Et sane viro vere Christiano summopere cavendum est, ut in omni conversatione sua non propriæ tantum conscientiæ consulat, sed & ædificationi alienæ; nec quærat quod sibi utile est, sed quod multis; videatque tam quid illis expediat, quam quid sibi liceat: ne libertate sua abutatur in perniciem fratris. Sed quatenus a rebus licitis abstinendum sit ob scandalum vitandum; nec paucis expediri potest, neque est præsentis instituti despicere.
units.tr: XIV. The seventh case is where what is sworn seems unlawful because it may thereby create a danger of scandal for another, by giving him, through our act, an occasion of ruin. Very many and very grave warnings against giving scandal are found in the Pauline Epistles, especially Rom. 14. and 1 Cor. 8. and 10. Indeed a man who is truly Christian must take the greatest care that in all his conduct he consults not only his own conscience but also the building up of others; nor should he seek what is useful to himself but what is useful to many; and he should consider what is expedient for them as much as what is permitted to himself, lest he abuse his liberty to the destruction of his brother. But how far one must abstain from things lawful in order to avoid scandal cannot be settled in a few words, nor is it the purpose of the present undertaking to examine it.

units.la: Dicendum videtur, quod ad præsens negotium attinet, unius scandali periculum, si nulla adsit alia ratio cur res illicita censeatur, non sufficere ad impediendam juramenti præstiti obligationem: sicut in præcedente casu de periculo tentationis jam actum est: quum utriusque periculi videatur esse eadem per omnia ratio.
units.tr: It seems necessary to say, as far as the present matter is concerned, that the danger of a single scandal, if there is no other reason why the thing should be judged unlawful, is not sufficient to annul the obligation of an oath already taken. This was already dealt with in the preceding case, concerning the danger of temptation, since the reasoning on both dangers seems to be the same in every respect.

units.la: XV. Emensus jam tandem de Materia Impossibili, Necessaria, & Illicita præcipuos Casus: ad reliqua Dubia pergo. Dubium Quartum est, de Juramento rei Liberæ; hoc est rei neque Necessariæ neque Illicitæ, sed Mediæ & Indifferentis. Quæ ἀδιάφορα cum ex duplici causa oriatur; sc. ex voluntate Legislatoris nec præcipientis nec prohibentis, & ex levitate Rei: occurrunt proinde in hac materia duo Casus. Casus prior est, cum res nullo aut præcepto aut interdicto divino vel humano legitimo ita determinata est, quin ut posset quisque pro hic & nunc secundum exigentiam circumstantiarum pro suo arbitrio facere vel non facere, prout ipsi visum fuerit expedire. ποιείτω quod vult faciat, non peccat; 1 Cor. 7. 36. Ut si Caius juret se Titio fundum venditurum, aut daturum mutuo centum. Respondendum breviter, Juramentum in hoc casu, & licitum esse, & obligare. Casus posterior est, cum res aut ob sui levitatem indigna est viri prudentis deliberatione, nec casu nuce interest fecerisne an non feceris; ut levare festucam de terra, fricare barbam &c. aut ob parvitatem materiæ non est multum æstimabilis; ut dare pomum puero, aciculam commodare, &c. Juramentum de re isto sensu adiaphora omnino est illicitum. Arguit enim sanƈti nominis Dei aut nimiam irreverentiam, si (ut fere fit) ex quodam habitu jurandi longo usu contracto, imprudenti forte exciderist; aut apertum contemptum, siquis id sciens prudensque admiserit. Scilicet non est Deus advocandus testis, nisi ubi dignus vindice nodus inciderit; ubi causa exigit, non justa modo sed & gravis. Et in hoc omnes consentiunt. Cæterum de Obligatione quid statuendum? Video quidem plerosque Casuistas Pontificios in ea esse sententia, juramentum de re exigua & parvi momenti esse sua natura nullum, & non obligare, quia sc. res levis non est idonea materia Juramenti, & lex non curat de minimis. Sed miror potuisse eos, qui alias videri volunt esse tam Lyncei, in re tam aperta execurire: nisi quod putidæ illi distinƈtioni Peccati mortalis & Venialis, quo velut fermento totam Theologiæ Moralis massam fœde corruperunt, locum relictum cupiant. Sed obligare Juramentum in re vel levissimi mo-
units.tr: XV. Having now at last gone through the principal cases concerning the matter that is impossible, necessary, and unlawful, I turn to the remaining doubts. The fourth doubt concerns an oath about a free matter, that is, a thing that is neither necessary nor unlawful, but intermediate and indifferent. Since indifferent things [ἀδιάφορα] arise from a twofold cause, namely the will of the lawgiver, who neither commands nor forbids, and the lightness of the thing itself, two cases occur in this matter. The first case is when a thing has been determined by no command or prohibition, divine or lawful human, so that anyone may, in the present circumstances and according to what they require, do or not do it at his own discretion, as seems to him expedient. Let him do what he will; he does not sin [ποιείτω], 1 Corinthians 7:36. For example, if Caius swears that he will sell a farm to Titius, or lend him a hundred. The answer in this case is briefly that the oath is both lawful and binding. The second case is when a thing, because of its triviality, is unworthy of the deliberation of a prudent person, and it makes no difference, even in a nut's worth, whether you did it or not, such as lifting a straw from the ground, rubbing one's beard, and so on; or when, because of the smallness of the matter, it is of little worth, such as giving an apple to a boy, lending a needle, and so on. An oath about a thing that is indifferent in this sense is wholly unlawful. For it shows either too great irreverence towards the holy name of God, if (as usually happens) it slips out by imprudence from a habit of swearing acquired through long use; or an open contempt, if someone admits it knowingly and deliberately. Certainly God is not to be called as witness except where a knot has arisen worthy of an avenger, where the cause demands not only a just but also a grave matter. All agree on this. But what must be decided about the obligation? I indeed see that most of the Papist casuists hold the view that an oath about a trifling and unimportant matter is, by its nature, null and does not bind, because a light thing is not a fitting matter for an oath, and the law does not concern itself with the smallest things. But I wonder that those who wish to appear so lynx-eyed in other matters could have stumbled so badly in a matter so plain; unless they desire to leave room for that foul distinction between mortal and venial sin, by which, like a leaven, they have shamefully corrupted the whole mass of moral theology. But that an oath binds, even in a matter of the very slightest

units.la: festucam ... : marginal fragments of the left page are not transcribed here. momenti constat; Primo, quia in re gravi & levi eadem est veritatis & falsitatis ratio.Secundo,quia in Assertorio Juramento qui aliter dicit quam res est, etsi in re levissima pejerat : ergo a si- mili & in Promissorio, qui aliter facit quam juravit. Tertio, quia aliter, quantum in se esset, Deum falsæ rei testem ifaceret. Quarto, quia omnis jurans tenetur facere totum quod promisit, quatenus potest & licet : sed dare puero pomum & possibile est & licitum; ergo tenetur præstare. Non debuit ergo sic jurari : sed ubi juratum est, debet impleri.
units.tr: festucam ...: marginal fragments of the left page are not transcribed here. momenti constat; First, because in a grave matter and a light one the reason of truth and falsehood is the same. Second, because whoever gives a different account from the fact in an assertory oath is forsworn, even in a very slight matter; therefore by parity also in a promissory oath, whoever acts otherwise than he swore. Third, because otherwise, so far as in him lies, he would make God a witness to a false thing. Fourth, because everyone who swears is bound to do all that he has promised, so far as he can and may; but to give a boy an apple is both possible and lawful; therefore he is bound to perform it. It ought not therefore to have been sworn in this way; but where it has been sworn, it must be fulfilled.

units.la: XVI. Reliquum est Dubium Quintum, ubi juratur in Materiam Indefinitam & incertam: & continet tres potissimum Calus. Primus Casus est, cum quis se tradit quodammodo in alienam potestatem, promittendo se facturum quicquid ille alter voluerit, Ut si princeps juraret se daturum aulico amico ob praestitum sibi fidele officium quicquid is petierit: aut si servus cujusquam vel amicus juraret se omnia heri jussa vel amici mandata facturum. In isto casu dico primum, Juramentum iftiusmodi si simpliciter intelligatur ut verba sonant, esse illicitum. Injuriam facit Deo, cujus unius servus est omnis homo, quisquis se facit g servum hominis, & alienæ temeritatis mancipium. Dico secundo, ut licitum esse possit, aliud aliquid necessario subintelligi. Ut exempli gratia, Juro me facturum quod voles: subintellige, si rem voles honestam, possibilem, æquam. Atque eatenus, & in eo sensu obligat. Videntur hac quasi solenni formula jurasse soliti olim Reges Persarum & Judæorum, idque indefinite ad ampliorem magnificentiæ suæ & gratiæ ostentationem; Pete quod vis, & dabitur tibi usque ad dimidium regni. Hac forma Rex Persarum h Assuerus Reginæ coujugi juravit: & cum hæc rem æquam & necessariam peteret, ille pro fide data rem fieri jussit. Eadem pene forma cum Salomon Reginæ matri promisisset, daturum se ei quicquid peteret; & ipsa Adoniæ nomine rem peteret, quæ Solomoni, cui comperta erat jamdiu hominis ambitio, visa est iniquior, Salomon non obstante Juramento postulatum matris non fecit. Quo facto satis indicavit, non se alia mente promisisse, quam si res justa postularetur: suoque exemplo nos docuit, ubi indefinite in alienam voluntatem JuJuratur, subintelligi semper oportere hanc conditionem, Si is id voluerit, quod ex æqui boni jure ab illo modeste expectari, a nobis honeste concedi fas est. Suppetit & tertium exemplum ejus formæ juramenti, quod narratur Math. 14. Herodis &c. Tetrarchæ, qui saltatriculæ ex fratre nepti gratiam faturus, juravit se ei daturum, quicquid peteret. Petiit illa rem iniquissimam; hominis innocentis & indemnati amputatum in patina caput. Rex fieri jussit ὅτι Religiosum scilicet & verecundum hominem puduit præsentibus tot convivis non adimplere id nefario licet facinore, ad quod se juramenti sacramento obstrinxerat. Esto hoc nobis exemplum in cautelam; ast illud Salomonis in imitationem. Et meminerimus Juramentum sic indefinite prolatum k cum sola justa exceptione tantum esse semper intelligendum; & extendendum ad ea solum quæ non sunt verisimiliter cogitata cum juraretur; non ad ea, quæ si tunc cogitata fuissent, non fuisset juratum.
units.tr: XVI. What remains is the Fifth Doubt, where one swears to an indefinite and uncertain matter. It contains chiefly three cases. The first case is when someone hands himself over, in a sense, into another's power, promising to do whatever that other wishes: for example, if a prince were to swear that he would give to a courtier friend, for a faithful service rendered to him, whatever the friend asked; or if a servant or friend of someone were to swear that he would do whatever his master had ordered or his friend had commanded. In this case I say, first, that an oath of this kind, if understood simply as the words sound, is unlawful. It does injury to God, whose alone every man is servant; whoever makes himself a servant of a man, the bondsman of another's rashness, does so. I say, second, that for it to be lawful, something else must necessarily be understood. For example: I swear that I will do what you wish; understand, if you wish something honourable, possible and fair. Thus far, and in that sense, it binds. Kings of Persia and Judea used to swear in this solemn formula, it seems, and indefinitely, to display their magnificence and favour the more: Ask what you will, and it shall be given you, even to half the kingdom. King Ahasuerus of Persia swore to his queen consort in this form; and when she asked for a fair and necessary thing, he ordered it done in fulfilment of his pledge. Solomon promised his queen mother almost the same form, that he would give her whatever she asked; and she asked a thing on behalf of Adonijah, which seemed to Solomon, to whom the man's ambition had long been known, too unfair. Solomon, notwithstanding the oath, did not grant the mother's request. By this act he sufficiently showed that he had not promised with any other intention than that a just thing would be asked; and by his own example he taught us that where one swears indefinitely to another's will, this condition must always be understood: if he wishes what, by the law of good and fair dealing, may reasonably be expected from him and honourably granted by us. There is also a third example of this form of oath, recounted in Matt. 14: Herod the tetrarch, who wished to gratify the dancing girl, his brother's daughter, swore that he would give her whatever she asked. She asked a most unjust thing: the head of an innocent and unconvicted man, cut off and brought on a dish. The king ordered it done, because [ὅτι] the religious and modest man was ashamed, with so many guests present, not to fulfil the wicked deed to which he had bound himself by the sacrament of an oath. Let this be a warning to us; but let Solomon's conduct be our pattern. And let us remember that an oath uttered indefinitely in this way is always to be understood with only a just exception, and extended only to those things which were not likely to have been thought of when it was sworn, not to those which, had they been thought of then, would not have been sworn.

units.tr: XVII. The Second Case

units.la: Conditio intelligitur. Si &c. quum sit. l. jus publicum. ff. de pact. præeminentias superioris alicujus potestatis; ut Regis, Civitatis, aut domini alicujus feudi: qualia sunt apud nos juramenta homagii, Juramentum Suprematus Regii, & similia. Licita esse hoc genus juramenta nemo non agnoscit, atque etiam obligare: sed ob illorum jurium plerumque incertitudinem, merito dubitari potest, quatenus obligent. Dicendum est, obligari subditum indubie ad conservandum quantum in ipso est omnia jura quæ νόμῳ[?] aut θέσμῳ, legibus aut moribus constat esse legitima; id est quæ aut jure scripto definita sunt aut longo temporis usu & diuturna (ut vocant) præscriptione invaluerunt: quatenus sc.sibi nota sunt, vel etiam posthac moraliter innotescere poterint. Non tamen pariter obligari ad omnia ea observanda quæ sunt dubii aut controversi juris: præsertim cum soleant fere qui potestate præditi sunt funiculos agrorum extendere, & ultra lapides clientium salire, nec jurium suorum finibus contenti esse. Debet tamen subditus animo esse semper parato, & illa quæ sunt dubia, ubi justa esse constiterit, agnoscere & tueri.
units.tr: A condition is understood. If etc., since it is. l. jus publicum. ff. de pact. eminences of some superior power, such as a king, a state, or the lord of some fief. Of this kind are the oaths of homage among us, the Oath of the Royal Supremacy, and similar oaths. Lawful oaths of this kind no one denies, and indeed they bind; but because those rights are for the most part uncertain, it may rightly be doubted how far they bind. It must be said that the subject is undoubtedly bound to preserve, so far as lies in him, all those rights which are established as legitimate by law [νόμῳ] or by ordinance [θέσμῳ], that is, by laws or customs: those which are defined by written law, or which have grown strong through long use and lasting prescription (as they call it), so far as they are known to him or may become morally known to him hereafter. Yet he is not equally bound to observe everything that belongs to disputed or doubtful right, especially since those who hold power are wont to stretch the measuring-lines of their fields and to leap over the boundary-stones of their clients, and are never content within the limits of their rights. Nevertheless the subject ought always to be ready in mind to acknowledge and defend those doubtful rights which are shown to be just.

units.la: XVIII. Ultimus Casus est, ubi exigitur Juramentum a membro alicujus communitatis, puta Civitatis. Academiæ, Collegii, aut societatis Mercatorum vel Artificum, ad observanda statuta, privilegia, consuetudines, & liberates illius communitatis. Quæritur, Qualis est obligatio? Respondeo, Imprimis Juratus obligatur ad omnia statuta fundamentalia, quantum in ipso est, simpliciter observanda. Fundamentalia autem dico, quæ necessario & proxime tendunt ad conservandum publicum statum, ordinem, & honorem totius corporis sive communitatis. Sed id secundo non semper et necessario ad rigorem literæ; sed prout in more posita sunt, & usu communi recepta, & prout approbata consuetudine ab aliis observantur. Tertio, ad minorum gentium statuta quod attinet, quæ pertinent ad externam tantum formam & decus: vel quæ aut ex conditione materiæ, aut ex forma sanctionis, aut alio probabili indicio vir prudens judicaret non fuisse condita cum intentione l rigidæ obligationis; obligatur ea ordinarie observare: sic tamen ut liceat ei quandoque justa de causa sine scrupulo conscientiæ id prætermittere quod statuto aliquo faciendum præscribitur; modo id fiat citra sca ndalum aut contemptum. Quarto, Ob-
units.tr: XVIII. The last case is when an oath is exacted from a member of some community, for instance a city, a university, a college, or a society of merchants or craftsmen, to observe the statutes, privileges, customs and liberties of that community. The question is: what is the obligation? I answer: first, the one sworn is bound to observe absolutely, so far as in him lies, all the fundamental statutes. By fundamental I mean those which necessarily and directly tend to preserve the public state, order and honour of the whole body or community. Second, this does not always and necessarily hold to the rigour of the letter, but as the statutes are laid down in practice and received by common usage, and as they are observed by others under approved custom. Third, as regards the statutes of lesser kind, which pertain only to external form and decorum, or which a prudent man would judge, from the nature of the matter, the form of the sanction, or some other probable indication, were not made with the intention of strict obligation: he is bound ordinarily to observe them, yet in such a way that it is sometimes lawful for him, for a just cause, to omit without scruple of conscience what a statute prescribes to be done, provided this is done without scandal or contempt. Fourth, ob-

units.la: {a} Juramentum non debet obligare quā volu-ntarie promissum, ut Gerson. de ult. ipi. Cit. lect. 4.
units.tr: {a} An oath ought not to bind as a voluntary promise, as Gerson, de ult. ipi., Cit. lect. 4.

units.la: Obligatio extenditur & ad statuta de suturo sancienda, modo sint possibilia, justa & honesta. Quinto, si aliquod statutum post juramentum præstitum abrogatur, vel in desuetudinem abeat; obligatio Juramenti quoad illud statutum cessat, ita ut non teneatur illud ultra observare: nisi juratum fuerit verbis specialibus in ipsam rem statuto decretam; in eo enim casu sublato statuto manet tamen obligatio. Sexto, cum statuta Communitatum fere plurima sint, & multa multis ignota; & difficillimum sit, imo vix possibile omnia & singula exacte & examussim observare: qui bona fide ita se comparaverit, ut nihil quod est officii sui lubens præterierit, debitamque adhibuerit moralem diligentiam: ut ea omnia sciret quæ ad ipsius officium pertinent; statueritque statui, honori, paci suæ Communitatis, quantum humana patitur infirmitas, fideliter & sine scandalo inservire; hunc ego non dubitarim fidem de statutis observandis a se datam bona conscientia hactenus liberasse, & debitum ad quod se obligavit æqui boni lege exsolvisse. Quod item & de publicis Regni legibus intelligendum est.
units.tr: The obligation extends also to statutes to be enacted in future, provided they are possible, just and honest. Fifth, if any statute is abrogated after the oath has been taken, or falls into disuse, the obligation of the oath as regards that statute ceases, so that he is not bound to observe it any longer; unless it was sworn in special words directed to the very matter decreed by the statute, for in that case, though the statute is removed, the obligation remains. Sixth, since the statutes of communities are for the most part very many, and many are unknown to many, and it is most difficult, indeed hardly possible, to observe all and each exactly and precisely: he who has so conducted himself in good faith that he willingly omitted nothing of his duty, applied due moral diligence to know all that pertains to his office, and resolved to serve faithfully and without scandal the state, honour and peace of his community, as far as human weakness allows, I would not doubt has by a good conscience discharged the pledge given to observe the statutes, and has paid, by the law of fair dealing, the debt to which he bound himself. The same is to be understood also of the public laws of the kingdom.

units.la: XIX. Atque hæc de prima casuum classe dicta sufficiant. Ne quis autem me existimet nimiam propterea jurandi licentiam voluisse permittere, quod toties dixerim hoc vel illud Juramenti genus non esse illicitum : illud necessarium duxi me vos mature submonere, non id ea mente aut hodie dictum, aut posthac dicendum, quasi cuivis licereputarem pro suo arbitrio cum voluerit sic jurare ; quum sciam juramentum rem esse sacram, nec nisi magna cogente necessitate, idque rarissime, & summa cum reverentia adhibendam. Sed id ita ubique intelligendum, non esse juramentum ex illa vel illa causa simpliciter & de toto genere illicitum. Exempli gratia, cum dixi Juramentum impeditivum majoris boni non esse illicitum, vel Juramentum de re adiaphora non esse illicitum : sensus fuit, non debere concludi Juramentum aliquod esse simpliciter & de toto genere illicitum, (modo habeat alias omnes debitas conditiones,) ex eo solum quod sit impeditivum majoris boni, aut ex eo solum quod sit de re adiaphora : sive quod eodem recidit, non esse ex hac parte aliquod impedimentum quin ut possit esse licitum tum, si fit alias necessarium & omni alia ex parte debite conditionatum.
units.tr: XIX. So much for the first class of cases; let these suffice. Lest anyone think that I meant to grant a wide licence to swear because I have so often said that this or that kind of oath is not unlawful, I have thought it necessary to warn you in good time. I have not said this, nor will I say it hereafter, with the idea that anyone may swear in this way whenever he likes, at his own discretion. I know that an oath is a sacred thing, to be used only under strong compulsion, and that very rarely, and with the utmost reverence. But this must be understood everywhere in this sense: that an oath is not simply and in its whole kind unlawful on account of this or that cause. For example, when I said that an oath hindering a greater good is not unlawful, or that an oath concerning an indifferent matter is not unlawful, my meaning was that no oath should be concluded to be simply and in its whole kind unlawful merely because it hinders a greater good, or merely because it concerns an indifferent matter (provided it has all the other due conditions). This comes to the same thing: on that side there is no obstacle to its being lawful, provided it is otherwise necessary and in every other respect duly conditioned.
