units.tr: SECTION I.

units.la: ABsolutis superiore Lectione praecipuis difficultatibus, quae ad Juramenti Materiam propius pertinebant: pergendum nunc porro ad ea dubia solvenda quae ad Causam ejus efficientem quoquo modo reduci posse videbuntur. Est autem Juramenti Causa Efficiens, quod ad nostrum institutum attinet, duplex. Altera quam Agentem dicimus, cujus propriae est effectio: altera, quae agentem ad operandum impellit, quam ὁρμητικήν seu Impulsivam causam solemus appellare. Agens rursus aut est proxima & principalis, aut minus principalis & ab effectu remotior. Cum enim ad Juramenti obligationem duas minimum personas concurrere necesse sit, velut terminos istius relationis; personam scilicet Jurantis, qui fidem suam alteri jurejurando confirmat, & personam ejus cui juratur, qui fidem alterius sibi juramento interposito firmari postulat, quem plerique Ciceronem secuti Deferentem vocant: utriusque personae suae sunt quasi partes in hoc negotio; sed Jurantis primae & potiores, secundae Deferentis. Possunt autem spectari in utroque Agente, imprimis conditio (sive ut ita dicam idoneitas) personae, deinde & extensio Obligationis. Sunt ergo in hoc genere Causae Efficientis illa dubia primo loco consideranda, quae oriuntur ex defectu alicujus conditionis requisitae ex parte Agentis principalis ad hoc, ut sit idoneus ad suscipiendum juramentum. Duo autem potissimum requiruntur, ut quis ad jurandum idoneus sit: judicium scilicet rationis, & legitima potestas. Oportet enim ad jurandum accedere animo, & deliberato, & ad implendum promissum parato. At neque deliberare potest, qui non est præditus judicio rationis: nec fidenter aliquid polliceri & cum effectu, qui sub aliena potestate est, & non sui juris.
units.tr: Having dealt in the previous lecture with the chief difficulties that pertain more closely to the Matter of the oath, we must now proceed to resolve those doubts which may seem reducible in some way to the efficient Cause of it. For the purposes of our present undertaking, the efficient cause of an oath is twofold. One is what we call the Agent, whose proper work is the effecting of the oath. The other is that which impels the agent to act, and which we are accustomed to call the ὁρμητικήν or Impulsive cause. The agent, in turn, is either the proximate and principal one, or one that is less principal and more remote from the effect. For since at least two persons must concur in the obligation of an oath, as the terms of that relation, namely the person of the Swearer, who confirms his word to another by an oath, and the person to whom the oath is made, who asks that the word of another be secured by an oath interposed, and whom most writers, following Cicero, call the Deferens, each of these persons plays, as it were, a part in the transaction: the part of the Swearer is the first and the more important, that of the Deferens the second. Moreover, in each agent one may consider especially the condition (or, if I may so put it, the fitness) of the person, and then also the extent of the obligation. Therefore, under this head of efficient cause, those doubts must be considered first which arise from the lack of some condition required on the part of the principal agent for him to be fit to undertake an oath. Two things above all are required for a person to be fit to swear: judgement of reason, and lawful power. For one must approach an oath with a mind that is both deliberate and ready to fulfil what is promised. But he cannot deliberate who lacks the use of reason, nor can he confidently promise anything with effect who is under another's power and not his own master.

units.la: II. Dubium itaque Primum est, Quatenus obligat juramentum ejus, cui deest judicandi facultas? Qui defectus cum possit a variis causis oriri, varii propterea in hoc capite occurrunt casus. Primus est de Pueris, quoad pervenerint ad usum rationis: quod qua demum ætate fiat, nec a quoquam definitum est, nec definiri posse puto: quum alii celerius maturescant, alii tardius. Jura quidem cum civilia Romanorum, tum plerarumque gentium municipalia certos annos constituerunt, ad quos antequam perventum fit, pueri nec ad juramentum assertorium præstandum sunt admittendi, nec cogendi ad promissorium. Qualis est apud nos annus ætatis decimus sextus, quo minor qui sic nec admittitur testis in judiciis, nec exigitur ab eo Juramentum aliquod fidelitatis: imo omne Juramentum ab eo præstitum est in jure nullum. Obtinent hæc in foro externo: coecæterum in foro conscientiæ interno non eadem est ratio. Instituendi quidem sunt a prima pueritia liberi & pupilli a parentibus & tutoribus, ut juramenti vim & religionem, perjuriique gravitatem & debitas ei poenas mature intelligant, & serio expendant: quo diligentius sibi caveant ne se temere tam foedo crimine polluant, sed a prava jurandi consuetudine discant ab initio abstinere linguam suam. Vix enim cogitari poterit, quis possit esse puerilis juramenti necessarius & legitimus usus, tum ob judicandi imperitiam, tum ob illud quoque quod sub potestate aliena sunt: nisi forte a parentibus in quorum potestate sunt pro jure suo ad aliquod mandatum suum fideliter exequendum exigatur. Quemadmodum Annibalem fama est novem ferme annorum puerum a patre Amilcare inter sacrificandum aris admotum, & jurejurando adactum, ut Romani nominis perpetuus hostis esset. Sed heu, proh pudor! ex collapsa dudum ubique apud homines Christianos disciplina domestica, audias passim in vicis & in triviis pariter pueros atque puellas, ubi vix dum articulate loqui didicerint, sacrum & verendum Dei nomen ore prophano & intrepide & impune temerantes: cujus vitii teterrimum fatorem, quo puerili velut recentes testæ penitus imbuti iunt, vix tandem senes facti deponunt. Sed nolo me aliorsum rapiat doloris & indignationis æstus: redeo prorenus ad rem. Dico ergo juramentum puerorum, antequam pervenerint ad annos (ut nostri loquuntur) discretionis, vel sint doli capaces, ob defectum judicii, nec licitum esse, nec obligare. At quamprimum sunt doli capaces, ut possint quæ sit juramenti natura & vis, etsi tenuiter, aliquatenus tamen intelligere; quod ordinarie & ut plurimum contingit completo jam fere primo ætatis septennio, in multis etiam maturius, aut qui sunt præcocioris ingenii, aut in quibus malitia supplet ætatem: juramentum puerile, etsi fit (nisi fortasse excipi debeat is unicus casus, si a parente exigatur) alias penitus illicitum; præstitum tamen obligat, nisi aliunde impediatur. Ratio est, quia actus ex sua natura obligatorius, qualis est ille jurandi actus, processit, ab animo judicandi facultate aliquatenus rpædito.[?]
units.tr: II. The first doubt, then, is: how far does the oath bind one who lacks the faculty of judgement? Since this defect may arise from various causes, various cases present themselves under this head. The first concerns children, insofar as they have reached the use of reason. At what age this happens has not been fixed by anyone, nor, I think, can it be fixed, since some mature more quickly and others more slowly. The civil laws of the Romans, and the municipal laws of most nations, have indeed set certain years, before which children are neither to be admitted to give an assertory oath nor compelled to give a promissory one. Among us the age is sixteen, before which a minor is not admitted as a witness in court, nor is any oath of loyalty demanded of him; indeed, every oath taken by him is void in law. These rules hold in the external forum; but in the internal forum of conscience the reasoning is not the same. Children and wards must indeed be instructed from earliest childhood by their parents and guardians, so that they may early understand the force and sanctity of an oath, the gravity of perjury and the penalties due to it, and weigh these seriously; so that they may take more careful heed not to stain themselves rashly with so foul a crime, but learn from the start to restrain their tongues from a wicked habit of swearing. For it can hardly be conceived what necessary and lawful use a child's oath could have, both because of their inexperience in judging and because they are also under another's power, unless perhaps it is demanded by a parent, in whose power they are, for the faithful carrying out of some command of his. Thus it is said that Hannibal, a boy of about nine, was brought by his father Hamilcar to the altar while sacrificing and bound by an oath to be an everlasting enemy of the Roman name. But alas, for shame! Since domestic discipline has long since collapsed everywhere among Christian people, one may hear everywhere in the lanes and crossroads boys and girls, scarcely yet able to speak articulately, profanely, boldly and with impunity, taking the holy and reverend name of God upon their lips. The foul stench of this vice, with which they are thoroughly imbued while still young, like fresh pots, scarcely do they finally lay it aside when they grow old. But I will not let the heat of grief and indignation carry me elsewhere: I return straight to the matter. I say, then, that the oath of children, before they reach the years (as our people put it) of discretion, or are capable of malice, is neither lawful nor binding, on account of the lack of judgement. But as soon as they are capable of malice, so that they can understand, though only faintly, in some measure, what the nature and force of an oath is (which ordinarily and for the most part happens once the first seven years of life are nearly complete, and in many earlier still, either in those of precocious talent or in whom malice makes up for age), a childish oath, though it is made (unless perhaps this one case is to be excepted, if it is demanded by a parent), is otherwise wholly unlawful; yet once made it binds, unless it is hindered by some other cause. The reason is that an act which is by its nature binding, such as the act of swearing, proceeds from a mind that has in some measure the faculty of judgement.

units.la: III. Secundus Casus est de amentibus & furiosis: & Tertius itidem de stultis & morionibus. Quorum utriusque generi hominum familiare vitium est, ex ore impuro etiam incogitantes juramenta importune eructare. Quod etsi est illis a nobis condonandum; & fortassis a Deo qui summe misericors est, nec mestem expectat ubi sementem non fecit, non imputabitur eis in peccatum, quia ex invincibili mentis errore promanat: certum tamen est, quod de omni juramento pronunciavit Servator, οὐ τῷ πονηρῷ εἶναι, ex instigatione Diaboli & communi pravitate cordis humani provenire, qua sumus omnes Adæ filii inflexiles ad bonum, ad omne mali genus cerci. De ejusmodi juramentis, vana quæstio est, & nulli usui, Sint ne licita an illlicita? quia expensio rei licitæ & illicitæ ad eos tantum pertinet, qui possunt aliquatenus judicare de rebus actis aut agendis, utrum sint suæ Regulæ (id est legi Dei & rectæ rationi) conformes vel non. Qua facultate cum destituantur qui sunt impotes mentis, frustra illis legem dixeris. Næ is cum ratione sua vel magis insanit, qui ab insano rationem factorum exposcit. Interim constat ejusmodi juramenta, in quantum sunt actus amentium, nullatenus obligare. Quod si quis alias furiosus & amens, lucidis tamen animi intervallis per certa tempora ita fruatur, ut fit per illa intervalla mentis suæ compos: juramenta ab illo tunc præstita non minus obligant ad suum implerionem, quandiu contigerit eum recto rationis usu frui, quam si ab homine sanæ & sedatæ mentis præstita suissent.
units.tr: III. The second case concerns the insane and the furious; and the third likewise concerns fools and dullards. It is a common fault of both these kinds of people that they thoughtlessly belch out oaths unseasonably from impure mouths. Although this must be pardoned them by us, and perhaps by God, who is supremely merciful and does not expect a harvest where he has not sown, it will not be imputed to them as sin, since it proceeds from an invincible error of the mind; yet it is certain that the Saviour pronounced concerning every oath that it is of the evil one [οὐ τῷ πονηρῷ εἶναι], arising from the instigation of the Devil and from the common perversity of the human heart, by which we all, the sons of Adam, are inflexible to good and prone to every kind of evil. Concerning oaths of this sort, the question whether they are lawful or unlawful is an idle one and of no use, since the weighing of what is lawful and unlawful pertains only to those who can in some measure judge of things done or to be done, whether they are in accordance with their rule (that is, the law of God and right reason) or not. Since those who are deprived of the mind's powers lack this faculty, one would speak to them of the law in vain. For he who demands an account of actions from a madman is himself more mad than the madman is with his own reason. Meanwhile it is clear that oaths of this kind, insofar as they are acts of the insane, do not bind at all. But if someone who is otherwise furious and insane enjoys, in lucid intervals of mind for certain times, a condition in which he is in command of his mind during those intervals, the oaths he takes then bind him to their fulfilment no less than if they had been made by a person of sound and calm mind, for as long as he happens to enjoy the right use of reason.

units.la: IV. Casus Quartus & quintus sunt de obligatione Juramenti,
units.tr: IV. The Fourth and Fifth Cases concern the obligation of an oath

units.la: IV. Casus Quartus & quintus sunt de obligatione Juramenti, quo quis aut ebrius pollicetur aut iratus minatur se aliquid facturum, quod sobrius & pacatus fieri nolet. Ratio dubitandi est, quod cum ad hoc ut juramentum aliquod obliget, requiratur aliquod saltem animi deliberati judicium: ebrietas & iracundia, quarum utraque est amentia quædam brevis, sic judicium perturbant, & rationis usum tollunt pro tempore, ut quoad alter crapulam edormierit, alteri nonnihil defecerit ætatis animi dolor, neuter sane a furioso multum distare videatur. Cæterum de ejusmodi Juramentis illud imprimis certum est, neutrum genus excusari posse a peccato: sed utrum ebrietas aut iræ impetus peccatum quod est in illo jurandi actu aggravet an extenuet potius non satis inter omnes convenit; neque profecto videtur isti problemati una affirmatione simpliciter & sufficienter respondéri posse, cum judicium hac in parte pendeat plurimum ex circumstantiis. Sed utcunque, est ea quæstio non hujus instituti. Evincit ratio dubitationis expedire, ne quis aut ebrius aut iratus quidquam omnino juret: quia in illa mentis intemperie non potest jurare in judicio; sed necesse est ut id temere effutiat quicquid demum id sit, quod suaserint (quæ nil moderabile suadent) vinum & dolor, quodque sanus & siccus indictum injuratumque magno redemptum cuperet. Sed tamen de Obligatione distinguendum est. Nam primo, aut res illicita est in quam juravit, aut licita & honesta. Si illicita fuerit (ut plerunque fit in his præsertim juramentis quæ iratis nimia vindictæ cupiditate obcæcatis ex animo quodam impetu excidunt) manifestum est non obligare: rei enim illicitæ nullam esse obligationem ante demonstratum est satis. Idcirco & prudenter ab Abigaile admonitus est, & monenti pie obsecutus est David, postquam indigna hominis ingrati contumelia paulo lo commotior, in internecionem Nabalis & universæ domus ejus jurasset: cum posthabito jure jurando manum abstinuit a sanguine. Quod si res jurata sit licita, ut sæpe sunt ea quæ ebrii magnifice pollicentur; tum dispiciendum est secundo, qualis quantusque fuerit ebrietatis excessus: num in eo gradu ut impediret tantum aut perturbaret usum rationis, an in eo ut ipsam mentem penitus auferret, hominemque summota ratione quasi in bestiam aut feram converteret. Rationis usu penitus sublato, qui juravit tenetur ubi ad sanam mentem redierit, & ebrietatis & temerarii etiam juramenti seriam agere pœnitentiam: non tamen obligatur ad faciendum quod se facturum juravit; quia quo tempore juravit, non habuit eum usum rationis qui necessarius esset ad judicandum de rebus agendis cum aliqua animi deliberatione. At rationis usu præpedito tantum, non autem ita sublato, quin ut posset quantumvis ebrius de rebus agendis aliquo modo judicare & statuere, videtur etiam aliquo modo obligari ad juramentum aliqua saltem ex parte adimplendum, si fieri possit sine suo admodum gravi incommodo; tum ratione antecedentis deliberationis ad obligandum sufficientis, tum in aliquam temeritatis suæ pænam, ut discat in posterum sapere, & sobriam vitam agere, ne id in se temere admittat ebrius, quod eum sobrium ringat. Sed si adimpletio promissi cedat juranti in grave damnum aut incommodum; ut si quis ebrius juraret fundum unde familiam alit venditurum vili pretio : videtur non obligari. Ob eam sc. rationem, quod vix ullum potest esse certius indicium emotæ fede sua mentis, quam cum quis vino saucius id se facturum magnifice pollicetur, quod est cum suo magno malo conjunctum. Quum ergo animus inter jurandum non fuit plene liber; propterea nec erit obligatio plena. Is itaque fortassis in hoc casu erit rei non bonæ exitus non pessimus, si utraque pars, jurans sc. & is cui juratur, viri boni & prudentis arbitrio rem totam permittat: qui statuat scilicet ex circumstantiis, quotam partem par sit jurantem ejus quod promisit, in ebrietatis & ex ebrietate temeritatis pœnam persolvere.
units.tr: The fourth and fifth cases concern the obligation of an oath by which someone, when drunk, promises or, when angry, threatens to do something that he would not wish to do when sober and calm. The reason for doubt is that, for an oath to bind at all, some measure of deliberate judgment is required. Drunkenness and anger, each of which is a kind of brief madness, so disturb the judgment and suspend the use of reason for a time, that once the one has slept off his drunkenness and the other's grief of spirit has subsided, neither seems to differ much from a madman. Yet concerning oaths of this kind one thing is especially certain: neither kind can be excused from sin. But whether drunkenness or the impulse of anger makes the sin committed in the act of swearing worse, or rather lessens it, is not agreed among all; nor indeed does it seem that this question can be answered simply and adequately with a single yes or no, since the judgment in this matter depends largely on the circumstances. However that may be, that question does not belong to the present undertaking. The reason for doubt shows that it is expedient that no one, whether drunk or angry, swear anything at all, because in that disorder of mind he cannot swear deliberately; he must rashly blurt out whatever it is that wine and grief have suggested (which suggest nothing moderate), and what a sober and dry man would wish, at great cost, to have neither said nor sworn. Yet the obligation must still be distinguished. For, first, the thing sworn to is either unlawful or lawful and honourable. If it is unlawful (as usually happens, especially with those oaths which burst from the spirit in a certain rush by men blinded by an excessive desire for vengeance while angry), it is clear that it does not bind, for it has been shown sufficiently that there is no obligation to an unlawful thing. Hence David was both wisely admonished by Abigail, and dutifully obeyed her when he had been a little too stirred by the unworthy insult of an ungrateful man, and had sworn the destruction of Nabal and his whole household; he set aside his oath and kept his hand from blood. But if the thing sworn is lawful, as are often those things which the drunk promise grandly, then, secondly, one must consider what was the degree and extent of the drunkenness: whether it was of such a degree as merely to hinder or disturb the use of reason, or of such a degree as to take away the mind altogether and, reason being removed, turn the man into something like a beast or a wild animal. Where the use of reason has been wholly taken away, the one who swore is bound, when he returns to his right mind, to do serious penance both for the drunkenness and for the rash oath; yet he is not bound to do what he swore he would do, because at the time he swore he did not have that use of reason which is necessary for judging about things to be done with some deliberation. But where reason has been only hindered, and not so taken away that, however drunk, he can in some way judge and decide about things to be done, he seems in some measure to be bound to fulfil the oath at least in part, if this can be done without great inconvenience to himself: partly on account of the preceding deliberation, which is sufficient to bind, and partly as a penalty for his rashness, so that he may learn in future to be wise and to live soberly, lest he rashly commit in himself, when drunk, what would displease him when sober. But if the fulfilment of the promise would bring grave loss or inconvenience upon the one who swore, as if a drunken man swore that he would sell at a low price the farm on which his family lives, he seems not to be bound. The reason is that there can hardly be any more certain sign of a mind that has been disturbed from its proper state than when someone, wounded by wine, grandly promises to do what is joined with his own great harm. Since, therefore, the mind was not fully free while he swore, the obligation will not be full either. In this case, then, perhaps the outcome will be not the worst for a bad matter, if both parties, the one swearing and the one to whom the oath is made, leave the whole affair to the judgment of a good and prudent man, who would determine, from the circumstances, what part of what he promised the one swearing ought to pay, as a penalty for his drunkenness and for the rashness arising from drunkenness.

units.la: V. Dubium Secundum est, de Juramento ejus qui non est sui juris, sed sub pote- state alterius: ut si filiusfamilias aut pu- pillus
units.tr: V. The second doubt concerns the oath of one who is not his own master but under the power of another, as a son under his father's authority, or a ward,

units.la: pillus qui sunt sub potestate parentum & tutorum, vel servus qui est in domini potestate, vel uxor sub mariti potestate, vel subditus alicujus principis, vel miles sub imperio ducis, vel alius quivis qui alterius potestati ita subjicitur ut non sit plenarie sui juris, juramentum aliquod praestet sine permissu superiorum: quaeritur an & quatenus valeat ejusmodi juramentum? Respondeo. Non licet ei qui alterius potestati subest, de his rebus in quibus subest, aliquod jurando statuere, sine consensu sui superioris: vel expresso, si commode haberi potest; vel saltem tacito; id est, ubi jurans potest verisimiliter praesumere superiorem, si consuleretur, non contradicturum. Si secus fecerit, peccat jurando: nec obligatur ad faciendum quod juravit; imo obligatur ad non faciendum, nisi accedat superioris, ubi rem rescierit, licentia. Id quod fuse explicatum est a Mose toto hoc capite, in casu voti vel juramenti, (nam quantum ad vim obligandi ex hoc ipso versu videtur esse eadem utriusque ratio) a virgine praestiti dum est in domo patris sui, vel a muliere in domo mariti sui. Summa est, Votum virginis, si pater rescierit nec contradixerit, ratum esse; quia
units.tr: who are under the authority of parents and guardians, or a slave under his master's power, or a wife under her husband's power, or a subject of some prince, or a soldier under a commander, or anyone else who is subject to another's power so that he is not wholly his own master. Does such a person's oath, made without the permission of his superiors, have any force, and if so, how far? I answer: a person who is under another's power may not bind himself by oath in matters in which he is subject, without the consent of his superior, either express, if that can conveniently be had, or at least tacit, that is, where the one swearing can reasonably presume that his superior, if consulted, would not object. If he acts otherwise, he sins in swearing, and he is not bound to do what he swore; indeed he is bound not to do it unless the superior's permission follows once he learns of the matter. Moses explains this at length in this whole chapter, in the case of a vow or oath (for as regards its binding force, the reasoning seems to be the same for both, from this very verse), made by a virgin while she is in her father's house, or by a wife in her husband's house. In short, a maiden's vow stands if her father learns of it and does not object, because by keeping silent he is seen to have consented;

units.la: Marginal notes at the right edge are cut off and largely illegible; only fragments such as "quia", "cont", "anal", "est", "nus" are visible. quia taccndo consensisse videtur: sin contradixerlt, irritum. Quod idem per analogiam de aliis omnibus statuendum est, qui alienæ potestati subsunt, quatenus subsunt; Ut ex antecedictis manifestum est, his duabus rationibus, Primo, quia injuriam alteri facit, qui quasi jure suo statuit de iis quæ sunt juris alicni: nemo autem tenetur alteri injuriam facere, ex quinta nostra hypothesi, cum nulla fit rei illicitæ obligatio. Secundo, tenetur quisque ex officio superiori in his quibus superior est subjici, atque ipsius voluntati parere: quam obligationem ex tertia nostra hypothesi subsequens juramentum tollere non potest. Proinde omnino dicendum est, Juramentum ejus qui sub alterius potestate est, absque ipsius consensu nec licitum esse, nec obligatorium. VI. Quod tamen non est ita absolute intelligendum, quin ut duplicem admittat exceptionem: quarum altera personam respicit jurantis, altera consensum superioris. Quod ad jurantem attinet, sciendum est vix quenquam qui gaudet usu rationis, ita plene sub alterius esse potestate, quin ut sit quantum ad aliqua saltem sui juris. Et de his ita licet unicuique statuere pro suo arbitrio, etiam inconsulto superiore, ut possit aliquo actu suo sine ejus licentia inducere sibi obligationem. Non debet Caii servus Titio operam suam locare aut herilium bonorum partem aliquam ei donare vel commodare, sine consensu ipsius Caii: quia in his quae ad obsequium praestandum, ad disponendum de bonis, vel ad quamcunque familiae administrationem spectant, habet pater-familias merum imperium. Potest tamen Caii servus de a peculio suo, vel Caii filius de peculio (quod vocant) castrensi vel quasi castrensi, aliquid Titio donare vel promittere, Caio inconsulto; & si promissionem juramento firmaverint, tenentur vel eo invito promissis stare: quia habet uterque peculii sui liberam potestatem & dispositionem, estque quoad hoc sui juris. Secundo, quod ad consensum superioris attinet, sciendum ad ratihabitionem juramenti a subdito praestiti, non necessario requiri consensum praecedaneum expressum, sed sufficere consensum tacitum, sive antecedentem sive subsequentem. Consensum tacitum antecedentem
units.tr: but if he objects, it is void. The same must be held by analogy for all others who are under another's power, so far as they are under it, as is clear from what was said above, for two reasons. First, because he who binds himself as if by his own right in matters that belong to another's right does an injury to that other, and no one is bound to injure another, by our fifth hypothesis, since no obligation arises from an unlawful thing. Second, everyone is bound by duty to submit to his superior in those matters in which the superior has authority, and to obey his will; and by our third hypothesis, a subsequent oath cannot remove this obligation. Therefore it must be said absolutely that the oath of one who is under another's power is neither lawful nor binding without that person's consent. VI. This, however, is not to be understood so absolutely as to admit no double exception: of these, one concerns the person of the one swearing, the other the consent of the superior. As far as the one swearing is concerned, it must be noted that scarcely anyone who has the use of reason is so wholly under another's power that he is not his own master at least in some matters. And in these matters each person may decide for himself, even without consulting his superior, so that by some act of his own, without that superior's permission, he may bring an obligation upon himself. A slave of Gaius ought not to hire out his labour to Titius, or give or lend to him some part of his master's goods, without the consent of Gaius himself, since in matters that concern the rendering of service, the disposing of goods, or any management of the household, the head of the family has absolute authority. Yet Gaius's slave may give or promise something to Titius out of his own private property (peculium), or Gaius's son out of what they call military or quasi-military peculium, without Gaius's knowledge; and if they confirm the promise by oath, they are bound to keep it even against his wishes, since each has free power and disposal over his own property and is in that respect his own master. Second, as regards the consent of the superior, it must be noted that for the ratification of an oath made by a subordinate, an express prior consent is not necessarily required, but a tacit consent, whether prior or subsequent, is sufficient. By tacit prior consent I mean the case where, from the fairness or triviality of the matter, or from some other probable cause, it can reasonably be presumed that the superior would consent, or at least not object, if he were consulted.

units.la: a Servus quod jura-mento servus de peculio ad ministra-tionem hab. l. 20. ff. de Ju-rand. tecedentem intelligo, cum ex rei æquitate vel levitate, vel alia probabili causa verisimililiter præsumi potest, superiorem facto consensurum, vel saltem non contradicturum si consuleretur. Ut si Caio absente, vel inconsulto, uxor ejus pauperem nudum trita veste donaret, aut stipem mendico erogaret: aut filius ejus vel servus Titio vicino petenti bovem, aut plaustrum, aut aliud quid rusticæ domesticæve supellectilis utendum commodaret; aut ad ædes extruendas, fruges comportandas, aut aliud opus necessarium perficiendum operam ei suam collocaret. Consensum tacitum subsequentem intelligo, cum superior cujus in potestate est quamlibet promissionem a subdito temere factam, si sibi commodum visum fuerit, rescindere; postquam promissum rescivit, non statim & palam contradicit, nec ullo certo indicio prodit quod hactenus factum est ita sibi improbari, ut impleri porro nolit. Juxta id quod a Mose perscriptum est hujus capitis versibus sexto, octavo, aliisque: ubi ad irritandum a patre vel marito filiæ conjugisve votum, requiritur dissensus fui & aperta & matura significatio Nec enim satis est patri ad irritandum ( sic in scholis loquuntur ) filiæ votum dixisse id sibi displicere : sed oportet ut aperte contradicat, ἐὰν διαπύῃ ... v. 6. & 9. ἐὰν ἀθετήσῃ..., v. 13. & 16. si rescindendo rescindat, & tollendo tollat. Quasi diceret, oportet ut facto constanter abnuat, & interposita omni authoritate sua prohibeat quod promissum est fieri. Requiritur etiam ut id statim fiat, ἐὰν ἡμέρᾳ ἀκούσῃ, v. 6, 8, 9, 13, 15. quo primum die aliquid ea de re inaudiverit. Quasi diceret, si diffensum suum vel uno die dissimulet, votum in perpetuum stabilivit: qui enim fero se nolle significat, putandus est aliquandiu voluisse.
units.tr: a Slave, on what he has by oath concerning a slave's peculium for administration: law 20, Digest, On Oaths. I understand antecedent tacit consent to be that which can reasonably be presumed, from the fairness or triviality of the matter or some other probable cause, to be what the superior would have consented to, or at least would not have opposed had he been consulted. For example, if in Gaius's absence or without his knowledge his wife gave a poor naked man a worn-out garment or gave alms to a beggar; or if his son or slave lent a neighbour Titius, who asked for it, an ox, a cart, or some other item of farm or household equipment; or if he put his labour at the disposal of someone building a house, gathering in crops, or doing some other necessary work. I understand subsequent tacit consent to be the case where a superior, in whose power a subject is, does not at once and openly object, after learning of a promise rashly made by the subject, though he could annul it if he thought it advantageous, and gives no clear sign that what has been done is so disapproved by him that he is unwilling for it to be carried out further. This accords with what Moses wrote in the verses of this chapter, the sixth, the eighth and others, where, for a father or husband to annul a daughter's or wife's vow, a clear and timely declaration of dissent is required. For it is not enough for the father to annul (as they say in the schools) the daughter's vow by saying that it displeases him; he must openly contradict it, [ἐὰν διαπύῃ] (v. 6 and 9), [ἐὰν ἀθετήσῃ] (v. 13 and 16), "if by annulling he annuls" and "by removing he removes." As if to say: he must steadfastly refuse by his action and, by exercising all his authority, forbid what has been promised to be done. It is also required that he do this at once, [ἐὰν ἡμέρᾳ ἀκούσῃ] (v. 6, 8, 9, 13, 15), "on the very day he hears anything about the matter." As if to say: if he conceals his dissent even for one day, he has established the vow for ever; for one who does not signal that he is unwilling is to be thought to have been willing for some time.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Post considerationem personæ Iurantis, ut Agentis principalis; consideranda proxime venit persona Deferentis juramentum, sive ejus cui juratur, cujus post ipsum jurantem sunt hac in re partes secundæ. De qua est dubium Tertium: ubi duo occurrunt Casus: prout ejus spectari potest vel Authoritas, vel Fides. Casus ergo primus est; ubi de ejus authoritate ambigitur qui exigit a nobis Juramentum. Si enim fit legitimus fuperior, atque ita a nobis agnoscatur, neque aliud a nobis Juramentum exigit quam quod est lege fancitum, aut diuturna & approbata consuetudine stabilitum: nemini potest esse dubium ejusmodi juramentum & licite præstari posse, & debere fideliter adimpleri. Ast ubi videtur is qui juramentum exigit, id nullo suo jure facere, sed jus & potestatem sibi indebitam usurpare: dubitari potest non immerito, liceatne jusjurandum ab eo sic delatum suscipere; & fi susceperimus, an & quatenus obligemur. Dicendum primo, debere hominem pium & fortem juramenta omnia ab eo qui non habet legitimam potestatem imposita, quantum in ipso est omnino declinare. Non modo quia folenne est τοῖς ἐξυσιαζόυσιν ad iniqua promittenda eos in quos tyrannidem exercent compellere: sed etiam quia tenetur quisque jus suum libertatemque pro virili tueri; nec fe facile alienæ tyrannidi in servitutem tradere. At fecundo, fi præter imperium vis insuper adhibeatur, cui resi-
units.tr: After considering the person of the one swearing, as the principal agent, the person to whom the oath is sworn comes next for consideration. After the swearer himself, he is the second party in this matter. About him arises the third doubt, in which two cases occur, depending on whether his Authority or his Faith is considered. The first case, then, is where there is doubt about the authority of the one who requires an oath of us. For if he is a lawful superior, and is acknowledged as such by us, and requires from us no other oath than one sanctioned by law or established by long and approved custom, no one can doubt that such an oath may be lawfully taken and ought to be faithfully kept. But where the one who requires the oath seems to do so without any right of his own, and to usurp a power not due to him, it may not unreasonably be doubted whether it is lawful to undertake an oath so imposed, and, if we have undertaken it, whether and how far we are bound. I say first that a pious and brave man ought, as far as lies in him, entirely to avoid all oaths imposed by one who lacks lawful power. This is not only because it is customary for those in power [τοῖς ἐξουσιάζουσιν] to compel those over whom they exercise tyranny to promise unjust things, but also because each person is bound to defend his right and liberty to the best of his ability, and not to surrender himself easily into servitude to another's tyranny. But I say secondly that if, besides the command, force is further applied, to which he cannot resist, so that there is no longer any room for refusal without the greatest danger,

units.la: G resistere non poterit, ita ut nullus jam fit fine summo discrimine recufandi locus : dicendum posse virum pium tale juramentum ob vitandum grave incommodum in se admittere, sed ægre tamen & gravate & cum aliqua reluctantis animi significatione ; dummodo tamen ipsa juramenti verba (quod in hoc genere rarissimum est) nihil contineant aut ex se illicitum, aut legibus publicis contrarium, aut juri alicujus tertiæ personæ derogatorium : Alias recusare debere, etiam cum vitæ discrimine,& ultima quæque pati potius quam inhonesto vinculo obligare caput. Dicendum tertio qui juramentum susceperit a persona justam authoritatem non habente delatam, sed nulla alia ex parte vitiosam,omnino teneri ad implendum quod juravit.
units.tr: a pious man may admit such an oath in order to avoid a grave harm, but with difficulty, reluctantly and with some sign of an unwilling mind; provided, however, that the words of the oath itself (which in this kind is very rare) contain nothing in themselves unlawful, nothing contrary to public laws, and nothing derogating from the right of any third person. Otherwise he ought to refuse, even at the risk of his life, and to suffer any extremity rather than bind his head with a dishonourable chain. I say thirdly that one who has undertaken an oath tendered by a person without lawful authority, but not otherwise defective, is wholly bound to fulfil what he has sworn.

units.la: VIII. Casus secundus est, si fit is cui jurandum est Infidelis, vel Hæreticus, vel qui nobiscum antea egit non bona fide ; Dico primo, licitum esse homini infideli aut hæretico aut perjuro fidem dare. Factum id ab Isaaco & Jacobo Patriarchis itemque a Josue & primoribus bus populi Ifraelitici : qui fædera cum Allophylis & Infidelibus pepigerunt fidemq; mutuam datis ultro citroque solennibus juramentis confirmarunt. Dico secundo, fidem his datam esse omnino servandam. Solent nostri Pontificiis objectare, quod doceant fidem cum hereticis non esse servandam: in quo fieri sibi clamant summam injuriam nostri feculi Jesuitæ. Pudet sc. eos in tam clara luce dogma tam alienum ab omni sana ratione, tam humanæ societati perniciosum, palam prositeri. Sed enim evicerunt nostri, idque prolatus tabulis, defendi illam conclusionem a nonnullis ejus Ecclesiæ doctoribus, sine ulla librorum aut prohibitione, aut expurgatione. Sed ut omnes verbo tenus negarent, illud Saltem constat, si de eorum hac in re sententia aut ex doctrinæ, suæ principiis, aut ex factis factorumque ratione, prout a suarum partium nec suspectæ fidei historicis narrantur, judicare licet non esse cur sibi calumniam a nostris fieri tam fidenter clamitent. Interim sententiam illam dum nolunt videri suam, aut falsam aut impiimpiam tacito agnoscunt. Increpant aliquoties Prophetæ Reges Judæ, & præ ceteris Ezekiel toto fere capite decimo septimo, quod fidem Babyloniæ regibus juratam non servassent. Locus est insignis, & quem memini alicubi Chrysostomum & fuse & pulchre admodum explicare. Quin & Gentilium historiis nobilitata est Reguli, aliorumque hac in parte fides: qui & hostibus & Pœnis (perfidissime genti) quod jurejurando intercedente promiserant, vel cum certo capitis periculo censuerint oportere præstari. Regulum hoc elogio ornat Silius, compellans eum quasi per apostrophen.
units.tr: VIII. The second case is if the one to whom the oath is sworn is an unbeliever, or a heretic, or one who has previously dealt with us not in good faith. I say first that it is lawful to give one's faith to an unbeliever, or a heretic, or a perjurer. This was done by the patriarchs Isaac and Jacob, and likewise by Joshua and the leaders of the people of Israel, who made covenants with the foreign and unbelieving peoples and confirmed the mutual pledge of faith with solemn oaths given on both sides. I say secondly that faith given to such persons is to be kept entirely. Our people commonly object to the Papists that they teach that faith is not to be kept with heretics, and in this the Jesuits of our age loudly cry that they suffer the greatest injury. They are ashamed, that is, to profess openly in so clear a light a doctrine so alien to all sound reason and so harmful to human society. But our people have proved, by producing the records, that this conclusion has been defended by some teachers of that Church, without any prohibition or expurgation of the books. But even if they all deny it in words, this at least is certain: if one may judge their opinion in this matter, either from the principles of their doctrine, or from their deeds and the reasons for them, as they are related by historians not suspect to their own party, there is no reason why they should so confidently cry out that they are being slandered by our people. Meanwhile, while they are unwilling that that opinion appear to be their own, they tacitly acknowledge it to be either false or impious. The prophets rebuke the kings of Judah several times, and above all Ezekiel, in almost the whole of the seventeenth chapter, because they did not keep the faith sworn to the kings of Babylon. It is a notable passage, and I remember that Chrysostom somewhere explains it both at length and very finely. Indeed, the faith of Regulus, and of others in this matter, is also made famous in the histories of the Gentiles: who, when they had promised by oath to enemies and to the Carthaginians (a most treacherous people), judged that the promise ought to be kept even at certain risk of life. Silius adorns Regulus with this praise, addressing him as if by apostrophe:

units.la: Qui longum semper fama glisscente per ævum, Infidis servasse fidem memorabere Pœnis.
units.tr: You will be remembered through all ages, with fame ever growing, as the one who kept faith with faithless Carthaginians.

units.la: Objicies fortasse vulgaria illa, Fallere fallentem pro fraude non habendum, & cum Cretensibus Cretizandum. Quibus addi possunt quæ adducuntur a Grotio duo illa; alterum Bruti dictum ex Apiano
units.tr: You will perhaps object those common sayings, that deceiving a deceiver is not to be counted as fraud, and that one must play the Cretan with Cretans. To these may be added the two sayings cited by Grotius: one the saying of Brutus from Appian,

units.la: Ἓντον πησον δὅτι ‘Ρωμαίοις περὶ τυραννους Ὁλ’ὅνορκον, cum tyranno nulla Romanis fides est aut juramenti religio: alterum e veteri Tragico, Fregisti fidem, inquit ille quidam; respondet alter, Quam neque dedi neque do infideli cuiquam. Respondeo, ista e communi vita sumpta ostendere magis quid facere soleat vulgus hominum, quam quid fieri debeat. Vel si sint pro veris admittenda, ibi solum probari, ubi juratum est sub conditione: vel expressa, ut si dicam, Juro me daturum tibi centum, si tu mihi fundum pignori datum intra mensem redemeris; vel saltem tacita, ut cum duo homines mutuis juramentis se obligant ad mutua promissa praestanda per respectum mutuum. Exempli gratia, Si Chremes herus juraret Sosiae servo se daturum ei annuatim decem aureos, Sosia vicissim Chremeti juraret se ei serviturum octo annis: qui horum utervis promissam fidem prior violaret, alterum fidei religione protenus liberaret. At si duo homines mutuo se obligent promissis diversi generis, aut non eodem tempore, aut alias citra mutuum respectum : violata ab uno fides non liberat alterum obligatione; sed uterque tenetur id fervare quod ipse juravit, etiamsi alter quod suarum erat partium non effecerit. Exempli gratia : Rex aliquis simpliciter & citra respectum ad fidelitatem subditorum jurat fe regnum administraturum juste & secundum leges : Subditi alio tempore simpliciter et citra respectum ad Principis officium jurant fe ei debitam fidelitatem & obedientiam prestituros. Utrique obligantur quod sui est officii fideliter facere, etsi defecerit altera pars a suo officio : ita ut neque Rex solutus fit suo juramento, si subditi debitum obsequium non prætiterint; nec Subditi suo, si Rex a justitiæ tramite deflexerit.
units.tr: [Ἓντον πησον δὅτι ‘Ρωμαίοις περὶ τυραννους Ὁλ’ὅνορκον] (with a tyrant the Romans have no faith or regard for an oath); the other from an old tragedian, where one man says, You have broken faith, and the other replies, Which I neither gave nor give to any faithless man. I answer that these sayings, taken from common life, show more what the common run of men is wont to do than what ought to be done. Or, if they are to be admitted as true, they prove this only where the oath was sworn under a condition, either expressed, as if I say, I swear that I will give you a hundred, if you redeem within a month the field given to you in pledge, or at least tacit, as when two men bind themselves by mutual oaths to perform mutual promises by mutual regard. For example, if Chremes, the master, swore to his servant Sosias that he would give him ten gold pieces a year, and Sosias in turn swore to Chremes that he would serve him for eight years: whichever of them first violated the promised faith would at once free the other from the bond of faith. But if two men bind themselves mutually by promises of different kinds, either not at the same time, or otherwise without mutual regard, faith violated by one does not release the other from obligation; rather each is bound to keep what he himself has sworn, even if the other has not done what belonged to his part. For example: some king swears simply, and without regard to the loyalty of his subjects, that he will govern the kingdom justly and according to the laws. Subjects at another time swear simply, and without regard to the office of the prince, that they will render him due fidelity and obedience. Each is bound to do faithfully what belongs to his office, even if the other party has failed in his duty; so that neither the king is released from his oath if the subjects have not rendered due obedience, nor the subjects from theirs if the king has turned aside from the path of justice.

units.la: IX. Hactenus de conditione utriusque persona Agentis : Jurantis sc. ut principalis, & Juramentum deferentis, ut minus principalis. Dubium quartum sequitur, de Extensione obligationis respectu utriusque personæ; ubi duo occurrunt Casus. Prior casus respicit perfonam Jurantis: An & quatenus Juramentum obliget Jurantis hæredes & successores ? Exempli gratia, Caius empto Titii fundo jurat simpliciter fe soluturum ei intra sex menses centum libras: Interea temporis moritur Caius : queritur an vi juramenti a Caio preftiti teneatur Caii hæres solvere promissas pecunias ? Respondetur, teneri quidem Caii hæredem ad folvendum, ratione rei quæ causam dedit juramento, in quantum fruitur commodo illius fundi pro quo promissæ sunt pecuniæ : heres enim de jure tenetur solvere justa debita defuncti in cujus bona fuccedit, & æquissimum est ut hæreditas transeat cum onere suo. Non tamen tenetur hæres vi juramenti a defuncto preftiti: ita ut fi non solverit, injustus tantum fit, non item perjurus. Cujus ratio est: quia juramentum est vinculum perfonale, & inducit obligationem spiritualem tantum in conscientiæ foro interiori, non autem civilem five temporalem in foro externo. At in personalibus nemo ligatur fine proprio consensu. Si dicatur Caium per actum suum personalem obligare posse se & hæredes suos ad aliquid faciendum, ut quotidie fieri videmus in syngraphis obligatoriis: ergo videri a pari posse eum & sacramento obligare hæredes; præsertim si expressis verbis dicat se jurare pro se & hæredibus suis. Respondeo non esse parem utrobique rationem. Quia Obligationem spiritualem quæ est in conscientia necesse est esse personalem; sicut est sua cuique conscientia propria, & quæ non possit transire in aliam personam: at obligatio temporalis sequitur rem temporalem; quæ, cum possit transire ad aliam personam, potest consequenter alteri personæ obligationem inducere. Tenetur ergo hæres ex equitate rei, non vi juramenti.
units.tr: IX. So far concerning the condition of both persons who act: the one swearing, as principal, and the one to whom the oath is tendered, as less principal. The fourth question follows, concerning the extent of the obligation with respect to each person, and two cases arise here. The first case concerns the person of the swearer: whether, and how far, an oath binds the swearer's heirs and successors? For example, Gaius, having bought Titius's farm, swears simply that he will pay him one hundred pounds within six months. Meanwhile Gaius dies. The question is whether Gaius's heir is bound, by virtue of the oath sworn by Gaius, to pay the promised money. The answer is that the heir is indeed bound to pay, by reason of the thing which gave cause for the oath, insofar as he enjoys the benefit of that farm for which the money was promised. For by law an heir is bound to pay the just debts of the deceased into whose goods he succeeds, and it is most equitable that an inheritance pass along with its burden. Yet the heir is not bound by virtue of the oath sworn by the deceased, so that if he does not pay, he is merely unjust, not also perjured. The reason is this: an oath is a personal bond, and it induces an obligation that is spiritual only, in the inner forum of conscience, and not civil or temporal in the outer forum. But no one is bound in personal matters without his own consent. If it be said that Gaius, by his personal act, can bind himself and his heirs to do something, as we see done every day in written obligations, then by the same reasoning he could bind his heirs by an oath as well; especially if he says in express words that he swears for himself and his heirs. I answer that the reasoning is not parallel on both sides. For the spiritual obligation which exists in conscience must be personal, just as each person's conscience is his own and cannot pass into another person. But temporal obligation follows a temporal thing, and since that thing can pass to another person, it can consequently induce an obligation in that other person. The heir is therefore bound by the equity of the thing, not by virtue of the oath.

units.la: X. Casus posterior
units.tr: X. Latter case

units.la: X. Casus posterior respicit personam ejus cui juratur: An qui juravit aliquid alicui facturum, eo defuncto obligetur id facere heredi ejus vel successori? Respondeo, ordinarie obligari. Certum est jurantem obligari, si expresserit id se facturum ipsi aut hæredi. Obligari etiam censendus est, etsi non sit expressum, ubi juramentum suscipitur ratione alicujus dignitatis : quia dignitas non variatur ex varietate personarum. Unde siquis subditus aut Miles juret fidelitatem Regi, vel Imperatori exercitus ; censebitur juramentum factum etiam quoad successores in eadem dignitate. Idem dicendum est in materia debiti, & plerisque aliis rebus, in quibus ratio aliqua officii aut contractus causam præbuit juramento. Siquæras unde fiat ut Juramenti vinculum, cum fit personale ex parte jurantis, non fit etiam personale ex parte ejus cui juratur, sed transeat ad hæredes & successores: five quod idem est, quare potest quis fe obligare alicui & successoribus ejus, etsi successores in juramento non exprimantur; non potest autem obligare fe & successores suos, etsi diserte exprimantur: Respondeo, discriminis rationem in hoc positam esse, quod in altero casu agatur de obligatione propria, in altero de obligatione aliena. Obligare potest quivis seipsum spiritualiter prout ipse voluerit & intenderit; & proinde poteft per actum proprium obligare se tam successoribus alterius, quam personae ipsius: at non potest quis alteri inducere obligationem, nisi ipse quoque voluerit; & proinde non potest actu suo obligare spiritualiter nisi seipsum tantum. Quod autem dixi in responsione ad dubium in hoc casu jurantem ordinarie obligari: id propterea dixi, quia fieri potest ut interdum non obligetur. Nam cum de jurantis intentione, ex natura rei & materiae subjectae praecipue judicari debeat: ubi ex natura rei promissae & aliis circumstantiis veri similiter praesumi potest jurantem intendisse promissionem tantum personalem ei cui juravit, et non successoribus ejus; obligatio juramenti non transfit ad successores.
units.tr: X. Casus posterior concerns the person to whom the oath is sworn: if someone has sworn that he will do something for another person, and that person has died, is he bound to do it for his heir or successor? I answer that, as a rule, he is bound. It is certain that the swearer is bound if he has expressed that he will do it for that person or for his heir. He is also to be considered bound, even if it is not expressed, where the oath is taken by reason of some dignity, because dignity does not vary with a change of persons. Hence if a subject or a soldier swears allegiance to a king or to the commander of an army, the oath will be considered made also with regard to successors in the same dignity. The same is to be said in the matter of a debt, and in many other matters, in which some ground of office or of contract has given cause for the oath. If you ask how it happens that the bond of the oath, since it is personal on the part of the swearer, is not also personal on the part of the person to whom the oath is sworn, but passes to heirs and successors; or, what is the same, why a man can bind himself to someone and his successors even though successors are not named in the oath, but cannot bind himself and his successors even when these are expressly named: I answer that the reason for the difference lies in this, that in the one case the matter concerns an obligation of his own, and in the other an obligation of another. Anyone can bind himself spiritually, in so far as he himself wills and intends; and therefore by his own act he can bind himself to the successors of another as well as to that person himself. But no one can induce an obligation in another person unless that person also wills it; and therefore he cannot by his act spiritually bind anyone but himself. But when I said in the answer to the question that in this case the swearer is as a rule bound, I said it because it may happen that at times he is not bound. For since the swearer's intention must be judged chiefly from the nature of the matter and of the subject matter, if from the nature of the promised thing and other circumstances it can reasonably be presumed that the swearer intended a promise merely personal to the person to whom he swore, and not to his successors, then the obligation of the oath does not pass to successors.

units.la: XI. Sed de Causis Agentibus haec dicta sufficiant: ad Impulsivas tran- sfeo.
units.tr: XI. But let what has been said about the efficient causes suffice; I pass on to the impulsive causes.

units.la: Quae partim internae sunt, partim externae. Internas dico, cum quis ex mero motu propriae voluntatis
units.tr: These are partly internal, partly external. I call them internal when someone, from the mere motion of his own will,

units.la: Prælectio Quarta.
units.tr: Lecture Four.

units.la: tatis fine alterius impulsu, sponte fe ad jurandum offert : vel ex impetu quodam iræ, amoris, alteriufve perturbari animi passionis ; vel etiam ex sola peccandi libidine & impia quadam jurandi consuetudine inter loquendum temere & fine judicio juramenta subinde fpargit. Quod vitium, ob peccati cum gravitatem tum frequentiam, optarim ut in sacris concionibus & sæpius et vehementius reprehenderetur ; quod video suis temporibus a sanctissimo viro JohanneChrysoftomo diligenter & acerrime factum : ne iustissimo Dei iudicio propter juramenta terra lugeat, & Dominus juret in ira sua, non se habiturum innoxios, qui verendum ipsius nomen ita contemptui habent, ut non vereantur sine necessitate sacrosanctam Dei majestatem testem & arbitrum ad ducere. Sed de toto isto juramentorum genere non est quod multa dicam. Omnino prohibitum est omne juramentum spontaneum, nisi causa subsit gravis & necessaria. Audire est operae pretium, quid de se Augustinus, Juro, inquit, sed quantum mihi videtur magna necessitate compulsus, cum video non mihi credi vult faciam, & ei qui mihi non credit non expedire quod non credit. Quasi diceret, tunc solum jurandum est, cum expedit ut nobis credatur, & injuratis non crederetur. Et in hoc casu (in quo solo licitum est) juramentum ultra praestitum vel maxime obligat: cum nullum vinculum arctius obliget, quam quod sponte suscept um est.
units.tr: ...of his own free will, at another's urging, offers himself to swear; or from some violent passion of anger, love, or another disturbance of the mind; or even from mere lust for sinning and a godless habit of swearing, so that in conversation he rashly and without thought scatters oaths from time to time. This vice, because of the gravity and frequency of the sin, I would wish to see reproved in sacred sermons more often and more vehemently. St. John Chrysostom did this carefully and sharply in his own time, lest by the most just judgment of God because of oaths the land mourns, and the Lord swear in his wrath that he will not hold guiltless those who hold his reverend name in such contempt that they do not hesitate, without necessity, to call the most holy majesty of God as witness and judge. But there is no need for me to say much about this whole kind of oath. Every voluntary oath is absolutely forbidden unless a serious and necessary cause lies behind it. It is worth hearing what Augustine says of himself: I swear, but as far as it seems to me, compelled by great necessity, when I see that I am not wished to be believed; I will do it, and it is not expedient for one who does not believe me that he should not believe. As if he meant that one may swear only when it is expedient that we be believed, and otherwise we would not be believed when we swear. And in this case (the only one in which it is lawful), an oath once given binds most strongly of all, since no bond binds more tightly than one undertaken of one's own accord.

units.la: XII. His itaque missis pergo ad causas impulsivas externas: quae duae sunt potissimum, Dolus & Vis.
units.tr: XII. Having set these aside, I now proceed to the external impelling causes, of which there are two chief ones: Deceit and Force.

units.la: Dubium ergo Quintum est, de obligatione Juramenti, quod dolo & astu elicitum est: id est, cum quis alieno verbo vel facto in errorem inductus, jurat se aliquid facturum, quod nisi ab alio deceptus non suisset juraturus. Cujus rei illustre habemus exemplum de Josue & Principibus populi Israelitici: qui a Gibeonitis simulantibus se peregrinos esse, qui e longinqua regione venissent ut foederis conjunctionem cum populo Dei quererent, decepti admiserunt eos in foedus, pacemque illis interposito jurejurando dederunt. Qui tamen postquam se deceptos senserunt, non ausi sunt rescindere juramentum, cujus religione se obstrictos sciebant, sed vitam ipsis & pacem prout pacti essent concesserunt : rationem tantum inierunt (impositā eis conditione, ut ad vilissima quæque ministeria adhiberentur,) qua Gibeonitæ & præsentis doli pœnas aliquas darent, & in officio continerentur, nequa Israelitis in posterum nocere possent. De quo facto sic Ambrosius, Josue pacem quam dederat revocandam non censuit, quia firmata erat sacramenti religione, ne dum alienam perfidiam arguit, suam fidem solveret. Quo uno exemplo satis constat juramentum dolo elicitum habere vim obligandi. Et ne quis existimet Josue cum suis fuisse hac in re plus æquo superstitiosos : non ipsi solum populo qui Gibeonitas putabat jurejurando non obstante occidendos esse, restiterunt, hac reddita consilii sui ratione, Juravimus sibi in nomine Dei Israel & ideo non possumus eos contingere : sed & Deus ipse duplici postea signo rem comprobavit. Altero, dum depugnanti Josue pro Gibeo-
units.tr: The fourth question, then, concerns the obligation of an oath that has been drawn out by deceit and cunning: that is, when someone, led into error by another's word or deed, swears that he will do something which, had he not been deceived by the other, he would not have sworn to do. We have a notable example of this in Joshua and the leaders of the people of Israel. The Gibeonites pretended to be foreigners who had come from a distant land seeking alliance with the people of God, and Joshua and the leaders, deceived, admitted them into covenant and gave them peace under a sworn oath. Yet when they perceived that they had been deceived, they did not dare to break the oath, by whose sacredness they knew themselves bound, but granted them life and peace as they had been pledged. They only devised a plan (imposing a condition that they be assigned to the lowliest of tasks) by which the Gibeonites would pay some penalty for the present deceit and be kept in subjection, lest they could ever harm the Israelites in the future. Of this deed Ambrose says: Joshua did not judge that the peace he had given should be revoked, because it was confirmed by the sacredness of an oath; lest, while he exposed another's faithlessness, he should break his own faith. From this one example it is sufficiently clear that an oath drawn out by deceit has binding force. And lest anyone think that Joshua and his men were in this matter more scrupulous than was right: they not only resisted the people, who thought the Gibeonites should be killed notwithstanding the oath, giving the reason for their decision, We have sworn to them in the name of the Lord God of Israel, and therefore we cannot touch them; but God himself afterwards confirmed the matter by a twofold sign. The first was when, as Joshua fought for Gibeon

units.la: {f} Jos.9 19 Gibeonitis adversus conjuratos in eorum perniciem Reges victoriam insignem, edito etiam illustri miraculo, concessit. Altero, cum post centum superque annos Saul regis injusta pacti cum Gibeonitis fœderis violatio triennii fame publica vindicata, septemque e liberis ejus publico suspendio ex Dei ipsius mandato tandem expiata est.
units.tr: {f} Jos. 9. 19 against the conspiring kings to their destruction, God granted a remarkable victory, with an illustrious miracle also displayed. The second was when, more than a century later, King Saul's unjust violation of the covenant with the Gibeonites was avenged by a public famine for three years, and at last, by God's own command, it was expiated by the public hanging of seven of his sons.

units.la: XIII. Est tamen in hoc casu aliqua distinctio admittenda.
units.tr: XIII. Yet in this case some distinction must be admitted.

units.la: Nam error ille, in quem inductus est alterius dolo cui juravit, si sit circa aliquam circumstantiam tantum, aut circa causam rei aliquo modo extrinsecam & quasi accidentariam; non tollit obligationem: ut ex errore Israelitarum circa Gibeonitas jam patuit. Quod idem dicendum est, Si Caius Titii viduam juraret se ducturum uxorem, putans eam esse divitem cum esset pauper; teneretur eam ducere, nec iste error tolleret obligationem: & sic de aliis juramentis ejusdem rationis. At si error sit circa substantiam ipsius rei, aut propriam ejus causam; ut si Caius juraret matrimonium contrahere cum hac fœmina particulari sub nomine Titiæ; putans eam esse Titiam quæ non est, & postea errorem suum deprehenderet: non teneretur juramento. Error enim circa substantiam rei, quæ fuit propria jurandi causa, irritam facit promissionem, & obligationem tollit.
units.tr: For that error into which someone is led by the deceit of the person to whom he swore does not annul the obligation if it concerns only some circumstance, or some cause of the thing that is in some way extrinsic and, as it were, accidental; as the error of the Israelites concerning the Gibeonites has already shown. The same must be said if Gaius, supposing a widow of Titius to be rich when she is poor, were to swear that he would marry her: he would be bound to marry her, and this error would not remove the obligation; and so with other oaths of the same kind. But if the error concerns the substance of the thing itself, or its proper cause; as if Gaius swore to contract marriage with this particular woman under the name of Titia, supposing her to be Titia when she is not, and afterwards discovered his mistake: he would not be bound by the oath. For an error concerning the substance of the thing, which was the proper cause of the swearing, makes the promise void and removes the obligation.

units.la: XIV. Dubium Sextum & ultimum est, de Vi: sive de Juramento per metum extorto contra voluntatem jurantis, ita ut metus ille si abesset, nollet jurare. Et est quæstio sane difficilis & intricata: conabor tamen summam rei expedire, quam potero & brevitate & perspicuitate.
units.tr: XIV. The sixth and last question is concerning Force: that is, concerning an oath extorted by fear, against the will of the one swearing, such that, were the fear absent, he would not wish to swear. This is a question certainly difficult and intricate; yet I shall try to set out the substance of the matter as well as I can, both briefly and clearly.

units.la: Casus ergo primus est, ubi metus est levis, & qui non facile cadit in constantem virum: ut si quis metu iniquæ censuræ, vel irrisionis, vel iræ & offensionis alicujus viri potentis, juramento se promitteret facturum aliquid quod sibi esset inconveniens, quodque ni metus ille esset, nec facere vellet nec promittere. Pro responsione illud imprimis repetendum est, quod in tota hac materia juramentaria est sanctissime observandum, si quid proponatur jurandum, quod est contra legem Dei, contra officium hominis Christiani, ftiani, contra bonos mores, contra leges Reip. contra antecedentem obligationem, aut alio quocunque refpe&tu illicitum ; non debere ullo aut commodi intuitu, aut periculi metu, ejusmodi juramentum aut prastari, aut prastitum adimpleri. Hoc supposito dico, viro forti(id est pio ; pius enim esse nequit qui non est fortis) simpliciter contemnendum esse inanem & levem metum, & omne ejusmodi juramentum constanter & intrepide recusandum. Nimirum est Vir justus fortis ut leo ; qua fortitudine qui deuitutus est, vix fieri potest ut faciat insigne aliquid viro bono dignum. Qui enim observat ventum non seminabit, & qui speculatur nubes non metet, inquit Solomon. Imo vix fieri potest quin ut multa sane faciat viro bono indigna : Timor enim hominis, eodem Salomone teste, adducit laqueum. At siquis forte præ animi angustia incautior laqueo se implicari passus fuerit, ligavit ligamen super animam suam, & tenetur id qnod promisit adimplere.
units.tr: The first case, then, is where the fear is slight, and one that does not easily fall upon a steadfast man: as if someone, from fear of unjust censure, or ridicule, or the anger and displeasure of some powerful man, were to promise by oath to do something unsuitable for himself, which, were it not for that fear, he would neither wish to do nor promise. In reply, it must first be repeated, which in this whole matter of oaths is to be most carefully observed: if anything is proposed to be sworn which is against the law of God, against the duty of a Christian man, against good morals, against the laws of the commonwealth, against a prior obligation, or unlawful in any other respect, then on no account, whether for the sake of advantage or from fear of danger, ought such an oath either to be performed or, once performed, to be fulfilled. With this assumed, I say that a brave man (that is, a pious one, for one who is not brave cannot be pious) must simply despise a vain and light fear, and must steadfastly and fearlessly refuse every oath of this kind. Indeed the just man is bold as a lion; and when one is deprived of this courage, it can hardly happen that he does anything noble and worthy of a good man. For "he who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap," says Solomon. Indeed it can hardly be avoided that he does many things unworthy of a good man: for, as the same Solomon bears witness, "the fear of man brings a snare." But if someone, through narrowness of spirit, has been somewhat too incautious and allowed himself to be entangled in a snare, he has bound a bond upon his own soul, and he is bound to fulfil what he promised.

units.la: Casus
units.tr: Case

units.la: SECT. XV.
units.tr: SECT. XV.

units.la: Casus secundus est, ubi gravis & justus est metus, & qui cadere potest in constantem virum: qualis est metus captivitatis, amissionis omnium bonorum, infamiæ, cruciatus, & quod est ipsius mortis. Dico primum ut supra, si juramentum contineat in se quid illiciti, ne vel mortis vitandæ causâ à viro honesto suscipi debere; nec suscepstum posse sine peccato servari. Audito Christiani aurcam hominis Ethnici hac de re sententiam: m Justum & tenacem propositi virum Non civium ardor prava jubentium, Non vultus instantis tyranni Mente quatit solida. Dico secundo, si res exigatur intentatâ vi aliqua aut gravi metu, quæ nec illicita est, nec cuiquam injuria, sed ipsi tantum juranti plus minúsve incommoda; ut siquis iter faciens inciderét in latrones, qui mortem ei strictis gladiis minarentur, nisi promissâ sub juramento certa pecuniæ summâ vitam redimat: licitum esse in hoc casu pecuniam promittere, & promissionem jurejurando firmare. Ratio est, quia è duobus propositis malis licet, & prudentem decet, minus eligere: & minus malum est pecuniæ jactura quàm vitæ. Dico tertio, Juramentum istiusmodi obligare, & pactum
units.tr: The second case is where the fear is grave and just, and such as may fall upon a constant man: such as fear of captivity, loss of all goods, infamy, torture, and finally of death itself. I say, first, as above, that if the oath contains anything unlawful, it ought not to be taken by an honest man, not even to avoid death, and once taken it cannot be kept without sin. I have heard the golden opinion of a Christian on this matter from a heathen man: The man who is just and firm of purpose is not shaken in his solid mind by the passion of citizens demanding wicked things, nor by the face of a threatening tyrant. I say, secondly, that if a thing is demanded under some threatened violence or grave fear, which is neither unlawful nor an injury to anyone, but only a greater or lesser inconvenience to the one swearing, as when someone travelling on a journey falls among robbers who threaten him with drawn swords unless he ransoms his life by promising a certain sum of money under oath, then it is lawful in such a case to promise the money and to confirm the promise by an oath. The reason is that of two evils one may, and a prudent man ought, choose the lesser; and the loss of money is a smaller evil than the loss of life. I say thirdly that an oath of this kind binds, and that the agreed price must by all means be paid to the robbers.

units.la: H cum prædonibus precium omninò esse persolvendum. Quod etsi videatur ex antedictis esse satis manifestum; tamen cùm habeat hæc assertio magni nominis adversarios, inque his Ciceronem (singularis judicii virum, & de jurisjurandi religione, quoad licuit homini Gentili, hoc uno dempto cætera female rectissimè sentientem:) non abs re erit assertionem hanc aliquot rationibus confirmare. Primo ergo, qui jurat rem licitam & possibilem, tenetur id præstare: atqui pactam prædoni pecuniam solvere nec illicitum est, nec impossibile: ergo tenetur. Secundo, elegit id quod tunc visum est ipsi melius, quodque si e duobus alterum ipsi esset jam nunc necessario eligendum, denuo eligeret: & videtur non posse honestè recusari, quod fuit prudenter electum. Tertio, quod ob certum finem promissum est, à promittente debet præstari, postquam consecutus est suum finem; quia omne sub conditione pactum, conditione illâ præstitâ debet & ipsum præstari: quo maximè fundamento nititur Voti conditionalis obligatio. Sed pactus cum latrone precium, eo fine id fecit, ut vitam suam redimeret: ergo postquam vitam redemit, assecutus finem quem intendebat, debet exsolvere quod promisit. Quarto, suspecta debet esse semper prudentia carnis, ut inimica cordis puritati, & tranquillitati conscientiæ tiæ insidiosa: Prudentia autem carnis, quæ demum est, si hæc non fit, ubi videtur honestas cum utilitate certare, honcito postponito, id quod utile est amplecti? Vix poterit de pecunia pacta solvenda multum deliberare, cui potiores sunt divitiis religio & fides, & qui posthabendum statuit tranquilitati mentis commodum temporale. Quinto, demum laudantur Ethnicis Regulus, aliique (ut dictum est superius) qui fidem hostibus servarunt, etsi iniquissimis conditionibus pactam: Laudatur & ipsi Ciceroni Pomponius tribunus, qui servavit quod terrore coactus juraverat, idque hoc adjecto epiphonemate, tantum temporibus illis jusjurandum valeat.
units.tr: Although this may seem sufficiently clear from what has been said, yet since this assertion has adversaries of great name, among them Cicero (a man of singular judgement, who, as far as a heathen could, thought most rightly about the sanctity of an oath in everything except this one point), it will not be out of place to confirm the assertion by several reasons. First, then, one who swears to do a lawful and possible thing is bound to perform it; but to pay the money agreed with a robber is neither unlawful nor impossible; therefore he is bound. Secondly, he chose what then seemed better to him, and if one of two options had to be chosen again now, he would choose the same; and it seems that what was prudently chosen cannot honestly be refused. Thirdly, what is promised for a certain end ought to be performed by the one promising once he has attained his end, since every promise made under a condition must itself be performed once that condition is fulfilled; and this is the chief foundation on which the obligation of a conditional vow rests. But he who agreed with the robber on a price did so for the end that he might redeem his life; therefore, once he has redeemed his life and attained the end he intended, he must pay what he promised. Fourthly, the prudence of the flesh must always be suspected, as hostile to purity of heart and insidious to tranquillity of conscience. Now what is the prudence of the flesh, if not this: where honesty and advantage seem to clash, to set honesty aside and embrace what is useful? Hardly could one deliberate long about paying the money agreed, to whom religion and faith are worth more than riches, and who judges temporal gain to be of less account than peace of mind. Fifthly, the heathen praise Regulus and others (as was said above) who kept faith with their enemies, though the terms they had agreed to were most unjust. Cicero himself also praises Pomponius the tribune, who kept what he had sworn under compulsion of terror, adding this exclamation: such was the value of an oath in those times.
