units.la: Ast excipiunt qui contra sentiunt; Imprimis, Non esse hostis, & latronis vel piratæ eandem rationem: cum hoste, perinde ac cum litis adversario, jure agendum (Gentium hic, ut illic civili:) & proinde fidem ei servandam; at cum prædone, velut humani generis communi hoste, nullam esse juris, ergo nec & fidei societatem. Respondeo: primo, peritos juris interpretes affirmare, esse aliquam vel cum latrone juris societatem; ut cui ex jure gentium depositum fit reddendum; ergo à pari & promissum solvendum. Secundo, etli latroni nihil deberetur, ut personae indignae; qua ratione nudae promissionis exsolutio posset fortassis excusatius evitari: at Deo saltem praestandam esse fidem. Objiciunt secundo, isto pacto honestum civem à sceleratis hominibus spoliari, quod cedit in malum publicum. Respondeo, imò vero honesti civis vitam servari, quod cedit in bonum publicum. Aut latrocinia, inquiunt tertio, & rapinae hac ratione stabilientur, si latronibus non modò impune erit, sed & lautè. Respondeo, id si fiat, per accidens fieri: ipsorum vitio, non illius; qui nec juvit ullo modo latrones, nec vel probavit promittendo vel probat promissum servando ipsorum factum; quin potius dum consuluit sibi, ipsorum quoque scelera ita impedivit, ut latrones essent solum, non item homicidae. Objiciunt quarto, Obligationem juramenti oriri ex actu judicii & voluntatis deliberato: ergo ubi voluntas non est libera, ita ut non tam actio dicenda sit quàm coactio, nullam videri esse qui (n) obligationem. Respondeo, Voluntatem cogi non posse, & hoc ab omnibus agnosci. Potest quidem esse coactio ex parte principii actionis externi & remoti; sed ex parte principii proximi, quae est in omnibus actibus humanis voluntas, nulla potest esse coactio. Juramentum ergo qui facit latroni, ut vitam servet volens facit, Non est ergo ejusmodi juramentum ἁπλῶς ἀκούσιον simpliciter involuntarium, sed mixtum; quod Aristoteli μὴ ἑκούσιον dicitur: actio sc. partim invita, quia fit non libenter; partim voluntaria, quia fit cum electione, etsi non liberrima, libera tamen satis ad hoc ut dici mereatur potius voluntaria quam involuntaria; quia agens data sibi duorum optione potestatem habet eligendi utrum ex his malit. Et vult, qui mavult. Non ergo recte dicitur eum coactum jurasse, qui cum poterat non jurasse maluit jurare. Mors enim interminata nisi juraret, permissum est ipsius arbitrio, malletne damnum interminatum pati, an juramenti obligatione ab illo damno liberari. Deliberavit, elegit obligari: ergo obligari voluit: & qui se voluisse obligari fatetur, absurde dixerit (a) se coactum esse, & propterea non obligari. Objiciunt quinto, Latroni nihil deberi, & proinde viatorem non obligari; cum omnibus obligatio dicat relationem ad debitum, ut ante dictum est: Latroni autem nil deberi probatur, quia nullum jus fundatur in injuria, & iniquissimum videtur ut quis ex facto suo injurioso jus aliquod sibi adquirat: ergo latroni, qui metum viatori incussit, & contra bonos mores extorsit ab eo juramentum
units.tr: But those who think otherwise object. First, an enemy and a robber or pirate do not fall under the same rule: with an enemy, one deals by law just as one does with an opponent in a lawsuit (the law of nations here, as civil law there), and so faith must be kept with him. But with a pirate, as a common enemy of the human race, there is no legal fellowship and therefore no fellowship of faith. I reply: first, that skilled interpreters of law affirm that there is some legal relation even with a robber, since a deposit must be returned to him under the law of nations; therefore, by parity, a promise must also be kept. Second, even if nothing is owed to a robber as an unworthy person, by which reasoning the performance of a bare promise might perhaps be avoided with a cleaner conscience, still faith must be kept at least toward God. They object secondly that by this course an honest citizen is robbed by wicked men, which tends to public harm. I reply: on the contrary, the life of an honest citizen is preserved, which tends to the public good. Or, they say thirdly, robberies and plunders would be established by this method, if robbers were not only to go unpunished but to profit handsomely. I reply: if that happens, it happens by accident, through their own fault and not his; he neither helped the robbers in any way, nor approved their deed by promising, nor approves it by keeping the promise. Rather, while he looks after himself, he also so checks their crimes that they are only robbers and not also murderers. They object fourthly that the obligation of an oath arises from a deliberate act of judgment and will; therefore, where the will is not free, so that the act is to be called compulsion rather than action, there seems to be no obligation. I reply: the will cannot be compelled, and everyone acknowledges this. There can indeed be compulsion on the part of the external and remote principle of the action, but on the part of the proximate principle, which in all human acts is the will, no compulsion is possible. Therefore the one who swears to a robber in order to save his life does so willingly. Such an oath is not therefore simply involuntary [ἁπλῶς ἀκούσιον], but mixed, which Aristotle calls not voluntary [μὴ ἑκούσιον]: that is, an action partly unwilling, because it is done not gladly, and partly voluntary, because it is done with choice, though not the freest choice, yet free enough that it deserves to be called voluntary rather than involuntary, since the agent, given a choice between two options, has the power to choose which of the two he prefers. And he wills who prefers. It is therefore not correct to say that he swore under compulsion who, when he could have not sworn, preferred to swear. For since death was threatened only if he did not swear, it was left to his own judgment whether he preferred to suffer the threatened harm or to be freed from that harm by the obligation of an oath. He deliberated, he chose to be bound; therefore he willed to be bound. And one who admits that he wished to be bound would absurdly say that he was forced (a), and for that reason is not bound. They object fifthly that nothing is owed to a robber, and therefore the traveller is not bound, since every obligation implies a relation to something due, as was said before. But that nothing is owed to a robber is proved because no right is founded on injustice, and it seems most unjust that anyone should acquire any right for himself from his own wrongful act. Therefore to the robber, who put fear into the traveller and extorted an oath from him against good morals,

units.la: (a) Sic Ferrar. Nazian. Greek notes printed in the right margin, not transcribed in full. mentum iniquum, jus nullum accrescit, proinde nec qui juravit obligatur. Respondeo, exurgere posse à Juramento duplicem obligationem: unam hominis cui juratur, ut parti; Deo per quem juratur alteram, ut testi & vindici. Multa possunt impedire priorem illam obligationem, ita ut jus nullum consequatur is cui juratur, nec ei quidquam in foro conscientiæ ex æquo bono à jurante debeatur: & de isto obligationis & debiti genere procedit objectio. Verum cessante obligatione respectu hominis injuriam aut vim inferentis, manet tamen Deo facta obligatio: cui & irreverentia fit, si quis juramentum admittat non intendens implere; & injuria, si admissum insuper habeatur.
units.tr: (a) So Ferrar., Nazian. [Greek notes printed in the right margin, not transcribed in full.] ...mentum iniquum (the word is split across the page): no right accrues, and therefore the one who swore is not bound either. I reply that two obligations can arise from an oath: one of the man to whom the oath is sworn, as to a party; and the other to God, by whom it is sworn, as witness and avenger. Many things can prevent the former obligation, so that the one to whom the oath is sworn acquires no right, and nothing is owed to him by the swearer in the court of conscience on the ground of equity; and it is of this kind of obligation and debt that the objection speaks. But although the obligation toward the man who inflicts the injury or force has ceased, the obligation to God remains. To Him irreverence is done if anyone admits an oath without intending to fulfil it, and injury is done if, once admitted, it is held in contempt.

units.la: Restat unus adhuc Casus, huic loco peculiaris: fiquis incidens in latrones cogatur,ne ab eis occidatur, juramento silentium promittere; sc. nunquam se ipsorum latrocinia cuiquam revelaturum, aut nomina magistratui proditurum. Difficile est hoc in genere aliquid statuere, inquit Fredericus Baldwinus, professor non ita pridem Wittenbergensis: sed addit tutius sibi videri si silentium non præstet, sed magistratui indicet, etsi juraverit se non indicaturum. Censet itaque que & rum pro conesse res hoc tur hor ut tur pte del va fec tia jur coeo at ar qu fi ri la c q h i que istusmodi juramentum non obligare; & affert suæ sententiæ tres rationes: quarum nulla mihi satisfaƈit, ut sunt ab eo propositæ, breviter & nudè sine ulteriore confirmatione. Primo ait, Juramentum hoc esse de reillicitâ. Si id constaret, confeƈta res esset, nec opus esset aliis argumentis. Sed hoc ab eo sumitur, non probatur. Si eo putetur esse illicitum, quia officium est boni civis homines facinorosos ad magistratum deferre, ut supplicio quod commeriti sunt afficiantur: conceditur id quidem, sed non propterea sequitur semper peccatum esse non deferre; cùm præcepta officiorum affirmativa obligent ad ea præstanda non simpliciter, sed cùm possumus & expedit pro exigentiâ circumstantiarum. Dicit fecundo, tale juramentum videri habere speciem quandam collusionis cum latronibus. Quod est ab eo ita timidè pronunciatum, ut non debeat putari multum fiduciæ posuisse in hoc argumento, [ Speciem collusionis, speciem quandum, & videtur habere. ] Quod sive sit verum, sive non: quis interim probaverit non licere homini viatori, si inciderit in latrones, in aperto vitæ periculo, aliquid facere quod videtur habere cum eis speciem quandam collusionis ? Quod tertio loco affert, hoc silentio justitiam impediri, improbos in impietate sua confirmari, alios hac occafione induci posse in discrimen vitæ : valeret quidem, si ex eorum manibus salvus & injuratus evasisset. Atqui supponimus, ni jurasset, occidendum. Quæro ergo, licuísne ci in tàm certo vitæ discrimine jurare silentium, vel non licuit: Si non licuit, (& sanè duo priora argumenta aut id efficiunt, aut nihili sunt) certò pereundum ei fuit, & quis tum superesset qui magistratui latrones indicaret? Quæ ex ipsius silentio incommoda sequi objiciuntur, ex ipsius morte (cùm mortuis indicium sit perpetuum silentium) non essent eadem insecutura? At si licuit jurare, licebit & juramentum observare: nisi forte (quod fieri potest) casus aliquis insperato emergens rem quo tempore jurabatur licitam reddiderit postea ex accidente illicitam. Stet ergo, donec contrarium firmioribus rationibus probetur, & in hoc casu & in cæteris ubi vigent dolus, metus, tyrannis & similia; virum bonum aut non debuisse jurare (quod durum videtur summo in vitæ discrimine, si res ipsa non sit illicita) aut debere quod juravit religiose observare. Atque hactenus de Juramenti causâ Efficiente. In quâ pertractandâ volueram esse brevior, sed res non tulit. Excrevit stylus dum ista meditor longius quàm expectabam; & tamen non pauca quæ possent utiliter dici, dum brevitati consulo, prudens prætermisi.
units.tr: There remains one further case, peculiar to this place: if someone, falling in with robbers, is forced, to avoid being killed by them, to promise on oath silence, that is, that he will never reveal their robberies to anyone or hand their names over to the magistrate. It is difficult to lay down anything in this kind of case, says Fredericus Baldwinus, a professor at Wittenberg not long ago; but he adds that it seems safer to him not to keep silence, but to inform the magistrate, even though he has sworn that he will not inform. He therefore holds that such an oath does not bind, and he offers three reasons for his opinion, none of which satisfies me as he puts them forward, briefly and bare, without any further support. First, he says, this oath is about something unlawful. If that were established, the matter would be settled and no other arguments would be needed. But this is assumed by him, not proved. If it is thought to be unlawful because it is the duty of a good citizen to bring wicked men before the magistrate so that they may be punished for what they have deserved, I grant that; but it does not follow that it is always a sin not to bring them forward, since the affirmative precepts of duty bind us to perform them not absolutely, but when we are able and when it is fitting, according to the demands of the circumstances. He says secondly that such an oath seems to have a certain appearance of collusion with the robbers. This he pronounces so timidly that one should not think he placed much confidence in this argument. [An appearance of collusion, a certain appearance, and it seems to have.] Whether that is true or not, who will prove that it is not lawful for a traveller who falls among robbers, in manifest peril of his life, to do something that seems to have a certain appearance of collusion with them? As to what he gives in the third place, that by this silence justice is hindered, the wicked are confirmed in their impiety, and others may be led by this occasion into danger of their lives: this would indeed have force if he had escaped safe and unsworn from their hands. But we are supposing that, had he not sworn, he would have been killed. I ask, then, whether it was lawful for him to swear silence in so certain a peril of his life, or whether it was not lawful. If it was not lawful (and certainly the two former arguments either establish this or are worth nothing), he was bound to perish, and who would then survive to inform the magistrate against the robbers? Would not the evils that are objected as following from his silence have followed from his death instead (since for the dead silence is perpetual)? But if it was lawful to swear, it will also be lawful to observe the oath, unless perhaps (which can happen) some case arising unexpectedly has made the thing, which was lawful at the time of swearing, unlawful afterwards through a later event. Let it stand, therefore, until the contrary is proved by firmer arguments, that both in this case and in others where deceit, fear, tyranny and the like prevail, the good man either ought not to have sworn (which seems hard in the greatest peril of life, if the thing itself is not unlawful), or ought to observe religiously what he has sworn. And so far concerning the efficient cause of the oath. In treating this I had meant to be briefer, but the matter did not allow it. My pen has grown longer than I expected while I was considering these things; and yet I have prudently passed over, for the sake of brevity, not a few things that might usefully have been said.

units.la: DE Juramenti Causis Materiali & Efficiente, in superioribus actum est : de Causa Formali nunc agendum. Cum autem duplex fit rei alicujus Forma; Externa, & Interna: quæ hujus sunt classis, ut duo capita ita revocanda sunt, ut quæ ad Juramenti verba aut signa pertinent, eo quod sensibus exterioribus percipiantur, Externæ Formæ nomine veniant; quæ vero ad ejusdem sensum & interpretationem, quod interioris mentis est opus, Formæ Internæ. Respectu Externæ Formæ, Juramentum aut signis solum constat, aut verbis solum, aut utrisque. Dubium itaque primum est de eo juramento, quod signo solum fit fine verbis. Fuerunt qui existimarent, nisi expresse adhibito aut verbo Juro, aut Dei nomine, dicendo Juro me facturum, vel per Deum faciam, Deum testor, Ita me Deus adjuvet, vel quid simile; nudam esse promissionem, non item Juramentum: & proinde obligare quidem sub pœna mendacii, sed non sub pœna perjurii; ita ut qui non fecerit quod pollicitus est, reus fit violatæ fidei, quæ & in promissionibus est fervanda, non autem ejus religionis quæ in juramento est. Dicitur & Bartolus à Caluistis in ea fuisse sententia, ut putaret verba saltem aliqua ad juramenti rationem sic esse necessaria, ut nisi verbis prolatis fiat testificatio, non sit formaliter juramentum, nec eo nomine obliget. Sed merito ab omnibus rejicitur utraque sententia. Cum enim verborum praecipuus usus sit, εἰς τὸ ἑρμηνεύειν, ut sc. interpretes sint τὸν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ νοηματῶν, eorum conceptum quae in mente sunt, & quorum sunt signa: si fieri posset ut illi mentis conceptus (etsi minus fortassis commodè, sufficienter tamen) aliqua alia ratione, ut scripto, nutibus, aliisve indiciis ita significentur, ut ab aliis intelligantur: nulla cogit necessitas ut verbis prolatis opus fiet. Sic muti, & quibus exsecta est lingua, & qui ex gravi morbo, vel jam morituri sermonis usum amiserunt, si debeant aut matrimonium contrahere, aut testamentum condere, aut aliud quodvis præstare,quod sine clarâ & indubitatâ assensus sui significatione fieri non potest; cum vivâ voce non possunt, solent nutu, manu sublevatâ, aut alio id genus indicio mentem suam interrogantibus significare. Quæ significatio non minus valida est ad omnem juris effectum, quàm ea quæ vivâ voce fit. Eadem prorsus & juramenti ratio est: in quo modò Deus quoquo modo testis invocetur, sive id ab aliquo expressè fiat verbis prolatis, sive tacitè signis quibuscunque sufficientibus ad hoc,
units.tr: Having dealt above with the Material and Efficient causes of an oath, we must now treat its Formal Cause. Since the form of anything is twofold, External and Internal, the two heads must be understood as falling under this division. Whatever belongs to the words or signs of an oath, because it is perceived by the outer senses, is called the External Form. Whatever belongs to its meaning and interpretation, which is the work of the inner mind, is the Internal Form. With respect to the External Form, an oath consists either of signs alone, or of words alone, or of both. The first question, then, concerns the oath made by a sign without words. Some have thought that unless the word I swear is expressly used, or the name of God, by saying "I swear that I will do it", "I will do it by God", "I call God to witness", "So may God help me", or something similar, the thing is a bare promise and not an oath. On this view it binds under the penalty of lying, but not under the penalty of perjury; so that one who does not do what he promised is guilty of broken faith, which must be kept in promises, but not of the religious obligation that lies in an oath. Bartolus is also said to have held this opinion among the Canonists, thinking that some words at least are so necessary to an oath that, unless words are spoken, the attestation is not formally an oath and does not bind under that name. But both opinions are rightly rejected by everyone. For the chief use of words is for interpreting [εἰς τὸ ἑρμηνεύειν], that is, that they may be interpreters of the thoughts in the soul [τὸν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ νοημάτων], the concepts of the mind of which they are the signs. If those concepts of the mind could be signified sufficiently (though perhaps less conveniently) by some other means, such as writing, nods or other indications, so as to be understood by others, then no necessity requires that words be spoken. Thus mutes, those whose tongue has been cut out, and those who through grave illness or at the point of death have lost the use of speech, if they must contract marriage, make a will, or do anything else that cannot be done without a clear and undoubted sign of their assent, cannot do so by the living voice; they are accustomed to show their mind to those questioning them by a nod, a raised hand, or some other such sign. This signification is no less valid for every legal effect than one made by the living voice. The reason for an oath is exactly the same. In it God need only be called on as witness in some way, whether this is done expressly by spoken words or tacitly by any signs sufficient for the purpose,

units.la: ut hi querum interest manifeste intelligant velle eum interposito Deo teste fidem suam obligare; ejusmodi actus & formaliter juramentum est, & omnino sufficit ad inducendam obligationem in conscientia. Quod facit quem adducit e vetere Comico senarium Johannes Stobaeus, (a) ὅρκος βέβαιος [illegible, ~12 letters] Firmum est juramentum, si vel annuero solum. Frustra ergo est, & egregius fui (b) impostor, siquis se juramenti vinculo aut penitus solutum, aut sal-
units.tr: so that those concerned clearly understand that he wishes to bind his faith by calling God to witness. An act of this kind is formally an oath, and it is wholly sufficient to create an obligation in conscience. This is what the verse which John Stobaeus cites from an old comic poet means: [ὅρκος βέβαιος] "An oath is firm, even if I merely nod assent." It is therefore vain, and a clever deceiver of himself, if anyone thinks himself either wholly freed from the bond of an oath, or sal-

units.tr: {a} Sen. 27.

units.la: {b} [illegible, ~10 letters] tem laxius obligatum eo putent, quòd verbum nullum juratorium emiserit. Si alteri quasi Deo teste & arbitro (c) interroganti, ita se gesserit omnino assensisse videretur; vel si ubi utile ei esset (respectu alicujus temporalis commodi) videri in aliena verba jurasse, amici alicujus operâ sciens lubens usus fuerit, qui falsò licet testaretur, tamen ipsum ita jurasse: ligavit eo facto ligamen super animam suam, & secundum omne quod egressum est ex interrogantis vel exigentis ore facere tenetur non minus, quam si egressum esset ex ore suo, si res sit licita & praestari debeat: sin illicitam sciverit, non poterit isthoc artificio perjurii crimen devitare.
units.tr: {b} ...ly more loosely bound by it, because he has uttered no oath-formula. If he so conducted himself before another who was questioning him, as though calling God to witness and as arbiter, it would seem that he had wholly assented. Or if, where it was useful to him (with respect to some temporal advantage), he knowingly and gladly made use of the services of a friend so as to appear to have sworn in another's words, and the friend, though falsely, testified that he had so sworn, he has by that act bound a bond upon his soul, and is obliged to do, according to all that has come out of the mouth of the questioner or the one demanding it, no less than if it had come out of his own mouth, provided the thing is lawful and ought to be performed. But if he knew it to be unlawful, he cannot escape the crime of perjury by this device.

units.la: SECT. II.
units.tr: SECT. II.

units.la: Porrò ut signo solo potest sine verbis, ita solis verbis potest & iæpissimè solet sine signis jurari: cum in aliis, tum vel maximè in iis juramentis, quæ incautis in sermone communi excidunt. Verba autem juramenti duobus adhuc modis considerari possunt: vel quantum ad res per quas juratur, vel quoad exprimendi modum & formulas loquendi quibus juratur. Dubium ergo Secundum est de Obligatione Juramenti, ratione ejus sive rei sive personæ per quam juratur: ubi duo occurrunt Casus. Casus prior est, an & Casus 3, quatenus obligetur qui jurat per aliquam creaturam ? Certum enim est & ab omnibus conceditur, & licitum esse & obligatorium Juramentum per Deum creatorem factum: Sed de Juramento per Creaturam nonnulla est dubitatio. Pro responsione tamen dico primò, Jurare per creaturam absolutè, ultimatè, & terminativè, ita ut constituatur in aliquâ creaturâ finis & vis juramenti sine relatione ad Deum, simpliciter illicitum esse. Ratio manifesta: quia exhibetur eo pacto Creaturæ reverentia soli Deo debita. Juramentum enim (ut antè dictum est) est cultus Latriæ, qui non debet exhiberi ulli creaturæ: quatenus jurans invocando Deum testem ut hi quorum interest manifestè intelligant velle eum interposito Deo teste fidem suam obligare; ejusmodi actus & formaliter juramentum est, & omnino sufficit ad inducendam obligationem in conscientia. Qui facit quem adducit è veteri Comico senarium Johannes Stobæus, (a) ὄρκιον βέβαιον Firmum est juramentum, si vel annuero solum. Frustra ergo est, & egregius fui (b) impostor, si quis se juramenti vinculo aut penitus solutum, aut saltem laxius obligatum eo putent, quòd verbum nullum juratorium emiserit. Si alteri quasi Deo teste & arbitro (c) interroganti, ita se gesserit omninò assensisse videretur; vel si ubi utile ei esset (respectu alicujus temporalis commodi) videri in aliena verba jurasse, amici alicujus operâ sciens lubens usus fuerit, qui falsò licet testaretur, tamen ipsum ita jurasse: ligavit eo facto ligamen super animam suam, & secundùm omne
units.tr: Moreover, just as an oath may be made by a sign without words, so an oath may be made by words alone, and very often is made without signs, both in other cases and especially in those oaths which slip out of careless people in ordinary speech. The words of an oath may be considered in two further ways: either as to the things by which one swears, or as to the manner of expression and the forms of speech by which one swears. The Second question, therefore, concerns the obligation of an oath with respect to the thing or person by which one swears, and here two cases arise. The first case is whether, and the second case is how far, a person who swears by some creature is bound. For it is certain, and is granted by all, that an oath sworn by God the Creator is lawful and binding. But there is some doubt about an oath by a creature. In reply, however, I say, first, that to swear by a creature absolutely, ultimately and terminatively, so that the end and force of the oath is placed in some creature without reference to God, is simply unlawful. The reason is plain: by this means the reverence due to God alone is given to a creature. For an oath (as was said before) is an act of latria, which must not be paid to any creature; insofar as the one swearing calls God to witness, so that those concerned clearly understand that he wishes to bind his faith by calling God to witness. An act of this kind is formally an oath, and it is wholly sufficient to create an obligation in conscience. This is what the verse which John Stobaeus cites from an old comic poet means: [ὄρκιον βέβαιον] An oath is firm, even if I merely nod assent. It is therefore vain, and a clever deceiver of himself, if anyone thinks himself either wholly freed from the bond of an oath, or at least more loosely bound by it, because he has uttered no oath-formula. If he so conducted himself before another who was questioning him, as though calling God to witness and as arbiter, it would seem that he had wholly assented; or if, where it was useful to him (with respect to some temporal advantage), he knowingly and gladly made use of the services of a friend so as to appear to have sworn in another's words, and the friend, though falsely, testified that he had so sworn, he has by that act bound a bond upon his soul, and is obliged to do, according to all that has come out of the mouth of the questioner or the one demanding it, no less than if it had come out of his own mouth, provided the thing is lawful and ought to be performed. But if he knew it to be unlawful, he cannot escape the crime of perjury by this device.

units.la: SECT. II.
units.tr: SECTION II.

units.la: Porrò ut signo solo potest sine verbis, ita solis verbis potest & iæpissimè solet sine signis jurari: cùm in aliis, tùm vel maxi- mè in iis juramentis, quæ incautis in sermone communi excidunt. Verba autem juramenti duobus adhuc modis considerari possunt: vel quantum ad res per quas juratur, vel quoad exprimendi modum & formulas loquendi quibus juratur. Dubium ergo Secundum est de Obligatione Juramenti, ratione ejus sive rei sive personæ per quam juratur: ubi duo occurrunt Casus. Casus prior est, an & quatenus obligetur qui jurat per aliquam creaturam? Certum enim est & ab omnibus conceditur, & licitum esse & obligatorium juramentum per Deum creatorem factum: Sed de Juramento per Creaturam nonnulla est dubitatio. Pro responsione tamen dico primò, Jurare per creaturam absolutè, ultimatè, & terminativè, ita ut constituatur in aliquà creaturà finis & vis juramenti sine relatione ad Deum, simpliciter illicitum esse. Ratio manifesta: quia exhibetur eo pacto Creaturæ reverentia soli Deo debita. Juramentum enim (ut ante dictum est) est cultus Latriæ, qui non debet exhiberi ulli creaturæ: quatenus jurans invocando Deum testem & vindicem, ipso facto agnoscit eum & cordis inspectorem, ut qui sciat an mens consentiat verbis; & justissimum ac potentissimum peccatorum cordis punitorem; quorum neutrum rei cuicunque creatæ potest competere. Imò istiusmodi Juramentum esset vel ex ipsorum Pontificiorum consessione, plane Idololatricum. Dico secundo, Jurare per Creaturas relativè & quasi transitivè, ut solent Pontificii: per B. Virginem, & alios Sanctos Sanctorumve reliquias; hoc est (ut ipsi exponunt) non ultimatè & terminativè, ita ut cultus in ipsis terminetur, sed relative & transitive, ita ut ipsos pertranseat & per ipsos deferatur sinaliter ad Deum: dico inquam, hoc esse saltem superstitiosum. Quia nullo aut rationis lumine, aut Scripturae testimonio constat, ullam Creaturam,quantumvis sanctam habere concreditam sive delegatam sibi à Deo potestatem, vel cognoscendi corda hominum, vel puniendi eorum perjuria. Dico tertio, inter jurandum tacito Dei nomine alicujus Creaturae mentionem facere, ut siquis juraret per caput, per animam, per salutem suam, aut per hunc ignem vel panem &c. (etsi propter periculum scandali, & quod mali speciem aliquam habere videatur, consultius esset ab ejusmodi formulis omnino abstinere) non tamen videri simpliciter illicitum præmur qua per sunt fit luter his apt alig Jud cran inte um hac run ex pin
units.tr: Just as a sign alone can serve without words, so words alone can serve without signs, and oaths are very often sworn in this way, both in other cases and especially in those oaths which slip out unguardedly in ordinary conversation. The words of an oath may be considered in two further ways: either with respect to the things by which one swears, or with respect to the manner of expression and the forms of speech in which one swears. The second question, therefore, concerns the obligation of an oath, with regard to the thing or person by which one swears, and two cases arise. The first case is whether and how far one who swears by some creature is bound. It is certain, and granted by all, that an oath sworn by God the Creator is lawful and binding. But there is some doubt about an oath sworn by a creature. In reply, I say, first, that to swear by a creature absolutely, ultimately, and terminatively, so that the end and force of the oath rests in some creature without reference to God, is simply unlawful. The reason is plain: by such a practice the reverence due to God alone is given to a creature. For an oath (as was said before) is an act of latria, which ought not to be paid to any creature, inasmuch as the one swearing, by calling on God as witness and avenger, thereby acknowledges him as the searcher of hearts, who knows whether the mind agrees with the words, and as the most just and most powerful punisher of sins committed in the heart; and neither of these can belong to any created thing whatever. Indeed, such an oath would be plainly idolatrous, even by the confession of the Papists themselves. I say, second, that to swear by creatures relatively and, as it were, transitively, as the Papists do, by the Blessed Virgin and other saints or relics of saints; that is (as they themselves explain it), not ultimately and terminatively, so that the worship ends in them, but relatively and transitively, so that it passes through them and is at last carried to God: I say, this is at least superstitious. For neither by the light of reason nor by the testimony of Scripture is it established that any creature, however holy, has been entrusted or delegated by God with the power either of knowing the hearts of men or of punishing their perjuries. I say, third, that to make mention of some creature while silently meaning the name of God in swearing, as if someone were to swear "by my head, by my soul, by my salvation," or "by this fire or bread," etc. (although, on account of the danger of scandal, and because it may seem to have some appearance of evil, it would be more prudent to abstain altogether from such formulas), nevertheless this is not to be regarded as simply unlawful for the sole reason that it must be sworn by God alone.

units.la: præcisè ob hoc quod per solum Deum fit jurandum. Ratio est : quia per istas formulas aut non juratur omninò , aut per Deum solum juratur. Quod ut clarius intelligatur , ne videar aut aliquid novi & fufpecti dogmatis invexisse in Ecclesiam, aut execrandæ illi jurandi per creaturas consuetudini, quæ passim (proh dolor ! ) nimium quantum invaluit, veniam indulsisse : Sciendum est in istiusmodi formulis, in quibus fit Creaturæ alicujus mentio, quasi per modum jurandi, per Deum tamen revera sæpè jurari interpretative. Ut in omnibus iis quæ ex communi more concipiendi habent in se vim quandam execratoriam : ut per animam , per salutem meam hoc vel illud faciam : quæ sunt perinde intelligenda acsi diceretur, Ne fit Deus animæ meæ propitius, Ne mihi Deus salutem donet æternam, ni fecero. Itémque in his in quibus res eæ nominantur, quæ sunt aptæ ex sui natura speciatim, nos excitare ad aliquam recordationem Dei: quomodo cum Judæi olim jurabant Per Cælum, Per hanc sacram victimam, &c. id ita aut intelligebant, aut intelligere debebant, ac si dixissent, Per Deum cujus est in cælo thronus, Per Deum cui hæc sacra fiunt, &c. Ast ubi ejusmodi rerum nomina adhibentur, quæ non habent ex naturâ sui aliquam specialem vel propinquam aptitudinem excitandi in nobis cogitationem aliquam de Deo, nec videntur implicare aliquid execratorium; ut siquis ad mensam vel ante focum juraret Per hunc panem, Per hunc ignem, &c. etsi propter modum exprimendi videantur istiusmodi formulae juramenti speciem habere; revera tamen & interpretative non sunt Juramenta, sed meræ potius obtestationes, ut in dubio tertio mox plenius explicabitur. Dico quarto, omne Juramentum quod per creaturas fieri videtur, sive licite sive illicite; hoc est, sive terminetur in creatura (sicut est cultus Imaginum apud vulgus Pontificiorum) quod est Idololatricum; sive juretur per creaturam transitive, ut inde mediate & ultimate deferatur ad Deum (quâ argutiolâ doctiores Pontificii suam οἰκονομίαν tueri conantur) quod tamen est superstitiosum; sive implicite & interpretative per Deum fiat adhibito tamen creaturæ nomine: si modo sit revera & formaliter Juramentum, & non tantum Obtestatio; non minus obligare jurantem ad faciendum id quod promisit, quam si per Deum ipsum distinctis verbis juratum suisset.
units.tr: The reason is that by such formulas either no real oath is made at all, or it is made by God alone. To understand this more clearly, and so that I may not seem either to have introduced into the Church some new and suspect doctrine, or to have granted indulgence to that accursed custom of swearing by creatures which, alas, has grown far too strong everywhere: it must be known that in such formulas, in which some creature is mentioned as if by way of swearing, God is nevertheless often sworn by in an interpretative sense. This holds for all those expressions which, by common usage of speech, have in themselves a certain force of cursing, such as "by my soul, by my salvation, I will do this or that"; these are to be understood just as if one said, "May God be not propitious to my soul," or "May God not grant me eternal salvation, if I do not do it." Likewise, in those expressions in which things are named which by their own nature are especially apt to stir us to some remembrance of God: as when the Jews of old swore "by heaven" or "by this sacred victim," etc., they either understood, or ought to have understood, these words as if they had said, "by God whose throne is in heaven," or "by God to whom these sacred things are offered," etc. But where names of such things are used which do not by their nature have any special or close aptitude for stirring in us some thought of God, and do not seem to imply anything of a cursing kind, as if someone at table or before the hearth were to swear "by this bread, by this fire," etc., then, although on account of the manner of expression such forms of oath may seem to have the appearance of an oath, nevertheless in truth and in interpretation they are not oaths but rather mere adjurations, as will be explained more fully in the third question shortly below. I say, fourth, that every oath which seems to be sworn by creatures, whether lawfully or unlawfully (that is, whether it terminates in the creature, as is the worship of images among the common people of the Papists, which is idolatrous; or whether it is sworn by the creature transitively, so that it is thence carried mediately and ultimately to God, a subtlety by which the more learned Papists try to defend their οἰκονομία, which is nevertheless superstitious; or whether it is made implicitly and interpretatively by God, the name of a creature being nonetheless used): provided it is truly and formally an oath, and not merely an adjuration, binds the one swearing to do what he has promised no less than if it had been sworn by God himself in express words.

units.la: Cujus ratio est, quia in omni Juramento, quod revera & formaliter est tale, Deus aliquo modo testis advocatur. Dico quinto, ut possit fortassis ex his quæ jam dicta sunt, aliquo modo defendi Juramenta istiusmodi non esse simpliciter & de toto genere illicita, si saltem eo etiam quo dictum est modo intelligantur: tamen cum certum sit ea nihilo esse minus obligatoria, quàm alia, nec ulla cogat necessitas ut iis utamur, (quia possumus ubi juramento est opus, aliis uti formulis, & ubi non est opus, oportet omnino non jurare : videri esse officium hominis Christiani, quisquis conscientiæ suæ tranquillitati ferió consultum cupit, ab ejusmodi formulis prorsus abstinere. Id quod iis omnibus non ægrè persuasum fore existimo, qui earum aut originem aut exitum penitus fuerint contemplati. Originem debent, partim Chaldæorum, Ægyptiorum, aliarúmque superstitiosarum gentium Idolomaniæ, qui per Solem, Ignem, & alias creaturas, quas pro Diis habuerunt, velut per numina jurarunt: partim reverentiæ nominis & majestatis divinæ apud populum Dei; quæ initio fortassis pia & justa, decursu temporis paulatim abiit in eam superstitionem, aucta præsertim ex prava consuetudine jurandi libidine, ut ordinarie mallent per obvia quaevis jurare, quam ἐπι τὸν ποιητὴν ϰῃ πα- τέρα τῶν ὅλων ἀναϰεκχεν, ut loquitur Philo, ad rerum universarum conditorem & patrem procurrere. Quod & veteres Græcos (quorum plerosque ritus & mores & Hebræorum æmulatione fluxisse quivis potest facile observare) fecisse adnotarunt Græco-
units.tr: The reason for this is that in every oath which truly and formally is such, God is in some way called upon as witness. I say, fifth, that perhaps from what has already been said it can in some way be defended that oaths of this kind are not simply and wholly unlawful, at least if they are understood in the manner just described. Yet since it is certain that they are no less binding than others, and since no necessity compels us to use them (for where an oath is needed we can use other forms, and where no oath is needed we ought not to swear at all), it seems to be the duty of a Christian man, whoever earnestly desires the tranquillity of his conscience, to abstain altogether from such formulas. I think that all those who have carefully considered either their origin or their outcome will not be reluctant to be persuaded of this. They owe their origin partly to the idolatry of the Chaldeans, the Egyptians, and other superstitious nations, who swore by the sun, fire, and other creatures which they regarded as gods, as if by divinities; partly to reverence for the name and majesty of God among the people of God, which at first was perhaps pious and just, but in the course of time gradually passed into that superstition, increased especially by the bad custom of swearing with license, so that they ordinarily preferred to swear by whatever lay at hand rather than "to have recourse to the Maker and Father of all things" [ἐπὶ τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων ἀναφεύγειν], as Philo says. The scholiasts of the Greek poets noted that the ancient Greeks (whose rites and customs, most of them, anyone can easily observe to have flowed from an imitation of the Hebrews) did the same.

units.la: Græcorum Poetarum Scholiastæ: qui eos non solitos scribunt facile per Deos jurare, ἀλλὰ ἢ πρὸς θεῶν ὀμνύειν ... per ea quæ præsto erant ad manum aut ante oculos, ut panem, ignem, aquam, avem, sceptrum, aut quid simile. At quod ex divini numinis reverentiâ quadam ortum videtur, abiit tandem in summam ejus irreverentiam & contemptum: ut ferè videre est astu Diaboli, & justo Dei peccatis peccata punientis judicio: pietatem postquam degenerare cœperit in superstitionem exire tandem in apertam impietatem. Etenim postquam ex superstitione jurari cœpum est per creaturas; eo tandem increvit licentiæ jurandi cacoethes, ut dum à Dei nomine temperarent, non sibi homines aut jurandi metam ullam figerent, aut ullo pejerandi metu ducerentur. Qui sceptrum non putat esse Deos, ut ille loquitur, putat & licere sibi per sceptrum juranti secus facere, quàm si per Deos juratum fuisset. De Manichæis ita Augustinus, Jurabant sæpissime, nulloque mentis scrupulo per Creaturas. Et proculdubio apud Judæos, ex quo invaluit mos iste jurandi per creaturas, plurimum immutam fuisse jurisjurandi reventiam, è Christi verbis, Matth. c. 5. & 23. apertissimè constat. Quorum verborum ex utriusque loci collatione is videtur esse scopus, ut duplicem
units.tr: The scholiasts of the Greek poets write that the Greeks were not accustomed to swear readily by the gods, but rather "by whatever was at hand or before their eyes, such as bread, fire, water, a bird, a sceptre, or something similar" [ἀλλὰ ἢ πρὸς θεῶν ὀμνύειν ... ]. But what seems to have arisen from a certain reverence for the divine majesty has at last passed into the highest irreverence and contempt for it: as is nearly always seen, by the craft of the Devil and by the just judgment of God, who punishes sins with sins; once piety begins to degenerate into superstition, it at last breaks out into open impiety. For after people began to swear by creatures out of superstition, the itch of swearing grew to such a degree of license that, while they refrained from the name of God, they set no limit for themselves in swearing and were restrained by no fear of perjury. He who does not think that the sceptre is a god, as that writer says, thinks it lawful for himself to act otherwise when he swears by the sceptre than if he had sworn by the gods. Of the Manichaeans Augustine says thus: They swore very often, and without any scruple of mind, by creatures. And undoubtedly among the Jews, from the time when this custom of swearing by creatures prevailed, the reverence due to the oath was greatly diminished, as is most clearly evident from the words of Christ in Matthew chapters 5 and 23. From a comparison of the two passages, the purpose of these words seems to be this: to correct their double (perhaps even triple) error.

units.la: Suid. 19. contra Faust. 22. cem (forte an & triplicem) ipsorum errorem corrigeret. Primum, quod sibi, modo à Dei nomine abstineretur, in rebus quamvis leviculis, jurandi libertatem & παῤῥησίαν quandam concederent. Alterum, quod putarent jurando non peccari, si vel per Deum juraretur, modo verum esset quod juraretur. Tertium, quod existimarent non esse perjurium, etsi res falsa juraretur, dum per creaturas id fieret, non autem per Deum. Sic enim illi perperam interpretabantur quod dictum erat, Non perjurabis, sed reddes Domino juramentum tuum. Docet itaque Christus Juramenta illa, in quibus rei alicujus creatæ, non item Dei nomen assumitur, non esse propterea aut minus vere Juramenta, aut minus obligatoria, quàm illa in quibus per ipsum Deum difertim juratur. Et hæc de priore Casu dicta sunto.
units.tr: Suid. 19. contra Faust. 22. The author corrects a double (perhaps even triple) error of theirs. First, they allowed themselves freedom and a certain boldness [παῤῥησίαν] in swearing, even about trivial matters, provided only that they abstained from the name of God. Second, they thought that no sin was committed in swearing, even by God's name, so long as what was sworn was true. Third, they judged that there was no perjury, even if a false thing was sworn, provided that it was done by creatures and not by God. For they misread what had been said: You shall not forswear yourself, but shall render to the Lord your oaths. Christ therefore teaches that those oaths in which the name of some created thing is invoked, and not the name of God, are not for that reason either less truly oaths or less binding than those in which God himself is expressly sworn by. And so much for the former case. ## SECT. III.

units.la: SECT. III.

Casus posterior est, cum per idola aut falsos deos juratur. Pro solutione dubii in hoc casu, dico primo, ejusmodi juramenta esse simpliciter illicita & plane idololatrica, & à Deo expresse prohibita. Deferunt enim cultum soli vero Deo debitum diis non veris; contra præceptum Dei, Deut. 6. 13. Deum tuum timebis & ipsi soli servies, & jurabis per nomen ejus. Et graviter Deus ipse, Jer. 5. 9. improperat populo suo hoc peccatum: Quomodo, inquit, propitius sim tibi? Filii tui dereliquerunt me, & juraverunt per eos qui non sunt dii. Dico secundo, Juramentum ejusmodi sub poena perjurii obligare, & servari debere: ita ut perjurus sit qui fidem sic datam fefellerit in re licita. Quo facit illud Augustini, , Et iterum, Si objicies, non esse hoc Juramentum, quia Deus testis non advocatur, siquidem deus falsus non est Deus; & proinde non obligare. Respondeo, etsi deus falsus sit revera non Deus, (quia ut Verum convertitur cum Ente, sic falsum convertitur cum Non-ente) est tamen Deus opinione ipsius qui jurat: quod sufficit ad inducendam obligationem: Et proinde tale Juramentum est ex hypothesi verum juramentum; supposita sc. erronea jurantis conscientia: quatenus tenetur in conscientia sua id praestare quilibet; quod secundum conscientiae suae judicium juramento firmavit. Deus enim verus, si fides vel per falsum deum facta violetur, in suam injuriam id factum interpretatur: quia sc. jurans, d quamquam sub falsis notis, generali tamen complexione numen divinum.
units.tr: The latter case is when people swear by idols or false gods. To resolve the doubt in this case, I say, first, that such oaths are simply unlawful and plainly idolatrous, and expressly forbidden by God. For they give to false gods the worship owed to the one true God alone, contrary to the command of God, Deut. 6. 13: You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him alone, and swear by his name. And God himself severely reproaches his people for this sin, Jer. 5. 9: How, he says, shall I be merciful to you? Your sons have forsaken me and sworn by those who are not gods. I say, second, that an oath of this kind binds under the penalty of perjury and ought to be kept, so that whoever breaks the pledge so given, in a lawful matter, is a perjurer. To this purpose is that saying of Augustine. And again: If you object that this is not an oath, because God is not called as witness, since a false god is not God, and therefore does not bind, I answer: although a false god is in truth not God (for as the true is convertible with being, so the false is convertible with non-being), he is nonetheless God in the opinion of the one who swears. That is enough to induce an obligation. Such an oath is therefore, on the hypothesis of the swearer's mistaken conscience, a true oath, since each person is bound in conscience to perform what he has confirmed by oath according to the judgment of his own conscience. For if the pledge made by a false god is broken, the true God takes it as an injury done to himself, since the one swearing, although under false names, yet by a general comprehension, intends the divine power.

units.la: d Grot. 2. de jur. bel. 13. num intuetur. Unde Augustinus, e Non te audit lapis loquentem; sed punit Deus sallentem. Respicit ut opinor, solennem illum ritum Romanorum, quo jurans lapidem silicem manu tenens hæc verba prolocutus, Si sciens fallo, ita me Jupiter bonis omnibus ejiciat, ut ego hunc lapidem, protenus lapidem à se projecit: quod qui fecit, Jovem lapidem jurare dicebatur. Qui ergo per Deum falsum pejerat, vindicem perjurii sentiet Deum verum, ὡς καταφρονήσας ὀρίοτητ@, ut ait author libri Sapientiæ, tanquam numinis & religionis contemptor. Imo ita fidenter pronunciat hac in re Augustinus, ut non vereatur affirmare, sine ulla dubitatione minus malum esse jurare per deum falsum veraciter, quam fallaciter per Deum verum Quod ejus dictum non est ἁπλῶς & omni ex parte intelligendum; sed secundum quid, & præcipe quoad rationem mendacii & perjurii. quod solum ibi confideravit. Dico tertio, ex hac vi obligatoria talis juramenti pendere solutionem illius quæstionis quæ à Publicola quodam proposita fuit B. Augustino,& ab illo suè tractatur tota Epistola 154. Liceatque ab eo exigere jujurandum, quem scimus juraturum per idola? Quod ille licere confirmat, cum exemplo Abrahæ, qui fœdus cum Abimelecho pactum dato acceptoque vicissim juramento confirmavit,
units.tr: d Grotius, 2. de jure belli, 13. Hence Augustine: e The stone does not hear you speaking, but God punishes you lying. He refers, I think, to the solemn Roman rite, in which the one swearing held a flint in his hand and uttered these words: If I knowingly lie, may Jupiter cast me out from all good things, as I cast this stone from me; and he then threw the stone away from himself. Whoever did this was said to swear by Jupiter the stone. Therefore whoever perjures himself by the false god will feel God the true avenger of perjury, as one who despises the sanctity of the oath [ὡς καταφρονήσας ὁρκιότητος], as the author of the Book of Wisdom says, as a contemner of the divinity and of religion. Indeed Augustine pronounces so confidently on this matter that he does not hesitate to affirm: without any doubt it is a lesser evil to swear truly by a false god than to swear falsely by the true God. This saying is not to be understood absolutely [ἁπλῶς] and in every respect, but in a certain respect, and especially as regards the nature of lie and perjury, which alone he was considering there. Third, I say that the solution of the question proposed to St. Augustine by a certain Publicola, and treated by him throughout Epistle 154, depends on the binding force of such an oath: And may one be permitted to require an oath of the man whom we know will swear by idols? Augustine confirms that it is lawful, citing the example of Abraham, who confirmed a covenant with Abimelech by an oath given and received in return,

units.la: s Sap. 14. 30. b ubi supra. mavit, Gen. 21. quod & à Jacobo itidem postea factum cum Labane, Gen. 31. tum etiam ratione ; quia alias nulla effet ratio accommoda paciscendi foedera, aut confervandæ fidei & pacis publicæ cum homine idololatra : nec fit ullâ Dei lege prohibitum uti illius fide inbonum, qui per falsos Deos male jurat. Si dicatur, hoc esse communicare malo alieno : respondet Augustinus — Non per hoc peccato ejus se sociare, quo per damonia juravit ; sed tantùm bono pacto ejus qui finem dedit, & servavit. Et de secundo dubio hactenus.
units.tr: s Wisdom 14. 30. b Ibid. He mentions, Gen. 21., which was afterwards likewise done by Jacob with Laban, Gen. 31. Then also on rational grounds: otherwise there would be no suitable reason for making covenants, or for preserving faith and public peace with an idolater. Nor is it forbidden by any law of God to use the good faith of one who swears wrongly by false gods. If it is said that this is to share in another's evil, Augustine answers: it is not by this that one associates oneself with his sin, by which he swore by demons, but only with the good faith of the one who made and kept the agreement. And so much for the second doubt.

units.la: SECT. IV.
units.tr: SECT. IV.

units.la: Sequitur Dubium Tertium ; quod respicit Juramentum, quantum ad modum exprimendi, & jurandi Formulas. Ratio dubitandi est, quòd cum certum sit omne id quod est verè & formaliter Juramentum obligare sub culpa & pœna perjurii, non item illas formulas quæ non sunt juramenta : opus est, ut ex illis formulis quæ juramenti speciem habere videntur, certo aliquo charactere vel notâ internoscere valeamus ; quænam sint & quæ non sint proprie & formaliter Juramenta. Quâ in re fateor Casuistarum, quotquot licuit in hac temporis angustiâ consulere, mihi neminem satisfacere: qui hanc quæstionem partim leviter attigerunt, partim non satis distinctè tractarunt. Ut ergo distinctius aliquid hac de re quantum ad alia festinanti licebit proponam; Sciendum nudæ assertioni vel promissioni superaddi plerunque ad fidem faciendam aliquam, quasi confirmationem: idque aut Asseveratione, aut Obtestatione, aut demum Juramento. Quæ tria, etsi videri possint non multum inter se distare, & gradu potius quàm specie differre: revera tamen intrinsecè, formaliter, & specificè ad invicem distinguuntur. Verùm est illa distinctio, ob affinitatem, & finis in quem tendunt, & vocum quibus exprimuntur, adeò sæpè obscura, ut difficile sit tria ista aut non penitus confundere, aut dextrè & peritè distinguere. Itaque quò melius isthæc internoscantur: quatuor mihi videntur esse consideranda, ex quibus velut criteriis de qualibet loquendi formulâ sitne Juramentum, an Obtestatio, an Asseveratio tantùm, poterimus aliquatenus dijudicare. Forma sc. verborum, eorundem propria & genuina vis, Mos gentis, & Intentio ipsius jurantis.
units.tr: There follows the Third Doubt, which concerns the oath as to the manner of expressing it and the formulas of swearing. The reason for doubting is this: since it is certain that everything which is truly and formally an oath binds under the guilt and penalty of perjury, and likewise that those formulas which are not oaths do not, we need some definite mark or sign by which we may distinguish, among those formulas which seem to have the appearance of an oath, which are properly and formally oaths and which are not. In this matter I confess that none of the casuists, as many as I have been able to consult in this brief time, satisfies me: some touched on the question only lightly, others did not treat it with sufficient precision. So, that I may propose something more distinctly on this matter, as far as the haste of my other business allows, it should be understood that to a bare assertion or promise there is often added, to make it believed, some confirmation: this is done either by Asseveration, or by Obtestation, or finally by an Oath. These three, although they may seem not much to differ from one another, and to differ rather in degree than in kind, are nevertheless in their inner nature, formally and specifically, distinct from one another. Yet that distinction, because of their affinity, the end at which they aim, and the words by which they are expressed, is so often obscure that it is hard either not to confuse these three altogether or to distinguish them skilfully and accurately. Therefore, that these may be better distinguished, I think four things must be considered, by which, as by criteria, we can in some measure judge of any form of speech whether it is an oath, or an obtestation, or only an asseveration. These are: the form of the words, the proper and genuine force of the same, the custom of the people, and the intention of the one swearing.

units.la: SECT. V.
units.tr: SECT. V.

units.la: Primo, ex ipsa verborum forma quandoq; facis constare potest, utrum juratum fit, vel non. Juro mihi te daturum centum. Iuro: vel per Deum dabo: vel Deo teste aut coram Deo spondeo me daturum: vel Dabo, ita me Deus adjuvet; aut aliquid simile si respondeatur, quin juratum sit nemini potesse esse dubium. Obligatur proinde, qui istiusmodi aliqua loquendi formula usus fuerit, ipso facto: & si rem promissam non fecerit, perjurii reus est. Ast illud, Dabit mihi centum? Dabo: nudam esse Promissionem vel ipsa verba ostendunt, nullâ adjecta ulteriore datæ fidei confirmatione. Dxti mihi te daturum centum? Dabisne? Certe dabo: credè mihi non fallam. Accessit quidem promissioni aliqua confirmatio: sed ex ipsa verborum forma satis constat hanc esse meram Affeverationem, non autem Juramentum, imò ne Obtestatio quidem: quum nec Deus testis adducatur, nec aliquod aliud fidei velut pignus. Quos mihi politicus es centum, qui sciam te daturum? Cape hanc dextram; Fide boni viri dabo; quam certum est solem hunc lucere, faciam; nulla mihi fit apud te in posterum fides ni fecero, &c. Plus quam meam Asseverationem ista continere verba ipsa indiindicant, nondum tamen juratum esse. Sunt ergo potius Obtestationes dicendae: in quibus sc. ad rei promissae vel etiam asseveratae, ulteriorem confirmationem, rem aliquam nobis charam, aut omnibus certam & manifestam, quasi fidei nostrae pignus interponimus. Ubi ergo ex ipsa verborum forma liquido satis constare poterit, sitne id quod ad confirmandam promissionem assumitur, proprie Iuramentum, vel Asseveratio mera, vel etiam Obtestatio; non opus erit ulteriori disquisitione.
units.tr: First, from the form of the words themselves it can sometimes be established whether something has been sworn or not. I swear to you that I will give you a hundred. I swear: or by God I will give; or I promise, with God as witness or before God, that I will give; or I will give, so help me God; or any similar form, if one of these is said, there can be no doubt that an oath has been sworn. Whoever uses any such form of speech is therefore bound by the very fact, and if he does not perform what he promised he is guilty of perjury. But that Will he give me a hundred? I will give: the words themselves show this to be a bare promise, with no further confirmation of plighted faith added. You told me you would give a hundred? Will you? Certainly I will give; believe me, I will not deceive you. Some confirmation has indeed been added to the promise, but from the form of the words it is clear enough that this is a mere affirmation, not an oath, and not even an obtestation, since neither is God called as witness, nor is anything else offered as a pledge of faith. How am I to know, you politician, that you will give me a hundred? Take this right hand; I will do it on the faith of an honest man; as surely as this sun shines, I will do it; may I have no faith placed in me hereafter if I do not do it, and so on. The words themselves show that these contain more than my mere affirmation, yet they are not yet an oath. They are therefore rather to be called obtestations, in which, I say, to add further confirmation to a promise or even an affirmation, we set before us as a pledge of our faith something dear to us, or something certain and manifest to all. Where, then, it can clearly enough be established from the form of the words whether what is taken up to confirm the promise is properly an oath, or a mere affirmation, or also an obtestation, no further inquiry will be needed.

units.la: SECT. VI.
units.tr: SECT. VI.

units.la: Sed quia sæpissimè contingit, ob formularum similitudinem, vel ambiguam alicujus vocabuli significationem, vel significandi latitudinem; vel aliâ aliquâ de causâ, ut non possit ex verbis prolatis sit necne juratum certò dijudicari: attendi debet secundo loco verborum propria vis & genuinus sensus, atque inde summi judicium. Videri enim potest ex formâ verborum, illas omnes locutiones, in quibus aut Dei nomen adhibetur, aut τὴ Græcorum cum accusativo casu, aut Latinum Per, aut Anglicum By, esse formaliter Juramenta. Quâ solâ ratione adductus Soto putavit tantum esse discriminis inter has for-mulas, Per fidem, & In fide; per veritatem & & In veritate, ut illas diceret esse formaliter Juramenta, non item iflas. At si verborum vis & genuinus sensus penitius introspiciatur, nullum erit discrimen inter praepositiones Per & In, si ad eandem rem applicentur : sed prout rescui applicantur sacra erit vel civilis, perinde de utraque judicari debet. Illa ergo formula Per Deum est ex vi verborum proprie Juramentum : quia res sacra est Dei nomen, & qui sic loquitur, Deum inducit testem, At illa Per Fidem (etsi ex more alicujus gentis, aut intentione dicentis poterit esse Juramentum) non est tamen Juramentum ex vi verborum, sed Asseveratio tantum, vel ad plurimum Obtestatio. Quia fides humana non est res sacra, sed civilis: & qui sic loquitur non adducit Deum testem, sed tantum pronunciat secundum fidem suam, sive declarat rem a se cum animi deliberatione serio & sincere dici. Istorum enim verborum Per fidem meam, sive in assertoria sive in promissoria materia, haec est genuina expositio: Ex animo loquor, vere id dico quod sentio ; pignero tibi fidem meam rem ita se habere ; si sciens fallo, nulla mihi in posterum fides habeatur, &c. Non est ergo fidei interpositio ex vi verborum Juramentum ; nisi forte ubi nos revocat ad Juramentum aliquod prius a nobis praestitum : ut in hac Academia, cum postulatur quis ad interrogata respondere virtute jujuramenti sub hac forma, Tu dices fide tuâ data huic Universitati----& cum indicuntur solenniter Convocationes, quibus interesse jubentur à Bedellis Doctores, Magistri Regentes & non Regentes, Per fidem, per fidem, per fidem. Quod idem mihi (etsi sciam multos aliter sentire) dicendum videtur de illo Pauli-no, vn̄ τὴν καύχησιν per gloriationem nostram quam habeo in Christo, quotidie morior: scilicet non esse proprie Juramentum, etsi illud vn̄ adjunctum habeat, sed seriam tantùm afseverationem; se, ut morti semper obnoxium, ita quotidie paratum esse, cum Deus voluerit, mori.
units.tr: But because it very often happens, on account of the similarity of formulas, or the ambiguous meaning or breadth of some word, or for some other reason, that it cannot be certainly determined from the words uttered whether or not an oath has been sworn, the second thing to be considered is the proper force of the words and their genuine sense, and from this the judgment is to be made. For it may seem, from the form of the words, that all those expressions in which either the name of God is used, or the Greek dia [διά] with the accusative case, or the Latin per, or the English by, are formally oaths. Moved by this alone, Soto thought there was such a difference between these formulas, per fidem and in fide, per veritatem and in veritate, that he held the former to be formally oaths and the latter not. But if the force of the words and their genuine sense are examined more closely, there will be no difference between the prepositions per and in, when they are applied to the same thing; rather, according as the thing to which they are applied is sacred or civil, a judgment must be made about each alike. That formula By God is, by the force of the words, properly an oath, because the name of God is a sacred thing, and whoever speaks in this way calls God in as witness. But By faith (although by the custom of some nation, or the intention of the speaker, it may be an oath) is not an oath by the force of the words, but only an affirmation, or at most an obtestation. For human faith is not a sacred thing but a civil one, and whoever speaks in this way does not call God as witness, but only declares according to his faith, or states that the thing is said by him with seriousness and sincerity after deliberation of mind. For this is the genuine explanation of these words By my faith, whether in an assertory or a promissory matter: I speak from my heart, I truly say what I think; I pledge to you my faith that the thing is so; if I knowingly deceive, let no faith be placed in me hereafter, and so on. The interposing of faith is therefore not an oath by the force of the words, unless perhaps where it recalls us to some oath previously taken by us; as in this University, when someone is required to answer questions under the force of his oath in this form: You will answer, by the faith you have given to this University; and when Convocations are solemnly announced, to which the Doctors, Regent and non-Regent Masters are ordered to attend by the Bedels: By faith, by faith, by faith. The same seems to me (although I know many think otherwise) to be said of that passage of Paul, by our glorying [ὑπὲρ τὴν καύχησιν] which I have in Christ, I die daily: namely, that it is not properly an oath, even though it has the by attached, but only a serious affirmation; that, as he is always liable to death, so he is ready every day, when God wills, to die.

units.la: SECT. VII.
units.tr: SECT. VII.

units.la: De illis autem Iosephi verbis ad fratres suos (a) Per vitam Pharaonis exploratores estis ; de quibus varie disputant interpretes; quid sit sentiendum, poterit fortassis ex his quæ jam dicta sunt haud incommode judicari. Sunt qui Iosephum diu jam inter aulicos Pharaonis versatum (quasi ipsi ex quotidiano convictu affricuissent ei aliquid de scabie sua) sic paulatim putant ipsorum moribus hac saltem ex parte assuevisse, ut didicerit tandem ad ipsorum exemplar per vitam Regis jurare; quomodo solitæ sunt posterioribus seculis Romani ex adulatione quadam jurare per genium Imperatoris. Sed non facile me patior de dictis factisque insignium pietate virorum sequius judicare quam res ipsa cogit. Video vetErum plerosque ita Sanctorum famæ detulisse, ut ingenio suo nimium indulserint, dum eorum apertos lapsus honesto aliquo velamine excusare conantur. Errore saltem aliquanto honestiore, quam est error eorum, qui postremo hoc seculo amant e diverso in piorum virorum lapsus curiosius inquirere, & ne desit quod calumnientur, vel recte facta pervertendo sincerum vas incrustare gestiunt. Mitius aliquanto alii Iosephi dictum illud interpretantur: eum sc. quo tectius rem gereret & ne fratribus alicunde forte suboleret quis esset, ni Ægyptiaci principis quam induerat personam perite sustineret, formulam hanc jurandi Aulicis regiis familiarem, illa tantum vice in compendium simulationis adhibuisse. At mihi non est volupe vel hanc culpam, etsi paulo leviorem, sanctissimo viro impingere sine necessitate. Tertia est eorum sententia, qui Iosephum liberant quidem ab omni culpa: sed ea ratione, quod putent ante interdicta a Christo id genus juramenta, licuisse cuivis sine peccato per creaturam jurare. Quam sententiam fateor mihi catenus probari, quod Iosephum immunem culpæ statuat: Sed rationem illius sententiæ non probari. Nam primo non constat Christum interdixisse speciatim Juramenta per Creaturas, magis quam ea quæ per Deum fiunt : Prohibuit enim utriusque generis omnia non necessaria. Nec opus fuit ista novo interdicto prohibere, quæ ex se erant semper illicita. Et quod specialiter dixit de Juramento per creaturas, eo tendit ut ostendat ejusmodi juramenta, contra quàm senserant Judæi, si præstita forent, non minus obligare quam quæ expresso Dei nomine fiunt. Secundo nec verum est licuisse piis ante Christum, ex quadam dispensatione sive indulgentia divinâ per creaturas jurare, cum is cultus soli Deo debeatur, ut eo Deut. 6. & Ierem. 5. ante probatum est. Qui posterior locus, etsi forsan eos qui per idola seu falsos Deos jurabant, peculiariter respiciat : vis tamen argumenti quo utitur Propheta, à genere ducti, eos etiam attinet, qui per creaturas jurant, quum & de Creaturis recto dicatur quòd non sunt dii. Tertio, ipsius Juramenti natura, ut ex ejus definitione constat, cum requirat ut Deus testis advocetur, satis ostendit nunquam licuisse per creaturas jurare : Vel ipsis Ethnicis fatentibus, qui θεῶν ... ad Juramenti essentiam pertinere docuerunt. Quæ cum ita sint, nec videatur hac ratione satis commodè excusari posse ab omni crimine Iosephum: restat quarta demum sententia, quæ
units.tr: Concerning those words of Joseph to his brothers (a) By the life of Pharaoh you are spies, on which the interpreters dispute in various ways, what ought to be thought may perhaps be judged without difficulty from what has already been said. Some think that Joseph, having long lived among Pharaoh's courtiers (as if they had rubbed some of their scabies off on him through daily association), had gradually grown so far accustomed to their habits, at least in this respect, that he finally learned from their example to swear by the life of the King, just as in later centuries the Romans, out of a certain flattery, swore by the genius of the Emperor. But I am not easily persuaded to judge the words and deeds of men distinguished for piety worse than the facts themselves compel. I see that most of the ancients so reported the fame of the saints that they indulged their own talent too much, while trying to excuse the saints' open lapses with some honourable veil. That is at least a more honourable error than the error of those who in this last age love to inquire more curiously into the lapses of godly men, and, lest there be nothing to slander, eagerly seek to daub the pure vessel by perverting even their right deeds. Others interpret that saying of Joseph somewhat more gently: that he used this form of swearing, familiar to royal courtiers, only on that occasion, as a shortcut of pretence, so that he might carry out the matter more guardedly, and lest the brothers somehow learn from elsewhere who he was, unless he skilfully maintained the character of the Egyptian prince which he had put on. But it does not please me to impute even this fault, though a slightly lighter one, to that most holy man without necessity. The third opinion is of those who indeed free Joseph from all fault, but on the ground that they think that before the prohibitions of Christ such oaths were permitted to anyone, without sin, to swear by a creature. I confess that this opinion pleases me so far as it holds Joseph free of blame, but the reasoning of that opinion does not please me. For, first, it is not established that Christ specifically forbade oaths by creatures rather than those made by God, for he forbade all unnecessary oaths of both kinds. Nor was there need to prohibit by a new interdict those things which were always unlawful in themselves. And what he said specifically about oaths by creatures tends to show that such oaths, contrary to what the Jews had thought, if they were made, bind no less than those made with the express name of God. Second, it is not true that before Christ it was permitted to the pious, by some divine dispensation or indulgence, to swear by creatures, since that worship is due to God alone, as was shown earlier from Deut. 6. & Jerem. 5. Although the latter passage perhaps refers in particular to those who swore by idols or false gods, yet the force of the argument which the Prophet uses, drawn from the genus, also touches those who swear by creatures, since it is rightly said of creatures too that they are not gods. Third, the very nature of an oath, as is clear from its definition, since it requires that God be called as witness, sufficiently shows that it was never permitted to swear by creatures, the heathens themselves confessing this, who taught that the appeal to the gods [θεῶν ...] belongs to the essence of an oath. Since these things are so, and it does not seem that Joseph can be sufficiently and conveniently excused from all crime on this ground, there remains at last a fourth opinion, which
