units.la: Arist.lib.2. Rhetor.
units.tr: Arist.lib.2. Rhetor.

units.la: Opin.4. quæ explicando genuinum sensum verborum Josephi, censet eum non omnino juravisse, & proinde nec male jurando peccasse. Si enim tunc juraretur per vitam Pharaonis: aut vita Pharaonis ut testis adduceretur, quod est valdè ineptum; aut aliquid execratorium vel imprecatorium in se contineret, quod quid sit, sine dura & coactâ admodum verborum interpretatione, non est facile hariolari. At verborum ejus facilis erit & simplicissimus sensus, si indicativa oratione ita exponantur, Per vitam Pharaonis exploratores estis; id est, quam verum & certum est Pharaonem vivere, tam verum & certum est vos esse exploratores: quemadmodum illud per hunc solem qui lucet verum tibi dico, idem valet, ac si diceretur, Tam verum est hoc quod ego tibi dico, quàm verum est Solem hunc lucere. Quorum neutrum, ut mihi videtur, est formaliter Juramentum; sed Asseveratio potiùs vehementiore obtestatatione confirmata. Non sum nescius ex adverso adduci posse nonnulla: quæ etsi non sint tanti, ut propterea mutandam esse putem sententiam meam; sunt tamen tanti, ut propterea æquum esse censeam, cuique ut liberum sit sequi sententiam suam, modò non damnet alienam, & hoc mihi interim concedat, ex vi saltem verborum, nisi aliunde constiterit, non posse clarè evinci Josephum phum jurejurando usum esse: cum ipsa verba nullam contineant, aut invocationem testis, aut vindictæ postulationem.
units.tr: Opin.4. which, in explaining the genuine sense of Joseph's words, holds that he did not swear at all, and therefore did not sin by swearing wrongly. For if then an oath were being taken by the life of Pharaoh, either the life of Pharaoh would be brought in as a witness, which is very absurd, or it would contain something execratory or imprecatory, and what that is, without a harsh and strained interpretation of the words, is not easy to guess. But the sense of his words will be easy and most simple if they are expounded as an indicative statement: By the life of Pharaoh you are spies; that is, as true and certain as it is that Pharaoh lives, so true and certain is it that you are spies. Just as the words by this sun which shines, I tell you the truth, amount to the same as if it were said, what I tell you is as true as it is true that this sun shines. Neither of these, as it seems to me, is formally an oath, but rather an assertion confirmed by a more vehement adjuration. I am not unaware that some arguments can be brought against this, which, though not so weighty that I think I should change my opinion on account of them, are yet weighty enough that I think it fair that each person be free to follow his own opinion, provided he does not condemn another's; and that he grant me meanwhile this: that from the force of the words alone, unless it has been established elsewhere, it cannot be clearly proved that Joseph used an oath, since the words themselves contain neither the invocation of a witness nor a demand for vengeance.

units.la: SECT. VIII.
units.tr: SECT. VIII.

units.la: Tertium dignoscendi juramenti ξεπ'ειον est Mos alicujus gentis, loci, vel communitatis. Potest enim fieri, ut locutiones aliquæ, quas nec ex forma, nec vi & germano sensu verborum liquet esse juramenta, ex usu tamen recepto alicujus populi, & communi hominum existimatione pro juramentis habeantur: & ut illæ vicissim, quas ex verbis judicares esse juramenta, habeantur pro non-juramentis. Ratio est: quia verba perinde valent ac nummi. Quæ utraque non φύσει valent & natura, sed θέσει, seu Instituto magis, at χρῆσει, sive usu vel maxime: hoc est, tanti sunt utraque quanti æstimantur. Cujus rei exemplum non est quod aliunde quæramus, quam ex formulis quibusdam nostratibus. Quum enim fidei & veritatis (in hoc præsertim negotio) eadem sit omnino ratio, ut qui veritate caret, careat & fide; quique fide, & veritate: ea tamen opinio apud nostræ gentis homines ex longo usu invaluit, ut qui In faith dixerit jurasse putetur, qui In truth non jurasse; &, quod non minus est à ratione alienum, ut In truth asseveratio afleveratio mera habeatur, [illegible, ~8 letters] etiam juramentum. Cujus rei rationem inceptus esset qui quaereret, extra eam quae ab {a} usu est, Quem penes arbitrium est, & jus, & norma loquendi. Unde sequitur eum, qui dum ad verborum solum formam aut vim attendit, indulget sibi libertatem ejusmodi locutionibus in communi sermone utendi sine aliquo delectu vel scrupulo, quae longo usu consecutae sunt apud nos vim & aestimationem juris-jurandi, & praeceptum Christi de non jurando violare, & fratri offendiculum praebere, & semet perjurii periculo exponere.
units.tr: A third mark for distinguishing an oath [ξεπ'ειον] is the custom of some nation, place, or community. For it may happen that certain expressions, which from their form and from the force and plain sense of their words are clearly not oaths, are nevertheless regarded as oaths by the accepted usage of a people and the common opinion of men. And conversely, those which from their words you would judge to be oaths are regarded as non-oaths. The reason is that words have the same value as coins. Both have their worth not by nature [φύσει] but by institution [θέσει], or rather by use [χρῆσει], and above all by use: that is, each is worth exactly what it is esteemed to be worth. For an example of this we need look no further than certain formulas among our own people. Since the reason for faith and truth (especially in this matter) is altogether the same, so that whoever lacks truth lacks faith too, and whoever lacks faith lacks truth, yet among the men of our nation long usage has prevailed to such an extent that whoever says "In faith" is thought to have sworn, but whoever says "In truth" is thought not to have sworn; and, what is no less contrary to reason, an "In truth" assertion is held to be a mere asseveration, [illegible, ~8 letters] even an oath. If anyone set out to inquire into the reason for this, he would be beginning beyond what is settled by usage, since the power and the rule of speaking rest with usage. Hence it follows that the man who, while attending only to the form or force of words, allows himself the liberty of using such expressions in ordinary speech without any discrimination or scruple, when by long usage among us they have acquired the force and estimation of an oath, violates the precept of Christ not to swear, gives offence to his brother, and exposes himself to the danger of perjury.

units.la: SECT. IX.
units.tr: SECT. IX.

units.la: Quartum & ultimum dignoscendi Juramenti χριτήριον est mens & Intentio jurantis. Esto enim non constet vel ex verbis ipsis, vel ex communi aestimatione hominum, aliquam sermonis formulam esse Juramentum: Siquis tamen ejusmodi formula usus, aut mentis suae errore aliquo putet se jurasse, aut ex aliqua dolosa intentione velit putari jurasse; ea formula etsi non sit revera, & ex se juramentum, habebit tamen quoad ipsum hominem, ad omnem obligandi effectum in conscientia Juramenti instar, ita ut non modo mendacii, sed & perjurii reus sit in foro interno, si fidem sic datam violaverit. Ut enim judice
units.tr: The fourth and last criterion for recognising an oath is the mind and intention of the one swearing. Suppose it is not established either from the words themselves or from common human judgement that some form of speech is an oath. If a person uses such a formula while mistakenly thinking, through some error of mind, that he has sworn, or while wishing, from some deceitful intention, to be thought to have sworn, then that formula, although it is not really and in itself an oath, will nevertheless have the force of an oath for that person, with respect to every binding effect in conscience. So he is guilty not only of lying but also of perjury in the internal court if he violates the pledge given in this way.

units.la: Apostolo,a qui æstimat aliquid esse κοινὸν, commune vel impurum, quod ex se non est κοινὸν, est illi tamen κοινὸν, ita ut ab eo teneatur abstinere, sicut à re verè communi & impurâ: Sic a lege contrariorum, qui aliquid æstimat esse ὅσιον, id est sacrum, quod ex se ὅσιον non est, est illi tamen ὅσιον, ita ut ab eo abstinere teneatur sicut a re verè sacrâ. Et si error mentis sufficit ad inducendum obligationem; multò magis mala voluntas sallendi proximum obligationem inducet. Quia justum est, ut vir impius & dolosus incidat in foveam quam fodit proximo suo, & ut illi laqueo quem tetendit alteri implicitus sit pes suus.
units.tr: As the Apostle judges, one who considers something to be κοινὸν [common] or unclean, although it is not common in itself, is nevertheless bound to it as common, so that he must abstain from it just as he would from a thing that really is common and unclean. In the same way, by the law of contraries, one who considers something to be ὅσιον [holy], that is sacred, although it is not holy in itself, is nevertheless bound to it as holy, so that he must abstain from it just as from a thing that is truly sacred. And if an error of mind is enough to induce an obligation, then a wicked will to deceive a neighbour will much more induce an obligation. For it is just that the wicked and deceitful man should fall into the pit he dug for his neighbour, and that his foot should be caught in the snare he set for another.

units.la: SECT. X.
units.tr: SECTION X.

units.la: Quatuor eorum quæ nunc exposui criteriorum is usus est, siquando quæstio vel scrupulus oriatur in conscientiâ, de aliquâ loquendi formulâ quæ videtur habere speciem Juramenti, habeáne vere & formaliter rationem, & consequenter vim Obligatoriam Juramenti, vel non? protinus ut ad hæc criteria recurratur, fiatque examen illius formulæ ad has velut notas διαγνωστικὰς, idque eo quo proposui ordine, incipiendo à primâ atque ita percurrendo singulas, fi opus fuerit: id est, nisi ante ex jam peracto examine satis constiterit quòd sit juramentum Potest enim constare affirmatio, sc. quòd sit juramentum, ex unius alicujus notæ examine: at non potest constare negatio, nisi peracto ad singulas notas toto examine. Cujus examinis duplex est finis: alter antequam juretur, ut cogitet quisque an expediat ejusmodi formulâ uti, vel non: alter postquam in ea verba juratum est, ut intelligat quantum obligetur.
units.tr: Of the four criteria I have now set out, this is their use: whenever a question or scruple arises in conscience about some form of speech that seems to have the appearance of an oath, whether it truly and formally has the nature of an oath and consequently the binding force of an oath or not, one should at once have recourse to these criteria, and examine that formula by these marks, which are διαγνωστικὰς [diagnostic], in the order I have proposed, beginning with the first and going through each in turn, if need be. That is, unless from an examination already completed it has been sufficiently established that it is an oath. For the affirmative, namely that it is an oath, can be established from the examination of a single mark; but the negative cannot be established unless the whole examination has been carried through all the marks. This examination has a twofold purpose: the one, before anyone swears, so that each may consider whether it is expedient to use such a formula or not; the other, after one has sworn in those words, so that he may understand how far he is bound.

units.la: SECT. XI.
units.tr: SECTION XI.

units.la: Egimus hactenus de Juramento eo, quod fit signo sine verbis, & de eo quod fit verbis sine signo: sequitur Juramentum ex utrisque conjunctis. Adhibentur autem cum verbis signa, ob majorem vel solennitatem actus, vel dignitatem personæ. Quartum ergo Dubium est de Juramento solenni: ubi Casus primus seu Quæstio prima est de ritibus & ceremoniis in solenni juramento adhibitis. De ritibus Gentilium multi multa scripsere; quæ nec est alias operæ pretium, nec est præsentis instituti percensere. Aunotavit præcipuos quosdam Alexander Neapolitanus, lib. 5. Genial. dier. c. 10. Sanctissima habebantur illa, quæ a aris Deorum tangentes conceptis verbis jurabant: Illis proxima, quibus b sovem lapidem. Conceptis autem verbis jurare di-
units.tr: So far we have treated of the oath that is made by a sign without words, and of that which is made by words without a sign; there follows the oath made by both joined together. Signs are added to words either for the greater solemnity of the act or for the dignity of the person. The fourth Question, therefore, concerns the solemn oath, where the first case, or first question, concerns the rites and ceremonies used in a solemn oath. Many have written much about the rites of the Gentiles; but it is neither otherwise worth the effort nor within the scope of the present undertaking to go through them. Alexander of Naples has noted certain principal ones, Genial. dier. lib. 5, c. 10. Those were held most sacred which were sworn in set words while touching the altars of the gods; next to these were those by which one swore while touching a stone of Jupiter. Now to swear in set words...

units.la: dicuntur, qui verba Juramenti præscripta recitant vel singuli, vel unus aliquis tantùm reliquis c in ejus præeuntis verba consensum suum d uno aut altero verbo signove significantibus. Apud Veteres Hebræos duo præcipuè ritus in sacris literis memorantur. Quorum alter peculiaris fuit iis juramentis ἐπαγγελίας quæ superiores pro authoritate suâ exigebant à suis inferioribus, ut mandata sua fideliter exequerentur. Cujus primum exemplum habetur Gen. 24. ubi Abraham ab Oeconomo suo Juramentum exigens fidelitatis, de uxore filio suo deligenda, jubet eum e manum femori suo supponere. Quod idem facere jussit f Iacob jam morituris Iosephum filium Gen. 47. cum ei curam demandavit sepulturæ suæ in terra Canaanitide. Quem ritum sive observarint in signum fidei, qua credebant in semen benedictum egressurum de femore Abrahæ: sive in commemorationem fœderis quod ante pactum erat cum Abraha cum circumcideretur: sive alia quacunque de causa; non tamen legimus id ullo expresso Dei mandato niti, sed fuisse, quantum nobis quidem constare potest liberæ omninò institutionis. Quò magis miremini illorum hominum perversam non sine superstitione severitatem, qui ritus omnes in cultu Dei decoris & ordinis gratia ab hominibus sine expresso Dei man nant, ut execranda & in Ecclesiis Christianorum non ferenda idola. Alter populi Dei inter jurandum erat elevatio manus dextræ cælum versus adhibita & in Juramentis ἐνιαῖος quæ quis sponte suscepit & non ex alterius imperio. Quem g ritum, sive ex Hebræorum imitatione, ut plurima alia, sive ductu quodam naturæ quasi Deum intuentes quem ὑψίστῳ ἀρχάτα νωμίν credid()erunt, plerarumque gentium populi observarunt. Hujus utique ut & superioris b primum exemplum habemus in Historia ipsius Abrahæ, Gen.14. sed & hoc nullo quod scimus speciali Dei mandato subnixum. Qui ritus nihilominus ita postea invaluit apud ejus posteros, ut per metonymiam adjuncti illa phralis levandi manum pro ipso actu jurandi frequenter posita reperiatur, imo & vox ipsa יָד quæ proprie dextram significat, Hæbreis & Arabibus pro juramento non raro accipiatur. Unde aliqui ipsorum interpretes illa verba Pf.144.8. & 11. de juramento intelligunt, Quorum os loquitur vanitatem, & dextra eorum est dextra iniquitatis, vel potius mendacii sive falsitatis; id enim proprie significant Hebræa יָמִין שֶׁקֶר. Quin & ipse Deus ubi ad modum humanum ἀνθρωποπαθῶς jurans inducitur, eo loquendi genere utitur. Ego levo ad cælum manum meam, & juro in dextra mea, Deut. 32.40. ad quem ritum alibi in libris Propheticis utriusque Testamenti non raro aliusum. Quem proinde ritum iterum jure miremini, in Christianis Ecclesiis non tolerari modò, sed & approbari ab ipsissimis illis viris, qui tamen alios veteris Testamenti ritus (cum sint ejusdem rationis omnes, ut liciti pariter, aut pariter illiciti,) à Christianis usurpari adeo non probant, ut ne tolerent quidem, sed è coetibus sacris penitus exterminandos clamitent. Quod attinet ad ritus Christianorum, ut reliquas priscæ Ecclesiæ ceremonias varias, variéque pro locorum & temporum varietate observatas missas faciam: Una feré est quæ a prisco saeculo ad nos usque derivata, etiamnum in usu est, sc. ut tactis sacrosanctis Dei Evangeliis in verba concepta juretur. Et hoc omne genus Juramenti, in quo præter verba prolata, adhibetur etiam aliquis externus visibilis motus corporalis: ut tactus altarium, femoris, aut libri, projectio lapidis, levatio manus, & similia, dici solet Juramentum corporale, Ballamoni σωματικὸς ἔρκος.
units.tr: are said to swear in set words, those who recite the prescribed words of the oath, either each for himself or, when only one person speaks, the rest giving their assent by one word or sign, following the words of the one who goes before. Among the ancient Hebrews, two rites are especially recorded in the sacred writings. The first was peculiar to those oaths [ἐπαγγελίας] that superiors, by their own authority, required of their inferiors, that they should carry out their orders faithfully. The first example of this is in Gen. 24., where Abraham, requiring an oath of fidelity from his steward concerning the choosing of a wife for his son, bids him put his hand under his thigh. Jacob likewise ordered Joseph, his son, to do the same when he was about to die, Gen. 47., when he committed to him the care of his burial in the land of Canaan. Whether they observed this rite as a sign of faith, by which they believed that the blessed seed would come forth from the thigh of Abraham; or in remembrance of the covenant which had been made with Abraham at his circumcision; or for any other reason, we do not read that it rested on any express command of God, but that, so far as we can ascertain, it was of entirely free institution. All the more may you marvel at the perverse and not wholly unsuperstitious severity of those men who condemn all the rites in the worship of God that men have introduced without an express command of God for the sake of decency and order, as if they were execrable idols that must not be tolerated in the churches of Christians. The second rite of the people of God in swearing was the lifting up of the right hand toward heaven, used in oaths [ἐνιαῖος] which a man undertakes of his own accord and not at another's command. This rite was observed by the peoples of most nations, whether by imitation of the Hebrews, as in many other things, or by a certain leading of nature, as if looking upon God whom they believed to be [ὑψίστῳ], the Most High. We have the first example of this, as of the former, in the history of Abraham himself, Gen. 14., but this too, so far as we know, rested on no special command of God. This rite nevertheless became so established afterwards among his descendants that, by metonymy, the phrase lifting the hand, which properly belongs to the act, is often used for the act of swearing itself; and indeed the word itself, [יָד], which properly signifies the right hand, is not seldom taken for an oath among the Hebrews and Arabs. Hence some of their interpreters understand those words of Ps. 144.8 and 11 concerning an oath: Whose mouth speaketh vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity, or rather of lying or falsehood, for the Hebrew [יָמִין שֶׁקֶר] properly means this. Indeed, when God himself is introduced swearing in human fashion [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς], he uses this manner of speaking: I lift up my hand to heaven, and swear by my right hand, Deut. 32.40. The prophetic books of both Testaments often allude to this rite elsewhere. Therefore you may again rightly marvel that this rite is not only tolerated in the churches of Christians, but even approved by those very men who, although all the Old Testament rites are of the same kind, so that they are equally lawful or equally unlawful, nevertheless do not approve of the other Old Testament rites being used by Christians, and so far from tolerating them, loudly cry out that they must be utterly driven out of sacred assemblies. As for the rites of Christians: to pass over the various other ceremonies of the ancient Church, observed in varying ways according to the variety of places and times, there is one which has come down to us from the early age and is still in use, namely that, with the holy Gospels of God touched, one swears in set words. And this whole kind of oath, in which, besides the words spoken, some external visible bodily motion is also used, such as touching the altars, the thigh, or a book, throwing a stone, lifting the hand, and the like, is commonly called a corporal oath, Balsamon's [σωματικὸς ἔρκος] bodily fence.

units.la: SECT. XII.
units.tr: SECTION XII.

units.la: De his ritibus qui in solennibus Juramentis solent adhiberi, Casus secundus, sive Quæstio secunda est, An & quatenus addant vim aliquam obligationi Jurisjurandi; Quod est quaerere, An Iuramentum solemne & corporale fortius obliget simplici: ita ut gravius sit perjurium violati solennis Iuramenti quam simplicis? Pro responsione dico primo, a Casuistis non modo Pontificiae partis sed & Ecclesiarum Reformatarum concedi, Solennitatem actus aggravare peccatum in Juramento, perinde ac in Voto: quum sit Juramenti & Voti in plerisque, maxime in virtute obligandi consimilis ratio. a Jurare corporaliter plus est quam instrumento aut nuda voce, inquit ex illis quidam: & alius, b Quanto plus crescunt solemnitates, tanto majus est perjurium. Dico secundo, Etsi perjurium concedatur esse gravius, non tamen magis obligare solenne Iuramentum ex se & natura sua quam simplex: quia obligatio Iuramenti quatenus juramentum est, (nam & obligat quatenus promissionem includit; sed inquam quatenus est Iuramentum) exurgit praecise ex eo quod Deus testis & vindex invocatur. Invocatur autem Deus testis & vindex, non minus in Simplici Iuramento, quam in Solenni & Corporali: nam illa invocatio fit praecise per prolationem verborum, quae eadem est in simplici & solenni; & non per aliquem motum corporalem aut signum concomitans, in quibus consistit Iuramenti solennitas. Dico ergo tertio, quod solennitas juramenti aggravet peccatum perjurii, id ex accidenti proprovenire; sed tamen necessario & inseparabiliter, non autem contingenter: idque duplici ratione. Primo, ob majorem deliberationem. Ad hoc enim adhibetur externorum rituum solennitas, ut majorem incutiat interiori menti actus reverentiam, & religionis quasi sensum quendam; ut ita agens majori cum animi attentione & deliberatione versetur circa illum actum: & omne peccatum caeteris paribus eo gravius est, quo fit contra actum voluntatis antecedaneum magis deliberatum. Secundo solennis juramenti gravius est perjurium propter majus scandalum: quia quo solennius aliquid fit, eo attentius & a pluribus observatur; & proinde si in eo peccetur, exemplum magis erit & notorium & perniciosum. Dico quarto, cum in Juramento quae pars est cultus Dei expedire concedatur ut ob majorem actus reverentiam adhibeatur quaedam ritum & ceremoniarum solennitas, atque etiam praescripta verborum formula: non videri dari posse justam aliquam rationem, cur ex aliis partibus publici cultus utraque exulare cogatur, & ritum (inquam) mediocris solennitas & certa formula verborum. Fateor mihi, etsi & apud memetipsum cogitando, & abs aliis scitando, saepius & ferio id quaesiverim, nunquam tamen hactenus occurrisse idoneam discriminis rationem, cur non ista aut a juramento ut superstitiosa additamenta amoveri debeant, aut in reliquo Dei cultu, ut utilia pietatis subsidia, retineri possint. Qui potest capere, capiat: ego quidem non intelligo.
units.tr: Concerning those rites which are customarily employed in solemn oaths, the second case, or second question, is whether and to what extent they add some force to the obligation of an oath. That is, does a solemn and bodily oath bind more strongly than a simple one, so that perjury in violating a solemn oath is graver than perjury in violating a simple one? In answer, I say first: the Casuists not only of the Papist party but also of the Reformed Churches concede that the solemnity of an act aggravates sin in an oath, just as it does in a vow, since the reasoning about the binding power of oath and vow is in most respects similar. "To swear bodily is more than to swear by instrument or bare voice," says one of them; and another: "The more the solemnities increase, the greater the perjury." I say second: although perjury is conceded to be graver, a solemn oath does not of itself and by its nature bind more than a simple one. For the obligation of an oath insofar as it is an oath (for it also binds insofar as it includes a promise; but I mean insofar as it is an oath) arises precisely from the fact that God is invoked as witness and avenger. God is invoked as witness and avenger no less in a simple oath than in a solemn and bodily one. For that invocation is made precisely through the utterance of words, which is the same in a simple and a solemn oath, and not through any bodily motion or accompanying sign, in which the solemnity of an oath consists. I say therefore third that the solemnity of an oath aggravates the sin of perjury, and that this comes about by accident; yet it does so necessarily and inseparably, not contingently, and for a twofold reason. First, on account of greater deliberation. For the solemnity of external rites is employed for this very purpose: that it may strike the inner mind with greater reverence for the act, and a kind of sense of religion, so that the agent engages with that act with greater attention and deliberation of mind. And every sin, other things being equal, is the graver the more it is committed against an antecedent act of the will that was more deliberate. Second, the perjury of a solemn oath is graver on account of greater scandal: for the more solemnly something is done, the more attentively and by more people it is observed; and therefore if sin is committed in it, the example will be more notorious and more pernicious. I say fourth: since it is conceded that in an oath, which is a part of the worship of God, it is expedient that a certain ritual and solemnity of ceremonies, and also a prescribed form of words, be employed for greater reverence of the act, it does not seem that any just reason can be given why both should be banished from the other parts of public worship, namely the ritual (I say) of moderate solemnity and a fixed form of words. I confess that, although I have often and earnestly sought this, both thinking it over myself and asking of others, I have never yet come upon a suitable reason for the distinction: why these things should be removed from the oath as superstitious additions, or else be retained in the rest of the worship of God as useful aids to piety. Let him who can grasp it grasp it; I, for my part, do not understand.

units.la: Restat Quintum Dubium, nullius fere difficultatis, & paucissimis absolvendum, de Juramento, ubi solennitatis aliqua pars ob dignitatem personae omittitur. Ut quando Principi, Satrapae, aut Magnati juramentum defertur munus aliquod honorarium suscipienti, omissis ritibus ordinariis (ut libri tactu, & oculo &c.) praelectis verbis in quae jurandum est, admonetur tantum ut promittat in verbo Principis, aut in verbo honoris sui &c. se fideliter praedicta observaturum. Cui monitioni si admota pectori manu respondeat tantum se id pollicerı, Juramentum jam pro praestito & perac�to habetur. In hoc casu dico breviter, juratum non minus obligari in conscientia, ad fideliter praestandum ea quae sic pollicitus est, quam si singula verba & syllabas ipse suo ore pronunciasset, & reliqua solennia exactissime persegisset. Atque haec de Juramenti Forma externa dicta sunto. Expectabatis forsitan, quod & mihi constitutum erat, ut hac praelectione complecterer & ea quae ad Internam formam pertinent. Sed continet ea pars dubia quædam singularis & momenti & usus, & indigna quæ in nimis arctum compingantur: illud præsertim, quonam sensu Iuramentum debeat intelligi. Itaque ne aut vobis aliquam injuriam faciam nimia prolixitate, aut rei ipsi nimia brevitate: dabo operam ut proxima prælectione, cum Finali causa (quæ nec multa continet dubia, nec multum difsicilia) unà etiam expediam ea quæ de Interna Forma supersunt dicenda.
units.tr: There remains the Fifth Doubt, of almost no difficulty and to be dispatched in very few words, concerning an oath where some part of the solemnity is omitted on account of the dignity of the person. For example, when an oath is administered to a prince, a satrap or a magnate, undertaking some honorary office, the ordinary rites (such as touching the book, and the eye, etc.) are omitted; the words to be sworn are read out beforehand, and he is merely admonished to promise, "in the word of a prince," or "in the word of his honour," etc., that he will faithfully observe what has been stated. If, to this admonition, he replies with his hand placed upon his breast that he so promises, the oath is held to be already given and completed. In this case I say briefly that the one who has sworn is bound in conscience to faithfully perform what he has so promised no less than if he had pronounced each word and syllable with his own mouth and carried through all the remaining solemnities most exactly. And let these things be said concerning the External Form of an oath. Perhaps you expected, as I too had intended, that in this lecture I would also embrace the matters pertaining to the Internal Form. But that part contains certain doubts of singular weight and use, and matters unworthy of being squeezed into too narrow a compass, chiefly this: in what sense an oath ought to be understood. Therefore, lest I either do you some wrong by excessive length, or do the subject itself wrong by excessive brevity, I will take care that in the next lecture, together with the Final Cause (which contains neither many doubts nor very difficult ones), I also dispatch what remains to be said about the Internal Form.
