units.la: SECT. I.
units.tr: SECT. I.

units.la: FORmam Juramenti tractandam proposuimus duplicem ; Externam,& Internam. Externa signorum & verborum, quæ exteriore sensu percipiuntur, rationem continet: quam superiore lectione absolvimus. Internam, quæ in verborum sensu & interpretatione, quod est interioris mentis opus, consistit, nunc aggredimur. Verborum autem sensum hic intelligo, non respectu formularum, quibus aliquid jurari significatur ; ( de hac enim inter dignofcendi Juramenti κρῑτήρια, dum in externa forma versaretur , ante dictum est : ) sed respectu ipsius promissionis, quæ jure jurando confirmatur, & in verbis continetur. Res sane magni momenti,& multiplicis usus : utroque nomine digna omni vestra attentione.Etenim & magni interest perspicere quo sensu juraveris ; quia pejeravit, qui quod promissum est non eo sensu perfecerit, quo promisit, aut promittere debuit: nec in solis Juramentis, sed & in Votis, Promissis, Fœderibus, Contractibus, aliisq; conventionibus omnibus, in quibus bona fide agier oportet, omnino videndum ut promissio eo prorsus sensu quo facta est adimpleatur. Ad rem ergo. Juramenti verba, aut clara sint necesse est, aut ambigua.
units.tr: WE have proposed that the form of an oath is to be treated in two parts: the external and the internal. The external form contains the account of the signs and words that are perceived by the outward sense, and this we completed in the previous lecture. The internal form, which consists in the sense and interpretation of the words, which is the work of the inner mind, we now take up. By the sense of the words I here mean not the sense with respect to the formulas by which something is signified to be sworn (for concerning these, as the criteria [κρῑτήρια] for recognising an oath, we said earlier, while we were dealing with the external form), but the sense with respect to the promise itself, which is confirmed by the oath and contained in the words. This is indeed a matter of great weight and of many uses, and on both counts it deserves your full attention. For it greatly matters to see clearly in what sense you have sworn, since he forswears himself who does not perform what was promised in the sense in which he promised, or was bound to promise. And this must be considered carefully not only in oaths but also in vows, promises, covenants, contracts, and all other agreements in which one ought to act in good faith: the promise must be fulfilled in precisely the sense in which it was made. To the matter, then. The words of an oath must either be clear or be ambiguous.

units.la: SECT. II.
units.tr: SECT. II.

units.la: {*}Dubium primum est de Obligatione Juramenti, cujus verba clara sunt, & habent sensum manifestum & indubitatum. Ubi quatuor occurrunt casus. Primus est, cum verba Juramenti aut Promissionis ita sunt clara, sive primo ex propria sua & communi significatione; sive secundo ex recepto loquendi more alicujus gentis vel civitatis; sive tertio ex mutuo consensu partium: ut de eorum sensu inter partes omnino constet. Exemplum Primi: Caius Titio, spondeo me fundum meum Tusculanum tibi daturum, si mihi infra mensem centum aureos dependeris. Exempla Secundi: Si Johannes cum Petro linguâ nostrâ vernaculâ sic contraheret, pro centum marcis, quas tibi debeo, dabo tibi cras de grege meo centum oves mascuias, Anglicè Fo̅r an hundreth marks an hundreth wea- thers: vel, Pro usu-fructu fundi tui solvam tibi quotannis tres modios frumenti, Anglicè Three bushels of wheat. Quorum in priori exemplo, etsi vocabulum illud an hundreth sit ita ambiguum, ut nunc idem significet quod Latinis proprie est Centum, hoc est quinquies viginti, nunc majorem summam scilicet sexies viginti; tamen ex passim recepto per universum regnum Angliæ illius vocis usu, mens ita contrahentium sic effet manifesta, ut de sensu verborum nulla posset oriri lis: quandoquidem In hundred, cum de pecuniis sermo est, Centum sive quinquies viginti; cum de pecore, sexies viginti denotare, nemo est apud nos qui non intelligat. In posteriore item exemplo, illa vox § Bu- sheli cum apud Meridionales Anglos ex usu communi modium Latinorum unicum significet, apud Septentrionales binos modios: usus locorum ambiguitatem ejus vocis ita definiret, ut utrovis loco contractus fieret, de sensu tamen verborum inter bonæ fidei visos nulla posset esse dissensio. Exemplum tertii: Caii agrum quendam e multis unum fundo suo vicinum Titius emere cupiens, de pretio cum eo aliquoties ante collocutus, ubi eum die quodam convenit, Dabin' mihi, inquit, agrum tuum eo quo dixi pretio? Dabo. Jura mihi te daturum. Juro. Etsi de eo agri qui Titii fundo vicinus est peculiaris nulla, facta fit mentio: certum est tamen ex antegressis sermonibus eundem illum agrum peculiarem intelligi. Et istiusmodi quidem Juramentum obligat jurantem ad praestandū bona fide id quod promisit eo sensu, in quem manifestum est, si abesset utrinque omnis dolus malus, utrumque contrahentium consensisse. Fidem violaret Caius, si Titio alium aliquem agrum daret, & non cum de quo ante collocuti fuerant: & pactus an hundred weathers, si non nisi quinquies viginti tradiderit, promissi fidem non implevit.
units.tr: The first doubt concerns the obligation of an oath whose words are clear, and which have a manifest and indubitable sense. Four cases arise here. The first is when the words of the oath or promise are so clear, whether first from their proper and common meaning, or second from the accepted manner of speaking of some nation or city, or third from the mutual agreement of the parties, that there is no doubt between the parties about their sense. An example of the first: I, Gaius, promise Titius that I will give him my Tusculan farm, if he pays me a hundred gold pieces within a month. Examples of the second: if John made this contract with Peter in our own vernacular, "For a hundred marks which I owe you, I will give you tomorrow a hundred wethers from my flock," in English, "For an hundreth marks an hundreth weathers"; or, "For the usufruct of your farm I will pay you each year three bushels of wheat," in English, "Three bushels of wheat." In the first of these examples, although the English word "an hundreth" is so ambiguous that it may now mean what the Latins properly call centum, that is five times twenty, and now the greater sum, namely six times twenty, nevertheless from the use of that word which is accepted everywhere throughout the kingdom of England, the intention of the contracting parties would be so plain that no dispute could arise about the sense of the words. For, since "a hundred," when we speak of money, denotes centum or five times twenty, and when we speak of sheep denotes six times twenty, there is no one among us who does not understand this. In the second example likewise, since the word "bushel" by common usage among the Southern English means a single modius of the Latins, but among the Northern English means two modii, the custom of the places would fix the ambiguity of that word, so that whichever place the contract was made in, there could be no disagreement about the sense of the words between parties acting in good faith. An example of the third: Titius, wishing to buy from Gaius one field out of many which lies next to his own farm, having often discussed the price with him beforehand, met him on a certain day, and said: "Will you give me your field at the price I named?" "I will." "Swear that you will give it to me." "I swear." Although no particular field next to Titius's farm was mentioned, it is certain from the earlier conversation that this very field was meant. An oath of this kind binds the one swearing to perform in good faith what he promised, in the sense in which it is evident that both contracting parties, if all wicked deceit were absent on both sides, had agreed. Gaius would violate his faith if he gave Titius some other field and not the one they had discussed before; and if he agreed to "an hundred weathers" and delivered only five times twenty, he has not fulfilled the faith of his promise.

units.la: SECT. III.
units.tr: SECT. III.

units.la: Casus Secundus est de Juramento, ubi verba secundum communem morem intelligendi satis ex le clara videntur; sed jurans tamen non habens intentionem se obligandi in eo sensu quem verba aperte prae se ferunt, sensum alium quendam sibi imaginatur, cujus verba ipsa propter alicujus dictionis aut phrasis ambiguitatem possunt esse aliquo modo capacia: quem celare cupit audientes, ita ut ipse verba accipiat in alio sensu, quam ab audientibus accipi putet aut cupiat. Haec est illa, quam cum nonnullis Casuistis & Scholasticis Jesuitae potissimum tuentur & exercent, verbalis Æquivocatio. Cujus exempla in juramentis Assertoriis fere adducuntur: quia ejusmodi æquivocationis ex ipsorum doctrinâ praecipuus usus est, cum quis interrogatus à Judice non competente, vel non secundum ordinem juris, vel habens alias causam veritatem dissimulandi rationabilem, commutat apertum sensum verborum in alium minus apertum, & ab eâ quâ de re agitur longius remotum, prout suis rationibus expedire videbitur. Ut si Ludovicus interrogatus an esset esse Gallus, juraret se non esse gallum, sc. gallinaceum : aut si servus cujusspiam interrogatus effetne herus intus, juraret non esse, id est non comedere : cum mens interrogantis utrobique sit satis aperta. Idem & in Juramento Promissorio contingere potest : ut siquis belli dux pactus cum hoste decem dierum inducias, castra ejus de nocte diriperet ; quòd inter pacifcendum dierum tantum mentio facta suisset, non item noctium. Historiam narrant Livius & alii de decem Romanis apud Hannibalem captivis, qui certis conditionibus postquam redituros se in ipsius castra juraverant ab eo dimissi sunt : a quorum unus minime Romani ingenii homo (inquit ille, b alii a duobus id factum narrant) jurisjurandi solvendi causa commenticio consilio regressus eodem die in hostium castra velut aliquid oblitus, ante noctem comites assequitur. Quæ ipsius fraudulenta calliditas tam turpis existimata est, ut non modò contemptus vulgò c dispretûsq; sit, & à Censoribus omnium notarum damnis & ingnominiis affectus ; sed & à Senatu comprehendendus, & custodibus publicis datis ad Hannibalem deducendus judicaretur. Defendunt tamen acriter hanc æquivocationem Jesuitæ: ita ut Joh. Molanus professor Lovaniensis cædem Johannis Huss, contra fidem publicam de salvo conductu datam, eo nomine defendat, quòd salvum veniendi, non item redeundi veniam habuerit. Eant nunc Iesuitæ & fidenter conquerantur magnam sibi injuriam fieri, quòd docere dicantur non esse fidem cum hæreticis servandam. Nam si istoc pacto servari possit fides: non est quòd de eâ, cum quibuscunque demum transfigi contigerit, aut servandâ aut violandâ multum sint solliciti. Sed Iesuitisimum hunc integris in eam rem editis libris refutarunt,& fusè & solidè Reverendus in Christo Pater Joh. Mortonus Episcopus nunc Dunelmenfis, Henr. Mafonus, noftrorumq; alii, ab iis qui pleniorem hujus rei tractationem desiderant consulendi. Statuendum est interim isto modo jurantem, & æquivocè jurando peccare; & tacitâ illâ æquivocatione non obstante obligari in conscientia ad promissum faciendum in eo sensu quem verba ex se reddunt, & sunt apta ingenerare in mente audientium: ni sic fecerit, perjurio non vacare.
units.tr: The second case concerns an oath where the words, according to the common manner of understanding, seem quite clear; yet the one swearing, not intending to bind himself in the sense which the words plainly show, imagines for himself some other sense, to which the words themselves may in some way be open because of the ambiguity of some word or phrase. He wishes to conceal this from his hearers, so that he takes the words in a different sense from the one he thinks, or wishes, his hearers to take them. This is that verbal equivocation which the Jesuits, above all, defend and practise together with some Casuists and Schoolmen. Examples of it are commonly brought forward in assertory oaths, because by their own teaching this equivocation is chiefly used when someone, questioned by a judge who has no authority, or not according to the order of law, or having some other reasonable cause for concealing the truth, changes the plain sense of the words into another less plain, and one further removed from the matter in hand, as his own reasons shall seem to require. For example, if Louis, asked whether he was Gallus (a Frenchman), were to swear that he was not a gallus (a cock); or if a servant, asked whether his master was within, were to swear that he was not, that is, that he was not eating; since the intention of the questioner in both cases is quite plain. The same can happen in a promissory oath too: for example, if a general, having agreed with the enemy on a truce of ten days, were to attack the enemy's camp by night, because in agreeing only days had been mentioned, and not nights. Livy and others relate the story of the ten Roman captives held by Hannibal, who, after swearing under certain conditions that they would return to his camp, were dismissed by him; one of whom, a man by no means of Roman character (he says, though others, b reporting it of two men, tell the story differently), in order to discharge his oath by a contrived plan, went back to the enemy camp on the same day, as if he had forgotten something, and before nightfall rejoined his companions. This fraudulent cunning of his was considered so disgraceful that he was not only despised and c scorned by the common people, and visited by the censors with every mark of infamy and disgrace, but was also judged to be seized by the Senate and, under public guard, to be led back to Hannibal. Yet the Jesuits defend this equivocation stoutly: so much so that Johannes Molanus, professor at Louvain, defends on this ground the killing of John Huss, contrary to the public faith of the safe-conduct given, because he had a licence to come safely, but not to go back. Let the Jesuits now go on and boldly complain that a great wrong is done to them, because they are said to teach that faith is not to be kept with heretics. For if faith can be kept in this way, there is no reason to be very anxious whether it is to be kept or broken with whomever it happens to be pledged. But this Jesuit subtlety has been refuted in full books written for that purpose, both fully and solidly, by the Reverend Father in Christ, John Morton, now Bishop of Durham, by Henry Mason, and by others of our own, to be consulted by those who desire a fuller treatment of this matter. Meanwhile it must be laid down that one who swears in this way, equivocating, sins; and that, notwithstanding that tacit equivocation, he is bound in conscience to perform the promise in the sense which the words themselves convey, and which are fit to produce that understanding in the minds of the hearers; unless he has done so, he is not free from perjury.

units.la: SECT. IV.
units.tr: SECT. IV.

units.la: Rationes istius assertionis aliquot dudum attuli, confirmandæ primæ nostræ hypothesi: addo nunc alias, sed breviter. Primò, quia juramentum debet simplicissimè & cum essectu intelligi; quæ summa est illus hypothesis: cum qua simplicitate pugnat illud quæsitæ ambiambiguitatis artificium. Secundo, quia magna est prophanatio nominis divini, eum ut cordis infpectorem & testem invocare, in testimonium veritatis eorum verborum, quæ cum eo quod jurans in corde reconditum fervat non concordant. Quod quid est aliud quàm Deum qui nec illudere scit nec illudi, quantum in ipso est impostorem facere & indignæ simulationis patronum? Tertio, quia ejusmodi æquivocatio ipsi institutioni & naturæ Juranienti adversatur: cujus præcipuus usus est, ut fit a ἀντιλογίας πέρας, ut finem statuat litibus & controversiis, & ut de rebus alioqui incertis habeatur aliqua certitudo quantum expedit rebus humanis; cum fit jurisjurandi religio b expediendarum litium maximum remedium. Ast æquivocatione tollitur omnis illa certitudo, quæ jurando quæritur: quæ enim potest esse certitudo illius refponfionis, cujus sententia incerta est? Nec expediuntur hac ratione lites, sed augentur magis. Quarto, quia sic jurans proximum suum decipit, & sciens fallit: contra quàm exigitur à jurante ne c jurec in dolo; & contra veterum formulam illam, Si sciens fallo. Quinto, quia ut affirmatio & negatio inAffertorio,sic est sponsio in Promiffsorio Juramento, cum contineat in fe responsionem ad quæstionem seu interrogationem à deferente propositam, nisi fit
units.tr: I have already offered several reasons for this assertion, to confirm our first hypothesis. I now add others, though briefly. (1) First, because an oath must be understood in the plainest sense and as it is actually meant. That is the whole point of this hypothesis, and the contrivance of a sought-after ambiguity is incompatible with that plainness. (2) Second, because it is a great profanation of the divine name to call on God as the searcher of hearts and witness, in attestation of words that do not agree with what the swearer keeps hidden in his heart. What is this but making God, who knows neither how to deceive nor how to be deceived, as far as in us lies, an impostor and a patron of unworthy pretence? (3) Third, because such equivocation runs against the very institution and nature of an oath. Its chief use is to be [a] the end of contradiction [ἀντιλογίας πέρας], to bring an end to disputes and controversies, and to give some certainty in matters otherwise uncertain, as far as human affairs require. For the sanctity of an oath is the greatest remedy for settling lawsuits. But equivocation destroys all that certainty which an oath seeks: for what certainty can there be in an answer whose meaning is uncertain? Lawsuits are not settled in this way; they are rather multiplied. (4) Fourth, because a person who swears in this way deceives his neighbour and deceives knowingly. This is contrary to what is required of the one swearing, that he not swear in deceit, and contrary to that old formula, If I knowingly deceive. (5) Fifth, because just as affirmation and denial belong to an assertory oath, so in a promissory oath there is a pledge, which contains within it an answer to the question or interrogation put by the examiner. Unless the answer fits and suits the question put, it is a lie and not the truth. For question and answer together form, as it were, one proposition, and this must be judged wholly false if the answer is given in a sense other than that in which the question was asked. [b] (See Digest, law 1, On the Law of Oaths.)

units.la: b l.1. ff. de jure jur. fit congrua & apta propositæ interrogationi, mendacium est non veritas. Nam ex interrogatione & responsione fit una quasi propositio: quæ omnino falsa censenda est, si alio sensu quàm quo proposita est interrogatio, responsio fiat. Neque vero multum adjuvat hac in re istius simulationis patronos restrictio illa quâ uti solent, &c. non licere nobis passim hac æquivocatione uti; Sed solum apud non judicem, eúmque qui jus non habet exigendi juramentum; vel qui sine justâ causâ nos adigit ad jurandum, aut rem indebitam petit, aut ex aliquâ simili causâ rationabili. Sed præterquam quod primò ista ab eis gratis dicuntur, sine ulla aut Scripturæ aut veteris Ecclesiæ authoritate, vel etiam solidâ & evidenti ratione: nec tollitur secundo, sed nec minuitur istâ restrictione vis eorum argumentorum, quæ jam adduximus in contrarium: sciendum tertio, etsi injusta vis concederetur impedire posse obligationem illam quæ homini fit, quia non est æquum ut ex actu injusto jus sibi quis acquirat, nullam tamen injuriam ab hominibus illatam justam nobis causam præbere posse injuriam faciendi Deo, tollendo &c. illam obligationem, quæ Deo fit ut cordium infpectori; cui, ex omni juramento nostro propter nominis sui invocationem, jus accrescit. Quarto, denique, Jesuitica hæc doctrina improbis hominibus pro sua libidine, mentiendi & pejerandi licentiam facit: etiam illa restrictione non obstante: quum ea manente, adhuc tamen an expediat vel non expediat uti equivocatione, penes ipsum jurantem solum sit tota judicandi potestas. Ideo siquis ad jurandum præter jus & fas adigatur: aut debet juramentum simpliciter recusare; aut ipsum in eo sensu quo proponitur sine ulla simulatione vel æquivocatione admittere.
units.tr: Nor does that restriction, which the defenders of this pretence habitually use, greatly help them in this matter: that it is not lawful for us to use this equivocation everywhere, but only before a judge who has no right to require an oath, or who without just cause binds us to swear, or who demands something not owed, or for some similar reasonable cause. But, apart from the fact that first, these things are asserted by them without warrant, with no authority of Scripture or the early Church, nor even solid and evident reason; second, the force of the arguments we have already adduced to the contrary is not removed or lessened by this restriction. It must be noted third that, even if one granted that an unjust force could prevent the obligation that arises toward a human being, since it is not fair that someone should acquire a right to himself by an unjust act, yet no wrong done by men can give us a just cause to wrong God, by annulling that obligation which is owed to God as searcher of hearts. To Him, by every oath we make, because His name is invoked, a right accrues. Fourth and finally, this Jesuitical doctrine gives wicked men licence to lie and to forswear themselves at their own pleasure, even with that restriction in place. For even with the restriction retained, the whole power of judging whether it is expedient or not to use equivocation still rests with the swearer alone. Therefore, if anyone is compelled to swear beyond right and lawful bounds, he must either simply refuse the oath, or admit it in the sense in which it is proposed, without any pretence or equivocation.

units.la: SECT. V.
units.tr: SECT. V.

units.la: Casus tertius huic affinis est de mentali (ut vocant) Reservatione quam eadem prorsus ratione tuentur Jesuitæ, & eadem restrictione definiunt, qua & verbalem æquivocationem. Ut enim in illa, ex detortis in alienum sensum verbis prolatis; sic in ista, ex assumento aliquo non exterius prolato, sed intus apud se in mente reservato, jurans interrogantem ludificatur. Sic Sacerdotem aiunt si à Magistratu hæretico rogetur an sit sacerdos, respondere posse se non esse sacerdotem; nempe Bacchi, aut Apollinis; & uxorem adulteram, si à marito Zelotypo de adulterio postuletur, jurare posse se adulterium non commisisse, nempe ut ipse dicat. Pariter & in promissorio Juramento, posse viatorem ob vitam redimendam jurare, latroni se certam pecuniae summum daturum, cum tamen in animo habeat nullam ei dare: dummodo sic intelligat, Dabo si debeam, vel Dabo si apud Magistratum petieris. Sed ut iisdem fere fundamentis nititur, sic iisdem argumentis evertitur, mentalis haec reservatio, quibus & illa verbalis equivocatio. Tollit enim omnem inter homines fidem & certitudinem. Deum impostorem facit, eos quicum agitur decipit jurisjurandi finem & usum pervertit, omne genus mendaciis & perjuriis latam fenestram aperit. Quia & aequivocatione illa tanto perniciosior est ista Reservatio, quanto huic quam illi difficilius occurritur. Praevisa vel insuspecta potest praecaveri Æquivocatio, ita explicando verba in quae jurandum est, ut nulla subesse possit ambiguitas, nulla reliqua sit evadendi rimula. Ast ne Reservationibus hisce quis utatur, nulla prorsus arte vel providentia effeceris. Vertumnum hunc quo nodo sic obstrictum teneas, ut non mutata subinde forma elabatur?
units.tr: The third case, related to this, concerns what they call mental reservation, which the Jesuits defend on exactly the same grounds and define with the same restriction as verbal equivocation. For just as in the one case words are twisted into a foreign sense, so in the other, the swearer mocks the questioner by means of some qualification not spoken aloud but kept inwardly in his mind. Thus, they say, if a priest is asked by a heretical magistrate whether he is a priest, he may answer that he is not a priest, meaning a priest of Bacchus or of Apollo. And an adulterous wife, if her jealous husband asks her about adultery, may swear that she has not committed adultery, meaning, as she herself understands it. Likewise in a promissory oath, a traveller who wishes to ransom his life may swear to a robber that he will give him a certain sum of money, although he has no intention of giving him anything, provided he understands it thus: I will give if I ought to, or I will give if you ask before a magistrate. But just as this mental reservation rests on almost the same foundations, so it is overthrown by the same arguments as that verbal equivocation. For it destroys all faith and certainty among men. It makes God an impostor, it deceives those with whom we deal, it perverts the end and use of an oath, and it opens a wide window for every kind of lie and perjury. And this reservation is all the more pernicious than that equivocation, in that it is harder to guard against than the other. An equivocation can be avoided if foreseen or suspected, by so explaining the words to be sworn to that no ambiguity can lie beneath them and no loophole for escape remains. But no art or foresight can ensure that a person does not use these reservations. Can you hold this Vertumnus so fast bound that he does not slip away by changing his shape again?

units.la: — * mille adde catenas,
units.tr: — * Add a thousand chains,

units.la: Effugiet tamen haec celeratus vincula Protei.
units.tr: Yet this wicked Proteus will slip out of the bonds.

units.la: Juramentum apud nos Fidelitatis, ea verborum accuratione & studio perscriptum, ut nullus aut effugio locus sit, sed fuisse tamen & sacrificuli, dum sibi quidlibet animo refervandi libertatem reservant, magna vultus constantia præstare non verentur. Ipsissimam enim illam clausulam, qua verbis conceptis spondent se omnia antedicta fideliter observaturos juxta tenorem verborum à se prolatorum, & juxta eorum verborum apertum & naturalem sensum & sententiam, sine ulla æquivocatione, aut mentali reservatione; intel-ligunt interim cum alia reservatione, quam tibi dicam.
units.tr: Our oath of Fidelity, drawn up with such precision and care of words that there is no place for escape, but ... the little priests, while reserving for themselves the freedom to keep back whatever they like in their minds, do not hesitate to put on a great show of steadfastness. For they pledge in words that they will faithfully observe all the things mentioned above, according to the tenor of the words they have uttered, and according to the plain and natural sense and meaning of those words, without any equivocation or mental reservation; yet meanwhile they understand it with another reservation, which I shall tell you of.

units.la: SECT. VI.
units.tr: SECT. VI.

units.la: Habent tamen paratam sibi hanc defensionem, quò se à perjurio liberent: nempe ex oratione verbali & mentali unam confici integram orationem compositam, in quâ totâ conjunctim acceptâ nulla sit falsitas. Ut exempli gratia, si sacrificulus verbis prolatis juret se non esse sacrificulum: adjectione illâ in animo reservata, sed non enunciatâ, Ut tibi dicam: oratio hæc tota, inquiunt, ex verbali & mentali composita, si integrè sumatur, erit vera; sc. Non sum sacrificulus ut tibi dicam. Nec videtur ratio aliqua obstare, quin liber-rum cuique sit orationem suam si libuerit ex terminis vocalibus & mentalibus componere. Cur enim in Precatione, si quis illa tantum verba Panem nostrum quotidianum ore protulerit, reliquo illa Da nobis hodie mente solùm cogitaverit; poterit illa integra oratio & licita esse, & Deo grata: non itidem licebit in juramento idipsum facere? Ut huic Jesuitarum argutiolæ plenè respondeatur, primò mirandum non animadvertere acutissimos disputandi artifices hac defensione omnem judiciorum, promissionum, contractumque humanorum fidem penitus labefactari. Quo enim utuntur argumento aliquid haberet ponderis, evinceret sane non minus licere istiusmodi reservationibus uti apud legitimum judicem, & in re debita (quod tamen illi dicunt fieri non oportere) quam apud judicem non competentem, aut in re indebita: quum Oratio ex verbali & mentali composita, sit omnino ejusdem utrobique aut veritatis aut falsitatis. Et hæc responsio sufficit ad hominem: sed ad rem ipsam dicendum secundo, Orationem ex verbali & mentali eo quo dictum est modo compositam admitti posse, ubi quis secum aliquid solus commentatur, ut in privata meditatione; aut quando cum solo Deo res est, ut in precatione vel gratiarum actione: aut ubi cum hominibus negotium est, ut in Juramentis, ubi sic ferendum est testimonium ut ab aliis audiatur & intelligatur, mixtam ex verbali & mentali orationem nullatenus esse admittendam. Hujus discriminis ratio manifesta est: quia tàm notum unicuique est, quod ipse intus in pectore suo occultum gestat, quam quod verbis palàm enunciat. Deo etiam cui nihil occultum est, vel abditissima cordium secreca a τετραχνηλισμένα sunt & perspectissima. Ita ut secum meditantibus, vel Deum precantibus, quod ad veri & falsi rationem attinet perinde est, sive totum id quod in mente est enunciant, sive partem tantùm, sive nihil. Cæterùm apud homines, quibus cogitata cordium ignorari necesse est, nisi quatenus sermone, alióve externo indicio significantur, orationis veritas & falsitas ex iis solis æstimanda est, quæ audientibus aliquid testari possunt. Quod cum reservationes illæ quæ in mente sunt efficere nequeant, in dijudicandâ orationis veritate verborum prolatorum tantùm, non autem reservationum mentalium ratio habenda est.
units.tr: Yet they have a defence ready to hand, by which they free themselves from perjury: namely, that from verbal and mental speech one may make up a single composite statement, in which, taken as a whole, there is no falsehood. For example, if a sacrificulus swears in spoken words that he is not a sacrificulus, while adding in his mind, but not uttering, as I tell you, the whole statement, they say, being made up of the verbal and the mental, will be true if taken in full: namely, I am not a sacrificulus, as I tell you. Nor does any reason seem to stand in the way of each person composing his statement, if he likes, from vocal and mental terms. For why, when someone in the Prayer has uttered only the words Give us this day our daily bread with his mouth, and has thought the rest, give us today, only in his mind, can that whole prayer be both lawful and pleasing to God, while in an oath it will not likewise be allowed to do the same thing? To answer this Jesuit subtlety fully, first, it is remarkable that these most keen artificers of disputation do not notice that by this defence all faith in judgments, promises and human contracts is utterly undermined. For if the argument they use had any weight, it would certainly prove that such reservations may be used no less before a lawful judge and in a matter that is due (which they nevertheless say ought not to be done) than before a judge without competence or in a matter that is not due, since a statement composed of the verbal and the mental is wholly the same, in either case, in truth or falsity. And this answer suffices against the man; but as to the thing itself, it must be said secondly that a statement composed of the verbal and the mental in the manner described can be admitted where someone is weighing something alone with himself, as in private meditation; or when the matter is with God alone, as in prayer or thanksgiving; but where the business is with men, as in oaths, where testimony must be given in such a way that it is heard and understood by others, a mixed statement of the verbal and the mental is in no way to be admitted. The reason for this distinction is plain: because what each person secretly bears inside his own breast is as little known to others as what he openly utters in words. Moreover, to God, to whom nothing is hidden, the most secret recesses of hearts are laid open [τετραχηλισμένα] and wholly visible. So that for those who meditate with themselves, or pray to God, it makes no difference, as regards the truth or falsity of the matter, whether they express everything that is in the mind, or only part of it, or nothing. But among men, to whom the thoughts of hearts must necessarily remain unknown, except so far as they are signified by speech or some other outward sign, the truth and falsity of a statement must be judged from those things alone which can bear witness to the hearers. Since those reservations which are in the mind cannot have this effect, in judging the truth of a statement regard must be had only to the words uttered, and not to mental reservations.

units.la: SECT. VII.
units.tr: SECT. VII.

units.la: Casus Quartus respicit post factum. Nam ut antequam juretur, & in ipso jurandi actu, oportet esse propositum adimplendi promissum eo sensu quo propositum est, sine aliquâ æquivocatione aut mentali reservatione: ita postquam juratum est adsit oportet studium & conatus, ut idoneo tempore fideliter idipsum & eodem sensu quo juratum est adimpleatur fine aliqua evasione aut effugio. Atque ut unum perjurii genus est, inter jurandum detorquere verba in alium sensum, quàm concipiunt audientes: sic alterium perjurii genus est, ubi recte juraveris, non sincerè agere, sed novo aliquo excogitato commento juramenti vim (salvis tamen verbis) declinare & eludere. a Verbis jurisjurandi artes mutantibus, quibus flagitii conscientia inerat, inquit de quibusdam Tacitus. Lepidum recitat ex Herodoto Stobæus de Archetimo quodam, qui apud Cydiam amicum nummos aliquot aureos depofuerat. Post aliquod tempus Archetimo depositum repetenti, Cydias præ auri cupidine acceptum negat. Res ad Judices delata: instat actor, negat reus: par utrique confidentia, testes nulli. Placuit judicibus, quòd deessent aliæ probationes, jurejurando litem terminari. Dies examini dictus. Cydias interea baculo ferulino scitè excavato nummos incluserat, simulans etiam adverfam valet udinem. Die condicto adest, baculum, velut qui è recenti morbo vixdum fatis convaluerat, manu gestans. Aris admovendus, Archetimo baculum tantisper tenendam porrigit, dum ipse jurisjurandi folennia perageret. Traditio baculo, tum demum summa cum animi vultúsque constantiâ præstito juramento, fatetur se ab Archetimo aurum accepisse, sed restitutisse fidenter asserit. Archetimus & offensus damno, & hominis conjunctam cum summâ impudentiâ summam perfidiam indignatus, baculum à se projectum tàm vehementi iƈtu pavimento impegit, ut ferula confracta, effusi nummi & Cydiæ fraudem, & totius rei veritatem patefecerint. Id Cydiæ factum ἐκ τίχνης πλασμένον ψευδῶ appellat historiæ scriptor, ex arte concinnatum mendacium: qui & idem observat Cydiæ κακλῶ βίᾳ καταςροφλῶ, velut justam perfidiæ mercedem, miserum vitæ exitum. Extant id genus exempla in historiis & in vita quotidiana compluria unde pauca quædam quæ nobis ex usu sient colligo. Primum, Homines vel improbos aliquâ saltem Juramenti religione & conscientia duci: adeo ut quibus justi & honesti vel nulla vel perexigua ratio est, ex quodam tamen naturæ sensu juramento se putent ad datam firmarámque fidem exolvendam obligari. Secundum, pravis affectibus ni fortiter resistatur, periculum esse ne scintilla illa quæ in nobis reliqua est luminis naturalis, ita ab illis aut penitus extinguatur, aut saltem miserè obruatur, ut de perjurio arte aliqua palliando magis, quàm sincerè evitando solliciti simus. Tertium, qui perjurii immunis esse cupit juramenti à se suscipiendi verba singula, eorúmque sensum & vim diligenter ex-penpendere debere: ut si non debeat servari, ne quidem suscipiatur; si tas sit suscipi, sine fraude & simulatione servetur. Impium est enim rem sacram præpropere vovare: & intempestivam, voto jam emisso, orditri inquisitionem. Et hæc de primo dubio. Cujus summa est; Juramenti verba ubi sunt ita ex se clara, ut deorum sensu inter bonæ fidei viros nullum possit esse dubium, obligari Jurantem in eo sensu quem manifeste reddunt: nec fas esse ipsi, aut inter jurandum, aut postquam juraverit, ea verba, quæ efitâ in compendium suum interpretatione alio detorquere.
units.tr: The Fourth Case concerns what is done after the fact. For just as, before an oath is taken, and in the very act of swearing, there must be a purpose of fulfilling the promise in the sense in which it is intended, without any equivocation or mental reservation, so after the oath has been taken there ought to be earnestness and effort that, at a fitting time, it be faithfully fulfilled in the same sense in which it was sworn, without any evasion or escape. And just as one kind of perjury is to twist the words, while swearing, into a sense other than the hearers conceive, so another kind of perjury is, having sworn rightly, not to act sincerely, but by some contrived new device to avoid and elude the force of the oath (while keeping the words intact). Tacitus says of certain men that they changed the arts of oath-words, in which there was a consciousness of crime. Stobaeus recounts from Herodotus an amusing story about a certain Archetimus, who had deposited some gold coins with a friend, Cydias. After some time, when Archetimus asked for his deposit back, Cydias, out of greed for the gold, denied that he had received it. The matter was brought before the judges; the plaintiff pressed, the defendant denied; the confidence of both was equal, and there were no witnesses. The judges decided that, since there was no other proof, the suit should be settled by oath. A day was set for the examination. Meanwhile Cydias had cleverly hollowed out a ferula staff and hidden the coins in it, pretending also to be ill. On the appointed day he appeared, carrying the staff in his hand, as one who had barely recovered from a recent illness. When he came to the altars, he handed the staff to Archetimus to hold for a while, while he himself performed the solemn rites of the oath. Then, having handed over the staff and sworn with the greatest constancy of mind and countenance, he confessed that he had received the gold from Archetimus, but boldly asserted that he had returned it. Archetimus, both offended by the loss and indignant at the man's great treachery joined with the utmost impudence, struck the staff he had been holding so violently against the pavement that the ferula broke, and the scattered coins revealed both the fraud of Cydias and the whole truth of the matter. The historian calls this deed of Cydias a lie fashioned by art [ἐκ τέχνης πλασμένον ψεῦδος], and he also observes that Cydias came to a wretched end of life [κακῷ βίῳ καταστροφή], as a just reward for his treachery. Many examples of this kind exist in histories and in everyday life, from which I gather a few points that are useful to us. First, even wicked men are generally moved by at least some religious fear and conscience of an oath, so that those in whom there is little or no sense of what is just and honourable nevertheless think, from a certain sense of nature, that they are bound by an oath to discharge a pledge given and confirmed. Second, unless one resists strongly the depraved affections, there is a danger that the spark of natural light that remains in us will be either wholly extinguished by them or at least miserably overwhelmed, so that we are concerned to cloak perjury by some art rather than to avoid it sincerely. Third, whoever wishes to be free of perjury ought to weigh carefully each of the words of an oath he undertakes, and their sense and force: so that if it ought not to be kept, it should not be undertaken at all; and if it is lawful to undertake, it should be kept without deceit or pretence. For it is impious to vow a sacred matter rashly, and it is untimely, once the vow has been uttered, to begin an inquiry. And this is said concerning the first doubt. Its sum is this: where the words of an oath are in themselves so clear that among men of good faith there can be no doubt of their sense, the one swearing is bound in the sense which they plainly express; nor is it lawful for him, either while swearing or after he has sworn, to twist those words to another meaning, devised for his own advantage.

units.la: SECT. VIII.
units.tr: SECT. VIII.

units.la: Dubium secundum, est, ubi de verborum sensu ambigitur. Casus autem sunt tres. Primus est, de Juramentis Spontaneis: ut in illis promissionibus, quæ fiunt ex mero motu propriæ voluntatis, ex animi quadam liberalitate, & non ex debito aliquo justitiæ aut obsequii. Respondetur communiter & vere; itiusmodi Juramenta esse ex ipsius jurantis mente accipienda: quia unusquisque sui optimus interpres est. Exempli gratia; Siquis apud nos voto, juramento, aut promissione se obstringeret dare alicui prochotrophio aut pauperibus bus alicujus villæ quolibet mense decem solidos : siquidem nobis Mensis nomen ambiguum est, si pauperes illi primùm pensionem sibi ex promisso deberi contenderent ad vicesimum octavum diem Januarii, & exinde deinceps reliquas vicesimo octavo quoquo die, accipiendo Mensem pro quatuor septimanarum spacio, quæ est una ejus nominis significatio ; ille contrà non deberi diceret ante ultimum diem Januarii, & sic deinceps, accipiendo Mensem pro duodecima ferè anni parte ut in Callendario in duodecim menses totus annus distribuitur, quæ est ejusdem vocis altera significatio : æquissimum est, ut vox ambigua ex ipsius potius quàm illorum mente accipiatur. Quia illa pensio non est eis debita ex justitia, & ante factam promissionem ; sed ex charitate, & vi promissionis liberæ, non alicujus pastionis aut contractus. Et de hoc genere juramenti debent illa verba intelligi, quæ citantur in glossa Juris Canonici, a Patet quod Deus non accipit sic juramentum, sicut ille cui juratur, sed potius sicut qui jurat intelligit. Sed ut hæc responsio rectius intelligatur, duo sunt observanda. Alterum, quòd hoc in spontaneis juramentis & promissionibus potissimum obtinet, cum ὑπ' ἐπαχλῶν diversa sit ratio, ut mox dicetur. Alterum, jurantem in præsenti casu obligari ad promissum servandum
units.tr: The second doubt arises where there is ambiguity about the sense of the words. There are three cases. The first concerns spontaneous oaths: those promises made from a mere motion of one's own will, out of a certain generosity of mind, and not from any debt of justice or obedience. The common and true answer is that such oaths are to be understood according to the mind of the one swearing, because everyone is the best interpreter of himself. For example, suppose someone among us bound himself by vow, oath or promise to give ten shillings every month to an almshouse, or to the poor of some village. Since the word month is ambiguous for us, suppose those poor claimed that the first payment was due to them under the promise by the twenty-eighth day of January, and thereafter the rest on the twenty-eighth day of each following month, taking month as a span of four weeks, which is one meaning of the word; while the other party said that nothing was due before the last day of January, and so on, taking month as roughly the twelfth part of the year, since the calendar divides the whole year into twelve months, which is the other meaning of the same word. It is most fair that the ambiguous word be understood according to his mind rather than theirs. For that payment is not owed to them by justice, nor was it owed before the promise was made; it is owed by charity and by the force of a free promise, not of any bargain or contract. It is of this kind of oath that those words should be understood which are cited in the gloss on canon law: a That God does not accept an oath as the one to whom it is sworn does, but rather as the one who swears understands it. But so that this answer may be better understood, two things must be noted. The first is that this holds chiefly for spontaneous oaths and promises, since the case is different for those [imposed by constraint, ὑπ' ἐπαχθῶν], as will soon be said. The second is that the one swearing in the present case is bound to keep the promise to be fulfilled

units.la: dum
units.tr: while

units.la: a Gloff. ad c.22.qu.5. c.11. dum eo sensu,quem ipse verbis suis, quo tem& shy;pore juravit,aut bona fide intendebat, aut voluit ab audientibus intelligi: non autem in eo sensu quemcunq; ipsi postea libuerit illis ver& shy;bis affingere. Deus enim qui aspicit cor, non luditur verbis : b Nec debet intentio verbis inservire, sed verba intentioni.
units.tr: in the sense which he himself intended in good faith at the time he swore, or wished to be understood by the hearers, and not in whatever sense he afterwards pleases to attach to those words. For God, who looks upon the heart, is not mocked by words. b The intention should not serve the words, but the words the intention.

units.la: SECT. IX.
units.tr: SECT. IX.

units.la: Casus Secundus est de Juramentis & pro& shy;missionibus c ἐπταχτοῖς, id eis quae juran& shy;ti ab alio deferuntur; five quae alius quif& shy;piam aliquo aut jure suo aut juris praetextu a jurante exigit. Qualia sunt ea impri­mis, quae a Rectoribus pro authoritate sua subditis imperantur, aut legibus sunt confti­uta: ut apud nos juramenta Suprematus Regii & Fidelitatis, & ea quae ex statutis Academiae ab eis exiguntur qui ad gradus promoventur, aliaque similia. Item ea quae ex justa con& shy;ventione pertium ab alterutro contrahentium postulantur: ut ea quae in pactis, faederibus, aliisque civilibus contractibus ad mutuam fidem confirmandam intervenium. Pro re­sponsione in hac casu dico, Istiusmodi jura& shy;menta regulariter intelligi debere in eo sensu, quem probabiliter judicari potest fuisse ab eo cui juratur, intentum: ita ut ju& shy;rans teneatur sub poena perjurii implere quod promisit (si sit res licita & honesta secundum intentionem deferentis) b Verba intelliguntur secundum mentem & intentionem ejus cui sit juramentum, ait Jurisconsultus. Ratio est, quia eum ob finem hoc juramenti genus suscipitur, ut is cui juratur ex interpolita fide habeat aliquam certitudinem, id quod sibi a jurante promissum est impletum iri: de promissione autem adimplenda nihilo certior effet, si verba ex mente jurantis, & non ex sua ipsius mente essent intelligenda. Alia enim ratio est Obligationis, ubi debitum fundatur in promissione: ubi vero promissio fundatur in devito, longe alia. Ipse Deus, qui nemini ex jure debitor est, ex promissionibus tamen suis gratuitis, facit se nobi debitorem: & qui Voto, Juramento, vel promissione spontanea se obligat ad aliquem actum charitatis, contrahit ipso facto debitum. Sed quia hoc debitum non fundatur in jure ejus cui facta est promissio, sed promanat ex mero actu libero & gratuito ipsius promittentis: omnino æquum est, ut ipse sit mentis suæ interpres, cuja potissimum interest, quantum & quatenus & quo sensu intendebat se obligare. Aut ubi contra promissio ipsa fundatur in debito aliquo antecedente; debito sc. aut subjectionis & obsequii ex authoritate superioris, aut justitiæ & pacti ex conventione partium quia is cui fit promissio jus habet eam exigendi, & ipsius maxime interest ut promissi fides fervetur : ratio postulat ut ex ipsius potius mente & interpretatione, quàm ex promittentis sensu, de promissionis obligatione judicetur.
units.tr: The second case concerns oaths and promises [imposed from outside, ἐπακτοῖς], that is, those which are laid upon the one swearing by another, or which someone demands of the one swearing either by his own right or under a pretext of law. Such are, above all, those things which superiors, by their authority, enjoin upon their subjects, or which are established by laws: for example, among us, the oaths of Royal Supremacy and Allegiance, and those which are exacted by the statutes of the university from those who are promoted to degrees, and other similar things. Likewise, those which are demanded by one of the contracting parties from the other by just agreement between the parties: for example, those which are interposed in pacts, treaties and other civil contracts to confirm mutual faith. In answer to this case I say that oaths of this kind ordinarily must be understood in the sense which can reasonably be judged to have been intended by the one to whom the oath is sworn, so that the one swearing is bound, under penalty of perjury, to carry out what he promised (provided the thing is lawful and honest according to the intention of the one imposing it). b The words are understood according to the mind and intention of the one to whom the oath is sworn, says the jurist. The reason is that this kind of oath is undertaken for this purpose: that the one to whom it is sworn may have some certainty, through the pledged faith, that what has been promised to him by the one swearing will be fulfilled. He would be no more certain of the performance of the promise if the words were to be understood according to the mind of the one swearing and not according to his own mind. For the reason of obligation is different where the debt is grounded in a promise, and quite different where the promise is grounded in a debt. God himself, who owes nothing to anyone by right, nevertheless makes himself our debtor by his gratuitous promises; and whoever binds himself by vow, oath or spontaneous promise to some act of charity thereby incurs a debt by that very fact. But because this debt is not grounded in the right of the one to whom the promise is made, but arises from the mere free and gratuitous act of the promiser himself, it is wholly fair that he himself should be the interpreter of his own mind, since it chiefly concerns him how far, how much, and in what sense he intended to bind himself. Or, on the contrary, where the promise itself is grounded in some prior debt, either a debt of subjection and obedience arising from the authority of a superior, or a debt of justice and pact arising from agreement of the parties, because the one to whom the promise is made has the right to exact it, and it especially concerns him that the faith of the promise be kept: reason requires that the obligation of the promise be judged according to his mind and interpretation rather than according to the sense of the promiser.

units.la: SECT. X.
units.tr: SECT. X.

units.la: Casus Tertius est, ubi diferens juramentum sensus ambigui, id tantum postulat ut in ea verba juretur; permittit interim jurantis ipsius arbitrio; quocunque voluerit sensu juramenti verba intelligere. Dico, merito suspectum esse debere latentis alicujus doli mali, & proinde recusandum esse viro pio & prudenti oblatum sub tali conditione juramentum: quod mihi videtur triplici de causa improbandum. Primo, refpectu ipsius Juramenti, in quo requiritur imprimis veritas: oratio autem indefiniti & ambigui sensus ante distinctionem factam non est propositio vera, imo ne propositio quidem; cum debeat propositio, ut ex ejus definitione vel pueris notum est, verum vel falsum significare fine ambiguitate. Secundo, respectu ejus cui jurandum est: finis enim juramenti proprius est, ut is cui juratur de re prius incerta habeat aliquam certitudinem: ex verbis autem incerti sensus quae po-teft test habere certitudo ? Tertiò, respectu ipsius jurantis: qui si juramentum sub eâ conditione præstet, aut proximo scandalum, at sibi laqueum parat. Istiusmodi enim collusio, ne cogitari quidem potest quò spectet alió, nisi ut aut nostro exemplo alii ad idem juramentum suscipendum (reluctante licèt conscientia) inducantur; quod est proximo scandalum præbere: aut ut aliud aliquid postea à nobis virtute illius juramenti faciendum exigatur, quod aut illicitum sit aut ineommodum; quod est nobismetipsis laqueum inducere. Caveat itaque vir prudens, ut sibi his artibus imponi patiatur: alteriúlve cujusquam aut gratiam aut metum tanti ducat, ut escam devoret, cui subesse hamum certò sciat. Sanè ut inter jurandum omnia rectè fiant, expedit ut de verborum sensu inter omnes partes quarum interest liquidò constet: id quod liquidò jurare veteribus dictum est:
units.tr: The third case is where the one who offers an oath, when the sense of the matter is doubtful, requires only that the words be sworn to, but leaves it to the discretion of the one swearing to understand the words in whatever sense he pleases. I say that such an offer must rightly be suspected of some hidden evil design, and therefore a godly and prudent man ought to refuse an oath offered on such a condition. This seems to me to be condemned for three reasons. First, with respect to the oath itself, in which truth above all is required: but a statement of indefinite and ambiguous sense, before any distinction has been made, is not a true proposition, indeed not even a proposition at all, since a proposition ought, as even children know from its definition, to signify something true or false without ambiguity. Second, with respect to the one to whom the oath is sworn: for the proper purpose of an oath is that the one to whom it is sworn may gain some certainty about a matter previously uncertain; but what certainty can come from words of uncertain sense? Third, with respect to the one swearing: who, if he swears under this condition, either gives offence to his neighbour or prepares a snare for himself. For such a collusion cannot be thought to aim at anything else, except either that by our example others are induced to take up the same oath (though their conscience resists), which is to give offence to a neighbour; or that something else is afterwards demanded of us by virtue of that oath, which is either unlawful or inconvenient, and this is to bring a snare upon ourselves. Let the prudent man therefore take care not to allow himself to be deceived by such tricks, and let him not value the favour or the fear of any other person so highly that he swallows the bait, knowing for certain that a hook lies beneath it. Surely, so that all things may be done rightly in swearing, it is expedient that the sense of the words be clearly agreed upon among all the parties whose interest is involved: this is what the ancients called swearing clearly:

units.la: Sic tamen & liquido juratus dicere posses.
units.tr: In this way, too, one who has sworn clearly could say:

units.la: Et ex veteri formula juratura à deferente juramentum dici solitum est, Qua de re peto liquido jures.
units.tr: And from the old formula used by the one who refers the oath to the one about to swear, it was customary to say: Concerning the matter about which I ask, swear clearly.

units.la: SECT. XI.
units.tr: SECT. XI.

units.la: Sed de his fatis. Pergo ad Dubium tertium, quod est de sensu Juramenti quoad latitudinem sive extentionem ejus: hoc est, an & quatenus sensus verborum ex scopo mitiendus est. Casus primus est, ubi Juramenti alicujus causa fuit particularis, verba tamen sunt generalia. Exempli gratia; Juramento Suprematus Regii causam dedit usurpatio Papalis, qui supremam in spiritualibus jurisdictionem in hoc regno sibi vendicabat: verbis tamen Juramenti ita asseritur suprematus regius, ut non Papa solum, sed & universi omnes alii quicunque excludantur a suprema potestate in hoc regno exercenda. Respondeo, tale juramentum obligare quoad verba ipsa in ultima sui latitudine. Ratio est, quia legis, licet ex particulari occasione latae; intentio tamen est generalis, omnia ejusdem generis vel rationis incommoda in futurum impedire. Et proinde etsi in proœmio legis mentio sæpe fiat particularis illius mali quod causam dedit legi ferendæ, verba tamen illa quibus lex ipsa continetur plerumque sunt magis generalia: id quod consulto & data opera factum est à Legum latoribus, & cætera quæ sunt consimilis rationis simul complectentur. Ut ergo de sensu Legis, non ex proëmio, sed ex corpore statuti (ut loquuntur) responsa petunt Consulti juris: sic & Juramenti justâ interpretatione, non ex præmissa recognitione, aliâve ejus præfatione, sed ex ipso quasi corpore Juramenti judicium sumere oportet.
units.tr: But enough of these matters. I proceed to the third doubt, which concerns the sense of an oath as to its breadth or extent: that is, whether and how far the sense of the words is to be judged from the purpose. The first case is where the cause of an oath was particular, yet the words are general. For example: the oath of Royal Supremacy was occasioned by the Papal usurpation, which claimed for itself supreme jurisdiction in spiritual matters in this kingdom; yet by the words of the oath the royal supremacy is asserted in such a way that not the Pope alone, but all others whatsoever, are excluded from exercising supreme power in this kingdom. I answer that such an oath binds as to the words themselves in their fullest extent. The reason is that a law, although enacted on a particular occasion, nevertheless has a general intention: to prevent in future all inconveniences of the same kind or reason. And therefore, although in the preamble of a law mention is often made of that particular evil which gave occasion to enact it, the words by which the law itself is contained are for the most part more general. This has been done deliberately and with set purpose by the framers of laws, so that they may embrace also other matters of similar reason. Just as lawyers seek the sense of a law not from the preamble but from the body of the statute (as they say), so too the just interpretation of an oath must be judged not from the preceding acknowledgement, or other preface to it, but from the very body of the oath.

units.la: SECT. XII.
units.tr: SECT. XII.

units.la: Casus Secundus est, quatenus Juramentum sit cum aliqua conditione intelligendum. Respondeo breviter. Primo, si verba continent conditionem expressam, non obligari jurantem, nisi præstita prius conditione. Ut si Caius promittat Titio se cras daturum centum, si Titius fundum ipsi hodie dederit: fundo non dato, non tenetur Caius promissione. Secundo, si conditio nulla sit expressa, debere tamen intelligi omnes illas conditiones sive exceptiones, quæ solent de jure & usu communi subintelligi : nempe hoc vel illud faciam , Si Deus permiserit , Salvo jure alterius, Rebus in eodem statu manentibus, Quoad potero & licebit, &c. ut fuit in explicatione secundæ hypothecæos fusiùs antè dictum.
units.tr: The second case is how far an oath is to be understood as having some condition. I answer briefly. First, if the words contain an express condition, the swearer is not bound unless the condition has first been fulfilled. For example, if Gaius promises Titius that he will give him a hundred tomorrow, provided that Titius has given him a farm today, then if the farm is not given, Gaius is not bound by the promise. Second, if no condition is expressed, yet all those conditions or exceptions which are customarily understood by common law and usage must be understood, namely: "I will do this or that, if God permits"; "saving the right of another"; "with things remaining in the same state"; "as far as I am able and it is lawful"; and so on, as was explained more fully earlier in the explanation of the second hypothec.

units.la: SECT. XIII.
units.tr: SECT. XIII.

units.la: Casus tertius est de Intentione Remota & Proxima. Videtur enim satisfecisse juramento, qui fecerit id quod intenderat intentione remota, & ut finem; etsi non faciat id quod verba ipsa sonant, quae fere continent intentionem proximam solum, sive mediorum. Exempli gratia, Si quis voto, juramento, vel promissione reciperet se pauperibus alicujus villae daturum quolibet mense decem solidos, nihil autem daret toto Januario aut Februario, sed Martio demum mense daret triginta solidos. Respondeo, jurantem, si intenderat obligare se tantum ad substantiam rei, non autem ad ejus rei circumstantiam sive modum, non simpliciter obligari ad illum modum faciendi, quem verba insinuare videntur. Unde si exemplo propositio totam trimestrem pensionem exhibuisset primo mense, sine dubio satisfecisset promissioni. Potest tamen fieri, ut per accidens & ex consequenti obligetur & ad ipsum modum rei: quia unusquisque obligatur (caeteris paribus, & si nihil aliud impediat) eligere in dubiis id quod est tutius. Ut in exemplo jam allato certe tutius est pensionem eo modo quo promissa est solvere; id est singulis mensibus decem potius quam tertio mense triginta. Tum ob
units.tr: The third case concerns the remote and proximate intention. For a person seems to have fulfilled an oath if he does what he intended by his remote intention, namely the end, even though he does not do what the words themselves say, which for the most part express only the proximate intention, that is, the means. For example, suppose someone vows, swears, or promises to give the poor of some village ten shillings every month, but gives nothing in January or February and then gives thirty shillings in March. I answer that if the one swearing intended to bind himself only to the substance of the thing, and not to its circumstances or manner, he is not simply bound to that manner of acting which the words seem to suggest. Hence, if in the example the promiser had paid the whole quarter's payment in the first month, he would without doubt have kept his promise. It may nonetheless happen that he is also bound, by accident and as a consequence, to the manner of the thing itself, because everyone is obliged (other things being equal, and if nothing else hinders) to choose in doubtful matters what is safer. Thus in the example just given, it is certainly safer to pay the sum in the way it was promised, that is, ten each month rather than thirty in the third month. This is so both because of the danger of sudden death and of uncertain events, and to avoid the scruples of conscience that might arise from a neglected circumstance.

units.la: Casus 51. Casus tertius est de Intentione Remota & Proxima. ob periculum repentinæ mortis & incertorum eventuum: tùm ad vitandum, qui vel ex neglecta circumstantia oriri possent, mentis scrupulos. Suaderem itáque homini pio, ut cujuslibet sui voti, juramenti, pacti, promissionisque fidem exolvere studeat, juxta verborum & intentionis suæ tenorem, quoad commodè fieri potest, etiam in levissimis circumstantiis: ne minutiora ista contemnendo, aut scrupulos sibi creet non necessarios, aut rebus gravioribus contemnendis paulatim & sensim assuescat. Cæterum illud unum utcunque admonitos omnes velim, ut summam & coronidem totius hujus dissertationis de Juramenti sensu & interpretatione, magnopere ut caveant, ne sibi nimium hac in re indulgeant; neu benigna nimis & laxa interpretatione, dum cupiditatibus suis plus æquo favent, Juramenti religionem minuant, & se perjurii periculo exponant. Atq; hæc de Formali Causa dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: Case 51. The third case concerns the remote and proximate intention. Therefore I would advise a godly person to take care to fulfil the faith of each of his vows, oaths, covenants, and promises, according to the tenor of the words and of his intention, as far as can conveniently be done, even in the slightest circumstances. He should do this so that by despising these smaller matters he does not create for himself unnecessary scruples, or gradually and imperceptibly grow accustomed to despising weightier matters. Yet I would wish all who have been warned in any way to take this one thing above all: that, in the chief and crowning point of this whole discourse on the sense and interpretation of an oath, they be most careful not to indulge themselves too much in this matter. Let them not, by an overly lenient and slack interpretation, while they favour their desires more than is right, diminish the sanctity of an oath and expose themselves to the danger of perjury. And let what has been said concerning the Formal Cause suffice.

units.la: SECT. XIV.
units.tr: SECT. XIV.

units.la: De Finali Causa paucula restant dicenda. Dubium Primum est, cum promittitur res ex se licita, sed aut malâ intentione, aut ob malum finem. Dicendum primò, simpliciter illicitum esse promittere aliquid quamumvis in se licitum, malo fine vel intentione. Ratio est, quia cùm quivis unus defectus in quolibet actu humano sufficiat ad hoc, ut totus actus sit malus, (Bonum enim ex causa integra est, malum ex partiali:) tùm præcipuè defectus ex parte finis, ut qui in moralibus primas tenet partes; quò fere putant id Christi dictum pertinere, Si oculus tuus fuerit nequam, & totum corpus tenebrosum erit. Dicendum secundò, si quis aliquid alteri juraverit ob finem inhonestum, sine conditione tamen turpi ab alio præstanda; obligari ad faciendum promissum. Ut si quis fœminæ polliceretur se ei dono missurum rem aliquam preciosam, intendens apud se ipsam eo munere ad impudicos amores pellicere, nullâ tamen ei palàm propositâ inhonestâ conditione, teneretur promissionem implere: quòd si proponeret ei unâ conditionem inhonestam, non teneretur promissio. Ratio utriusque; est, quia rem preciosam licitum est alteri dare: sed dare sub conditione turpi, illicitum.
units.tr: A few things remain to be said concerning the Final Cause. The First Question is this: when something lawful in itself is promised, but with a bad intention or for a bad end. I say, first, that it is simply unlawful to promise anything, however lawful in itself, with an evil end or intention. The reason is that any single defect in any human act is enough to make the whole act bad (for good comes from a whole cause, evil from a partial one), and especially a defect on the part of the end, which holds the first place in moral matters. To this, they think, the saying of Christ refers: If your eye be evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. I say, second, that if someone has sworn something to another for a dishonourable end, but without any dishonourable condition to be performed by the other, he is bound to do what he promised. For example, if someone promised a woman that he would send her some precious gift, intending by that gift to entice her to shameful loves, yet without openly proposing any dishonourable condition to her, he would be bound to fulfil his promise. But if he proposed a dishonourable condition to her, the promise would not bind him. The reason for both is that it is lawful to give someone a precious thing, but to give it under a shameful condition is unlawful.

units.la: Dicendum tertiò, Quod promissum est sub conditione malâ, præstitâ conditione debere adimpleri, si res saltem sit licita. Ut si quis alteri pro adulterio, aut falso testimonio, aut alio quolibet inhonesto vel turpi officio pecuniæ summam promiserit: tenetur, ubi alter conditionem pactam præstiterit, promissis stare & pactam pecuniam dissolvere. Sic Thamari nurui sui obligatum se Judas b Judas rectè putavit, pactam fcortationis mercedem hædum promissum mittere. Ratio est, quia etsi pactum fuerit illicitum, tamen res pacta non est illicita: Ergo fieri non debuit, sed factum valet. Et ex antedictis satis claret Juramentum illicitum de re licita posse obligare.
units.tr: I say, third, that what is promised under an evil condition must be fulfilled once the condition has been performed, provided that the thing itself is at least lawful. For example, if someone promised another a sum of money for adultery, or for false witness, or for any other dishonourable or shameful service, he is bound, once the other has performed the agreed condition, to keep his promise and pay the agreed money. So Judah rightly judged himself bound to his daughter-in-law Tamar, to send the promised kid as the agreed wage for harlotry. The reason is that even if the agreement was unlawful, the thing agreed upon is not unlawful. It ought not, therefore, to have been done, but once done it is valid. And from what has been said above it is clear enough that an unlawful oath concerning a lawful matter can bind.

units.la: SECT. XV.
units.tr: SECT. XV.

units.la: Dubium Secundum respicit jurantis intentionem. Intentionem dico, non eam quæ fertur objectivè in materiam juramenti, sive rem promissam; quâ quaeritur, quid jurans intenderit promittere, & quo sensu, & ad quid se obligare: de hac enim intentione modò actum est, cum de Juramenti sensu & interpretatione disseruimus: sed Intentionem eam intelligo, quæ fertur objectivè in ipsum actum jurandi: quâ quaeritur, an intenderit jurare, aut se obligare, vel non. De quâ multa disputant subtiliùs quam utiliùs Scholastici. Quæ ex usu fient ad vitæ institutionem pleraque in pauca contraham. Casus itaque primus est, cum quis ex consuetudine quadam jurandi, incogitans verba profundit juratoria —— ᾧ ὄρκῳ ἐπ' ἀκροῖς ἀπὸ τοῖς γελοίοις. Dico primò, certum esse ejusmodi Jurationem esse grave peccatum. Non solum originaliter, & ratione causæ; quia profluit ex habitu quodam pravo : sed etiam formaliter, & ratione ipsius actus; in quantum actus ex naturâ suâ religiosus, temere fit, non in judicio, & sine debitâ reverentiâ. Dico secundo, Juramentum illud, si fuit jurandi actus ex animi praecipitantia prorsus indeliberatus, non obligare: sed si adfuit aliqua animi deliberatio quantumvis exigua, aliquatenus obligare. Ratio utriusque membri assertionis est: quia ut actus aliquis humanus sit obligatorius, requiritur deliberatus animus, & pro mensura deliberationis, assurgit etiam obligationis mensura.
units.tr: The Second Question concerns the intention of the one swearing. I say intention, not that which is directed objectively at the matter of the oath, that is, the thing promised, by which it is asked what the swearer intended to promise, in what sense, and to what he bound himself. For we have already dealt with that intention when we discussed the sense and interpretation of an oath. I mean rather that intention which is directed objectively at the very act of swearing, by which it is asked whether he intended to swear or to bind himself, or not. On this the Scholastics dispute more subtly than usefully. I shall summarise in a few words what is most useful for the conduct of life. The first case, then, is when someone, from a certain habit of swearing, thoughtlessly pours out oaths, with an oath on the lips, from jests [ᾧ ὄρκῳ ἐπ' ἀκροῖς ἀπὸ τοῖς γελοίοις]. I say, first, that it is certain that such swearing is a grave sin: not only originally, and by reason of its cause, since it flows from a depraved habit, but also formally, and by reason of the act itself, insofar as an act which is by its nature religious is performed rashly, not in judgement, and without due reverence. I say, second, that such an oath, if it was an act of swearing made wholly without deliberation from the haste of the mind, does not bind; but if there was some deliberation of mind, however slight, it binds to some degree. The reason for each part of this assertion is that for any human act to be binding, a deliberate mind is required, and the degree of obligation rises in proportion to the degree of deliberation.

units.la: SECT. XVI.
units.tr: SECT. XVI.

units.la: Casus secundus, cum quis honoris aut urbanitatis gratia (sic enim Casuistae loquuntur) temere jurat in re fortuitis levi. Exempli gratia, si quis cum altero contendens, & honoris quasi praerogativam ei deferens, ut saepe fit, juraret se non exiturum domo, non discubiturum ad mensam, non bibiturum; nisi ille alter praeiverit, aut prior discubuerit, aut praebiberit. Imo cum saepissime fiat, ut sic contendentium uterque idem juret; si ejusmodi juramenta essent obligatoria, necesse esset e duobus alterum pejerare; quia necesse est alterutrum id facere; quod uterque juravit se non facturum. &turum. Dico primo ut supra, Juramentum istiusmodi esse temerarium, & peccato non carere, quia caret judicio. Secundo, esse tamen obligatorium ex sui natura, nisi forte fuerit actus omnino indeliberatus. Sed tertio, obligationem illam aut impediri posse aut tolli; ita ut perjurus non sit, qui secus quàm juratum est fecerit. Nimirum potest impediri obligatio, si intelligatur cum tacitâ conditione sive exceptione, hoc sensu, Si tibi placuerit, vel si res meo arbitrio permittatur, non ibo nisi tu præiveris. Potest etiam tolli: quia cum processerit ex respectu quodam ad honorem alterius, potest ille alter suo jure cedere, & tunc cessabit obligatio; uti (Deo volente) cum de vinculi solutione agam plenius ostendam.
units.tr: The second case: when someone, out of courtesy or politeness (for so the casuists speak), swears rashly about a trivial and chance matter. For example, if someone, contending with another and as it were conferring on him the precedence of honour, as often happens, swears that he will not leave the house, will not sit down at table, will not drink, unless the other man goes first, or sits down first, or drinks first. Indeed, since it very often happens that each of two contending parties swears the same thing, if oaths of this kind were binding, one of the two would necessarily be forsworn, since one of them must do what each swore not to do. I say first, as above, that an oath of this kind is rash and is not free from sin, because it lacks judgement. Second, that it is nevertheless binding by its nature, unless perhaps it was an act wholly undeliberate. But third, that this obligation can either be hindered or removed, so that the one who acts otherwise than he swore is not forsworn. Indeed the obligation can be hindered if it is understood with a tacit condition or exception, in this sense: If it pleases you, or if the matter is left to my judgement, I will not go unless you go first. It can also be removed, because since it arose from a certain regard for the honour of the other, that other man can yield his right, and then the obligation will cease; as I will show more fully, God willing, when I treat of the loosing of the bond.

units.la: SECT. XVII.
units.tr: SECT. XVII.

units.la: Casus Tertius, cum quis dubius est juraverit, necne, an teneatur Juramento? Aliqui putant non obligari: ex illa regula Juris, In dubiis melior est conditio possidentis. Sed quum valeat illa regula in his tantum, quæ ad commutativam Justitiam pertinent; ut si Caii hæ res dubitet an bona defuncti quæ ad ipsum ex testamento devenerunt bonè parta fuerint necne: Alii; & fortasse rectius, putant obligari, nisi posse dubitationem deponere. Ratio, quia in dubiis eligendum quod tutius: & est certè tutius obligatum fe putare, quàm non obligatum ; quia ex illo error exponit sed ad summum non nisi temporali incommodo, ex hoc perjurii periculo.
units.tr: The third case: when someone doubts whether he has sworn or not, whether he is bound by the oath. Some think he is not bound, by that rule of law: "In doubtful matters the condition of the possessor is the better." But since that rule holds only in those matters which pertain to commutative justice, as when Gaius doubts whether the goods of a deceased person, which came to him by will, were lawfully acquired or not; others, and perhaps more rightly, think he is bound, unless he can set aside the doubt. The reason is that in doubtful matters what is safer is to be chosen; and it is certainly safer to think oneself bound than not bound, because error in the former case exposes one only to temporal inconvenience at most, while in the latter it brings the danger of perjury.

units.la: SECT. XVIII.
units.tr: SECT. XVIII.

units.la: Casus Quartus : cum quis volens jurare, non tamen intendit fe obligare, an nihilominus obligetur ? Scholasticorum & Cafuistarum plurimi, præsertim qui ante Cajetanum fuerunt, negant obligari. Et quidem excusat se à perjurio Cydippe Ovidiana istiusmodi defensione.
units.tr: Fourth Case: when someone wishes to swear but does not intend to bind himself, is he nonetheless bound? Most of the Scholastics and casuists, especially those who came before Cajetan, deny that he is bound. Ovid's Cydippe indeed excuses herself from perjury with this kind of defence: "The mind is what swears; we have sworn nothing with it."

units.la: a Quæ jurat mens est : nil conjuravimus illâ. At fanior est Cajetani sententia, & qui eum secuti sunt Scholasticorum, deliberate jurantem, sive intendat se obligare, sive non obligare tamen. Etenim & actus jurandi est ex se obligatorius, & procedit ab animo deliberato: ergo necessario sequetur obligatio, nisi aliunde impediatur. Cum ergo obligatio ex jurejurando necessario & naturaliter profluat, non est in potestate hominis eam impedire, vel summovere: nemo enim potest, positis rerum naturis, earum necessarios effectus impedire. Annon deberet beret omnibus ludibrium, qui cum manum & sigillum syngraphæ obligatoriæ opponeret, profiteretur tamen se nullum habere intentionem semet obligandi ? Imò illa intentionis suæ professione non obstante, annon facto ipso obligaretur tamen ? Obligatur pariter & qui jurat ipso jurandi actu, quicquid aut intendit, aut se intendere profiteatur : quia intendens causam, intendere præsumitur & ejus causæ necessarium effectum.
units.tr: But the opinion of Cajetan is sounder, and so is that of the Scholastics who followed him: one who swears deliberately is bound, whether he intends to bind himself or not. For the act of swearing is binding in itself and proceeds from a deliberate mind; therefore obligation necessarily follows, unless it is hindered by something else. Since obligation arising from an oath flows necessarily and naturally, it is not within a man's power to prevent or remove it: for no one can, given the natures of things, impede their necessary effects. Would not anyone who set his hand and seal to a binding bond, yet professed that he had no intention of binding himself, be made a laughing-stock by everyone? Indeed, notwithstanding his profession of intention, would he not in fact be bound all the same? Likewise he who swears is bound by the very act of swearing, whatever he intends or professes to intend: for one who intends a cause is presumed to intend its necessary effect.

units.la: Atque ita tandem difficilem hanc & diffusam de Juramenti Vinculo dissertationem auspice Dei bonitate, comite patientiâ vestrâ, per quatuor Causarum genera deductam, ut potui, absolvi: reliquam tractationis partem, quæ de Vinculi Solutione est, propedi-em (Deo annuente) unica prælectione comp!
units.tr: And so, with God's goodness as my guide and your patience as my companion, I have, as far as I was able, worked through this difficult and extended dissertation on the bond of an oath, arranged under the four kinds of cause. The remaining part of the treatment, which concerns the dissolution of the bond, I shall (God willing) complete shortly in a single lecture.

units.la: Prælectio
units.tr: Lecture
