units.la: SECT. I.
units.tr: SECT. I.

units.la: VInculi illius sive ligaminis, quod qui jurat ligat super animam suam, & de quo tam multa hactenus disseruimus, Solutio hondiernum pensum est, & totius propositæ tractationis novissima pars. De qua solutione, antequam ad species defcendatur, duo sunt in genere observanda. Obfervandum primo; vinculi solutionem peculiarem esse juramento promissorio, in assertorio locum non habere. Omni Juramento, sive Assertorio, sive promissorio debet inesse Veritas: sed cum hoc discrimine, quod ad juramentum Assertorium unica sufficiat veritas de præsenti, cum in promissorio duplex requiratur; una sc. de præsenti, altera de futuro. Veritas de præsenti respicit ipsum actum jurandi: & consistit in hoc, ut jurans quando jurat verum dicat; hoc est, ut mens sit congrua verbis, & ut habeat intentionem servandi id quod promittit. Qui actus jurandi in Promissorio, quoad veritatem & falsitatem omnino convenit cum actu jurandi in Assertorio. Materia enim illius veritatis in utroque actu, cum sit de præsenti, transit in quandam quasi necessitatem immutabilem; in quantum Juramentum quamprimum præstitum est, statim aut b verum fuit aut falsum : quam veritatem aut falsitatem, ubi actus ille semel transierit, tam impossibile esse mutari, quam impossibile est id quod factum est infectum fieri posse. Obligatio ergo illa, qua tenetur jurans de præsenti verum dicere, cadit super ipsum actum jurandi, éstque illi actui inseparabiliter conjuncta; & proinde soluti non potest, nec a Juramento separari: & juramenti Assertorii præter istam de præsenti nulla est ulterior Obligatio, quia materia ejus est factum aliquod præteritum aut præsens.
units.tr: Of that bond or tie, which he who swears binds upon his soul, and about which we have disputed so much hitherto, the solution is today's task and the final part of the whole treatment proposed. Before we descend to the species, two things are to be observed in general about this solution. The first thing to observe is that the loosing of the bond is peculiar to a promissory oath and has no place in an assertory oath. Every oath, whether assertory or promissory, must contain truth, but with this difference: for an assertory oath a single truth, regarding the present, suffices, whereas a promissory oath requires a twofold truth, namely one regarding the present and another regarding the future. The truth regarding the present concerns the act of swearing itself, and consists in this, that the one swearing speaks truly when he swears; that is, that his mind agrees with his words, and that he has the intention of keeping what he promises. This act of swearing in a promissory oath agrees entirely with the act of swearing in an assertory oath as regards truth and falsity. For the matter of that truth in each act, since it concerns the present, passes into a certain almost unchangeable necessity: as soon as the oath has been taken, it was at once either true or false, and once that act has passed, this truth or falsity can no more be changed than what has been done can be made undone. The obligation therefore, by which the one swearing is bound to speak truly in the present, falls upon the act of swearing itself and is inseparably joined to that act; so it cannot be loosed nor separated from the oath. In an assertory oath, apart from this present obligation, there is no further obligation, because its matter is some past or present fact.

units.la: Sed in promissorio juramento, cujus Materia est res de futuro præstanda, requiritur etiam veritas altera, de futuro sc. quæ respicit Materiam Juramenti: & consistit in hoc, ut jurans quod promisit efficiat esse verum; hoc est, ut adimpleat promissum. Dum igitur materia juramenti promissorii, nempe res de futuro præstanda, propter futurorum eventuum incertitudinem multiplici mutationi & varietati obnoxia sit: hinc fit, ut Obligatio quæ cadit super illam Materiam, & qua tenetur jurans de futuro promissum adimplere, mutabilis sit & a juramento separabilis. Et hoc ipsum est, quod vinculi solutionem dicimus. Unde etiam sequitur id quod secundo loco observandum est; sc. solutionem vinculi in juramento promissorio non intelligi debere respectu Obligationis illius prioris, quæ nascitur ex veritate de præsenti, & est ei cum Juramento Assertorio communis: sed intelligi solum respectu obligationis posterioris, quæ nascitur ex veritate de futuro, & est ipsi propria & peculiaris. Hoc est, Omnis promisforiè jurans, ipso facto & vi ipsius actus jurandi, simpliciter & insolubilitur obligatur de præsenti bonâ fide & animo intendere id postea efficere quod promisit: sed postquam juratum est, multis de causis fieri potest ut non obligetur de futuro illud ad postea implendum quod ante promiserat & intenderat.Verbo sic,Perjurus est semper, qui c non intendit quod promittit: non est semper perjurus, qui d non perficit quod promisit.
units.tr: But in a promissory oath, whose matter is a thing to be performed in the future, there is also required the other truth, regarding the future, which relates to the matter of the oath: it consists in this, that the one swearing makes good what he promised, that is, fulfils the promise. Since the matter of a promissory oath, namely a thing to be performed in the future, is subject to manifold change and variety on account of the uncertainty of future events, it follows that the obligation which falls upon that matter, by which the one swearing is bound to fulfil in the future what he promised, is changeable and separable from the oath. This is precisely what we call the loosing of the bond. Whence there also follows what is to be observed in the second place: the loosing of the bond in a promissory oath must not be understood with respect to that earlier obligation which arises from the truth regarding the present, and which it shares with an assertory oath, but only with respect to the later obligation, which arises from the truth regarding the future and is proper and peculiar to it. That is, everyone swearing promissorily, by the very fact and force of the act of swearing, is simply and indissolubly bound in the present, in good faith and with the intention of afterwards doing what he promised; but after he has sworn, it can happen for many reasons that he is not bound in the future to fulfil afterwards what he had promised and intended beforehand. In short: he is always perjured who does not intend what he promises; he is not always perjured who does not perform what he promised.

units.la: SECT. II.
units.tr: SECT. II.

units.la: Ut autem, licitè & sine perjurio alióve peccato non adimpleatur quod promissum est, ex horum altero contingere necesse est: vel quòd nulla ab initio fuerit obligatio, vel quòd ea postea (soluto vinculo) sublata sit. Si res promissa erat cum juraretur aut impossibilis, aut illicita, Juramentum eâ de re præstitum nullam inducebat obligationem, neq; indiget solutione, sed poenitentiâ: quandoquidem sic jurando etsi admissum sit grave peccatum, nullum tamen vinculum est concontractum. Rei enim impossibilis, & rei item illicitæ nullam esse obligationem ante ostendimus. Solutio ergo vinculi supponit antecedentem obligationem: eámque postea aliunde sic tolli significat aut saltem impediri, ut qui prius juramenti vinculo ita constrictus tenebatur, ut non liceret ei sub poena perjurii aliter facere quam promiserat, ad promissum suum adimplendum jam non ultra teneatur. Itaque quod nunc agitur hoc est, ut certam rationem investigemus, quâ is qui se juramenti vinculo obligavit ad aliquid faciendum, possit esse securus in conscientiâ suâ se ab eo vinculo liberari, nec ad illud faciendum quod promisit ultra obligari. Cujus rei cum quinque omninò modi soleant assignari, singuli sunt à nobis suo ordine examinandi.
units.tr: For the promise to be fulfilled lawfully, and without perjury or some other sin, one of two things must have happened: either there was never any obligation from the start, or the obligation was later removed by the bond being loosed. If the thing promised was, when the oath was taken, either impossible or unlawful, the oath sworn about that matter created no obligation and needs no release, only repentance. Although a grave sin has been committed by swearing in this way, no bond has been formed at all. We have already shown that there is no obligation to an impossible thing or to an unlawful thing. The loosing of a bond therefore presupposes a prior obligation, and means that this obligation is afterwards removed or at least prevented by some other cause, so that the person who was previously bound by the bond of an oath, so that he could not act otherwise than he had promised without the penalty of perjury, is no longer bound to fulfil his promise. What we now have to do, then, is to investigate a sure reason by which a person who has bound himself by the bond of an oath to do something may be secure in his conscience that he is freed from that bond and is no longer bound to do what he promised. Since five modes of this are usually listed, each of them must be examined by us in its turn.

units.la: SECT. III.
units.tr: SECT. III.

units.la: Primus Casus est de Dispensabilitate Juramenti: An & quatenus Superioris dispensatio ejus obligationem tollere valeat? Dispensatio autem, ut ea vox communiter, accipitur, exemptionem significat alicujus personæ à lege communi factam ex speciali indulgentiâ ab habente authoritatem. Ut si quis legi alicui subditus, Principis beneficio ex speciali gratiâ ab illius legis obedientiâ tiâ eximatur: & ut fieri quotidie videmus in Academiis, ubi ex rationabili causa difpenfationes solent concedi particularibus personis, ut liceat eis in aliquibus aliter quàm statutum est facere. Fundatur autem dispensationis jus in ἐπιεικεία illa, quæ postulat ut de rigore legis nonnunquam aliquid remittatur ut æquitati sit locus. Cum enim leges necesse esset verbis generalibus ferri, & ad id respicere quod communiter & plerumque bonum & utile est publico; quod tamen sæpius contingere potest esse pro hic & nunc inutile vel saltem minus bonum: æquum utique visum est, ut ubi observatio ejus quod lege sancitum est videtur esse alicui privatæ personæ valdè onerosa vel incommoda, & ex ejus omissione publico non multum incommodari, Princeps vel alius legitimus superior potestatem haberet determinandi legem in eo casu non videri servandam: & hoc est quod dicimus in lege difpensare. Quam autem potestatem habent Principes seculares dispensandi in legibus suis, eandem sibi arrogant Pontifices Romani difpensandi in votis & juramentis. Quorum in hoc genere audaciam, dum subditos Regum à fidelitate sua absolvunt, Principum contractus & fœdera rescindunt, Votorum & Juramentorum vel arctissima quæque vincula commutando, relaxando, dispensando, concontraria jubendo, alióve artificio pro libitu & utilitate dissolvunt, utinam eorum nonnulli, qui rectissime damnant, non pessime imitarentur. Sed enim ut alii de facto exerceant, solus interim Papa vendicat sibi quasi de jure debitam hanc dispensandi in juramentis potestatem. Conquesti sunt graviter hac de re, & in papalium dispensationum abusus acriter invecti, etiam ante Lutherum multi ad quorum scripta remitto istarum rerum studiosos; atque aliquot argumentis contendo Juramenti vinculum esse simpliciter indispensabile, ita ut nec Papa nec alius quisquam ullam habeat omnino potestatem cum eo dispensandi. Primo, quia obligatio Juramenti est de Jure divino naturali: Jus autem naturale non subest foro humano; quum Deus solus sit author & dominus naturæ, nec hactenus potuerit unquam ostendi, Deum ulli hominum generi aut ordini authoritatem concessisse dispensandi in his quæ sunt juris naturalis. Secundo, quia concessa hac dispensandi potestate; everteretur funditus præcipuus juramenti finis, qui est assecuratio (ut ita dicam) rei promissæ: nullam enim posset habere certitudinem is cui juratur impletum iri quod promissum est, si cum jurante posset dispensari ne impleret. Tertio, quia juramentum eodem ipso actu & in eodem instanti, quo jurandi inducit obligationem.
units.tr: The first case concerns the dispensability of an oath: whether and to what extent the dispensation of a superior can annul its obligation. Dispensation, as the word is commonly understood, means the exemption of a person from a common law, granted by one who has authority, as a special indulgence. For example, when someone subject to a law is, by the favour of the prince and by special grace, released from obedience to that law; and as we see every day in the universities, where dispensations are customarily granted to particular persons for a reasonable cause, so that they may do certain things otherwise than the statute prescribes. The right of dispensation is founded on that equity [ἐπιεικεία], which requires that something sometimes be relaxed from the strictness of the law so that there may be room for fairness. For since laws must necessarily be enacted in general terms, and have regard to what is commonly and for the most part good and useful for the public, yet what is good in general may often turn out to be for the here and now useless, or at least less good; it has seemed altogether fair that, where observance of what the law has enacted appears to be very burdensome or inconvenient to some private person, and where its omission would not greatly harm the public, the prince or another lawful superior should have the power to determine that in that case the law is not to be regarded as binding. This is what we mean by dispensing with a law. But the power that secular princes have to dispense with their own laws, the Roman Pontiffs claim for themselves to dispense with vows and oaths. Would that some of those who most rightly condemn their audacity in this kind of thing, while they absolve the subjects of kings from their allegiance, rescind the contracts and treaties of princes, and by changing, relaxing, dispensing with, or ordering the contrary of even the tightest bonds of vows and oaths, or by some other trick dissolve them at will and for convenience, did not imitate them so badly! But while others exercise this power de facto, the Pope alone claims for himself, as though de jure, the power of dispensing with oaths. Many have complained severely about this matter, and have attacked the abuses of papal dispensations bitterly, even before Luther; I refer those who wish to study these things to their writings. And I contend by several arguments that the bond of an oath is simply indispensable, so that neither the Pope nor anyone else has any power whatever to dispense with it. First, because the obligation of an oath is of divine natural law; but natural law is not subject to a human tribunal, since God alone is the author and lord of nature, and it has never yet been shown that God has granted to any kind or order of men authority to dispense in those things which belong to natural law. Second, because if this power of dispensing were granted, the chief end of an oath, which is the assurance (so to speak) of the thing promised, would be utterly overthrown; for the one to whom an oath is sworn could have no certainty that what was promised would be done, if the one swearing could be dispensed from doing it. Third, because an oath, by that very act and in the same instant in which it is sworn, brings about the obligation [of keeping the promise].

units.la: b Et tamen de ... Dico quod contra jus naturale potest dispensare; ad 15. qu. 6.; cap. authoritatem. gationem fervandi promissionem, acquirit etiam simul ei cui juratur jus ad rem promissam: qui duo effectus Juramenti ita conjuncti sunt, ut posito altero vel sublato, alterum quoque necesse sit simul poni vel tolli. Si ergo supponeretur dispensatione tolli obligationem jurantis, sequeretur eădem tolli quoque jus ejus cui juratur. Et inde etiam ulterius sequeretur, dispensationem illam aut inanem esse aut iniquam: inanem & supervacaneam, si volente eo cui juratur fieret; si invito, iniquam & injustam. Illo enim volente, remitti potest obligatio (ut mox ostendam) etiam sine dispensatione: nolenti autem jus suum adimere, injuria est.
units.tr: b And yet ... I say that he can dispense against natural law; cf. 15 qu. 6; cap. authoritatem. obligation of keeping the promise, it at the same time also gives the one to whom the oath is sworn a right to the promised thing. These two effects of an oath are so joined together that, when one is posited or removed, the other must necessarily be posited or removed at the same time. If therefore it were supposed that the obligation of the one swearing were removed by dispensation, it would follow that the right of the one to whom the oath was sworn would be removed as well. And from this it would further follow that such a dispensation is either empty or unjust: empty and superfluous if it were done with the consent of the one to whom the oath was sworn; unjust and wrongful if it were done against his will. For if he is willing, the obligation can be remitted (as I will show presently) even without dispensation; but to take away his right against his will is an injury.

units.la: Quarto, quia in Juramento promissorio non tantum proximo fit obligatio, quatenus est promissorium; sed & Deo, quatenus est Juramentum. Ergo dato sed non concesso, prælatum habere potestatem tollendi obligationem, quâ homo obligatur homini respectu promissionis: præsumptio tamen esset non ferenda, si terra & cinis assumeret sibi potestatem tollendi authoritate suâ obligationem, qua homo obligatur Deo ut testi & vindici. Quinto denique quia dispensatio humana est res fori externi: obligatio vero juramenti est intus in conscientiâ, quæ uni Deo subest ut judici, & in quam homo non habet imperium. Quisquis ergo vendicat sibi jus dispensandi fandi in Juramento, assumit sibi potestatem divinam erigendo sibi tribunal in foro interno, & exercendo dominium in hominum conscientias. Et est ipsa dispensatio invalida, & de jure nulla: sicut sententia prolata a Judice in foro non suo, quia prolata est a non Judice, est ad omnem juris effectum invalida.
units.tr: Fourth, because in a promissory oath the obligation is not only to the neighbour, insofar as it is promissory, but also to God, insofar as it is an oath. Therefore, even granting, though not conceding, that a superior has the power to remove the obligation by which a man is bound to another man with respect to a promise, it would still be an intolerable presumption if dust and ashes were to assume to themselves, by their own authority, the power of removing the obligation by which a man is bound to God as witness and avenger. Fifth and finally, because human dispensation is a matter of the external forum; but the obligation of an oath lies inwardly in the conscience, which is subject to God alone as judge, and over which man has no dominion. Whoever therefore claims for himself the right to dispense with an oath assumes a divine power, by setting up for himself a tribunal in the internal forum and exercising lordship over men's consciences. And such a dispensation is invalid and, in law, null: just as a sentence pronounced by a judge in a forum not his own is, because it is pronounced by a non-judge, invalid for every legal effect.

units.la: SECT. IIII.
units.tr: SECT. IIII.

units.la: Torquent hic se mirum in modum Dispensationum Patroni, ut primi argumenti (quod sibimet unum objicere solent) viam declinare videantur. Sudant nimirum hoc saxum versando, (tuendam enim sibi vident utcunque Papæ hac ex parte authoritatem, ne culinæ suæ male sit,) nec tamen proficiunt hilum: dum quo se solide tueantur non habent, nec inter ipsos adhuc unquam convenire potuit, quo jure Papa hanc sibi arroget dispensandi potestatem. Quod vel unum malæ defensionis conscientiam arguit. Quemadmodum enim in bello suscipiendo, sic & in exercenda potestate, causa quæ parum constanter assignatur, facile præsumitur esse parum justa. Sunt imprimis qui potestatem hanc dispensandi in Juramentis & Votis, ab illa absoluta & Oecumenica Papæ authoritate arcessunt, quâ mundi dominus est,
units.tr: The patrons of dispensations twist themselves about in a remarkable way, and seem to evade the first argument, which they are accustomed to raise against themselves. They sweat over rolling this stone, since they see that they must somehow defend the Pope's authority in this matter, lest his kitchen go badly; yet they make not the least progress, because they have no solid ground on which to defend themselves, and they have never yet been able to agree among themselves by what right the Pope claims this power of dispensing for himself. This alone shows a conscience conscious of a poor defence. For just as in undertaking a war, so also in exercising power, a cause that is assigned with little consistency is easily presumed to be little just. First, there are those who derive this power of dispensing in oaths and vows from that absolute and ecumenical authority of the Pope by which he is lord of the world,

units.la: Opin. 6 est, & totius Orbis Imperator. Quia enim omnis jurans aut vovens est Papæ lubditus: propterea inquiunt, in omni voto aut Juramento fubintelligi debere illam conditionem, a fi Domino Papæ placuerit. Unde sequitur, quamprimum Papa significaverit (id quod dispensando facit) sibi non placere ut ratum fit quod juratum est, obligationem protinus cessare. Quæ sententia fi obtineret, posset Papa pro libitu suo juramenta quævis rescindere, five subesset justa aliqua causa, five non. Rejectâ itaque hac crassiore sententiâ, alii, inque his moderni aliquot Jefuitæ, negant Pontificem dispensare posse in Juramentis, aut regum contractus diffolvere, neque id ab eo fieri, proprie loquendo; tollendo fc. obligationem, ut (stante obligatione) ab ea eximendo privatam aliquam personam: sed dicunt eum dispensare improprie tantum; b declarando fc. Juramentum in eo casu non obligare, propter aliquod bonum quod impediretur, aut malum quod sequeretur, fi Juramentum illud servaretur. Sed contra, præterquam quod res ipsa clamat Papam hac in re potestatem exercere plufquam declaratoriam, aut (quod tandem est) sub declaratoriæ potestatis obtentu posse eum de fæderibus, Votis, Juramentis & Contractibus Regum & aliorum quorumcunque pro suo arbitrio statuere: quum fit ipse in hoc casu supremus ac solitarius Judex, cujus sententia omninò stari oporteat sine aliqua appellatione, Vel primo aperte causa justa est, cur non debeat res juramento promissa præstari, ut si fit impossibilis, turpis, inhonesta, vel quovis modo illicita: & tunc potest jurans propriâ authoritate, imò verò tenetur retractare quod juravit, non expectatâ Papæ vel alterius cujusquam dispensatione: ubi enim nulla est obligatio, conscientia libera est, nec dispensatione opus est. Vel secundo, Aut nulla apparet justa causa cur non servetur fides juramento data: & tunc omninò servanda est: & peccat quisquis dispensationem aut petit aut concedit; quia manet obligatio, quæ humanâ authoritate tolli nec potest nec debet. Vel denique dubia res est, nec satis constat propter aliquas difficultates ex utraque parte utrum jurans teneatur adimplere quod promisit: & tunc quidem utile erit viros divini juris peritos prudentes & pios consulere, & ex ipsorum sententiâ quid facto, est usus statuere. Quâ in re, cùm peritâ magis quàm potestate constet, cur potiores sint Papæ quàm alterius cujusquam partes non intelligo; nisi certum effet Papam cæteros pietate & prudentia anteire: quod non est credibile, certe non est necessarium. Alii tertiò, declaratoriâ hæc dispensatione ne non contenti, ut quæ Pontificiam potestatem nimium imminuat, responsionem excogitarunt miræ subtilitatis: nempe prælati c dispensatione re verâ tolli Juramenti obligationem, quæ est juris divini naturalis; non tamen propterea dicendum,præIatum difpenfare in jure divino & naturali. Quia inquiunt, lex illa naturæ divina est, ut juramentum quandiu vis ejus & obligatio manet fervetur: & cum hac lege Præl atus non difpenfat, sed per dispensationem suam tollit illam juramenti vim, quâ jurantem ante difpenfationem verè obligavit. Sed hæc subtilitas fi ad vivum resecetur, aut mera nugatio est & nihil dicit, aut implicat contradictionem: & eam etiam refellit Jesuita d Achorius; qui tamen & ipse eo nomine e Sayro monacho vapulat. Sic isti Cadmei fratres, dum fe mutuis ictibus conficiunt, nec certam defensionis suæ rationem afferre valent, causam quam tuendam susceperunt defendi non posse reipsa confitentur. Concludo itaque nec Papæ nec Principi, nec Synodo, nec Senatui, nec ulli Præl ato vel Ecclesiastico vel fecular i jus esse in fæderibus, contractibus aut Juramentis dispensandi; aut quenquam à vinculo quo ante factam dispensationem obstrictus tenebatur absolvendi.
units.tr: Opin. 6 is, and emperor of the whole world. For, they say, since everyone who swears or vows is the Pope's subject, it must be understood in every vow or oath that this condition is implied: if it pleases the Lord Pope. Hence it follows that as soon as the Pope signifies (which he does by dispensing) that it does not please him that what has been sworn should stand, the obligation ceases at once. If this opinion held, the Pope could annul any oaths at his pleasure, whether or not some just cause existed. Therefore, with this cruder opinion rejected, others, and among them some modern Jesuits, deny that the Pontiff can dispense in oaths or dissolve the contracts of kings, and say that this is not done by him properly speaking, that is, by removing the obligation so as to free some private person from it while the obligation remains; they say instead that he dispenses only improperly, b by declaring that in that case the oath does not bind, on account of some good that would be hindered or some evil that would follow if the oath were kept. But on the contrary, besides the fact that the matter itself cries out that the Pope exercises in this business a power more than declaratory, or (what in the end comes to the same) that under the pretext of a declaratory power he can decide at his own discretion about treaties, vows, oaths and the contracts of kings and of any others whatever, since in this case he is the supreme and sole judge, whose sentence must altogether be abided by without any appeal: either, firstly, there is openly a just cause why the thing promised by oath should not be performed, as if it is impossible, base, dishonourable, or in any way unlawful; and then the one swearing may, on his own authority, indeed is bound to retract what he has sworn, without waiting for a dispensation from the Pope or anyone else; for where there is no obligation, the conscience is free and no dispensation is needed. Or, secondly, no just cause appears why the faith given by oath should not be kept; and then it must altogether be kept, and whoever either seeks or grants a dispensation sins, because the obligation remains, which cannot and must not be removed by human authority. Or finally, the matter is doubtful, and it is not sufficiently clear, on account of some difficulties on either side, whether the one swearing is bound to fulfil what he promised; and then indeed it will be useful to consult prudent and pious men learned in divine law, and to decide from their opinion what use should be made of the matter. In this affair, since it rests more on skill than on power, I do not see why the Pope's side should be preferred to that of anyone else; unless it were certain that the Pope surpasses all others in piety and prudence, which is not credible, and certainly not necessary. Thirdly, others, not content with this declaratory dispensation, which diminishes the Papal power too much, have devised a response of remarkable subtlety: namely, that by the prelate's dispensation the obligation of the oath, which is of natural divine law, is in fact removed; yet it should not therefore be said that the prelate dispenses in divine and natural law. For, they say, that law of nature is divine, that an oath should be kept as long as its force and obligation remain; and the prelate does not dispense with this law, but by his dispensation he removes that force of the oath by which he had truly bound the one swearing before the dispensation. But if this subtlety is cut down to the quick, it is either mere trifling and says nothing, or it involves a contradiction; and the Jesuit Achorius also refutes it, d though he himself on that account is beaten by the monk Sayro. e Thus those Cadmean brothers, while they destroy one another with mutual blows, and cannot bring forward any sure ground for their defence, in fact confess that the cause they undertook to defend cannot be defended. I conclude therefore that neither the Pope, nor a prince, nor a synod, nor a senate, nor any prelate, whether ecclesiastical or secular, has the right to dispense in treaties, contracts or oaths, or to absolve anyone from the bond by which he was bound before the dispensation was granted.

units.la: SECT. V.
units.tr: SECT. V.

units.la: Isti de dispensatione quæstioni primæ, proxima est ei affinis de juramenti commutatione quæstio, five Casus secundus. Est autem Commutatio (ut ipsum nomen indicat) nihil aliud quam translatio obligationis ab unâ materiâ ad aliam; quæ sive major, sive minor, sive equivalens, videtur esse aliquo respectu commodior. Differt autem Commutatio à Dispensatione quodammodo sicut Species à suo Genere, vel Pars a suo Toto. si enim sufficeret ad solvendum vinculum tam una quam altera: solveretur & vinculum ex Toto per Dispensationem, per Commutationem vero ex parte solum. Summa doctrinæ Casuistarum de Commutatione fere hæc est. Primo posse privatum quemvis sua authoritate sine superioris dispensatione commutare votum aut juramentum in id quod est evidentur melius. Quod confirmant exemplo ipsius Dei, qui promissa sua temporalia non semper implet ad literam, sed sæpe ea commutat in melius: & adducunt in hanc sententiam dictum Gregorii, Propositum aut promissum non infringi, qui in melius id commutat. Secundo, non posse commutari promissum in id quod est evidenter pejus, aut de quo dubium est an sit melius, sine authoritate susuperioris, qui habet legitimam potestatem in ea parte judicandi & determinandi. Tertiò, Commutatione omnino tolli obligationem præexistentem à materiâ priori: & induci de novo obligationem in materiâ diversâ. Sed tota ista doctrina falso nititur fundamento, dispensabilitate sc. Iuramenti; quæ cum nulla sit, ut modò probavimus ruat necesse est hæc ei superstructa Commutatio. Dico ergo breviter, non posse remitti vel solvi juramenti vinculum, aut ex toto per Dispensationem, aut ex parte per Commutationem sine consensu omnium partium. Præcipuè autem requiritur consensus ejus cui juratur; quia ei jus acquiritur, quod sine ipsius consensu non debet ei surripi. Exemplum autem à Deo sumptum non est simile: qui promissiones Dei, ut sunt omnes gratuitæ ita temporales sunt etiam conditionales, & intelligendæ cum exceptione crucis, & beneplaciti sui utilitatis nostræ. Nec vero est Voti & Iuramenti, respectu commutationis, ratio per omnia similis. Votum enim cum soli Deo nuncupetur, poterit fortasse voventi aliqua licentia concedi permutandi id ipsum in aliud quod sit evidenter melius & Deo gratius; cum nulla fiat istâ permutatione injuria alicui tertiæ personæ; at in Iuramento, quod homini factum est, sieret illi homini a injuria, si absq; ejus consensu & præter ipsius voluntatem in aliud commutaretur. Ut si Caius juratus solvere Titio decem libras, daret ei equum decem librarum pretio æstimatum; non censendus esset satisfecisse Juramento. Iniquum enim, ut quis cogatur rem sibi debitam commutare invitus. Neutro ergo istorum modorum solvi potest juramenti vinculum, aut obligatio tolli.
units.tr: Closely related to the question of dispensation is the question of the commutation of an oath, or the Second Case. Commutation, as the name itself shows, is nothing other than the transfer of an obligation from one matter to another, and whether the change is greater, lesser or equivalent, it is seen to be in some respect more advantageous. Commutation differs from dispensation somewhat as a species differs from its genus, or a part from its whole. For if either were enough to loose the bond, the bond would be loosed entirely by the whole through dispensation, but only in part through commutation. The sum of the Casuists' doctrine on commutation is roughly this. First, any private person may, on his own authority and without a superior's dispensation, commute a vow or oath into something evidently better. They confirm this by the example of God himself, who does not always fulfil his temporal promises to the letter but often changes them for the better, and they cite to this effect the saying of Gregory: a purpose or promise is not broken by one who changes it for the better. Second, a promise may not be commuted into something evidently worse, or about which it is doubtful whether it is better, without the authority of a superior who has lawful power to judge and determine in that matter. Third, by commutation the prior obligation arising from the former matter is wholly removed, and a new obligation is induced in a different matter. But this whole doctrine rests on a false foundation, namely the dispensability of an oath; since that is no foundation at all, as we have just proved, the commutation built upon it must necessarily fall. I say therefore, briefly, that the bond of an oath cannot be remitted or dissolved, either wholly by dispensation or in part by commutation, without the consent of all parties. Especially the consent of the one to whom the oath is sworn is required, because a right is acquired by him, and it must not be taken from him without his consent. The example taken from God, however, is not similar. His promises, which are all gratuitous, are also temporal and conditional, and are to be understood with the exception of the cross and of his own good pleasure for our advantage. Nor is the reasoning in every respect alike for a vow and an oath with regard to commutation. For a vow, since it is made to God alone, may perhaps be granted to the one vowing some licence to exchange it for something that is evidently better and more pleasing to God, since no injury is done to any third person by such an exchange. But in an oath, which is made to a man, injury would be done to that man if it were changed into something else without his consent and against his will. As if Caius, sworn to pay Titius ten pounds, should give him a horse valued at ten pounds, he would not be judged to have satisfied the oath; for it is unjust that someone be compelled to change, against his will, a thing owed to him. Therefore the bond of an oath cannot be dissolved by either of these methods, nor the obligation removed.

units.la: SECT. VI.
units.tr: SECT. VI.

units.la: Sed posse videtur reliquis qui supersunt tribus modis: Irritatione sc. Superioris, Cefsatione Materiæ, & Relaxatione Partis. Casus ergo Tertius est de solutione vinculi per Irritationem à Superiore factam. Significat autem Irritatio (sic enim, Barbarè licet, cum Cafuistis loquendum est,) actum legitimi superioris, quo authoritate sua irritum facit sive annullat juramentum à subdito sine ipsius consensu præstitum. Rescindere enim posse legitimum superiorem vota & juramenta eorum qui sub ipsorum sunt potestate, & non sui juris, sufe docet c hoc ipso capite Moses: uti nos ubi de Causa efficiente egimus d ante ostendimus. Ratio est, quia is qui alienæ potestati subest, non est sui juris, non habet potestatem se obligandi in iis rebus in quibus subest, nisi ex voluntate superioris cui subest: & proinde non debet aliquo actu suo inducere sibi obligationem sine illius consensu, vel expresso, vel rationabiliter præsumpto. Jura enim Prælatorum in subditos, ex lege Dei immota & æterna, perpetua sunt. Officia insuper Subditorum erga prælatos, obsequiique jus & subjectionis, ex eadem perpetua lege, perpetua sunt & indispensabiliter obligatoria. Quæ obligatio antecedens (ex tertia nostra hypothesi) impedit effectum Juramenti subsequentis, ne possit obligare: semper enim obligatio prior præjudicat posteriori; & irritum facit omnem actum inductivum novæ obligationis sibi contrariæ.
units.tr: But it seems that the remaining three ways are possible: by annulment, that is, of the superior; by cessation of the matter; and by relaxation of the part. The Third Case, then, concerns the dissolution of the bond by annulment made by a superior. Now annulment (for thus, however barbarous, we must speak with the Casuists) signifies an act of a lawful superior by which, on his own authority, he makes void or annuls an oath sworn by a subject without his consent. That a lawful superior can rescind the vows and oaths of those who are under his power and not their own masters, Moses teaches in this very chapter, as we showed earlier when we treated of the efficient cause. The reason is this: one who is under another's power is not his own master, and has no power to bind himself in those matters in which he is subject, except by the will of the superior to whom he is subject. Therefore he ought not, by any act of his own, to bring upon himself an obligation without that superior's consent, either expressed or reasonably presumed. For the rights of superiors over subjects, grounded in the unchanging and eternal law of God, are perpetual. Moreover, the duties of subjects toward superiors, and the right of obedience and subjection, by the same perpetual law are perpetual and indispensably binding. This prior obligation (by our third hypothesis) hinders the effect of a later oath, so that it cannot bind; for a prior obligation always prejudices a later one, and it makes void every act that induces a new obligation contrary to it.

units.la: Dicendum ergo in hoc casu primo, non debere subditum in iis rebus in quibus alteri subest jurare se facturum quidquam, absque præsumpto saltem superioris sui consensu. Secundo si juraverit & res sit licita, obligari ad faciendum quamdiu non videtur id esse contra voluntatem, dignitatem, aut utilitatem superioris. Tertio, superiorem, si expresso consensu suo, sive antecedente sive subsequente, promissionem subditi semel confirmaverit, e non posse eandem postea irritam facere, aut obligationem ejus tollere. Quarto, si superior quamprimum rem rescierit, statim, dissensum suum palam & peremptorie subdito significaverit, prohibuerit que id in quod juratum est fieri : cessare continuò obligationem illam Juramenti transitoriam; & subditum vi obligationis officii, quæ permanens est & perpetua, teneri contrà quàm juraverat facere. Unde fiquis alienæ potest ti subditus, puta domini aut patris aut principis vel sponte suâ, vel vi & metu adductus, aliquod forte Juramentum præstaret, in quo dominum patrem aut Principem fi adesset non fuisse confeluurum crederet: jurando peccavit contra officium debitum, & omnino tenetur illud juramentum ut officio suo contrarium, non fervare. Stet ergo solvi vinculum Juramenti ex irritatione legitimi superioris.
units.tr: Accordingly, in this case it must be said: first, a subject ought not to swear that he will do anything in those matters in which he is under another's authority, without at least the presumed consent of his superior. Second, if he has sworn, and the thing is lawful, he is bound to do it for as long as it does not appear to be contrary to the will, dignity or advantage of the superior. Third, if the superior has once confirmed the subject's promise by his express consent, whether given beforehand or afterwards, he cannot afterwards make it void or remove its obligation. Fourth, if the superior, as soon as he has learned of the matter, at once openly and peremptorily signifies to the subject his dissent, and forbids what was sworn to be done, then that transitory obligation of the oath ceases at once, and the subject, by the force of the obligation of duty, which is permanent and perpetual, is bound to act contrary to what he had sworn. Hence if a subject under another's power, such as a master, father or prince, of his own accord or driven by force and fear, should perhaps make some oath in which he believed the master, father or prince, if present, would not have consented, he has sinned by swearing against his due duty, and he is wholly bound not to keep that oath, as being contrary to his duty. It stands, therefore, that the bond of an oath is dissolved by the annulment of a lawful superior.

units.la: SECT. VII.
units.tr: SECT. VII.

units.la: Casus quartus est de solutione vincult per cessationem materiæ, aut mutationem aliquam notabilem factam circa causam Juramenti principalem. Tunc enim cessasse materiam censendum est, cum rerum status inter tempus jurandi & tempus adimplendi ita immutatus est, ut si quo tempore jurabatur prævideri potuisset is qui postea insecurus est rerum status, non omnino juratum fuisset. Respondetur breviter, cessante Juramenti, Voti, aut promissionis materia, cessare simul ejusdem & obligationem: quemadmodum in naturalibus & artificialibus, deficiente materia, dedeficere necesse est & actionem agentis. Nec enim potest ignis urere, si desit materia combustibilis: nec faber, ni adsint ligna, scamnum facere. Si quis ergo miles juret obsequium belli Imperatori: finito demum bello, cum ipse desierit esse imperator, non ultra tenetur ex juramento obsequium ei præstare. Et si pater aliquis juraret, le testamentum in quo filium instituisset hæredem nunquam mutaturum: comperto tamen postea filium heredem institutum patri venenum miscuisse, pater non ultra tenetur juramento, sed eo non obstante poterit mutato testamento alium hæredem instituere. Idem dicendum est, cum quis juravit statuta alicujus Collegii sive communitatis sibi prælecta observare: si postea contigerit ea statuta revocari vel abrogari, jurans absolvitur à vinculo illius juramenti. Ratio est, quia radice obligationis sublatâ, tollitur una pullulans inde obligatio: fuit autem Materia illa quæ causam dedit jurationi, radix ejus obligationis quæ ex illa juratione insecuta est. Iuramentum enim sequitur naturam & conditionem actus cui adjungitur, id est Materiæ circa quam versatur, sicut accessorium sequitur naturam sui principalis : & quæ accessorium locum obtinent, inquiunt jurisconsulti, extinguuntur, cum principales res peremptæ fuerint.
units.tr: The fourth case concerns the dissolution of the bond by the cessation of the matter, or by some notable change made in the principal subject of the oath. The matter is then deemed to have ceased when the state of affairs has changed between the time of swearing and the time of performance, so that, if the later state of affairs could have been foreseen at the time of swearing, the oath would not have been taken at all. I answer briefly: when the matter of an oath, vow or promise ceases, its obligation ceases with it, just as in natural and artificial things the action of the agent must fail when its matter fails. Fire cannot burn if there is no combustible material, and a carpenter cannot make a bench unless there is wood. So if a soldier swears obedience to a commander in war, and once the war is over the commander is no longer commander, he is no longer bound by the oath to render him obedience. And if a father swore that he would never change the will in which he had named his son heir, but afterwards discovered that the son, the appointed heir, had put poison in his drink, the father is no longer bound by the oath, and notwithstanding it he may change the will and appoint another heir. The same must be said when someone has sworn to observe the statutes of a college or community committed to him: if those statutes are afterwards revoked or abrogated, the one who swore is released from the bond of that oath. The reason is that when the root of an obligation is removed, the obligation that sprang from it is removed too. Now the matter that gave occasion to the swearing was the root of the obligation that followed from that swearing. For an oath follows the nature and condition of the act to which it is joined, that is, of the matter with which that act is concerned, just as an accessory follows the nature of its principal; and, as the jurists say, accessories are extinguished when the principal things have perished.

units.la: Casus ultimus est, de solutione vinculi per Relaxationem Partis, ejus sc. cui juratum est: ut si Caius Titio aliquid promiserit, an remittente Titio obligationem, Caius promissi religione exolutus sit? Ubi imprimis observandum hunc loquendi modum Remittere Juramentum, & alium ei consimilem, Juramenti gratiam facere, apud bonos authores non uno semper sensu accipi. Summuntur enim interdum cum relatione ad juramentum præstandum, & sic is dicitur alteri remittere juramentum, vel juramenti gratiam facere, qui cum alter ille paratus est jurare, contentus voluntate non postulat ab eo Juramentum, sed injurato credit, vel alia quacunque de causa jusjurandum ab eo, a quo exigendi jus habet, non, exigit. Plerumque tamen sumuntur cum relatione ad Juramentum præstitum: & sic is dicitur alteri remittere vel gratiam facere, qui ei id quod promissum est condonat, nec rem virtute juramenti debitam, cum exigendi jus habeat, exigit. Sic de Tiberio Suetonius, a Equiti Romano jurisjurandi gratiam fecit ut uxorem in stupro generi compertam dimitteret, quam se antea nunquam repudiaturum juraverat. Et Impp. Antoninus & Verus rescripserunt b gratiam se facere jurisjuraudi ei qui juraverat se ordini non interfuturum, & postea Duumvir creatus est. Et hæc est illa remissio sive gratia Juramenti, quam Relaxationem vocant Casuistæ. De qua dico primum, Relaxationem istam in Juramentis, fœderibus, Pactis, aliisque Contractibus humanis locum habere, non item in Votis. Ratio discriminis est, quia Vota Deo fiunt ut parti: ab homine autem ea sola relaxari fas est, quæ homini facta sunt: Dico secundo, si juretur in gratiam alterius, id est per respectum ad honorem, obsequium, utilitatem, aliúdve ejus bonum vel commodum: juramentum non obligare, nisi is in cujus gratiam juratur, id gratum ratúmque habuerit. Sicut juris notoratis interpretatione, non obligat Caium ad solvendum Titio centum chirographum, etsi Caii manu subscriptum, sigilloque firmatum; nisi id Caius Titio tradiderit, Titiusque aut alius ejus nomine & vice sic traditum acceperit. Dico tertio, Juramentum sic præstitum, si is cui juratur ratum habuerit & velit servari, non posse c ab alia quacunque tertia persona relaxari. Ratio est, quia nemo potest jus alteri acquisitum, nisi ipse consenserit, adimere. Unde sequitur quod ante diximus, per dispensationem tertiæ personæ non tolli obligationem juramenti, absque consensu partium. Dico quarto, si
units.tr: The last case concerns the dissolving of a bond by relaxation on the part of the one to whom the oath was sworn. For example: if Gaius has promised something to Titius, is Gaius released from the bond of his promise when Titius remits the obligation? Here first it must be noted that the expressions to remit an oath and to grant the favour of an oath are not always taken in one sense by good authors. Sometimes they are used with reference to the oath to be sworn. In that sense, someone is said to remit an oath or grant its favour to another when, though that other is ready to swear, he is content with his word and does not ask for an oath, believing him without one, or for some other reason does not require the oath from one from whom he has the right to demand it. More often, however, they are used with reference to the oath already sworn. In that sense, someone is said to remit or grant favour to another when he forgives him what was promised, and does not exact the thing owed by virtue of the oath, although he has the right to exact it. Thus Suetonius tells of Tiberius that he granted to a Roman knight the favour of his oath, so that he might dismiss a wife caught in adultery with his son-in-law, whom he had earlier sworn never to repudiate. And the Emperors Antoninus and Verus rescripted that they granted the favour of the oath to one who had sworn that he would not attend a meeting of his order, and was afterwards made a duumvir. This is that remission or favour of an oath which the casuists call relaxation. Concerning it I say, first, that this relaxation has a place in oaths, covenants, pacts and other human contracts, but not in vows. The reason for the difference is that vows are made to God as a party, and only what was made to a man may be relaxed by a man. Second, if an oath is sworn in favour of another, that is, with regard to his honour, service, advantage, or other good or benefit, the oath does not bind unless the one in whose favour it was sworn has approved and ratified it. Thus, by the interpretation of the law of notes, a written obligation for one hundred, even though signed in Gaius's hand and sealed with his seal, does not bind Gaius to pay Titius, unless Gaius has delivered it to Titius, and Titius, or someone in his name and place, has accepted it as delivered. Third, an oath so sworn, if the one to whom it was sworn has ratified it and wishes it kept, cannot be relaxed by any other third person. The reason is that no one can take away a right acquired by another unless that other has consented. Hence it follows what we said before: the obligation of an oath is not removed by the dispensation of a third person without the consent of the parties. Fourth, if the one to whom the oath was sworn has remitted it and does not wish it kept, then:

units.la: {c} Non debet alii nocere, quod inter alios actum est. l. 10. ff. de Jurejur. is cui juratum est remiserit jujurandum & nolit servari; jurantem obligatione protenus solvi nec in conscientia teneri id facere quod se ante facturum juraverat. Ergo Caius Titio juratus solvere centum, si postea Titius ei debitum remiserit, non ultra tenetur juramento. Ratio est quia potest quilibet suo jure cedere; & rem sibi debitam condonare. Debito autem soluto, d cessare ipso facto obligationem necesse est; cum terminus obligationis sit debiti solutio, ut ex obligationis definitione patuit, sicut apud nos, ex ipsâ formulâ syngraphæ obligatoriæ constat, soluta pecuniâ obligationem solvi. Si dicas debitum hic non solvi, quia promissum non impletur Respondeo, ad omnem juris effectum perinde esse sive realiter impleatur, sive ab eo cujus interest pro impleto habeatur. Ratio est, quia acceptatio ejus cujus interest, est interpretative acceptio rei: atque ita, cessante quasi materia, cessat obligatio, eadem fere ratione qua in proximo antecedente casu dictum est. Et hoc ipsum est quod e Acceptilatione Iurif-Consulti vocant per quam (civilem licet solutionem, & non veram) non minus tamen obligationem tolli docent, quàm per veram solutionem. Si iterum dicas, ut relaxatione tolli possit obligatio hominis facta, videri tamen obligationem Deo factam manere; sicut an-te tè responsum est casu Iuramenti metu extorti. Respondeo, ex relaxato eo quo jam dictum est modo vinculo nullam fieri Deo injuriam, sicut fit in violatione Iuramenti coacti: quia promissio facta præcisè in favorem alterius, in Deum dirigitur solum ut testem promissionis homini factæ, & vindicem violatæ ejus fidei quæ alteri astringitur: quam fidem cum non violarit, sed promissioni satisfecerit, omni prorsus obligatione solutus est, & apud Deum & apud hominem. Dico quinto, solutionem vinculi quæ fit per relaxationem partis, eousque extendi, quò parti relaxanti placuerit; ut fi Caius Titio juraverit solvere centum, Titius autem ei postea quinquaginta remiserit; solvitur obligatio g ex parte tantum non ex toto. Tollitur fc. vinculum quoad quinquaginta remissos, manet quoad quinquaginta non remissos. Rursum, fi Caius Titio juraverit solvere centum infra viginti dies, Titius autem videns Caium non pesse constituto die fine aliquo suo incommodo pecuniam solvere, concedat ei adhuc viginti dies alios: Relaxatio hæc quæ fit per dilationem five prorogationem temporis, eatenus solvit Iuramenti vinculum, ut non teneatur pecunias solvere prout initio juraverat intra dies viginti; tenetur tamen, idque ex primi juramenti vinculo intra dies quadraginta easdem solvere. Dico sexto, Relaxationem partis valere ad vinculum juramenti solvendum, quantum ipsius interest: non tamen valere in praejudicium tertiae personae. Ratio est, quia potest quilibet per actum suum de jure proprio quantum vult remittere: Sed non potest quisquam de alieno jure quicquam demere, ipso vel inconsulto vel invito. Debet itaque unusquisque sic cedere jure suo, ut salvum sit interim alteri cuique jus suum. Sic Abraham de bonis jure belli acquisitis post reportatam de quatuor Regibus victoriam, Gen. 14. h jure suo cessit cum suam praedae partem Regi Sodomorum universam condonavit; reservata tamen tribus Ducibus belli sociis quae eis obtigisset justa portione. Unde Caius juratus solvere Titio & Julio centum, si Titius ei suam partem debiti condonet, solutus est juramenti vinculo quoad illam partem quae Titio debebatur; manet tamen obligatio quoad partem Julio debitam. Ex eodem fundamento fit, ut relaxatio partium ex consensu nihil efficiat in contractu Sponsaliorum. Quia ibi non utilitas tantum hominis spectatur, sed & institutum Dei: cui magna fieret injuria, si contractus ille etsi ex communi contrahentium consensu violaretur. Quia virtus illa & efficacia quam habet haec de qua nunc agitur relaxatio ad tollendam obligationem, supponit actum illum qui obligationem induxerat, non spectavisse ad aliud aliquid, præter bonum & commodum partis relaxantis tantum. Si alterius cujufquam interfit ex aliquo suo jure Obligationem non solvi, Obligatio non solvitur.
units.tr: {c} One ought not to harm another by what was done between other people. l. 10. ff. de Jurejur. The one swearing is at once released from the obligation and is not bound in conscience to do what he had sworn to do. So if Gaius swore to Titius to pay one hundred, and Titius afterwards remitted the debt to him, Gaius is no longer bound by the oath. The reason is that anyone may give up his own right and forgive a debt owed to him. But once the debt is paid, the obligation must cease by the very fact, since the end of an obligation is the payment of the debt, as is clear from the definition of obligation; just as among us, from the very wording of a written bond, it is evident that when the money is paid the obligation is discharged. If you say that the debt is not paid here, because the promise is not fulfilled, I answer that for every legal effect it is the same whether it is really fulfilled or is regarded as fulfilled by the one whose interest it is. The reason is that the acceptance of the one whose interest it is amounts, by interpretation, to acceptance of the thing; and so, the matter as it were having ceased, the obligation ceases, for nearly the same reason as in the immediately preceding case. This is what the jurists call acceptilation, through which, (though it is a civil and not a true payment), they teach that the obligation is removed no less than by true payment. If you say again that although the obligation of a man may be removed by relaxation, the obligation made to God seems to remain, as was answered before in the case of an oath extorted by fear: I answer that when the bond has been relaxed in the way just described, no wrong is done to God, as happens in the violation of a coerced oath. For a promise made solely in favour of another is directed to God only as witness of the promise made to the man, and avenger of the violated trust that binds one person to another. Since he has not violated that trust, but has satisfied the promise, he is wholly released from every obligation, both before God and before man. Fifth, I say that the dissolving of a bond by relaxation on the part of one party extends only as far as the relaxing party chooses. For example, if Gaius has sworn to Titius to pay one hundred, and Titius afterwards remits fifty to him, the obligation is dissolved only in part, not in whole. The bond is removed as to the fifty remitted, and remains as to the fifty not remitted. Again, if Gaius has sworn to Titius to pay one hundred within twenty days, and Titius, seeing that Gaius cannot pay by the appointed day without some loss to himself, grants him another twenty days, this relaxation, which comes by deferral or extension of time, loosens the bond of the oath only so far that he is not bound to pay the money within twenty days as he first swore; but he is bound, and by the bond of the first oath, to pay the same within forty days. Sixth, I say that the relaxation of a party is valid to loosen the bond of an oath as far as his own interest goes, but is not valid to the prejudice of a third person. The reason is that anyone may by his own act remit as much as he likes of his own right; but no one may take anything from another's right, whether that other is consulted or unwilling. Each person must therefore give up his right in such a way that meanwhile the right of each other person remains safe. Thus Abraham, after the victory won over the four kings, Gen. 14. h, gave up his right to the spoils taken by right of war when he remitted the whole of his share of the booty to the king of Sodom, yet reserving to the three allied commanders their just portion of what had fallen to them. Hence, if Gaius swore to Titius and Julius to pay one hundred, and Titius remits to him his part of the debt, Gaius is released from the bond of the oath as to that part which was owed to Titius; but the obligation remains as to the part owed to Julius. On the same ground, the relaxation of the parties by consent has no effect in the contract of betrothal. For there not only the advantage of the persons is regarded, but also the institution of God, and great wrong would be done to him if that contract were violated even by the common consent of the contracting parties. For the power and efficacy which this relaxation, of which we are now speaking, has to remove an obligation, presupposes that the act which had introduced the obligation did not look to anything else besides the good and advantage of the relaxing party alone. If it is in the interest of some other person that the obligation should not be discharged on account of some right of his, the obligation is not discharged.

units.la: SECT. IX.
units.tr: SECT. IX.

units.la: Eorum igitur quæ de vinculi Juramentorii solutione hactenus dicta sunt, breviter hæc summa est. Nec dispensatione alicujus fuperioris nec ulla commutatione solvi posse Juramenti vinculum, quin ut jurans adhuc in conscientia sua obligatus maneat, adimplere id quod promisit. Sed posse tamen id vinculum aut rescindi & irritum reddi authoritate superioris legitimam potestatem habentis, aut deficiente materia cessare, aut ab eo cui promissio facta est relaxari, ita ut obligandi vim penitus amittat. Absoluta jam tandem (Deo aspice) pro modulo tenuitatis meæ, quâ potui brevitate perspicuitate, fide, promissa cum hoc publicæ professionis munus auspicarer tractatione: Coronidis loco, monita quædam pauca, velut Corollaria, quæ nobis ad vitæ conscientiæque institutionem ex usu esse poterunt, de Juramentorum usu & abusu, attexenda duxi. Idque non per modum parænefeos, ut sol-
units.tr: The sum, then, of what has been said so far about the dissolution of the bond of an oath is this. The bond of an oath can be dissolved neither by the dispensation of any superior nor by any exchange, so that the swearer remains bound in conscience to perform what he promised. Yet that bond can be rescinded and made void by the authority of a superior who has lawful power, or can cease when its matter fails, or can be relaxed by the one to whom the promise was made, so that it entirely loses its force of obligation. Now at last, having finished (God is my witness) the treatment I promised, to the best of my modest ability, with such brevity, clarity and good faith as I could manage, and having begun it as the duty of my public profession, I have judged it fitting to add, as a crown to the whole, a few admonitions in the manner of corollaries, which may be of use to us for the guidance of life and conscience, concerning the use and abuse of oaths. I do this not by way of exhortation, as sacred orators do when they speak to the people in sermons, but, mindful that we teach in the School and not in the Church, by means of certain theses or practical conclusions briefly set forth and clearly explained.

units.la: {Q} lens lent Oratores sacri in concionibus ad populum, sed memores nos in Scholâ docere, non Ecclesiâ, per theses quasdam sive Conclusiones Practicas breviter propositas & dilucidè explicatas.
units.tr: {Q} Let them be read as they are written, that is, as lessons delivered in the School and not as sermons to the people.

units.la: SECT. X.
units.tr: SECT. X.

units.la: Conclusio Prima, & est contra Anabaptistas & Socinianos. Juramenti usus est licitus. Probatur primò, ex usu veteris Testamenti. Jurabant pii a Patriarchæ: jure-jurando terminari controversias instituit in lege b Moses: conditiones in jurando observandas præscripserunt c Prophetæ. Neque potest reddi justa aliqua ratio, cur piis sub veteri Testamento jurare licuerit, fidelibus sub novo non item liceat; cum non pertinuisse jusjurandum ad legem Ceremoniarum per Christum abrogandam, & ex ejus fine patet, cujus est perpetuus usus; & ex forma, quæ nihil videtur habere cum typo commune, Secundò, ab exemplis d Dei, e Angelorum, f Apostolorum; quorum illi ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, hi historicè & ἐν πνεύματι in sacrâ Scripturâ sæpè jurantes inducuntur. Tertiò, a consuetudine omnium populorum: qui ductu luminis naturæ ad fidem firmandam in civilis societatis commoditatem jurisjurandi religionem adhibendam censuerunt: quo nullum potest esse Legis naturalis indicium. cium certius. Quarto, a fine Juramenti; quæ est confirmatio fidei in rebus dubiis, ubi aliæ probationes deficiunt. Qui finis cum sit necessarius ad tollendas & terminandas lites: media ad illum finem necessaria, necesse est ut sint saltem licita. Quinto, à natura Juramenti, nihil in se continentis quod sit intrinsecè malum. Neque enim malum est Actus religiosus; neque malum est Rei dubiæ confirmatio; neque malum est divini testimonii advocatio: ex quibus quasi membris integratur juramenti essentialis definitio.
units.tr: First Conclusion, and it is against the Anabaptists and the Socinians: the use of an oath is lawful. It is proved, first, from the use of the Old Testament. The godly swore from the time of the Patriarchs; Moses instituted in the law that controversies be ended by an oath; the Prophets prescribed the conditions to be observed in swearing. Nor can any just reason be given why it was lawful for the godly to swear under the Old Testament but is not likewise lawful for the faithful under the New. The oath did not belong to the ceremonial law, which was abrogated by Christ; this is clear from its end, whose use is perpetual, and from its form, which seems to have nothing in common with a type. Secondly, from the examples of God, of Angels, and of Apostles: the first swear anthropopathōs [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς], in human fashion; the second swear historically; and the third swear in the Spirit [ἐν πνεύματι]; all are introduced in Holy Scripture as swearing often. Thirdly, from the custom of all peoples, who, led by the light of nature, judged that the religion of an oath should be employed to confirm faith for the benefit of civil society; and no surer sign of the law of nature can exist. Fourthly, from the end of an oath, which is the confirmation of faith in doubtful matters, where other proofs fail. Since this end is necessary for ending and settling disputes, the means necessary to that end must at least be lawful. Fifthly, from the nature of an oath, which contains nothing in itself that is intrinsically evil. For it is not evil to be a religious act; it is not evil to be the confirmation of a doubtful matter; and it is not evil to be the calling upon the testimony of God. From these, as from members, the essential definition of an oath is put together.

units.la: SECT. XI.
units.tr: SECT. XI.

units.la: Conclusio secunda. Juramenti usus in sermone quotidiano non est licitus. Probatur primo, à natura juramenti. Quia actus omnis religiosus, cum sit pars cultus Dei, debet præstari cum debitâ reverentiâ, & cum aliquâ animi cum præparatione tum attentione: quæ omnia abesse necesse est, cum temere adhibentur & sine judicio, vel incautis & incogitantibus excidunt verba juratoria. Secundo, à fine Juramenti, quæ est rei dubiæ confirmatio. Quum in sermone quotidiano de rebus fere levibus colloquia ferantur, quæ aut non sunt dubia, aut non tanti ut egeant religiosa confirmatione. Aut si tanti essent, non multo confirmatior esset fides apud eos quicum agitur,
units.tr: Second Conclusion: the use of an oath in everyday speech is not lawful. It is proved, first, from the nature of an oath. Because every religious act, since it is a part of the worship of God, ought to be performed with due reverence, and with some preparation and attention of mind; all of which must be absent when oaths are used rashly and without judgment, or when oath-words slip out from the careless and the thoughtless. Secondly, from the end of an oath, which is the confirmation of a doubtful matter. Since in everyday speech conversations are carried on about things that are for the most part trivial, which are either not doubtful or not of such weight as to need a religious confirmation. Or if they were of such weight, faith would not be much more confirmed among those with whom one deals

units.la: ex ejus hominis juramento, qui temere & multum jurat: cujus fere ea est apud plurimos existimatio, ut ei vel injurato credatur, fi putetur vera dixisse; vel jurato non credatur, fi putetur falsa. Tertio, a causa unde promanant ejusmodi juramenta. Quæ vel est vitiosus habitus, ex longo usu & peffimâ consuetudine contractus cujusmodi habitus cordis prophani, & tantum non athei, fructus & indicium est: vel effrænis aliqua animi perturbatio, velut impotentis iræ, aut intemperantis lætitiæ; quibus dum calent animi, facile difpumant in contumeliam Dei. Quo mihi videntur quasi peculiariter respicere verba illa Jacobi c. 5. verf. 12. Ante omnia, inquit, nolite jurare, neque per cœlum, neque per terram, &c. Hortatus nempe erat fideles ad ferendum patienter injurias versibus aliquot immediate præcedentibus: & versu sequente docet quibus fe rebus exercere deceat hominem Christianum, five doleat, five lætetur. Locus sane dignus, in quo explicando doêti viri sese exerceant, & cujus fcopus & vis ex verborum serie, aliquanto quàm ab Interpretibus factum est, accuratius investigetur. Poterit forte assis obiter in hanc rem aliquid compendii afferri ex ista qualicunque verborum (ut mihi sonare videntur) paraphrasi. Ponite vobis ante oculos veterum prophetarum & piorum exempla.
units.tr: by the oath of a man who swears rashly and often; the common opinion of most people about such a man is that, if he swears, he is believed when he is thought to have spoken truly, and is not believed when he is thought to have spoken falsely. Thirdly, from the cause from which such oaths spring. This is either a vicious habit, contracted by long use and a very bad custom, a fruit and sign of such a habit of a profane heart, and hardly of an atheist; or some unrestrained disturbance of the mind, such as of ungoverned anger or of immoderate joy; while minds are heated by these, they easily break out into insults against God. For this reason, it seems to me, the words of James, chapter 5, verse 12, look especially to this: Above all things, he says, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth, etc. He had indeed exhorted the faithful to bear injuries patiently in the few verses immediately before, and in the following verse he teaches with what things a Christian man ought to occupy himself, whether he grieves or rejoices. It is certainly a passage worthy of learned men exercising themselves in its explanation, and whose scope and force should be investigated more accurately from the sequence of the words than has been done by the Interpreters. Perhaps something of brevity may be offered on this matter in passing, from this paraphrase of the words, such as it is (as it seems to me to sound). Set before your eyes the examples of the old prophets and the godly.

Quin con-“ tinete vosmet sive commotiores sive hi-“ lares intra debitos modestiæ fines, nec cœ-“ lum terræ miscete , nec omnia clamoribus “ & jurationibus implete : sed tranquillo “ animo si quid affirmandum sit , nudè & “ simpliciter affirmate ; si quid negandum , “ nudè & simpliciter negate. At si vos porrò “ stimulet acrior ex utravis parte animi im-“ petus , non ferentis se intra pectoris an-“ gustias concludi, sed aliquâ exire gesti-“ entis : vestræ erit prudentiæ,animi illum ar-“ dorem in honorem Dei convertere. Quà “ tandem arte quæritis ? dicam. Angitur ani-“ mi quis vestrum? non ex impatientia pro-“ rumpat statim in juramenta & blas-“ phemias, quod ira æstuantibus proclive est: “ sed oret potius & precetur Deum, ut “ quoad illa mala auferantur, det sibi pa-“ tientiam.
