Si quis Apostoli verba simplicius intelligi malit, utatur suo judicio. Exposui tantum quod mihi videtur non improbabile: nemini legem dico. Sed ut redeam ad institutum cursum; si tamen digressus sum: illud iterum certum est Jacobi verba jurandi illud cacoethes, quod apud omnes & summae & abjectissimae fortis homines passim jamdiu inveteravit, omnino damnare. Multas implerem paginas, si quae in priorum Patrum & veterum ex omni gente Doctorum Hebraeorum, Graecorum, Latinorum, imo & hominum etiam Ethnicorum scriptis adversus hanc impium consuetudinem occurrunt, in unum congerer e. Accipite e plurimis unum & alterum. Ex Hebraeis sapientissimum virum Siracidem e Ne assuesce os tuum ad jurandum. Sicut servus continuo verberatus non caret livore, sic qui Dei nomen crebro in os suum assumit, non erit purus a peccato. Et vir multijurans implebitur iniquitate. E Graecis Eusebium philosophum Gentilem, f Multi, inquit, hortantur homines; τὸ ὀμνύειν εἶναι, id est, ut verum jurent: ego autem existimo τὸ ἀρχὴν μηδ' ἀπλῶς ὀμνύναι, ut ne quidem omnino facile jurent. E Latinis Augustinum. g Jurationem cave quantum potes. Melius quippe nec verum jurare, non quia peccatum est verum jurare, jurare. jurare, sed quia gravissimum est falsum jurare: quò citius cadit, qui jurare consuevit. Et alibi h, falsa juratio exitiosa: etiam vera periculosa. Sed quid opus est aliunde testimoniis, quum prohibita sit quotidiana hæc & non necessaria juratio, ita ut vix aliud quidquam in sacris literis difertius: & ab ipso Christo, μηδ' ὅλως, Ego autem dico vobis, Ne jurate omnino; & ab ejus Apostolo B. Jacobo loco jam citato k πρὸ πάντων δέ, Ante omnia ne jurate.
units.tr: Examples. If you suffer any evil, follow their patience. If you cannot attain that, at least, which unless you wish to be most careless, can very easily be guarded against, above all take care that you do not, either being too impatient in grief, or on the contrary too exuberant in gladness, rashly do by swearing anything unworthy of the Christian name and insulting to the majesty of God. Rather, restrain yourselves, whether more disturbed or cheerful, within the due limits of moderation; do not mix heaven with earth, nor fill everything with outcries and oaths; but with a tranquil mind, if anything is to be affirmed, affirm it plainly and simply; if anything is to be denied, deny it plainly and simply. But if a sharper impulse from either side stirs you further, one that will not bear to be confined within the narrow bounds of the breast, but eager to break out in some gesture, it will be a matter of your prudence to turn that ardour of mind to the honour of God. By what art, you ask? I will tell you. Is any of you afflicted in mind? Let him not break out at once into oaths and blasphemies out of impatience, which is natural to those who are seething with anger; but let him rather pray and beseech God to give him patience until those evils are taken away. On the contrary, Is anyone of a joyful and cheerful disposition? Let him not even in this way open his mouth to oaths, which is the custom of the Bacchantes; but let him rather sing hymns and Psalms in praise of God, who has granted such happy days to him. If anyone prefers to understand the Apostle's words more simply, let him use his own judgment. I have only set out what seems to me not improbable; I do not impose a law on anyone. But to return to the course I had set; if indeed I have digressed: it is again certain that the words of James utterly condemn that disease of swearing, which has long since spread widely among all men, both of the highest and of the most abject rank. I would fill many pages if I were to gather into one place whatever occurs in the writings of the earlier Fathers and of the ancient teachers of every nation, Hebrews, Greeks, Latins, and even Gentiles, against this impious custom. Take one or two out of many. From the Hebrews, the most wise man Jesus the son of Sirach: Do not accustom your mouth to swearing. As a servant constantly beaten does not lack a bruise, so he who often takes the name of God into his mouth will not be free from sin. And a man who swears much will be filled with iniquity. From the Greeks, the Gentile philosopher Eusebius: Many, he says, exhort men that swearing [τὸ ὀμνύειν εἶναι], that is, that they swear truly; but I think that to begin with, not to swear at all [τὸ ἀρχὴν μηδ' ἀπλῶς ὀμνύναι], so that they should not swear even at all readily. From the Latins, Augustine: Avoid swearing as much as you can. For it is better not to swear even the truth, not because it is a sin to swear the truth, but because it is most grievous to swear falsely: and he who is accustomed to swear falls more quickly. And elsewhere: A false oath is destructive; even a true one is dangerous. But what need is there of testimonies from elsewhere, since this daily and unnecessary swearing is forbidden, so that scarcely anything in the sacred writings is more clearly stated? It is forbidden by Christ himself, not at all [μηδ' ὅλως]: But I say to you, do not swear at all; and by his Apostle, the blessed James, in the passage already cited: above all things [πρὸ πάντων δέ], do not swear.

units.la: SECT. XII.
units.tr: SECT. XII.

units.la: Conclusio tertia. Nisi ex causa justa gravi & necessaria non est jurandum. Est Juramentum ex eo rerum genere, quæ nec per se sunt malæ quales sunt actus furti, homicidii, sacrilegii, perjurii, & omnium vitiorum; nec per se expetendæ, quales sunt actus charitatis, justitiæ, obedientiæ & omnium virtutum: sed quæ eò tantùm l bonæ sunt quia necessaria, ex hypothesi sc. finis, nec expetendæ nisi in ordine ad illum finem; qualia sunt omnia illa quæ ordinata sunt ad subveniendum alicui defectui, ut Medicina. Ut enim pharmacum non propter se repertum est sed propter sanitatem, nec ullus esset ejus usus, nisi essent humana corpora morbis obnoxia, (m Honora medicum propter necessitatem:) sic Juramentum in-
units.tr: Third conclusion. An oath is not to be sworn except for a just, weighty and necessary cause. An oath belongs to that class of things which are not in themselves evil, as are the acts of theft, murder, sacrilege, perjury and all vices, nor in themselves to be desired, as are the acts of charity, justice, obedience and all the virtues. It is rather one of those things which are good only because they are necessary, good by hypothesis, that is, for the sake of an end, and to be desired only in relation to that end. Such are all those things which are ordained to remedy some defect, as medicine is. For just as a drug was not discovered for its own sake but for the sake of health, and would have no use at all if human bodies were not liable to disease (Honour the physician for the sake of necessity), so the oath is ordained

units.la: l Non in bonis, id est per se expetendis, sed in necessariis juratio ordinatur ad aliud, habet ergo rationem medii, 1. de ferm. Aug. ftitutum est ad fidem inter homines firmandam ; nec ullus effet ejus usus, fi non effet gens humana ignorantiæ & perfidiæ heu nimis obnoxia : quo fortasse spectant illa Christi verba η ἐκ τῆς πονηρᾶς ἐστιν. Ergo sicut vitandus est medicinæ usus, ubi ad vitæ conservationem & valetudinem tuendam non videtur esse quodammodo necessaria : sic & Juramentum vitandum, ubi conservandæ humanæ societatis o necessitas, veritatis manifestatio, & fidei confirmatio, non videtur ipsius usum aliquo modo efflagitare. Salutare monitum est illud Epicteti (ut illi-us Stoici omnia) ὅρκον ἀποφεύγειν, εἰ μὲν οὖν τ' ἐς ἀπαν, εἰ δὲ μὴ, ἐκ τῆς ἐνόντων. Jusjurandum detita, si possibile est, omnino : si non, saltem quantum potes. Sancta res est Juramentum : sed quo sanctior, eo periculosior, si indebitè adhibeatur. Sicut pharmacum, quo majoris est efficaciæ & virtutis, eo magis corpori nocet, si temere & imperitè sumatur. Juramenti assertorii in Rep. necessarius usus est : in publicis præsertim judiciis, ad veritatem eruendam circa facta particularia ; quo pertinent juramenta testium, calumniæ, purgationis, &c. Extra judicium & in rebus privatis usus ejus rarior est : potest tamen quandoque esse necessarius ; ubi sc. multum interest, ut ei quod assertorie dicitur fides habeatur, & asserenti nisi juret non credetur.
units.tr: ¹ Not among goods, that is, things to be desired in themselves, but among necessary things: the oath is ordained to something else, and so has the character of a means. (Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 1.) It was instituted to confirm faith among men, and it would have no use at all if the human race were not so lamentably prone to ignorance and faithlessness. To this perhaps refers the saying of Christ, [ἐκ τῆς πονηρᾶς ἐστιν], "is of the evil one." Therefore, just as the use of medicine is to be avoided where it does not seem in some measure necessary for preserving life and maintaining health, so too the oath is to be avoided where the necessity of preserving human society, the manifestation of truth and the confirmation of faith do not seem to demand its use in some way. That saying of Epictetus (as with all his Stoic sayings) is a wholesome warning: [ὅρκον ἀποφεύγειν, εἰ μὲν δυνατόν, ἐς ἅπαν, εἰ δὲ μή, ἐκ τῶν ἐνόντων], "Avoid the oath, if possible altogether; if not, as far as you can." An oath is a holy thing, but the holier it is, the more dangerous it becomes if it is used improperly, just as the drug which is of greater strength and power harms the body the more if it is taken rashly and unskilfully. The use of the assertory oath is necessary in the commonwealth, especially in public courts, for bringing out the truth about particular facts; to this belong the oaths of witnesses, of calumny, of purgation, and so on. Outside a court, and in private affairs, its use is rarer; yet it may sometimes be necessary, namely where it matters greatly that what is asserted should be believed, and the one asserting will not be believed unless he swears.

units.la: Enchirid. Epicteti: ὅρκον ἀποφεύγειν. deretur. Juramenti Promissorii in judiciis usus nullus: at extra judicium plurimus, cum publicus tum privatus. Publicum imprimis ad continendum subditos in fidelitate sua erga Principes; ad firmandum foedera & contractus Regum & Rerumpublicarum: ad servandum leges & statuta, & consequenter honorem, ordinem, & pacem Collegiorum & Societatum; ad publica munera fideliter administranda; atque id genus alia. Ad privatos etiam contractus confirmandos, ut de praestatione rei inter emptorem & venditorem; de solvendo debito; de depósito reddendo; de mutuo, commodo, fidei commisso, &c. juramentum à Veteribus frequentissime adhibitum est. Sed in negotiis privatis plerisque aliae iniri possunt rationes, minore cum conscientiae scrupulo, & fortasse efficaciores ad cavendam improborum hominum perfidiam, quàm sunt Juramenta: ut per pignora, fideiussores, chirographa, testes & alia quae inducant obligationem in foro externo. Et ubi ista commode adhiberi possunt, omnino satius esset à juramentis abstinere: ne aut frequenter & levi de causa jurando, res sacerrima ex nimis familiari usu abeat in contemptum; aut dum multa juramus, labamur quandoque in perjurium. Rectè Augustinus, Nemo novit nisi qui expertus est, quàm fit fit difficile consuetudinem jurandi extinguere, & non temere facere, quod aliquando facere necessitas cogit.
units.tr: Enchiridion of Epictetus: [ὅρκον ἀποφεύγειν]. Be believed. The promissory oath has no use in judicial proceedings, but outside court it has very many, both public and private. Its public use is above all to keep subjects in their allegiance to princes, to confirm the treaties and contracts of kings and commonwealths, to keep laws and statutes and, consequently, the honour, order and peace of colleges and societies, to administer public offices faithfully, and other things of that kind. The ancients also very frequently used the oath to confirm private contracts, such as the delivery of goods between buyer and seller, the payment of a debt, the return of a deposit, or loans, commodatums, trusts and the like. But in private business many other means can be used with less scruple of conscience, and perhaps more effective in guarding against the faithlessness of wicked men than oaths: pledges, guarantors, written bonds, witnesses, and others which create an obligation in the external forum. Where these can conveniently be used, it would be altogether better to abstain from oaths, lest either the most sacred thing come into contempt through over-familiar and frequent swearing over slight matters, or, while we swear much, we slip at some time into perjury. Augustine rightly says: No one knows, except one who has experienced it, how difficult it is to extinguish the habit of swearing and not to do rashly what necessity sometimes compels us to do.

units.la: SECT. XIII.
units.tr: SECT. XIII.

units.la: Conclusio Quarta. Grave peccatum est Juramentum ab alio indebite exigere. Exigit autem indebite, Primo qui cogit aliquem Juramentum præstare, quod non est aut legibus scriptis sancitum: aut moribus (id est usu) receptum, & longi temporis Præscriptione sine intermissione vel contradictione stabilitum. Secundo, qui exigit ab alio juramentum quod aperte repugnat, vel ex eo sensu quem verba præ se ferunt secundum communem usum loquendi, videtur repugnare alicui juramento ab eo prius legitime & licite præstito. Tertio, qui jurare cogit in rem illicitam, quæ sc. est contra officium Deo, aut superioribus debitum, contra leges Regni, contra bonos mores, aut alias inhonesta & quæ servari non debeat. Quarto, qui Juramentum defert ambigui sensus, aut quoquo modo captiosum: quo conscientiæ, vitæ, libertati, aut fortunis proximi sui laqueum injiciat. Quinto, qui sine necessitate aut metu cogit, aut authoritate impellit, aut consilio, exemplo, dolo malo, aliove artificio aut ratione inducit alium ad jurandum, quem scit juraturum contra conscientiæ suæ judicium. Utinam meminerint omnes qui in magna potestate, conscientiæ, famæ, nomini suo quàm fœdum & indelebilem characterem inuflerit Jeroboamus filius Nebat, quòd populum Israeliticum pellexerit ad peccandum: & quantopere gravem Dei iram in se provocent, qui potestate suâ quam Deus uni cuique dedit ad constructionem & non ad ruinam, abutantur in perniciem aliorum.
units.tr: Fourth conclusion. It is a grave sin to demand an oath from another unduly. One demands unduly: first, he who compels someone to give an oath that is not sanctioned by written law, or established by custom (that is, by usage) and by long prescription without interruption or contradiction. Second, he who demands an oath from another which openly contradicts, or which, in the sense the words bear in common usage, seems to contradict, an oath previously given by that person lawfully and licitly. Third, he who compels someone to swear to an unlawful thing, that is, one contrary to the duty owed to God or to superiors, contrary to the laws of the realm, contrary to good morals, or otherwise dishonourable and not to be kept. Fourth, he who brings an oath of ambiguous or in any way captious sense, by which he casts a snare upon his neighbour's conscience, life, liberty or fortune. Fifth, he who, without necessity or fear, compels, or by authority drives, or by counsel, example, malicious deceit, or other artifice or argument induces another to swear, whom he knows will swear against his own conscience. Would that all who hold great power would consider how foul and indelible a mark Jeroboam the son of Nebat stamped upon his own conscience and name, because he led the Israelite people into sin; and how greatly they provoke the grave wrath of God who abuse for the destruction of others the power that God has given each one for building up and not for ruin.

units.la: SECT. XIV.
units.tr: SECT. XIV.

units.la: Couclusio Quinta. Juramentum oblatum reluctante vel dubitante conscientiâ non est fuscipiendum. Probatur Primo; quia a quod non est ex fide peccatum est. Secundo, quia jurandum est in judicio: quod certè is non facit, qui contra conscientiæ suæ judicium facit. Tertio, quia id necesse est fieri alicujus temporalis commodi intuitu aut ad evitandum aliquod damnum, aut ad consequendum aliquod lucrum, aut ad conciliandum alicujus hominis gratiam, aut quid simile. Quàm autem indignum est homine Christiano, Deum mundo, cælum cœno, animam corpori gaudium æternum lucro temporali, spem vitæ futuræ præsenti otio, internam pacem externæ posthabere! Quarto, quia sic jurans perjurii (gravissimi peccati) periculo se evidenter exponit. Qui enim spe metúve alicujus temporalis commodi vel incommodi induci potest ut juraret quod non debuit, hunc vix credibile est non pofle pari spe metúve induci ne adimpleat quod juravit. Perjurium autem vel ipsis etiam Ethnicis inter gravissima illa crimina est habitum, quæ credebantur Deorum immortalium iram non in reos tantum, sed & in posteros ipsorum, imò & in universas gentes accersere. Quo magis nobis metuendum est, qui Deum illum verum & unum colimus, qui folenniter edixit fe non habiturum insontem, quisquis nomen ipsius in vanum affumeret: ne dum quacunq; oculos obvertimus tàm uberem & luxuriantem undique Juramentorum & perjuriorum segetem, albescentemque jamdiu ad meflem conspicimus; Deus juftiffimus judex, ad tàm perfidam & prosanam gentem penitus excindendam, peracutam judiciorum falcem celerrimè immittat. Iratum sensimus jamdiu clementiffimum Patrem, et læsam infinities victamque (fi fas dicere) peccatis nostris infinitam Dei patientiam in furorem versam. Non facile est dicere, ob quæ potissimum peccata, ubi omnia sunt summa. Sed profecto qui ferió cogitaverit, ex quo nos Deus propriore flagello percutere cœpit, de his gravissimis jurandi pejerandique peccatis quàm non doluimus, imò potius quàm immensum increverit, hinc infrænata & impunita juran-di & blasphemandi licentia, illinc pejerandi sub Religionis obtentu fœda hypocrisis: vix fieri potest quin ut ei in mentem subinde veniat illud Jeremiæ Prophetæ, A juramentis terra luget.
units.tr: Conclusion Fifth. An oath offered when the conscience is reluctant or doubtful is not to be taken. This is proved first: whatever is not of faith is sin. Second, because an oath must be sworn in truth and judgment, which he certainly does not do who acts against the judgment of his own conscience. Third, because such an oath is necessarily made for the sake of some temporal advantage, either to avert some loss, or to obtain some gain, or to win the favour of some man, or for something similar. How unworthy it is for a Christian to prefer God to the world, heaven to mire, the soul to the body, eternal joy to temporal gain, the hope of future life to present ease, and inner peace to outward things! Fourth, because one who swears in this way plainly exposes himself to the danger of perjury, the most grievous of sins. For one who can be moved by the hope or fear of some temporal gain or loss to swear what he ought not to swear is hardly likely to be incapable of being moved by the same hope or fear not to keep what he has sworn. Moreover, perjury was counted among the gravest crimes even by the heathens themselves, who believed that it brought the wrath of the immortal gods down not only on the guilty but also on their descendants, and indeed on whole nations. How much more must we fear, who worship that one true God, who solemnly declared that he would not hold guiltless whoever takes his name in vain! Not to mention that, wherever we turn our eyes, we see on every side so rich and luxuriant a crop of oaths and perjuries, already long white for the harvest, that we may well expect the most just Judge of God to send in at once the sharp sickle of judgments to cut down utterly so faithless and profane a nation. We have long felt our most merciful Father angry, and his infinite patience, wounded countless times and (if it is right to say so) overcome by our sins, turned into fury. It is not easy to say which sins above all have provoked this, where all are so grievous. But surely whoever has seriously considered, since God began to strike us with a more direct scourge, how little we have grieved over these most grievous sins of swearing and forswearing, or rather how immensely they have grown, on the one hand an unbridled and unpunished licence of swearing and blaspheming, and on the other a foul hypocrisy of perjury under the cover of religion, can hardly help having from time to time that saying of the prophet Jeremiah come to mind: Because of oaths the land mourns.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, viri, patres & fratres, exorandi fumus qui adsumus omnes, & quotquot ubiam sunt hominum, qui pacì cum publicæ Regni & Ecclesiæ, tùm privatæ cordis & conscientiæ suæ bene cupiunt: ut contemptum nominis divini & fidei violatæ crimen ipsi imprimis sedulo caveamus. juramenta non necessaria omnino fugiamus, ab aliis indebitè delata constanter recusemus, à nobis debitè ritéque præstita fideliter expleamus; deinde ut peccandi licentiam & in aliis quoq;quantum in nobis est strenuè coerceamus; Deum denique Opt. Max. assiduè precemur, ut flagello ejus edocti admonitique & sub potenti ejus manu humiliati, ad ipsius misericordiam confugiamus, justitiam agnoscamus, gratiam imploremus, in peccatorum nostrorum remissionem, vitæ emendationem, et animarum salutem, per et propter merita Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Cui cum Patre et Spiritu Tri-uni Omnipotenti Deo sit regnum, potentia et gloria in Seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: Since this is so, brothers and fathers, we who are present here, and all who are anywhere in the world who sincerely wish well to the public peace of the Kingdom and the Church, and to the private peace of their own hearts and consciences, must earnestly beseech one another, and above all take diligent care that we ourselves do not commit the crime of contempt for the divine name and of broken faith. Let us altogether avoid oaths that are not necessary, steadily refuse those that others have unduly imposed on us, and faithfully carry out those that we have rightly and properly given. Then let us also firmly restrain, as far as lies in us, the licence to sin in others as well. Finally, let us constantly pray to God the Best and Greatest that, taught and admonished by his scourge and humbled under his mighty hand, we may take refuge in his mercy, acknowledge his justice, and implore his grace, for the forgiveness of our sins, the amendment of our lives and the salvation of our souls, through and for the merits of our Lord Jesus Christ. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the Triune Almighty God, be kingdom, power and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.
